captions.mask-of-agamemnon: The gold funerary mask Heinrich Schliemann found in Grave Circle A at Mycenae and famously named for Homer's king — though modern archaeology dates it centuries before the Trojan War. Whether or not it ever covered Agamemnon's face, it remains the West's most iconic image of the Mycenaean warlord who led the fleet to Troy. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.
captions.child-murder-mykonos-vase-detail: On the Mykonos vase the horse's belly opens into massacre — among Greece's earliest pictures of Troy's fall.
captions.painter-odysseus-and-his-men-blinding-po: The oldest surviving Cyclops scene — Nobody's cunning stake earns Poseidon's endless enmity after the lotus and the cave.
captions.perseus-beheading-medusa-boeotian-relief: A Boeotian relief pithos shows Perseus beheading Medusa — among the earliest narrative images of the Gorgon episode.
captions.painter-stheno-and-euryale-pursuing-pers: The name-vase of the Nessos Painter, National Archaeological Museum, Athens (inv. 1002): after Medusa's beheading, the immortal Gorgon sisters Stheno and Euryale race in pursuit of Perseus — among the earliest monumental images of the sisters who could not die.
captions.menelaus-and-hector-fighting-over-the-bo: The name-vase Euphorbos plate in the British Museum (GR 1860,0404.1): Menelaus and Hector fight over the fallen Trojan while labels in the archaic alphabet name the dead man ΕΥΦΟΡΒΟΣ. One of the earliest labelled Homeric scenes in Greek art — Panthous' son who wounded Patroclus before Hector finished the kill.
captions.painter-the-eurytios-krater-corinthian-c: This black-figure Corinthian column-krater, found at Caere (Cerveteri) in Etruria and now in the Louvre, is the artifact that gives King Eurytus his place in the art record and lends the vase painter his conventional name. The upper frieze of side A shows Eurytus of Oechalia reclining at a symposium beside the hero Heracles, with his daughter Iole and his son Iphitos among the banqueters — the very household whose archery contest and broken promise would later end in the sack of Oechalia. Painted around 600 BC, it is one of the earliest narrative scenes of the Eurytus saga in Greek art and a touchstone of the early Corinthian black-figure style.
captions.the-eurytos-krater-heracles-in-the-house: This Late Corinthian black-figure column-krater, now in the Louvre (E635), is the earliest surviving image to name Iole. The frieze shows the banquet of King Eurytus of Oechalia, where Heracles reclines among the king and his sons after the archery contest; the inscribed female figure Iole stands at the right of the scene, the bride who was offered as the prize and then withheld. The vase fixes in painted clay the moment that sets the whole tragedy of Heracles' death in motion, and is a key early witness to the myth tradition recorded later by Apollodorus.
captions.painter-heracles-and-nereus-black-figure: On the shoulder of this Boeotian black-figure lekythos, attributed to the Istanbul Painter and now in the Louvre (CA 823), the hero Heracles grapples with the Old Man of the Sea to wrest from him the way to the Hesperides. Nereus, true and shape-shifting, was renowned for changing into many forms to slip a captor's grasp; here the Archaic painter fixes the moment of the seizing hold, a favorite subject of sixth-century Attic and Boeotian pottery in which the bearded sea-god, sometimes given a coiling fish-tail, is pinned by the inescapable arms of Heracles.
captions.painter-heracles-pholus-and-the-centaurs: A small Corinthian black-figured skyphos (drinking cup, 9.7 cm high) attributed to the artist conventionally named the Pholoe Painter after this very subject. It shows the climactic battle that erupts after the communal wine-jar is opened at Pholus's cave: Heracles drives off the wild centaurs who swarm at the scent of the wine, the episode in which an errant arrow accidentally wounds Chiron and ultimately costs the gentle Pholus his life. Found at Corinth, the vase places Pholus at the center of the centaur-war cycle so often depicted in archaic Greek art. Now in the Louvre, Paris (accession MNC 677 / L 63).
captions.gorgon-pediment-of-the-temple-of-artemis: Carved in limestone for the west pediment of the Temple of Artemis on Corfu (Corcyra) around 580 BCE and now in the Archaeological Museum of Corfu, this is the earliest monumental Greek pediment to survive and the earliest securely identified image of Chrysaor. At its center the winged, snake-haired Gorgon Medusa kneels in the archaic 'running' pose, girt with serpents and flanked by guardian lions in Mistress-of-Animals fashion. At her side stand the two offspring who, in myth, sprang from her severed neck: the winged horse Pegasus and, here at her flank, the small human figure of Chrysaor, 'he of the golden sword.' Following the archaic convention of identifying a figure by placing its children nearby, the sculptors mark Medusa as their mother even as the composition fixes the instant of her death and their birth.
captions.group-heracles-and-alcyoneus-black-figur: Cabinet des Médailles amphora: Heracles grapples Alcyoneus — vase-painting's stock image of the Giant Apollodorus ranks with Porphyrion among the greatest of the earthborn.
captions.painter-perseus-fleeing-the-gorgons-dino: The name-vase of the Gorgon Painter, a monumental Attic black-figure dinos (mixing bowl on stand) made in Athens and found at Caere in Etruria. Around its shoulder runs the pursuit of Perseus by the Gorgons after the murder of Medusa: the hero sprints away at the left while behind him surge his immortal pursuers, Stheno and Euryale, their winged bodies and tusked, frontal faces enlivened with crimson detail. The scene is one of the earliest and most influential depictions of the Gorgon chase in Greek art, defining the running winged type that would echo across vase-painting for a century. The vessel (height c. 93 cm) entered the Louvre with the Campana Collection in 1861 (Department of Greek, Etruscan and Roman Antiquities, accession E 874).
captions.309-heracles-deianira-and-nessus-attic-b: Louvre E 803: the river-crossing confrontation that seeds the poisoned 'love-charm' — the feast's dark punchline already painted in sixth-century black-figure.
captions.bellerophon-pegasus-and-the-chimera-lako: On the fragmentary interior of this archaic Spartan drinking cup, Pegasus rears with hooves striking down at the Chimera while the hero Bellerophon attacks below — one of the earliest Greek images of the winged horse in combat. Rendered in the silhouette technique of Lakonian black-figure vase painting, with incised detail and added colour, the scene shows Pegasus as a sturdy winged steed mid-leap. Such cups carried the deeds of heroes into the world of the symposium, and the recurrence of Pegasus and the Chimera on sixth-century pottery attests to how early the myth of Medusa's immortal offspring entered Greek visual tradition.
captions.corinthian-vase-depicting-perseus-androm: This black-figure Corinthian vase preserves one of the earliest surviving depictions of the Andromeda episode. The sea-monster Cetus (Greek Ketos) rears as a great serpentine fish-beast at the right, its gaping jaws turned toward the hero, while Perseus strides forward to attack and the chained Andromeda waits beside the rock. The painter labels the figures in archaic Greek, fixing the iconography that would shape every later telling: the monster sent by Poseidon against Aethiopia, the exposed princess, and the rescuer who slays the beast and wins her.
captions.hydria-with-the-fight-of-achilles-and-me: Walters hydria: Achilles and Memnon duel while Thetis and Eos look on — Troy's two greatest living heroes before either falls.
captions.perseus-rescuing-andromeda-corinthian-am: An Archaic black-figure amphora of Corinthian manufacture showing the hero Perseus defending the bound princess Andromeda from the sea-monster Ketos, the pair pelting the beast with stones. It is among the oldest surviving depictions of the rescue that led to the marriage of Perseus and Andromeda — the union that produced Gorgophone, 'the Gorgon-slayer's daughter.' The vessel is held in the Altes Museum, Berlin.
captions.amphora-with-the-birth-of-athena: Louvre amphora F 32: Athena springs fully armed from Zeus' head as Olympians look on — the Hesiodic birth fixed in Archaic black-figure.
captions.exaleiptron-with-the-birth-of-athena: Louvre exaleiptron CA 616: Hephaestus' axe and the armed goddess rising from the skull — the same cosmogonic birth on a perfume vessel.
captions.harpies-and-a-male-figure-ivory-relief: A small ivory relief of about 570 BC in the Archaeological Museum of Delphi shows bird-bodied Harpies confronting a male figure in a scene linked to the Argonaut cycle — the same narrative in which Ocypete and her sisters torment Phineus until the Boreads intervene. Archaic ivory carving here already fixes the Harpy as a winged female monster, the visual type Ocypete inherits as one of the swift daughters of Thaumas and Electra (or of Typhon and Echidna, in variant genealogies).
captions.kleitias-caeneus-group-detail-of-the-fra: François Vase detail: the Caeneus group in the centauromachy — the Lapith once called Caenis named among Peirithous' wedding warriors.
captions.kleitias-the-calydonian-boar-hunt-detail: On the famous François Vase, an Attic black-figure volute krater signed by the painter Kleitias and the potter Ergotimos around 570 BC, the uppermost frieze of one side is given over to the hunt of the Calydonian Boar. A long line of named heroes and hounds, their identities inscribed beside them, presses the great boar that ravaged the lands of Calydon after King Oeneus neglected Artemis. Among the labelled figures appear Meleager and Atalanta, the central pair of the saga, alongside the leading huntsmen of the age. As one of the earliest and most detailed narrative renderings of the hunt that bears Calydon's name, the panel is a key witness to how Greeks of the archaic period pictured the city's defining myth. Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Florence.
captions.kleitias-the-francois-vase-attic-black-f: One of the most celebrated vessels of Archaic Greek art, this monumental Attic black-figure volute krater (c. 570–565 BC) carries some 270 figures across six superimposed friezes, 121 of them identified by painted inscriptions. Among the named heroes is Akastos (Acastus), the Argonaut and future king of Iolcus, who appears in the Calydonian boar hunt band near its top. Signed twice — 'Ergotimos made me; Kleitias painted me' — it is now in the National Archaeological Museum in Florence (inv. 4209) and remains the richest single visual compendium of early Greek myth, making it the earliest secure labeled image of Acastus.
captions.kleitias-the-francois-vase-detail-of-the: This detail from the upper neck frieze of the François Vase shows the hunt for the Calydonian Boar, the great beast charging left as nineteen hunters close in with spears, arrows and stones. Every participant is labeled: Peleus and Meleager thrust at the boar's head, with Atalanta and Melanion, the Dioskouroi, the fallen Ancaeus — and Akastos (Acastus), here recorded among the company of heroes who joined the hunt. The detail, in the National Archaeological Museum in Florence, is one of the few ancient images that names Acastus directly, anchoring his role as an Argonaut-generation hero in the visual record.
captions.painter-corinthian-column-krater-of-the-: This Late Corinthian red-ground column krater (formerly Berlin Antikensammlung F1655, lost in 1945 and since held by the State Historical Museum in Moscow) is the masterpiece of the painter who takes his name from it. One side shows the departure of the seer Amphiaraos; the reverse and handle zones stage the funeral games held for Pelias — a wrestling match and a chariot race — with the figures labelled by painted inscriptions in the Corinthian alphabet. These games are the great public event of Amythaon's own family: Pelias and his brother Neleus were sons of Amythaon's mother Tyro, and the named competitors and judges (among them Amythaon's brother Pheres, alongside Akastos, Argeios, Euphemos and Kastor) are his close kin. The vase is the most important early visual witness to the saga of the children of Tyro, the Aeolid house to which Amythaon belongs, and a cornerstone document of named-figure narrative in archaic Greek vase painting.
captions.painter-neoptolemus-sacrificing-polyxena: This Attic black-figure Tyrrhenian amphora, made in Athens and recovered in Italy, shows Neoptolemus performing the grim sacrifice demanded by his dead father's ghost. The rigid, shrouded body of Polyxena, daughter of Priam, is held horizontally over the tomb of Achilles by three armed warriors as Neoptolemus draws the knife across her throat. One of the earliest narrative depictions of the episode, the vase is among the prized archaic holdings of the British Museum, where it captures the cruelty that haunts the Greek victory.
captions.painter-perseus-and-the-gorgons-castella: Attic black-figure Tyrrhenian neck-amphora in Frankfurt (β 319): the three Gorgons — Stheno and Euryale still with their heads — pursue Perseus while Athena intervenes, a high-archaic staging of the immortal sisters' vengeance.
captions.painter-return-of-hephaestus-laconian-ky: Rhodes AM 10711: archaic Laconian cup of Hephaestus' return — the smith-god's expulsion and homecoming told as procession, not cradle scene.
captions.76-achilles-lying-in-wait-for-troilus: Attic black-figure hydria in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (45.11.2). Achilles lurks behind the fountain as Troilus and Polyxena approach to water their horses — the ambush that ends the youth before Troy falls, already a favourite subject of sixth-century Athenian painters.
captions.76-hector-and-cebriones: Attic black-figure amphora (British Museum): Hector and Kebriones named together — Priam's bastard son as the charioteer who will fall before Patroclus in Iliad 16.
captions.athenian-plate-with-heracles-and-apollo-: On this early Attic plate, Heracles and Apollo grapple over the golden-horned Ceryneian Hind, each laying a hand on the slender deer at the centre of the composition. The image visualises the climactic moment of the third Labour, when the god intervenes to protect his sister Artemis' sacred creature; Heracles must hold the hind without harming it. The compact tondo format makes the contested deer the literal pivot of the scene, a popular sixth-century treatment of one of the hero's gentler, capture-not-kill Labours.
captions.corinthian-krater-herakles-and-hesione: On this Archaic Corinthian krater in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (63.420), Heracles confronts the Trojan sea-monster while Hesione stands as the stake of Laomedon's broken bargain. Painted about 560 BC, the vase is among the earliest surviving images of the princess who will pass from Heracles' rescue to Telamon's bed — Troy's sister-story to Andromeda.
captions.painter-heracles-iolaus-and-the-lernaean: Side A of an Attic black-figure amphora in the Louvre (E 851) shows Iolaus at his most essential labour: beside Heracles as the hero grapples the many-headed Lernaean Hydra. The charioteer who will sear each stump with a brand is already present in the Archaic visual formula — Iolaus as the indispensable second hand of the second labour.
captions.relief-from-samothrace-agamemnon-talthyb: An Archaic marble relief from Samothrace, now in the Louvre (Ma 697), names Agamemnon in archaic Ionic letters at the head of three advancing figures — the high king, the herald Talthybios, and Epeios. Often read as Agamemnon's initiation into the Samothracian mysteries, it is among the earliest securely labelled images of the Mycenaean warlord who will lead the fleet to Troy.
captions.the-dioscuri-idas-and-lynceus-driving-ca: This Archaic limestone metope, carved around 560 BC for the Treasury (or monopteros) of the Sicyonians at the Panhellenic sanctuary of Delphi and now in the Archaeological Museum of Delphi, depicts the cattle raid in which the Messenian brothers Idas and Lynceus join their cousins the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux. Four heroes stride in profile beside the rustled herd, their names once inscribed above them. The episode is the prelude to the quarrel over the spoils that would ignite the fatal feud between the Apharetids and the Dioscuri—the conflict in which Lynceus, the lynx-eyed Argonaut lookout famed for sight that could pierce wood and earth, was struck down by Pollux's spear. As one of the few securely identified Archaic Greek images naming Lynceus, the relief is a cornerstone witness to his myth.
captions.tydeus-and-ismene-corinthian-amphora-lou: A Corinthian black-figure amphora in the Louvre names Ismene beside Tydeus — a rare archaic image of the Theban princess in the cycle of the Seven against Thebes. The vase preserves a darker local strand in which Ismene herself falls in the war her brothers began.
captions.painter-the-calydonian-boar-hunt-tondo-o: Calydon, the eponymous hero who gave his name to the Aetolian city, is almost never shown in person, but the myth that immortalised his city is one of the oldest hunting legends in Greek art. In this tondo from a Laconian black-figure kylix, painted around the mid-sixth century BC and attributed to the Naucratis Painter, a ring of spear-armed hunters and a hound close in on the monstrous boar that the offended Artemis loosed upon the fields of Calydon. The compact circular composition, with hunters advancing from both sides toward the bristling beast, is the standard archaic schema for the Calydonian hunt and one of the earliest surviving images of the saga set in Calydon's territory. Musée du Louvre, Paris (inv. E 670).
captions.achilles-fighting-memnon: Leiden vase — the Aethiopian king against Achilles, the duel that ends Memnon's brief aristeia.
captions.caeneus-and-the-centaur-attic-black-figu: Louvre CA 2494: invulnerable Caeneus driven into the earth by a centaur — the burial-death after Poseidon granted Caenis manhood and unpierceable flesh.
captions.exekias-akamas-and-demophon-exekias-alte: Another angle of Exekias' signed amphora: Acamas beside Demophon — Phaedra's sons as warriors with horses.
captions.exekias-akamas-and-demophon-exekias-amph: Exekias' Berlin neck-amphora, side B: Theseus' sons Akamas and Demophon lead their horses — Attic black-figure naming the Athenian princes, not Antenor's Trojan Acamas.
captions.exekias-akamas-and-demophon-exekias-side: Further view of the same Berlin vase: the Theseid brothers named in clay a generation before Troy's sack stories send them to recover Aethra.
captions.exekias-exekias-amphora-altes-museum-dis: The amphora on display in Berlin: Exekias' signature piece that pairs Heracles' lion with Akamas and Demophon — Acamas of Athens fixed in the museum case.
captions.heracles-and-alcyoneus-kylix: Attic kylix: Heracles confronts the Giant Alcyoneus — the earthborn who could not be killed on his native soil until the hero dragged him from Pallene.
captions.herakles-carrying-the-erymanthian-boar-t: An Attic black-figure amphora (inv. 16442) in the Museo Gregoriano Etrusco of the Vatican Museums, painted in Athens in the mid-sixth century BC. Heracles, club at the ready, advances with the bound boar slung across his shoulders toward Eurystheus, who has sunk down into a sunken pithos so that only his head and pleading hands rise above the rim. The painter relishes the contrast between the hero's effortless mastery of the great beast of Mount Erymanthus and the king's undignified panic, illustrating the tradition that the animal was delivered alive to Mycenae.
captions.mourner-psychostasia-dinos-hermes-weighi: On the rim of this Attic black-figure dinos (Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna, Antikensammlung IV 3619), found at Caere, the rare scene of the psychostasia unfolds: Hermes holds aloft a balance, and in each pan crouches a small winged figure. These winged souls are the Keres, the death-fates of Achilles and Memnon, weighed as the two heroes fight to the death between their grieving mothers Thetis and Eos. The heavier Ker tips the scale and seals its bearer's doom, dragging him down to Hades. The painter renders the abstract Hesiodic notion of fated death as a literal weighing of winged spirits, the canonical iconography by which the Keres entered Greek vase painting.
captions.painter-attic-black-figure-neck-amphora-: Vatican amphora: Athena strides into the duel as Olympians close on the Gigantes — sixth-century Athenian pottery that echoes the peplos woven with the Gigantomachy for the Panathenaia.
captions.painter-telamon-in-the-amazonomachy-tyrr: Attic black-figure Tyrrhenian amphora in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens (inv. 27524): beside Heracles, Telamon fights the Amazon Ainipe — the Salaminian hero named among the companions who sacked Troy in the generation before Homer's war.
captions.painter-theseus-and-peirithoos-abducting: On this Attic black-figure amphora by the Amasis Painter (Athens, National Archaeological Museum, inv. 404), Theseus and Peirithoos seize the young Helen — the partnership of the two heroes before the Centauromachy and the chair of forgetfulness. Bold silhouette and incision fix Peirithoos as Theseus's comrade in a deed that later myth would call reckless. The vase is among the earliest clear images of the Lapith king named beside his Athenian friend.
captions.sthenelos-bandaging-the-wounded-finger-o: Wellcome ink drawing after a Chalcidian neck-amphora: Sthenelus binds Diomedes' wounded finger — Capaneus' son as the comrade who tends the Argive champion in the Iliad's orbit.
captions.zeus-battling-typhon-chalcidian-black-fi: The canonical ancient image of the Typhonomachy on a Chalcidian hydria in Munich: Zeus strides forward to hurl his thunderbolt against a winged, snake-legged Typhon whose lower body coils into serpents — Hesiod's youngest child of Gaia and Tartarus (Theogony 820–868), blasted down a maimed wreck when the new order of Zeus was tested one last time.
captions.attic-heracles-killing-the-stymphalian-b: This Attic black-figured amphora, said to have come from the Etruscan site of Vulci, shows Heracles bringing down the birds of Lake Stymphalus with a sling rather than the bow of the literary tradition—a variant the early painters favoured for its dynamic silhouette. The dark figures stand out against the reserved clay ground in the classic black-figure technique, the hero braced mid-throw amid the falling birds. The vase entered the British Museum in 1843 (GR 1843.11-3.40) and is a key early witness to how Archaic Athens visualised the sixth Labour.
captions.dionysus-and-oenopion: British Museum amphora B 210 shows Dionysus with Oenopion — the Chian king often named as the wine-god's son, who brought viticulture to Chios. Archaic vase-painting keeps the island's legendary wine-king beside his divine father.
captions.e-heracles-fighting-geryon-with-the-dyin: On this Attic black-figure amphora (42 cm high), attributed to the workshop known as Group E and dated about 540 BC, Heracles drives his attack against the triple-bodied Geryon, the three-warrior giant of the western island of Erythia. Geryon is rendered in the canonical three-bodied form, three armoured men fused at the waist and bristling with shields and spears, while the herdsman Eurytion sprawls dying on the ground beneath the duel. The vase compresses the climax of Heracles' tenth labour, the slaying of the herdsman, his dog, and the giant himself, into a single heraldic confrontation. From the Canino Collection, it entered the Louvre in 1848 (Department of Greek, Etruscan and Roman Antiquities).
captions.exekias-achilles-and-ajax-playing-a-boar: Signed by the great Athenian potter-painter Exekias, this Attic black-figure belly amphora carries on Side A the most celebrated image of Ajax in all of ancient art: the two foremost Greek warriors of the Trojan War, Achilles at left and Ajax (Aias) the son of Telamon at right, lean over a low table absorbed in a quiet game of dice, spears still in hand and shields propped behind them. Tiny inscriptions name the heroes and even record their throws, while the helmeted Achilles calls 'four' and the bareheaded Ajax answers 'three.' Dated to about 540-530 BC, the scene fuses stillness and latent menace, a private moment of camaraderie shadowed by the deaths that await both men. The vase was found at Vulci in Etruria and is preserved in the Museo Gregoriano Etrusco of the Vatican Museums (inv. 16757).
captions.exekias-the-dionysus-cup: Munich kylix: Dionysus reclines in a ship whose mast sprouts grapevines, dolphins circling — the Homeric Hymn's Tyrrhenian pirates transformed, the god's voyage as black-figure miracle.
captions.exekias-the-suicide-of-ajax-boulogne-amp: Exekias shows Ajax planting his sword after the arms contest — shame after Odysseus wins Achilles' armor, fixed in Archaic black-figure quiet.
captions.painter-ajax-and-glaucus-fight-over-the-: Drawing after a lost Chalcidian black-figure amphora (formerly Pembroke-Hope, Deepdene; LIMC Achilleus 850): Ajax and the Lycian Glaucus struggle over Achilles' corpse while Paris and Aeneas look on and Athena, aegis snaking, aids the Greek. Homer's Glaucus — Hippolochus' son, Sarpedon's peer — appears here not in the famous armour-exchange of Iliad 6 but in the later fight for the fallen hero, named among the Trojan allies who will not leave Achilles' body uncontested. Colorized reconstruction after A. Rumpf, Chalkidische Vasen (1927), pl. 12.
captions.painter-geryon-and-orthrus-attic-black-f: Side B of an Attic black-figure neck-amphora attributed to the Swing Painter shows the two-headed Orthrus beside his master, the three-bodied Geryon, guarding the red cattle of Erytheia. The hound is rendered in the bristling silhouette typical of archaic vase-painting, his twin heads turned toward the threat that will end him — Heracles, who in Hesiod's account slays both the watchdog and the herdsman Eurytion before driving off the herd. Made at Athens and found at Vulci, the amphora is one of the canonical sixth-century witnesses to Orthrus' two-headed form and his role as Geryon's guard-dog. Cabinet des médailles, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris (De Ridder 223 = Luynes 715).
captions.painter-heracles-and-the-ceryneian-hind: On this Attic black-figure amphora (British Museum, B231), Heracles kneels astride the captured Ceryneian Hind, gripping its golden antler as he subdues the swift, divinely sacred deer of Artemis. The scene distils the third Labour into a single charged moment: the hero must take the beast alive rather than slay it, and the painter shows the muscular tension of restraint rather than the kill. The golden-horned hind, sacred to Artemis and hunted for a whole year through Arcadia, was among the most popular of the Labours in sixth-century vase-painting.
captions.achilles-ambushing-troilus: Etruscan wall painting in the Tomb of the Bulls at Tarquinia. Achilles crouches in ambush as Troilus rides past on horseback — one of the earliest monumental images of the Trojan prince's death, painted more than a century before the Classical vase tradition fixed the fountain scene.
captions.heracles-cerberus-and-eurystheus-caereta: The last Labour on an archaic Caeretan hydria: Heracles hauls three-headed Cerberus before Eurystheus, who has flung himself into a pithos in panic.
captions.monteleone-chariot-achilles-and-memnon-p: Etruscan bronze chariot panel — Achilles and Memnon's combat carried west of Greece, the Aethiopis in ivory and bronze.
captions.the-gorgons-stheno-and-euryale-pursuing-: On this Attic black-figure lekythos, now in the Cabinet des Médailles of the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris (inv. 277), the two immortal Gorgons Stheno and Euryale stride forward in furious pursuit. They are the surviving sisters of Medusa, whom Perseus has just beheaded, and Greek myth holds that they alone could never be slain. The painter renders them in the canonical archaic Gorgon type — broad grimacing faces, bared tusks, and lolling tongues — caught mid-run with the swift winged gait that signals their flight after the hero. This is one of the rare works to name Euryale explicitly alongside her sister rather than folding the trio into the single figure of Medusa.
captions.athena-and-enceladus: Attic black-figure: Athena spears the Giant Enceladus as the Gigantomachy turns — the earthborn who will be crushed under Sicily.
captions.herakles-and-the-lernaean-hydra-caeretan: On this archaic Caeretan black-figure water-jar (hydria), the hero Herakles strides against the Lernaean Hydra, whose many serpentine necks fan out from a single coiled body in a writhing tangle. The painter gives the monster the multiplying heads of the myth, and beside Herakles his nephew Iolaos assists with the torch used to cauterize the severed stumps so they cannot regrow. Produced in Etruria around the late sixth century BC, the vase is among the earliest and most vivid surviving images of the Second Labour. It is held by the J. Paul Getty Museum (Getty Villa, inv. 83.AE.346).
captions.painter-heracles-eurystheus-and-the-erym: Side A of an Attic black-figure amphora attributed to the Antimenes Painter, now in the Louvre (inv. F 202). The scene captures the comic climax of the Fourth Labour: a striding Heracles hoists the live Erymanthian boar above his head, about to hurl it down upon his taskmaster, while a terrified King Eurystheus has dived into a half-buried bronze storage jar (pithos), throwing up his arms with only his head and hands visible. The motif of the cowering king in the jar, faithful to Apollodorus' account (Bibliotheca 2.5.4), became one of the most popular Heraclean subjects in sixth-century Athenian vase painting.
captions.49-neoptolemus-killing-priam-attic-black: Attic amphora — Achilles' son fetched from Scyros in the Little Iliad, already the killer of Priam at the altar.
captions.620-heracles-and-the-nemean-lion-attic-b: On this Attic black-figure wine-jug (oinochoe) found at Vulci, the hero locks his arms around the great cat of Nemea in the wrestler's grip that ancient artists favoured for the encounter: because no weapon could pierce the beast's invulnerable hide, Heracles is shown subduing it with his bare hands rather than sword or club. The two figures interlock in a tense, near-symmetrical knot of limbs, the lion rearing on its hind legs, a compact rendering of the deed that opens the cycle of the Twelve Labours. British Museum, London (accession GR 1836.2-24.92).
captions.athena-and-enceladus-ec8465: Attic black-figure amphora from Vulci: Athena closes on the Giant Enceladus in the Gigantomachy — the earthborn who will be crushed beneath Sicily, not the icy moon that later borrowed his name.
captions.centaurs-and-caeneus-bronze-relief-olymp: Olympia bronze relief: centaurs overwhelm Caeneus — portable testimony to the gender-changed Lapith's distinctive death.
captions.chrysaor-from-the-gorgon-pediment-of-the: A close-up of the small human figure beside the great Gorgon on the west pediment of the Temple of Artemis at Corfu (c. 580 BCE, Archaeological Museum of Corfu): Chrysaor, the son who in Hesiod's Theogony leapt from Medusa's neck together with Pegasus at the moment Perseus beheaded her. Dwarfed by his monstrous mother and placed at her flank to declare his parentage in the archaic manner, this carving is the figure's earliest appearance in surviving art. Chrysaor is rarely depicted alone in ancient or later art, so the Corfu pediment, where he stands as one of Medusa's twin-born children, remains the principal monument to him.
captions.heracles-at-pholus-attic-black-figured-h: This Attic black-figured hydria (a calpis-type water vessel, 24.5 cm high) depicts the hospitable reception that defines Pholus in myth: the centaur welcoming Heracles to his Arcadian cave on the hero's Erymanthian-boar quest. Pholus is rendered as a typical centaur with a man's torso joined to a horse's body, greeting his guest in the moment before the fateful opening of the communal centaur wine-jar. The scene crystallizes the friendship between host and hero that Apollodorus records (Bibliotheca 2.5.4) and which would end in Pholus's accidental death by one of Heracles' poisoned arrows. Now in the Louvre, Paris (accession MNE 940).
captions.oinochoe-with-odysseus-and-ajax: Louvre oinochoe F 340: the two heroes of the arms dispute face each other — the contest antiquity painted as often as it told.
captions.painter-ajax-carrying-the-dead-achilles-: On the principal face of this Attic black-figure amphora, Ajax the Great strides forward beneath the limp, fully armed body of Achilles, whom he hoists across his shoulders to rescue the fallen hero's corpse from the Trojan battlefield. The rescue of Achilles' body, a deed that Ajax shared with Odysseus, was a favorite subject of Archaic vase painters because it dramatized Ajax's role as the bulwark of the Greek army. Attributed to the Antimenes Painter and dated to about 520-510 BC, the vessel renders the strain of the burden in the bent legs and lowered head of Ajax. It is held in the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore (inv. 48.17).
captions.painter-dike-and-adikia-nikosthenic-neck: On the reverse of this early Attic bilingual neck-amphora (Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna, AS IV 3722) the personified Dike, Justice, is shown thrashing the haggard, tattooed figure of Adikia, Injustice, with a hammer or double axe. It is the canonical archaic image of Dike as an active enforcer rather than a passive allegory: the stern maiden who watches mortal wrongs and punishes them, foreshadowing the sword and scales of her later iconography. The scene gives visual form to Hesiod's vision of Dike as the daughter who reports the crooked judgements of men to her father Zeus.
captions.painter-the-birth-of-athena-attic-black-: On this late-archaic Attic neck-amphora from Vulci, now in the British Museum (1836,0224.10), Athena springs fully armed from the head of the enthroned Zeus while the divine company looks on. The museum reading of the scene names Eileithyia twice over: the goddess of birth stands at each side of the emerging Athena, framing the miraculous labor between Hermes and Hephaistos. It is the canonical iconography of the doubled Eileithyiai as midwives, their presence marking the threshold moment when a new divinity first comes to the light.
captions.paseas-heracles-leading-cerberus-from-th: An early Attic red-figure plate showing Heracles, club raised, leading a two-headed Cerberus up out of the realm of the dead. The painter, conventionally called the Cerberus Painter after this very subject, renders the hound with serpents bristling along its neck — the snaky mane that Apollodorus describes when he writes of 'the heads of all sorts of snakes' on the monster's back. The composition concentrates the entire twelfth labour into a single taut moment of restraint. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (01.8025).
captions.silver-didrachm-of-taras-dolphin-and-whe: Munich didrachm: the dolphin-rider with a wheel reverse — Taras as the face of Magna Graecia's richest mint.
captions.euphronios-heracles-wrestling-antaeus-at: On this celebrated Attic red-figure calyx krater signed by the pioneer painter Euphronios, Heracles pins the Libyan giant Antaeus to the ground in a sprawling, anatomically charged wrestling match. Antaeus, son of Poseidon and Gaia, was invincible so long as he touched his mother the Earth, forcing every passing stranger to wrestle him to the death; the painter shows Heracles already mastering the unkempt, contorted giant — the prelude to lifting him bodily off the ground to break his strength. The two combatants' interlocked, straining bodies make this one of the masterpieces of early red-figure vase-painting. Now in the Musée du Louvre, Paris (G103).
captions.euphronios-hypnos-and-thanatos-carry-sar: An Attic red-figure calyx-krater painted by Euphronios and potted by Euxitheos, counted among the masterpieces of Greek vase painting. The principal scene, drawn from Homer's Iliad, shows the winged brothers Hypnos and Thanatos lifting the body of the slain hero Sarpedon from the Trojan battlefield under the direction of Hermes. Long displayed at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, the krater was repatriated to Italy in 2008 and is now shown at Cerveteri, near the necropolis from which it was looted.
captions.1410-achilles-and-memnon-between-thetis-: Attic black-figure — the two mothers watch as Achilles and Memnon fight for Troy's last eastern ally.
captions.euphronios-heracles-geryon-and-the-slain: On this Attic red-figure kylix, signed by the painter Euphronios and the potter Kachrylion, the two-headed hound Orthrus lies dead at the feet of his foes. Sprawled on the ground with both canine heads collapsed and his serpent tail trailing behind him, Orthrus has already fallen in the cattle-raid of the tenth labour: at left Heracles closes on the herd, while at right the three-bodied giant Geryon — Orthrus' master — still stands armed for the fight. The vase, found at Vulci and acquired for the Munich collection in 1831, is one of the finest archaic depictions of the watchdog of Erytheia, fixing his characteristic two heads and snake-tail. Staatliche Antikensammlungen, Munich (inv. 2620).
captions.euphronios-herakles-fighting-the-three-b: This Attic red-figure cup by the celebrated late-archaic painter Euphronios, made about 510 BC, sets the combat of Heracles and Geryon across its exterior. Geryon appears as three fully armed bodies joined at the trunk, one already collapsing as Heracles presses his assault, with Athena and Iolaos attending the hero in the surrounding cast; the reverse shows hoplites driving off the giant's coveted herd of cattle. Euphronios exploits the new red-figure technique to model the overlapping warriors' anatomy in subtle detail, turning the monstrous triple form into a study of overlapping muscular bodies. Staatliche Antikensammlungen, Munich (inv. 2620).
captions.heracles-slays-alcyoneus-paestum-metope: Metope from the Heraion at the mouth of the Sele (Paestum Museum): Heracles kills the Giant Alcyoneus — archaic stone of the Gigantomachy's hardest duel.
captions.oltos-heracles-brings-the-erymanthian-bo: The comic emblem of the Labours: Heracles delivers the live Erymanthian boar while Eurystheus hides in a pithos — Oltos' kylix made the cowering taskmaster the cycle's punchline.
captions.painter-neoptolemus-slays-eurypylus-atti: Shoulder of Martin-von-Wagner-Museum L 309 (from Vulci): Neoptolemus has cut down Eurypylus and pursues the charioteer until Apollo steps in with the bow. The Mysian son of Telephus — Troy's late ally from the Little Iliad cycle — dies in black-figure before Achilles' son.
captions.painter-tyrrhenian-pirates-into-dolphins: The Micali Painter's Tyrrhenian pirates becoming dolphins — the Homeric Hymn miracle after they seize the young god.
captions.silver-stater-of-taras-youth-on-dolphin: Early Tarentine stater: Taras riding the dolphin Poseidon sent to save him — the city's founder as civic badge on both faces. Berlin.
captions.theseus-and-antiope-pedimental-group-fro: Archaic marble from Eretria: Theseus carries off the Amazon Antiope — the abduction that sparks Athens' Amazon war and, in many tellings, makes her the mother of Hippolytus. Now in the Archaeological Museum of Eretria.
captions.statue-of-an-archer-from-the-west-pedime: The Aphaia pediment archer — traditionally identified as Teucer, the bastard brother who outlives Ajax and loses Telamon's hall.
captions.achilles-bandaging-the-wounded-patroclus: The Sosias Painter's cup — Achilles binding Patroclus' wound, the friendship Homeric art never stopped restaging before the fall.
captions.herakles-and-pholos-attic-red-figure-oin: An Attic red-figure oinochoe of about 500–490 BC shows Heracles with Pholus in the cave hospitality scene that opens the Pholoe adventure. Where black-figure predecessors fixed the silhouette of host and guest, the red-figure painter gives the civilized centaur and the hero clearer gesture and drapery on the brink of the wine-jar disaster. National Archaeological Museum, Madrid.
captions.onesimos-theseus-sciron-and-procrustes-c: Louvre cup G104: Sciron among Theseus' Isthmus labours beside Procrustes — the cliff and the bed as paired Athenian propaganda.
captions.painter-helios-rising-in-his-quadriga-at: On this black-figure lekythos Helios rises in his four-horse chariot while Nyx and Eos drive away — the sun god's daily birth painted for an Attic grave. Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
captions.painter-heracles-and-geras-villa-giulia-: Attic red-figure pelike in the Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia, Rome (inv. 48238), attributed to the Matsch Painter: Heracles, club planted and lion-skin over his shoulders, converses with Geras, who stands as an emaciated, bald old man with crooked back and walking stick. Where the Louvre pelike stages a beating, this vase freezes the quieter moment before or beside the struggle — Old Age as a named daemon Heracles can face and talk to. The reverse shows Dionysos with a maenad.
captions.painter-heracles-and-the-stymphalian-bir: On this small Attic black-figure amphora the hero confronts the man-eating birds of the Stymphalian marsh, the sixth of his twelve Labours. Heracles is shown attacking the flock as the birds scatter into flight, the vase compressing the whole episode—the scaring-up of the birds and their destruction—into a single charged image. Acquired by the Louvre with the Campana Collection in 1861, the vessel (about 20 cm high) belongs to the Department of Greek, Etruscan and Roman Antiquities and is among the earliest narrative depictions of the Labour to survive.
captions.painter-herakles-and-pholos-attic-black-: A black-figure lekythos in the Walters Art Museum (48.229) attributed to the Beldam Painter stages another version of Heracles' visit to Pholus — one of the parerga that vase-painters loved beside the canonical labours. Draped figures and the centaur host evoke the wine-sharing that turns fatal on Mount Pholoe. The vessel is a compact Classical-period witness to Pholus as the hospitable counterpart of the wilder Centaurs.
captions.painter-hermes-and-maia-attic-red-figure: This detail from an Attic red-figure belly-amphora, attributed to the Nikoxenos Painter and dated to around 500 BC, shows the nymph Maia standing beside her son Hermes amid an assembly of Olympian deities. Eldest of the Pleiades and daughter of the Titan Atlas, Maia bore Hermes to Zeus in a cave on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia; here the vase painter places mother and divine-messenger son together among the gods, a rare ancient image naming Maia in her own right rather than only as 'mother of Hermes.' The amphora is held in the Staatliche Antikensammlungen in Munich (Inv. 2304).
captions.painter-oeneus-with-coat-and-sceptre-att: On this Attic white-ground lekythos, the aged king of Calydon stands robed in a heavy mantle and grasping a sceptre, his name inscribed beside him to leave no doubt of his identity. To the left the painter sets the related episode of Deianira and the centaur Nessus, binding Oeneus to his celebrated daughter and the chain of myth that flowed from his house. The work, now in the Staatliche Antikensammlungen in Munich, is among the rare ancient images to name and depict Oeneus himself rather than the more famous hunt he convened, presenting him with the gravity of an enthroned patriarch.
captions.painter-peleus-consigns-the-young-achill: This white-ground lekythos attributed to the Edinburgh Painter shows Peleus, king of Phthia, handing over his infant son Achilles to the wise centaur Chiron, who will rear and educate the boy on Mount Pelion. The scene distills Peleus's role as the mortal father at the heart of the Achilles saga: having won the goddess Thetis, he entrusts their child to the gentlest of the centaurs for a heroic upbringing. The vessel is held by the National Archaeological Museum of Athens.
captions.painter-pholos-drawing-wine-for-herakles: On this Attic black-figure lekythos attributed to the Gela Painter, Pholus draws wine from the communal jar for his guest Heracles — the courteous act that, in Apollodorus, releases the scent that maddens the wild centaurs and ends in Pholus's own death by a poisoned arrow. The vase isolates the hospitable moment before the battle, making the gentle centaur the focus rather than the melee. Museo Archeologico Regionale, Palermo (NI 1904).
captions.peleus-seizing-thetis: On this Boeotian black-figure dish the hero Peleus locks his arms around the sea-nymph Thetis, who twists and shape-shifts in a desperate bid to escape his grip. Warned by the prophecy that Thetis would bear a son greater than his father, the gods steered her away from Zeus and toward a mortal husband; to win her, Peleus had to wrestle her down as she transformed in turn into fire, water, a lion and a serpent. The vase captures the decisive moment of that struggle, the founding episode that would lead to the birth of Achilles. Now in the Musée du Louvre (CA 2569).
captions.pinax-with-persephone-and-hades-enthrone: A terracotta pinax from the Mannella sanctuary of Persephone at Locri Epizephyrii, now in the Cleveland Museum of Art. Hades and Persephone sit enthroned as a married pair — not the snatch from the meadow but the cult image of underworld sovereignty, offered by Locrian worshippers who knew the king of the dead as a consort as much as a abductor.
captions.stone-figurine-of-hypsipyle-with-ophelte: An eroded stone figurine from the shrine of the hero Opheltes at Nemea, now in the Archaeological Museum of Nemea, shows a woman — almost certainly Hypsipyle — holding a child to her breast. Late Archaic or early Classical in date, it is among the rare cult objects that place the Lemnian exile at the heart of the Nemean hero-cult she accidentally founded.
captions.theseus-and-antiope-athenian-treasury-de: Delphi metope: Theseus carries off Antiope — the abduction that brings Amazon vengeance to Athens and sires Hippolytus.
captions.theseus-and-sciron-metope: Metope from the Athenian Treasury at Delphi: Theseus against Sciron — the cliff-robber carved into Panhellenic stone for every pilgrim to see.
captions.douris-eos-lifting-the-body-of-memnon-do: Louvre G 115: winged Eos gathers Memnon's corpse after Achilles' kill — the Aethiopis as a mother's recovery of Ethiopia's champion.
captions.douris-peleus-and-thetis-attic-red-figur: The tondo of this Attic red-figure drinking cup shows the hero Peleus wrestling the shape-shifting Thetis to win her as his bride. As the mortal grasps the struggling sea-goddess, she transforms her body to escape him — here a lion springs from her shoulder and a serpent coils about Peleus's arm — visualising the metamorphic ordeal Peleus must endure before the gods grant him the immortal Nereid. The cup is preserved in the Cabinet des Médailles, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris.
captions.makron-eumolpus-among-the-eleusinian-god: Attic red-figure skyphos in the British Museum (1873,0820.375; Cat. Vases E140), signed by the potter Hieron and painted by Makron: Triptolemos sits in his winged chariot amid the Eleusinian circle, and the name ΕΥΜΟΛΠΠΟΣ is inscribed beside the sweet-singing founder of the Mysteries. Demeter, Persephone, Eleusis, Zeus, Dionysos, Amphitrite and Poseidon complete the gathering — Eumolpus already cast as Poseidon's son and cult singer decades before Euripides' Erechtheus. Found at Santa Maria di Capua; Beazley ARV² 459.3.
captions.makron-kylix-of-hieron-and-makron-the-ju: On this Attic red-figure drinking cup, painted by Makron and signed by the potter Hieron and found at Vulci, the exterior unfolds the prelude to the Trojan War. One frieze shows the Judgement of Paris; the other shows Paris leading Helen away from Sparta. It is in this abduction scene that Timandra, sister of Helen and daughter of Tyndareus and Leda, makes one of her only securely identified appearances in ancient art: an accompanying inscription names her, and she is shown — in a chiton, mantle and fillet, arms flung outstretched — rushing forward to intervene as her sister is carried off, only to be held back by one of Paris's companions. The cup is one of the masterpieces of early-classical Athenian vase painting and is held in the Antikensammlung, Berlin (inv. F 2291).
captions.makron-paris-abducting-helen-detail-with: Detail of the abduction frieze on the same Berlin kylix (Antikensammlung F 2291): the inscription TIMA(N)DRA names Helen's sister as she strains forward, arms outstretched, while a companion restrains her. Beside the departing pair stand Icarius and Tyndareus — the Spartan household watching Helen leave. This is the clearest surviving letter-perfect portrait of Timandra in Attic vase-painting.
captions.painter-hermes-stealing-the-cattle-of-ap: Attic red-figure (Vatican): newborn Hermes drives off Apollo's cattle — the Homeric Hymn theft painted for a drinking party.
captions.painter-psychostasia-volute-krater-fragm: These fragments of an Attic red-figure volute-krater (Bibliotheque nationale de France, Cabinet des Medailles 385), an early work of the Kleophrades Painter found at Tarquinia, preserve another psychostasia. Zeus presides with thunderbolt and staff while Hermes, holding the kerykeion, lifts the balance to weigh the souls of two hoplites, most likely Achilles and Memnon. The Ker that sinks lower marks the warrior doomed to fall. The composition translates the moment of fate into a divine accounting, the Keres as the measurable weight of each man's death set in the gods' scales.
captions.painter-running-gorgon-pursuing-perseus-: Attributed to the Berlin Painter, one of the foremost red-figure artists of late-archaic Athens, this amphora in the Staatliche Antikensammlungen, Munich (inv. 2312) shows a single Gorgon in full flight, while the reverse depicts Perseus escaping with his sickle and winged boots. The pursuing sister is one of the two undying Gorgons, Stheno or Euryale, who chase the hero after Medusa's death. The painter softens the older grotesque mask into an elegant, dynamic figure, her drapery and limbs swept by the speed of the chase — an image of Euryale and her sister in their defining mythic role as the immortal avengers of Medusa.
captions.coinage-of-skione-founded-by-protesilaus: Skione coinage — the city that claimed Protesilaus as founder, the landing hero turned cult name.
captions.douris-death-of-pentheus-douris-cup-kimb: Douris' cup — the Theban king ripped apart on Cithaeron, red-figure violence for the god he refused.
captions.douris-heracles-sailing-the-sea-in-the-g: The tondo of this Attic red-figure kylix, painted by Douris around 480 BC, shows Heracles crossing the Ocean seated in the great golden cup of the sun-god Helios, the vessel the hero borrowed to reach Erythia, the far-western island where Geryon pastured his red cattle. Curled inside the circular bowl-within-a-bowl, Heracles rides the waves on the outward leg of his tenth labour, the episode whose goal is the killing of three-bodied Geryon and the driving home of his herd. The image is a witty pictorial pun, the painted drinking cup depicting a mythical voyage made in a cup. Museo Gregoriano Etrusco, Vatican Museums (no. 205336).
captions.douris-jason-and-the-dragon-douris-cup: Attic red-figure kylix: the dragon of the fleece swallows and disgorges Jason while Athena watches — one of antiquity's strangest images of the quest.
captions.douris-theseus-plunges-sciron-into-the-s: Douris' Berlin kylix from Vulci: Theseus kicks Sciron from the cliff toward the waiting turtle — the Isthmus brigand's death as Attic red-figure justice.
captions.makron-hermes-and-herse: Attic red-figure cup (Louvre G494): Hermes pursues Herse — the desire that makes Aglauros' envy fatal in Ovid's later telling.
captions.painter-achilles-mourns-patroclus-attic-: At Leiden, Antilochus stands left of grieving Achilles — the messenger who brought news of Patroclus' death — while Thetis brings new arms. Rijksmuseum van Oudheden.
captions.painter-apollo-and-idas-fighting-for-mar: On this Attic red-figure psykter (a wine-cooling vessel) in the Staatliche Antikensammlungen in Munich, the earliest surviving depiction of the myth unfolds in vivid combat. The god Apollo and the mortal hero Idas seize the Aetolian princess Marpessa between them, each refusing to yield her. According to Homer's Iliad, Idas alone among men dared draw his bow against a god for the sake of his bride; here the painter freezes that audacious confrontation, which Zeus would soon interrupt to let Marpessa herself choose her husband. The scene captures the central scandal of her story: a woman desired by an immortal who nonetheless preferred a man who could grow old beside her.
captions.painter-heracles-and-geras-louvre-g234: Attic red-figure pelike in the Musée du Louvre (G234), the name-vase of the Geras Painter: Heracles, in lion-skin with club raised, seizes the shrunken personification of Old Age by the head while Geras leans on a staff and begs. No literary myth of this encounter survives — the scene is known only from a handful of Athenian vases — yet the painter labels the wizened nude ΓΕΡΑΣ and makes the contrast unmistakable: the ageless hero confronting the one foe no labour can finally defeat. Side B shows Poseidon.
captions.painter-heracles-and-linus: Attic red-figure kylix: young Heracles turns on his music-master Linus with the stool or lyre that will kill him. The cup is the clearest archaic image of the Thracian (or Theban) Linus — brother of Orpheus in some genealogies — whose pedagogy ends in the hero’s rage.
captions.painter-heracles-strangling-the-serpents: Louvre stamnos: the infant in the cradle throttles Hera's snakes while Iphicles recoils — the Theban birth that proves Zeus' son.
captions.painter-herakles-and-linos: Boston MFA stamnos 66.206: Heracles and Linos locked in the music-lesson murder that Apollodorus and later mythographers retell. Museum clay keeps the singing-master distinct from Pope Linus — a mythic death, not a papal name.
captions.painter-idas-and-marpessa-separated-from: On this Attic red-figure psykter (wine-cooler), the Messenian hero Idas grips the Aetolian princess Marpessa, whom he has carried off in his chariot, while Zeus intervenes to part the rivals from the god Apollo, who also desired her. The vase crystallizes the climax of the myth: ordered by Zeus to choose, Marpessa picked the mortal Idas over the deathless Apollo, fearing the god would abandon her when age came. Painted around 480 BC and attributed to the Pan Painter, it survives among the Staatliche Antikensammlungen in Munich (inv. 2417), one of the earliest images to set the mortal suitor against the sun-bright Olympian.
captions.painter-odysseus-and-the-sirens-the-sire: Odyssey 12 on an Attic stamnos — the hero lashed to the mast while his crew rows past the meadow of bones, hearing the song that kills every man who reaches it unbound.
captions.painter-the-embassy-to-achilles-attic-re: Louvre G146 names the ambassadors: Phoenix, Ajax, and Odysseus before Achilles in his hut — persuasion, pride, and the cost of wrath in three registers.
captions.painter-triptolemus-in-the-winged-chario: Louvre G 187, the eponymous cup of the Triptolemos Painter: the Eleusinian hero sits in his winged, serpent-drawn chariot — the image that fixed Triptolemus' mission in the Athenian imagination for a century of vase-painting.
captions.philomela-and-procne-preparing-to-kill-i: Procne and Philomela prepare to kill Itys — the sisters' revenge banquet before the feathers close the myth.
captions.phineus-and-the-boreads: Attic red-figure — Phineus and the Boreads, the Argonautica mercy that clears the prophet's table of Harpies.
captions.the-embassy-to-achilles-attic-red-figure: Munich hydria: Phoenix and Odysseus stand before sulking Achilles — Iliad 9 made visible, the foster-father's Meleager parable still to fail.
captions.gigantomachy-poseidon-fighting-polybotes: Tondo of an Attic red-figure kylix (Cabinet des Médailles, Paris): Poseidon spears the Giant Polybotes while carrying the island of Nisyros on his shoulder — the myth that explains the volcanic islet off Cos. The Painter of the Paris Gigantomachy makes Polybotes the sea-god's named antagonist.
captions.342-red-figure-lekythos-with-nike-holdin: On this Attic red-figure lekythos attributed to the Painter of London E 342, the winged goddess Nike strides forward in a long flowing chiton, holding out a fillet (woolen band) of the kind tied around a victor's head — the tangible token of triumph she bestows. Vase-painters of Classical Athens frequently showed Nike in motion, hurrying with wreaths, ribbons or libation vessels to honor winners of games and battles, making her the constant attendant of victory. The vessel is now in the Walters Art Museum, Baltimore (inv. 48.254).
captions.birth-of-erichthonius-athena-receiving-t: On this Attic red-figure stamnos the moment of Erichthonius' birth is rendered with archaic clarity: the earth-mother Gaia rises from the ground to lift the swaddled infant upward, placing him directly into the outstretched arms of a fully armed Athena, who will become his foster-mother and protector. Hephaestus, whose unfulfilled pursuit of the virgin goddess caused the seed to fall upon the earth, looks on. The child is the autochthon of Athens, sprung from the very soil of Attica — the vase makes that claim literal, showing him handed up out of the ground. Now in the Staatliche Antikensammlungen, Munich, the piece is among the earliest surviving depictions of the Athenian foundation myth.
captions.death-of-actaeon-louvre-krater-full: Full view of the same Louvre crater: Actaeon's doom and the parental pair — Autonoe among the Cadmean women whose house Artemis and Dionysus both shatter.
captions.death-of-actaeon-reported-to-autonoe-and: Louvre krater CA 3482: while Artemis drives deer and Actaeon dies, a messenger reports to his parents — Autonoe and Aristaeus named in the scene. Cadmus' daughter as grieving mother, not only as Bacchant.
captions.demophon-freeing-aethra-attic-white-grou: This ancient Athenian white-ground cup, now in the Staatliche Antikensammlungen in Munich, illustrates the other great episode of Aethra's life: her old age as a captive at Troy. Having been carried off by the Dioscuri in retaliation for Theseus' abduction of Helen, the aged Aethra served as Helen's handmaid until, at the fall of Troy, her grandsons Demophon and Acamas recognized and rescued her. The vase captures the freeing of the white-haired queen, a beloved Athenian subject that completes her story as both mother of a hero and grandmother delivered from bondage.
captions.east-pediment-of-the-temple-of-zeus-at-o: Olympia's east pediment — Zeus between Oenomaus and Pelops before the fatal chariot race for Hippodamia.
captions.heracles-and-the-nemean-lion-metope-from: Olympia's metope opens the Labours — the weary hero after the Nemean Lion, Athena looking on in Severe-style calm.
captions.hermonax-the-birth-of-erichthonios-erech: On this red-figure stamnos by the painter Hermonax, the goddess Gaia (Earth) rises from the ground to hand the newborn Athenian child up to a waiting Athena, while Hephaestus looks on. The infant is the earth-born first king of Athens, named Erichthonios on the vase but repeatedly identified or merged with Erechtheus in the ancient tradition; Homer's Iliad (2.547) already calls the autochthonous king reared by Athena 'Erechtheus,' and later authors treat the two as the same Earth-born ruler. Now in the Staatliche Antikensammlungen, Munich (inv. 2413), the scene fixes the moment that gives Erechtheus his defining myth: a child of the soil itself, raised on the Acropolis under the protection of the city's patron goddess.
captions.marble-cult-mask-of-achelous: This Early Classical marble mask renders Achelous in his characteristic hybrid guise: a bearded human face bearing the horns and ears of a bull, the iconographic shorthand by which Greek art identified the great river-god. Such masks reflect the widespread cult of Achelous as the personification of flowing fresh water and fertility, venerated across Greece. Now in the Antikensammlung, Berlin (inv. 141684).
captions.oedipus-and-the-sphinx: An Attic red-figure amphora shows Oedipus before the Theban Sphinx — the same riddle scene that later painters would enlarge into Romantic and Symbolist drama. Ceramic, Musée du Louvre, Paris.
captions.olympia-west-pediment-of-the-temple-of-z: Olympia's west pediment — Apollo calm above the Lapith wedding brawl, Eurytion's outrage carved as order versus chaos.
captions.original-the-hestia-giustiniani: A marble statue of the veiled goddess of the hearth, a Roman copy after an early Classical Greek original of about 470 BC in the Severe style. The heavy peplos, grave frontal stance and modestly drawn veil convey Hestia's austere domestic dignity. The statue takes its name from the Giustiniani collection in Rome, where it was long held.
captions.painter-achilles-killing-penthesilea-pen: Munich kylix tondo: Achilles drives his spear into the falling Amazon — the Aethiopis duel that later tradition said left him stricken with love.
captions.painter-amymone-with-her-father-danaus-a: On this Attic red-figure neck amphora (BnF Cabinet des Médailles, De Ridder 359), a hydria-bearing woman runs toward a bearded man with a staff — conventionally read as Amymone (or a sister) approaching Danaus. The Providence Painter gives the Argive father a rare vase presence beside the Danaid he will later arm for the wedding night.
captions.painter-antilochus-attic-red-figure-neck: Louvre G 213: the Tithonos Painter names Antilochus on an Attic neck-amphora — Nestor's swift son isolated as a Trojan-War presence in early Classical vase painting.
captions.painter-boreas-and-oreithyia: Attic pointed amphora: Boreas seizes Oreithyia — the classical image of the parents who will raise Chione beside the winged Argonauts Zetes and Calais.
captions.painter-boreas-and-oreithyia-attic-red-f: This Attic red-figure pointed amphora in the Staatliche Antikensammlungen, Munich (56 cm high), is the very name-vase of the anonymous master scholars call the Oreithyia Painter. Boreas, the winged North Wind, takes hold of the Athenian princess Oreithyia as her sister Herse rushes in from the left in a vain attempt to help. The vase preserves the classical Athenian image of the abduction by the Ilissus, the myth by which the wind-god became a kinsman of Athens and which Pausanias records was also figured on the chest of Cypselus at Olympia.
captions.painter-oedipus-and-the-sphinx-of-thebes: On this Attic red-figure kylix tondo, travelling Oedipus listens as the crowned Sphinx poses her riddle — the Theban monster in its earliest Greek vase form. Ceramic, Vatican Museums (Gregorian Etruscan Museum).
captions.pyxis-with-zeus-and-aigina-attic-red-fig: An Attic red-figure pyxis (a lidded cosmetic box) showing the abduction of Aigina, one of the daughters of the river-god Asopus, by Zeus. The vase painter captures the pursuit in motion, with the god seizing the fleeing nymph; the reverse of the vessel depicts her father Asopus and her sisters reacting to the loss. The composition belongs to the classic Greek iconographic type of divine pursuit and abduction. Dating to the early Classical period, the pyxis is held in the Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge (GR.10.1934).
captions.the-charioteer-of-delphi: A rare surviving Greek bronze of a victorious charioteer, dedicated at Apollo's sanctuary at Delphi to commemorate a chariot-race triumph. Its calm, austere features exemplify the Early Classical severe style. It is preserved in the Delphi Archaeological Museum.
captions.the-mourning-athena: A small marble relief showing Athena, helmeted and leaning on her spear, bowing her head before an upright stele. Its quiet, pensive pose has made it one of the most touching images of the goddess to survive from the Classical period. It is displayed in the Acropolis Museum, Athens.
captions.deianeira-watching-heracles-fight-achelo: Louvre G365: Heracles seizes bull-bodied Achelous while Deianira looks on — the Calydonian contest that wins the bride and breaks the river's horn.
captions.electra-and-orestes-at-the-tomb-of-agame: This Melian terracotta relief in the Louvre (MNB 906) shows Electra and Orestes meeting at Agamemnon's tomb — the recognition that opens Aeschylus's Libation Bearers. The fifth-century plaque is among the earliest surviving images of the sister who keeps vigil until her brother comes home to kill. Louvre, Paris.
captions.heracles-and-the-cretan-bull-olympia-met: Marble metope from the Temple of Zeus at Olympia: Heracles grapples Poseidon's white bull — the seventh Labour — locking horns and neck as he prepares to bring the beast alive to Eurystheus. The original relief is in the Archaeological Museum of Olympia.
captions.melian-relief-of-the-birth-of-erichthoni: A small terracotta plaque (11 cm high) of the so-called Melian type, dating to the first half of the 5th century BC, staging one of the central Athenian foundation myths. Athena, at left, receives the infant Erichthonius handed up from the earth by Ge (Gaia) in the center, while Cecrops, the serpent-legged primal king, looks on at the right. The relief situates Cecrops as the human witness who legitimizes the divine origins of the Athenian royal line. It is held in the Antikensammlung Berlin (inv. TC 6281).
captions.metope-of-the-augean-stables-twelfth-met: This Early Classical marble high-relief was the last of the twelve metopes ringing the Temple of Zeus at Olympia, the very sanctuary in Elis that Augeas ruled. It shows the climax of the fifth Labour: a now-matured, weary Heracles braces a long bar against the stable foundations while the helmeted Athena, his patroness, calmly points to the spot where he should breach the wall to let the diverted river sweep away the dung of Augeas' immense herds. Augeas himself is absent — the metope distils the Labour to the moment of triumph over his impossible task, the work that the Elean king would refuse to reward. Excavated at Olympia and now in the Archaeological Museum of Olympia, it is the most celebrated ancient image of this Labour.
captions.painter-castor-on-the-niobid-krater: On this celebrated Attic red-figure calyx-krater, now in the Louvre (G341), Castor is shown as a youthful horse-tamer, identified by the inscription of his name beside the figure. As one of the Dioscuri, the mortal twin brother of Pollux and brother of Helen and Clytemnestra, Castor was renowned in antiquity as a master horseman and athlete; the painter accordingly equips him with horse and spears. The vase, attributed to the workshop of the Niobid Painter at the height of the early Classical style, is one of the few ancient images to label the hero by name.
captions.painter-gathering-of-the-argonauts-attic: On the principal face of this Attic red-figure calyx-krater, the Niobid Painter arranges the heroes of the Argo across several registers in the moments before their voyage — the scene most often read as the gathering of the Argonauts around Heracles. Amphidamas of Arcadia, named in the Argonaut catalogue as a son of Aleus who sailed from Tegea (Apollonius, Argonautica 1.161–171), belongs to precisely this assembled company; he is not individuated but stands among the anonymous crewmen the painter ranges across the vessel. The krater, dated about 460–450 BC and now in the Louvre (G 341), is one of the masterworks of early Classical Athenian vase painting, exploiting the calyx form's broad field to stack figures on uneven ground-lines in a way that anticipates the lost monumental wall paintings of the period.
captions.painter-the-boreads-rescuing-phineus-fro: On this Attic red-figure column-krater in the Louvre (inv. G364), the winged Boread brothers Zetes and Calais are shown in furious flight, driving the snatching Harpies away from the table of the blind Thracian seer Phineus. The sons of Boreas, the North Wind, were uniquely able to pursue the wind-swift monsters through the air, and as Argonauts they delivered Phineus from the curse that had let the Harpies foul his every meal. The painter sets the two sprinting youths, wings outstretched, in dynamic pursuit, capturing the moment that makes the Boreads heroes of the Argo's voyage. It is the single most celebrated ancient image of Zetes and his twin in action.
captions.painter-theseus-and-peirithoos-penthesil: In the tondo of the great Attic red-figure kylix by the Penthesilea Painter (Ferrara, Museo Archeologico Nazionale, inv. 44885), Theseus on horseback and Peirithoos with spears stand at an altar — the two friends paired at the heart of the largest known cup of its kind. Around them run the deeds of Theseus; the interior names Peirithoos as the constant companion, not a side figure. Found at Spina and dated about 460–450 BC, the cup is a Classical document of their sworn brotherhood.
captions.painter-triptolemus-with-demeter-and-per: Attic red-figure stamnos by the Niobid Painter: Triptolemus stands between the two Eleusinian goddesses, the mortal youth framed by Demeter and Persephone as he prepares to carry the Mysteries' grain across the world.
captions.rhea-handing-a-swaddled-stone-to-cronus: Met pelike: Rhea offers Cronus the wrapped stone in place of the infant — the trick that lets Zeus survive the Titan's swallowings.
captions.riace-bronze-a-museo-nazionale-della-mag: A second view of the great Riace warrior on display in the National Museum of Magna Grecia in Reggio Calabria, where the two bronzes are the centerpiece of the collection. The figure's anatomical naturalism, inlaid copper lips and nipples, and silver teeth mark the technical peak of fifth-century Athenian bronze-casting. Catalogued in the Erechtheus image group on the strength of the scholarly proposal that this heroic spearman embodies the Athenian king who fell to Poseidon's trident after slaying Eumolpus, the photograph lets the viewer study the statue's poise and gaze from a different angle than the standard frontal portrait.
captions.riace-bronze-a-statue-a: One of the two life-size Greek bronze warriors recovered from the sea off Riace, Calabria, in 1972, now in the National Archaeological Museum of Reggio Calabria. The nude, bearded fighter once held a spear and shield, his weight poised in the balanced contrapposto of the Severe Style. The bronzes carry no inscription, so their identity is debated; among the proposed readings, Salvatore Settis and Vinzenz Brinkmann argue that Statue A is Erechtheus, the autochthonous king of Athens, paired in a lost Athenian monument with his adversary Eumolpus, son of Poseidon. The identification remains uncertain, but it is the depiction cited on Erechtheus's own entry, making this commanding warrior the figure's most prominent possible likeness.
captions.the-artemision-bronze: Monumental ancient Greek bronze recovered from a shipwreck off Cape Artemision, now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens. The god strides forward with his arm drawn back to hurl a weapon now lost — a thunderbolt if he is Zeus, a trident if Poseidon — making it one of the finest surviving bronzes of the Severe style.
captions.exedra-of-the-epigoni-argive-votive-monu: Thersander, the son of Polynices to whom the conquering Epigoni handed the kingdom of Thebes, is almost never shown in surviving figural art; his most concrete monument is sculptural and votive. This semicircular limestone exedra stands on the south side of the Sacred Way at Delphi, dedicated by the Argives to commemorate the Epigoni, the descendants of the Seven against Thebes who avenged their fathers by taking the city. Pausanias (Description of Greece 10.10.4) records that the bronze statue group it once carried portrayed the victorious Epigoni and named Thersander among them, alongside Sthenelus, Diomedes, Promachus and Polydorus. Only the curved base survives today; the figures are lost, but the structure remains the principal ancient memorial to Thersander's role in the second war on Thebes.
captions.exedra-of-the-epigoni-at-delphi-curved-b: A closer view of the Argive exedra of the Epigoni at Delphi, the fourth monument west of the entrance to the Sanctuary of Apollo. The Argives erected it to honour the Epigoni who, ten years after the disastrous campaign of the Seven against Thebes, captured the city and installed Thersander, son of Polynices, on its throne (Pausanias 9.5.14). The lost bronze group that stood on this base is the only ancient sculptural ensemble known to have included a portrait statue of Thersander, set among his fellow avengers; the weathered semicircular foundation is what endures of that dedication, anchoring his memory in the physical landscape of Delphi.
captions.exedra-of-the-epigoni-at-delphi-dedicato: The surviving inscription on the Argive Epigoni exedra at Delphi names the dedication that once held Thersander's bronze among the avengers of the Seven. With the statues gone, the cut letters are the monument's last explicit voice — the civic claim that the Epigoni, and with them the Theban kingship of Polynices' son, stood here on the Sacred Way as Argos's thank-offering to Apollo.
captions.ajax-and-cassandra-attic-red-figure-cup-: Attic cup — Ajax dragging Cassandra from the Palladium, the Little Ajax crime already fixed in clay.
captions.artemis-and-enceladus-temple-e-metope-se: Classical metope from Temple E at Selinus: Artemis spears the falling Giant — Enceladus in stone combat, the Gigantomachy carved for a Sicilian temple that stands over the myth's volcanic ground.
captions.calchas-as-haruspex-etruscan-bronze-mirr: An Etruscan engraved mirror names Calchas (Chalchas) as a winged haruspex reading a liver — the Greek mantis recast in Italian ritual guise, proof of how early the Trojan seer travelled west of the Adriatic.
captions.centaurs-fighting-caeneus-lycian-sarcoph: Lycian sarcophagus short side: two centaurs hammer Caeneus into the ground — the same burial reserved for the Lapith who could not be pierced.
captions.death-of-pentheus-louvre-g445: Louvre G445 — Attic death of Pentheus, the spy in women's dress becoming the sacrifice the Bacchae demands.
captions.death-of-sarpedon-bell-krater: Attic red-figure bell-krater of the Sarpedon type: winged Sleep and Death lift the hero's body — the Euphronios theme repeated for another symposium.
captions.eos-and-tithonos-kylix: Eos and Tithonos on a kylix — archaic vase-painting of Dawn carrying off the Trojan prince.
captions.eriphyle-suckling-alcmaeon-with-amphiara: Attic hydria: Amphiaraus leans on his staff while Eriphyle suckles infant Alcmaeon — domestic calm before the necklace, the Seven's failure, and the sons' return.
captions.gaia-on-an-attic-red-figure-cup: Detail from an Attic red-figure vessel of the fifth century BC in which Gaia rises from the earth as a half-figure — the primordial mother made visible at the edge of the painted surface. Classical vase-painters rarely isolate her as a standalone portrait; here she appears as the living ground from which gods and heroes emerge.
captions.heracles-and-alcyoneus-red-figure-amphor: Red-figure amphora of the same combat: Alcyoneus as the sleeping or fallen Giant Heracles must finish — not the Pleiad Alcyone, but the Gigantomachy's immortal-on-his-soil foe.
captions.menelaus-recovering-helen-attic-red-figu: On this Attic red-figure crater in Munich, Menelaus finds Helen at the sack of Troy and raises his sword — then drops it as her beauty stays the blow. The vase paints the Ilioupersis reunion that ends the war he sailed to start: the Spartan husband reclaiming his wife. Staatliche Antikensammlungen, Munich.
captions.myron-athena-and-marsyas: After Myron: Athena has discarded the aulos; Marsyas starts forward to claim the pipes — the step before hubris and Apollo's knife.
captions.painter-attic-red-figure-lekythos-herakl: On this Classical Attic red-figure lekythos (Ashmolean Museum, Oxford, AN1890.26; attributed in Beazley's catalogue, ARV 627.1, to an imitator of the Villa Giulia Painter), the legendary family of Heracles is shown in a quiet domestic register rather than in heroic action. Deianeira sits enthroned on a chair, and on her lap the infant Hyllos stretches out both hands toward his father Herakles, who stands before them, while a mirror hangs suspended in the background as a marker of the household interior. The vase is among the rare ancient depictions to name Hyllus by name, presenting the eldest son of Heracles and Deianira as a reaching child long before he would behead Eurystheus, marry Iole, and lead the first attempted return of the Heraclids to the Peloponnese.
captions.painter-polynices-offering-the-necklace-: Attic red-figure oinochoe in the Louvre (G 442): Polynices extends the cursed necklace of Harmonia while Eriphyle reaches for the bribe that will send Amphiaraus to die at Thebes. The vase freezes the price of the Seven's war in a single exchange of gold for a husband's life.
captions.painter-psamathe-fleeing-among-the-nerei: Detail from an Attic red-figure vase of the Classical period, attributed to the Achilles Painter. The larger composition shows Peleus wrestling and seizing the sea-goddess Thetis; among the sister Nereids fleeing the struggle is Psamathe, here identified by inscription. The scene resonates with her own myth, for Psamathe was likewise captured on the shore by Peleus's father Aeacus — escaping into the form of a seal before he overpowered her and she bore him Phocus, whose name means 'seal.' Such named appearances in 5th-century BC Attic pottery are the principal ancient depictions of the Nereid.
captions.painter-theseus-and-sinis-amphora: Troilos Painter amphora in Rome: Theseus and the pine-tree brigand — Sinis' death as symposium-side myth.
captions.painter-theseus-and-sinis-kylix: Munich kylix: Theseus bends the pine with Sinis — the Pine-bender caught in his own torture, Attic red-figure for the Isthmus road.
captions.perseus-and-the-graiai-attic-pyxis: An Attic red-figure pyxis in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens (inv. 1291): Perseus flies past the Graiai on the lid of a Classical cosmetics box. The grey sisters appear in the vase-painter's shorthand as aged women at the edge of the hero's path — living proof that the eye-theft episode was already painted for Athenian households centuries before Apollodorus wrote it down.
captions.polygnotos-theseus-in-the-amazonomachy: Red-figure Amazonomachy with Theseus among the fighters — Athens' mythic war against the warrior women.
captions.relief-of-phrixos-on-the-golden-ram-meli: Melian terracotta relief in the Metropolitan Museum (Rogers Fund, 1912; inv. 12.229.20): Phrixus alone on the ram, carried over the sea toward Colchis. Classical plaque sculpture isolates the boy-hero of the fleece's origin — no Helle in frame, only the flight that leaves the Golden Fleece for Jason.
captions.rondanini-medusa: The Gorgon's face made classically beautiful — calm, symmetrical, winged, with snakes knotted beneath the chin. The type is often connected with the gorgoneion on Phidias' Athena; this copy, named for the Palazzo Rondanini in Rome where Goethe admired it, defined the 'beautiful Medusa' for the modern imagination.
captions.scylla-boeotian-red-figure-bell-krater-d: On this Boeotian red-figure bell-krater Scylla is rendered in the canonical classical scheme: a beautiful maiden from the waist up, her lower body merging into a coiling fish-tail (kētos), with the foreparts of savage dogs bursting from her loins.
