The painter captures the horror Homer describes in Odyssey 12—the woman's face above, the pack of ravening hounds below that snatched six of Odysseus' comrades from the deck. The vessel, 22.5 cm high, was acquired by the Louvre in 1900 and is displayed in the Department of Greek, Etruscan and Roman Antiquities (inv. CA 1341).
captions.stater-of-elis-for-the-olympic-festivals: A silver stater struck by Elis, the Peloponnesian kingdom that mythic tradition credits Oxylus with founding after the Return of the Heraclids. There is no surviving ancient portrait of Oxylus himself; the coinage of his realm is the closest material legacy of his foundation. The obverse shows an eagle with spread wings perched on an olive branch, and the reverse a thunderbolt (fulmen) - both emblems of Olympian Zeus, whose great sanctuary at Olympia lay within Elean territory and whose festival Elis administered. Now in the Cleveland Museum of Art (acc. 1916.995).
captions.telephus-seated-on-the-altar-with-bandag: Telephus on the altar with bandaged thigh — the Mysian king wounded by Achilles when the Achaeans mistook Mysia for Troy.
captions.thamyris-and-the-muses: Another Attic vase of Thamyris with the Muses — the challenge scene repeated for another symposium, the bard forever about to lose his voice.
captions.thamyris-and-the-muses-hydria: Attic hydria: Thamyris among the Muses before the contest that costs him sight and song — the Thracian bard as vase-painting cautionary tale.
captions.thamyris-vase-detail: A closer view of the same hydria type: the musician who challenged the Muses — lyre still in hand at the edge of hubris.
captions.the-abduction-of-antiope-by-theseus: A fifth-century relief (National Archaeological Museum, Athens) of Theseus seizing the Amazon Antiope — the war-bride whose capture opens the Amazonomachy in Athenian myth.
captions.votive-relief-of-amphiaraus-from-oropos: Marble votive from the Amphiareion at Oropos, now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens: Amphiaraus appears in the healing type of Asclepius, accompanied by a younger attendant. The relief shows the seer's afterlife as oracle-hero — swallowed by the earth before Thebes, worshipped where the sick slept for dreams.
captions.workshop-lekythos-with-hermes-and-herse: White-ground lekythos (Madrid): Hermes and Herse meet — the named encounter before Roman poets thicken the jealousy plot with Aglauros' stone.
captions.temple-of-hephaestus-athens-south-colonn: A view along the southern flank of the Hephaisteion, the Classical Doric temple whose pronaos frieze on the east end depicts the battle of Theseus and the Pallantides in the presence of the seated gods. The Pallantides were the sons of Pallas, son of Pandion II, who marched on Athens to seize the throne from Theseus and were ambushed and killed. Erected in the marble-quarrying decades after the Persian Wars, the temple program weaves the destruction of Pallas's rival house into Athens's civic-heroic self-image, making this monument — rather than any single portrait — the enduring artistic witness to Pallas the Pandionid.
captions.the-temple-of-hephaestus-athens: A Doric temple overlooking the ancient Agora of Athens, dedicated to Hephaestus and to Athena as patrons of crafts. Built in the fifth century BC, it is among the best-preserved of all ancient Greek temples, its colonnade and much of its sculptural decoration still standing.
captions.phidias-assembly-of-the-gods-east-frieze: On the same British Museum Block V that holds the peplos scene, the seated Olympians — including Zeus and Hera — turn their backs to the central ritual as if awaiting the outcome of Athens' founding sacrifice. Under Joan Connelly's reading of Euripides' Erechtheus, this divine assembly frames Queen Praxithea's consent: the gods preside while the royal household prepares the daughter's offering that will save the city. The slab keeps Praxithea's myth inside the Parthenon's most contested relief.
captions.phidias-the-peplos-scene-east-frieze-blo: Carved in low relief at the very center of the Parthenon's east frieze, above the temple's main door, this marble block shows five figures: a bearded man and a child handling a folded cloth, and a woman turning toward two girls who balance stools on their heads. Long read as priests handling Athena's peplos, the scene was reinterpreted by Joan Connelly as Athens' foundation myth — King Erechtheus preparing his youngest daughter for sacrifice while Queen Praxithea, the standing woman, receives the burial garments her elder daughters carry. Under this reading the central female figure is Praxithea herself, the mother who, in Euripides' lost Erechtheus, consented to give a daughter's life to save the city. Now in the British Museum, London (Elgin Collection).
captions.phidias-weavers-ergastinai-of-the-east-f: A marble block from the same central east frieze of the Parthenon, retaining traces of ancient pigment, showing draped women (the ergastinai, weavers of the sacred robe) approaching a group of officials at the head of the Panathenaic procession. As part of the continuous scene that culminates in the so-called peplos block, this section belongs to the procession in which the family of Erechtheus and Queen Praxithea stand at the focal point of the frieze — the ceremonial gathering that the Connelly interpretation links to Athens' founding sacrifice. Now in the Musée du Louvre, Paris (Ma 738 / MR 825).
captions.great-eleusinian-relief-demeter-triptole: The monumental Pentelic-marble votive from Eleusis, now National Archaeological Museum, Athens (NAMA 126): Demeter offers ears of wheat to the youth Triptolemus while Persephone crowns him — the canonical image of the Eleusinian envoy who carries Demeter's gift of agriculture to humankind.
captions.painter-amymone-aison-painter-oinochoe: Kerameikos oinochoe: Amymone among satyrs — Attic red-figure of the Danaid before Poseidon's rescue, hydria in hand for her father's water-quest.
captions.painter-athena-pursuing-aglauros-attic-r: On this Attic cup the goddess herself pursues Aglauros — a rare vase naming the middle daughter of Cecrops in the aftermath of the opened basket, when Athena's anger still runs through Athens.
captions.painter-cecrops-on-an-attic-red-figure-c: A detail of an Attic red-figure cup (kylix) attributed to the Codrus Painter, made in Athens in the third quarter of the 5th century BC, showing the Athenian king Cecrops. The cup, 12 cm high with a diameter of 31.2 cm, depicts the birth of Erichthonius from the earth, the autochthonous heir of Athens whom Cecrops' daughters would later be charged to guard. Cecrops appears here in his canonical form as a witness to the city's foundational miracle. The vessel is preserved in the Antikensammlung Berlin (Altes Museum, inv. F 2537).
captions.painter-deeds-of-theseus-cup: Kodros Painter's deeds-of-Theseus cup: Sinis among the Isthmus cycle — the Pine-bender as one panel in Athens' favourite hero comic-strip.
captions.painter-return-of-hephaestus-attic-red-f: Munich pelike: Dionysus leads the cast-out smith back to Olympus with his thiasos — the visual tradition that follows Hera's rejection of the lame newborn Hephaestus.
captions.painter-themis-and-aegeus: This Attic red-figure kylix, attributed to the Kodros Painter and found at Vulci, shows the Athenian king Aegeus consulting the oracle. He stands before the seated goddess Themis, who holds a phiale and laurel branch as she delivers the cryptic prophecy concerning his childlessness. Rendered against the lustrous black ground typical of high-classical Athenian pottery, the cup is among the most celebrated ancient depictions of Aegeus. It is held in the Antikensammlung, Berlin (inv. F 2538).
captions.phidias-athena-parthenos-reconstruction: A marble statuette regarded as the most faithful surviving copy of the colossal gold-and-ivory Athena Parthenos that Phidias created for the Parthenon. The goddess stands fully armed, a winged Nike on her outstretched hand and her shield resting at her side. It is held in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.
captions.phidias-dione-and-aphrodite-parthenon-ea: Two reclining goddesses from the Parthenon's east pediment in the British Museum are traditionally read as Dione supporting Aphrodite — Homer's mother of the love-goddess watching Athena's birth. Whether or not the names are certain, the marble pair remains Dione's most famous monumental presence.
captions.west-pediment-of-the-parthenon-cecrops-a: Marble figures from the west pediment of the Parthenon, traditionally identified as Cecrops seated with his daughter Pandrosus. The west pediment depicted the very contest in which Cecrops figures most prominently in myth: the strife between Athena and Poseidon for possession of Attica, judged in Athena's favor. As the founding king who established the goddess' cult, Cecrops was placed among the divine and heroic spectators of the contest. These surviving statues are now housed in the Acropolis Museum, Athens.
captions.aison-theseus-slaying-the-minotaur-tondo: Attic red-figure tondo: Theseus drags the slain Minotaur from the labyrinth while Athena stands by — Athens' founding exploit in a single charged cup.
captions.silver-stater-of-elis-olympia-eagle-seiz: A Classical-period silver stater of Elis, the land Oxylus the Aetolian asked for as his reward for guiding the sons of Aristomachus across to the Peloponnese (Pausanias 5.3.6-5.4.2). The obverse depicts an eagle - the bird of Zeus of Olympia - clutching a hare, while the reverse bears a striding figure of Nike, the goddess of victory presiding over the Olympic games held in Oxylus' kingdom. Standing in for any direct image of the hero, the coin embodies the prestige and divine patronage of the Elean state he is said to have established. Munzkabinett, Berlin.
captions.alkamenes-statue-of-procne-and-itys: The statue of Procne and Itys — maternal grief cast in marble at the hinge of the bird-metamorphosis tale.
captions.painter-helen-and-her-sisters-meidias-pa: Another museum photograph of the same Meidias Painter hydria in Athens (Kerameikos 2712) shows the Helen-and-sisters tableau from a further angle, clarifying the crowded late-fifth-century composition in which Phylonoe appears. For a figure attested in little more than Apollodorus's note of Artemis's gift of immortality, these Kerameikos plates remain the visual record.

A closer view of the Kerameikos hydria's shoulder frieze isolates the clustered Tyndarid sisters in the Meidias Painter's fine-line manner. Phylonoe belongs to this named Spartan group beside Helen — one of the few ancient images in which the princess Artemis made immortal can be read among her siblings rather than lost in a generic gathering of women.
captions.bellerophon-and-the-chimera-attic-red-fi: Attic epinetron in Athens: Bellerophon on Pegasus drives his spear into the Chimera — the aerial kill fixed on a domestic wool-working tool.
captions.mende-the-nike-of-paeonius: This Classical marble statue, signed by the sculptor Paeonius of Mende, was dedicated by the Messenians and Naupactians at Olympia around 420 BC to commemorate a victory, probably over Sparta in the Peloponnesian War. The goddess Nike is shown descending from the sky, her drapery billowing back in the rushing wind as she sweeps down on a triangular pillar, an eagle of Zeus beneath her feet to signify her flight through the heavens. Though her face and wings are lost, the wind-blown chiton and the buoyant, forward-leaning pose perfectly capture Nike as victory made flesh, swooping earthward to crown the victors. Now in the Archaeological Museum of Olympia.
captions.adrastos-in-his-chariot-attic-amphorisko: Attic red-figure amphoriskos in the Metropolitan Museum (Rogers Fund, 1919; inv. 19.192.44): Adrastos, king of Argos, drives his chariot with his name inscribed on the vase. Classical pottery gives the leader of the Seven a labelled portrait — the host who married his daughters to Polynices and Tydeus and led the Argive army to Thebes.
captions.aison-theseus-and-the-amazons-aison-kyli: Attic red-figure: Theseus locked with Amazons — the Athenian campaign that answers the abduction of Antiope or Hippolyte.
captions.heracles-and-apollo-struggling-over-the-: This bronze Corinthian helmet, now in the Cabinet des Médailles in Paris, carries an incised relief showing Heracles and Apollo contending over the Ceryneian Hind. The episode follows Apollodorus' account, in which Artemis and Apollo confront Heracles for seizing the goddess's sacred animal; here the deer stands between the two figures as the prize of their tug-of-war. The choice of subject for a warrior's helmet underlines the Labour's heroic prestige, framing the wearer in the image of Heracles' year-long pursuit and divine confrontation.
captions.painter-acrisius-orders-danae-and-perseu: Side B of the Hermitage calyx-krater (ARV² 360.1): King Acrisius commands that Danaë and the infant Perseus be shut in the chest — the Argive oracle made into Attic red-figure before the sea takes them.
captions.painter-attic-red-figure-hydria-the-rape: On this celebrated Attic red-figure hydria in the British Museum (E 224), the Meidias Painter stages the abduction of Hilaeira and Phoebe in the rich, crowded manner of late Classical vase-painting. The Dioscuri seize the daughters of Leucippus amid a throng of named companions, their names once inscribed beside the figures so that Hilaeira herself can be read in the scene. The vase is among the earliest and finest surviving images of the Leucippides myth, and it remains the canonical ancient counterpart to Rubens's later Baroque treatment of the same seizure.
captions.painter-diomedes-and-glaucus-exchanging-: Gela pelike: after the day's slaughter, Diomedes and Glaucus refuse to fight and trade armour — gold for bronze, Iliad 6's pause that closes the aristeia with guest-friendship.
captions.painter-eumolpos-with-demeter-and-persep: Attic red-figure three-handled skyphos in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens (inv. 1341 / CC 1355), attributed to the manner of the Jena Painter (Beazley ARV² 1517.10): a torch-bearing male stands between Demeter and Persephone in an Eleusinian night scene. The figure is generally read as Eumolpos — the Mysteries' ancestral singer — though some scholars prefer Iakchos; either way the vase places a young cult hero inside Demeter's torchlit circle at Tanagra's findspot. High Classical pottery keeping the founder of Eleusis among the goddesses he served.
captions.painter-helen-and-her-sisters-meidias-pa: Attic red-figure hydria from the Kerameikos, Athens (inv. 2712): Helen sits brooding with Eros on her lap while her Spartan kin gather around her — Phylonoe, Hermione, Clytemnestra nursing Orestes, and the wider Tyndarid sisterhood. LIMC records Timandra among the named women of this upper zone, the second major vase on which Helen's less-famous sister enters the pictorial record of the house of Tyndareus. Below, maenads tear Pentheus; above, the cursed daughters of Leda share one quiet, doomed household.
captions.painter-maenads-killing-pentheus-meidias: Meidias Painter circle — maenads killing Pentheus, late-classical vase fury for Dionysus' Theban revenge.
captions.painter-poseidon-and-a-young-warrior-eum: On this Lucanian red-figure pelike, found at Heraclea in Lucania and now in the Museo Archeologico Nazionale della Siritide in Policoro (inv. 35304), the sea-god Poseidon rides forward accompanied by a young, beardless warrior who is generally identified as his son Eumolpus; the reverse shows Athena in a chariot, casting the pair as the opposed champions of Poseidon's Eleusis and Athena's Athens. Eumolpus, the Thracian leader and reputed founder of the Eleusinian Mysteries, fell in that war when Erechtheus killed him in battle, whereupon Poseidon avenged his son by striking the Athenian king down with his trident. Standing at his divine father's side, the youthful figure on this vase is the principal ancient image cited for Eumolpus himself, and it heads his own entry in the visual record. The pelike, about 45 cm tall, was excavated at Policoro in 1963.
captions.painter-squat-lekythos-depicting-eutychi: An Attic red-figure squat lekythos of the late fifth century BC, painted with three personifications identified by name: Eutychia (Good Luck), Eunomia (Good Order), and Paidia (Play). At the centre Eunomia walks solemnly to the right in a girded peplos, diadem, and decorated hair-band, holding a necklace between her outstretched hands. The Athenian vase-painters of the circle around the Meidias Painter favoured such serene, richly adorned maidens to embody the well-ordered civic ideal of eunomia. It is held in the Walters Art Museum, Baltimore.
captions.painter-tyndareus-and-leda-before-the-eg: Tyndareus and Leda before the egg — the royal pair whose daughter’s hand draws every Achaean prince to Sparta.
captions.the-death-of-canace-lucanian-red-figure-: Painted on the shoulder of an early Lucanian red-figure hydria (kalpis) from Canosa, this is the earliest surviving image of Canace's tragedy and likely reflects Euripides' lost tragedy Aiolos. Canace lies dying upon a bed, the sword her father sent her still in her hand, while her brother Macareus stands with bowed head and bound wrists and King Aeolus presses forward, gesturing with his staff. The compressed, theatrical grouping turns the vase into a frozen stage scene of incest discovered and a daughter condemned. Museo Archeologico, Bari (inv. 1535).
captions.painter-squat-lekythos-aphrodite-and-ero: An Attic red-figure squat lekythos in the manner of the Meidias Painter, showing Aphrodite enthroned in a garden with Eros and a company of named female personifications: Peitho, Eudaimonia, Paidia, Eunomia, and Kleopatra. Each figure is labelled by an inscription, with Eunomia (Good Order) standing among the spring-bright attendants of the love goddess as the gentle ideal of a well-governed community. The vase exemplifies the late-fifth-century Athenian taste for crowding mythic scenes with abstract civic and erotic virtues personified as elegant women.
captions.apulian-red-figure-skyphos-depicting-the: South Italian skyphos in Karlsruhe: Actaeon set upon by his hounds as Artemis enacts his destruction — the myth on painted clay long before Titian.
captions.chimera-of-arezzo: The Etruscan bronze in Florence freezes the monster Bellerophon must kill — lion, goat and serpent in one snarling body, wounded as if mid-fight.
captions.painter-death-of-talos-volute-krater: The name-vase in Ruvo: winged figures pull the bronze pin from Talos' ankle as ichor drains — Apollonius' Crete automaton dying on Attic red-figure clay.
captions.painter-lucanian-red-figure-column-krate: Lucanian krater — the children of Heracles, the exile line that will reclaim the Peloponnese in the Return.
captions.painter-lucanian-red-figure-pelike-the-c: This Lucanian red-figure pelike, attributed to the circle of the Karneia Painter (LCS I 283) and now in the National Archaeological Museum of Policoro, stages the opening tableau of Euripides' tragedy Children of Heracles, the play in which Macaria appears. Heracles' orphaned children — the Heraclids — are shown as suppliant youths gathered at the altar of a sanctuary at Marathon in Attica, the refuge where Athens shelters them against the pursuing Eurystheus. It is within this very crisis that the oracle demands the voluntary death of one of Heracles' offspring for victory, and Macaria, daughter of Heracles and Deianira, freely offers her life. Painted in southern Italy around the close of the fifth century BCE, the vase is among the earliest surviving artistic responses to the drama that preserves Macaria's self-sacrifice, the legend that also named the spring at Marathon after her.
captions.painter-sacrifice-at-pylos-nestor: Attic vase of Nestor's Pylian sacrifice — the household Chloris ruled as Neleus' queen and mother of Nestor, Periclymenus and Pero. The mother stays offstage; her son's court keeps her name alive.
captions.votive-relief-of-archinos-to-amphiaraos: Marble shrine-relief of the offering of Archinos to Amphiaraos: the hero-healer stands treating a youth's shoulder, while the same youth sleeps on a couch as a sacred snake glides over him — incubation made visible. The inscription names Amphiaraos; the piece is the classic image of the Oropos oracle-cult that followed the seer's disappearance into the earth.
captions.medea-s-gift-to-creusa-louvre-ca-2193: Apulian crater: Creusa receives Medea's bridal gifts while the children stand by — the poisoned robe and diadem frozen in clay.
captions.painter-odysseus-and-diomedes-capturing-: The Lucanian red-figure vase that named its painter freezes Iliad Book X: Odysseus and Diomedes seize the Trojan spy in his wolf-skin as he prowls toward the Achaean ships. Dolon's night raid ends before it begins — the doomed volunteer of the Doloneia.
captions.painter-dioskouroi-with-tyndareus-and-le: Dioskouroi with Tyndareus and Leda — Helen's Spartan house, the court where the suitor-oath is sworn.
captions.terracotta-figurine-of-scylla: This late Classical terracotta statuette gives Scylla three dimensions: the cliff-monster of the strait modeled with a woman's torso rising from a serpentine sea-coil, girdled at the waist by the heads of dogs—the 'twelve feet and six necks' of the Homeric description compressed into a votive-scale image. Such figurines circulated as apotropaic and decorative objects in the Greek world. The piece is held at the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.
captions.votive-relief-of-the-alliance-between-co: This Classical Attic votive relief, now in the Acropolis Museum in Athens, commemorates the renewed alliance sworn between Athens and the island city of Corcyra (modern Corfu) in 375 BC. Personifications of the two allied states clasp hands beneath the protecting figure of Athena: the female figure on the relief is identified as Corcyra herself, the eponymous nymph of the island, here standing for her city as a political embodiment, though some readings name her Hera, the island's chief goddess. Corcyra was the naiad daughter of the river-god Asopus and the nymph Metope, carried off by Poseidon to the then-nameless island he afterwards called by her name, where she bore him Phaeax, ancestor of the Phaeacians. As the rare ancient image associated with this otherwise sparsely depicted nymph, the relief preserves her memory in the civic form her name eventually came to signify.
captions.cephisodotus-eirene-and-ploutos-plaster-: A full-length plaster cast in the Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow, reproducing Cephisodotus's Eirene group and showing the tender exchange of gazes between the goddess of Peace and the child Wealth she carries. The casting preserves the gentle inclination of Eirene's head toward Ploutos and the soft fall of her drapery, the spring-bloom serenity for which the type was prized in antiquity. As a teaching cast of the lost Athenian bronze, it transmits the Hellenic image of Peace as nurse and mother of abundance — the personified Eirene who, with her sisters Eunomia (Good Order) and Dike (Justice), was numbered among the Horai, daughters of Zeus and Themis.
captions.silver-stater-of-elis-olympia-laureate-z: A later Classical silver stater of Elis, now in Berlin's Münzkabinett, pairs a laureate head of Olympian Zeus with an eagle perched on an Ionic capital — the god and bird of the sanctuary Oxylus's kingdom administered. Where no ancient portrait of the Aetolian guide survives, the Zeus coinage of Elis-Olympia remains the material face of the realm myth credits him with founding after the Return of the Heraclids.
captions.1714-chryses-ransoming-chryseis-from-aga: Chryses ransoming Chryseis — the refused ransom that brings Apollo's arrows and Achilles' wrath into the same book.
captions.group-apulian-red-figure-chous-with-kall: South Italian chous (Getty): Callisto mid-metamorphosis into a bear — the Arcadian turn that places mother and son among the stars.
captions.lucanian-red-figure-nestoris-melampus-he: A Lucanian red-figure nestoris of about 360 BC, now in the National Archaeological Museum of Naples, carries one of the rare ancient images of the seer Melampus at work. The scene is set in a sanctuary: Melampus stands ministering while a seated priestess attends, and the two stricken daughters of King Proetus — driven mad and roaming the hills — are gathered for their cure. Artemis appears at the center with Dionysus and a satyr rendered in pale added color, framing the rite as a divine purification. It is the visual counterpart to the myth in which Melampus, son of Amythaon, healed the Proetids of their frenzy in return for a share of the Argive kingdom, and it remains a key witness to how South Italian painters imagined the prophet-healer in action.
captions.painter-boreas-abducting-oreithyia-apuli: On this South Italian (Apulian) red-figure wine jug in the Louvre, the painter renders the canonical Athenian myth of the wind-god's bride. Boreas, the bearded and winged North Wind, grasps Oreithyia, daughter of King Erechtheus, and lifts her from the ground in the act of carrying her off. The scene belongs to a long iconographic tradition in Greek vase painting, where Boreas is regularly shown as a powerfully winged male figure abducting the struggling Athenian princess, the union that would produce the winged Boreads Zetes and Calais.
captions.painter-diomedes-and-odysseus-stealing-t: Apulian vase — Diomedes and Odysseus stealing Rhesus' horses, the Doloneia in red-figure.
captions.amykos-and-the-argonauts-bnf-hydria: Paris BnF hydria (De Ridder 442): Amykos bound or confronted among the Argonauts — Apollonius' Bithynian bout fixed in clay.
captions.asteas-krater-of-the-madness-of-heracles: A red-figure calyx krater from Paestum, signed by the painter Asteas, this is one of the most celebrated depictions of the madness of Heracles and the only ancient image to name Megara by inscription within the scene. Driven mad by Hera, the hero hurls one of his sons onto a pyre already heaped with the family's burning possessions, believing the boy to be a child of his enemy Eurystheus. At the right, Megara recoils in terror, clutching her breast and tearing at her hair as she lunges toward the door of the house, while the goddess Mania, the personification of frenzy, hovers above. Every figure is identified by an accompanying inscription. The vase, 55 cm high, was found near Salerno and is now in the Museo Arqueologico Nacional, Madrid (inv. 11094).
captions.bronze-mirror-with-perseus-and-the-graia: An engraved Praenestine bronze mirror in the Metropolitan Museum of Art showing Perseus among the Graiai — one of the rare ancient images of the grey sisters. Long before Burne-Jones friezed the shared eye, Italic craftsmen cast the encounter onto a woman's mirror: the daughters of Phorcys as guardians on the road to Medusa.
captions.death-of-sarpedon: Lucanian red-figure hydria in the Museo Nazionale della Siritide, Policoro: Sarpedon's corpse amid Amazons and attendants — South Italian vase-painting keeping the Lycian prince's death in circulation.
captions.didrachm-of-phaistos-talos: Silver didrachm of Phaistos in the Cabinet des Médailles: winged Talos as the city's bronze guardian — Crete minting its automaton into civic identity.
captions.group-the-chimera-on-a-red-figure-apulia: On this red-figure Apulian dish in the Louvre (inv. K 362), a South Italian painter of the Lampas Group gives the Chimera her full Hesiodic three-form: a striding lion whose back sprouts a goat's head and whose tail terminates in a rearing serpent. The composition isolates the monster against the curve of the plate, emphasizing the uncanny fusion of three creatures into a single body that the Iliad calls 'of divine stock, not of men.' The vessel, from the Campana Collection acquired in 1861, belongs to the rich Apulian tradition of mythological pottery that flourished in Magna Graecia in the fourth century BC.
captions.leto-with-artemis-and-apollo-escaping-fr: A Hellenistic Greek relief, now in the Michael C. Carlos Museum in Atlanta, depicting the goddess Leto fleeing with her twin children Apollo and Artemis from the pursuing serpent Python. The scene draws on the tradition (preserved by Hyginus) in which Python, fated to die at the hands of Leto's offspring, hunted the pregnant goddess across the world before she could give birth — the prelude to Apollo's later return to Parnassus to slay the dragon. The carving is a rare ancient depiction that frames Python not in its death but as the threatening pursuer of the unborn god.
captions.loutrophoros-with-perseus-and-andromeda: This South Italian red-figure loutrophoros gives the myth its theatrical Apulian treatment, with Perseus confronting the sea-serpent Cetus as Andromeda stands chained for the sacrifice. The vase belongs to a wider repertoire of Magna Graecia ceramics that dwelt on the Perseus saga, and its monster — a long-bodied marine beast with snapping jaws — repeats the ancient image of the ketos sent from the sea, the prey-maker that the hero must kill to free and win the princess.
captions.lysippos-hermes-fastening-his-sandal: A marble statue in the Louvre of Hermes pausing to lace a winged sandal — the messenger caught in the ordinary instant before flight. The bent pose, credited to a Lysippan type, turns divine haste into a moment of private concentration; copies were prized across the Roman world as images of readiness and departure.
captions.oeneus-atalanta-and-meleager-engraved-et: This engraved bronze mirror from Etruria gathers Oeneus together with the central figures of the Calydonian hunt he hosted: his son Meleager, the huntress Atalanta, and another companion identified as a son of Thestius. The fine incised drawing names its protagonists in the Etruscan manner, attesting how thoroughly the Calydonian saga circulated beyond Greece into Italy. Held in the Louvre's Department of Greek, Etruscan and Roman Antiquities (inv. Br 1749), it preserves a rare ancient depiction in which Oeneus stands among the heroes of the hunt rather than apart from them.
captions.painter-parthenopaios-with-atalanta-apul: Side A of this Apulian red-figure calyx-krater by the Lycurgus Painter (Trendall–Cambitoglou RVAp 16/6) names Parthenopaios seated on a kline beside a veiled Atalanta — his mother in the Arcadian tradition — with an old man (often read as Teiresias) and a woman in attendance, while gods watch from above. It is one of the rare ancient vases to label the youngest of the Seven Against Thebes by name, fixing the beautiful Arcadian warrior in South Italian mythological painting. Museo Archeologico, Milan (A 0.9.1872 / St. 6873).
captions.painter-plate-with-bellerophon-on-pegasu: An Apulian red-figure plate attributed to the Baltimore Painter, a leading South Italian vase-painter of the late 4th century BC, showing Bellerophon seated on a galloping Pegasus and thrusting downward at the Chimera that rears beneath the horse. Held in the deposits of the Museo Nazionale Romano (Palazzo Massimo, Rome), it documents the spread of the Bellerophon myth into the Greek colonies of southern Italy and the ornate, theatrical style those workshops brought to heroic combat scenes.
captions.painter-theseus-and-peirithoos-in-the-un: Karlsruhe BL B 4: Hades and Persephone enthroned while Theseus and Peirithoos sit among the damned — Heracles with Cerberus nearby, the Chair of Forgetfulness as South Italian underworld map.
captions.plautios-heracles-iolaus-and-eros-relief: A repoussé and engraved bronze relief from the foot of the Ficoroni Cista, the celebrated 4th-century BC Praenestine (Etrusco-Latin) toilet box now in the Villa Giulia, Rome. The vignette shows three figures: Hercules at the right, a winged Eros at the centre, and Iolaus at the left. As Heracles' nephew and constant companion, Iolaus is here drawn into the hero's intimate circle, the small-scale metalwork demonstrating how the pairing of the two Theban kinsmen passed from Greek myth into the decorative repertoire of central Italy.
captions.portrait-statue-of-mausolus: Colossal marble from the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus (British Museum): the satrap-king whose tomb gave every later mausoleum its name. Hellenistic drapery and beard fix Mausolus as the mortal for whom Artemisia raised the Wonder of the World.
captions.punishment-of-dirce-pelike: Lucanian pelike in Policoro: Dirce's punishment with the twins present — South Italian vase-painting of the myth the Farnese Bull later monumentalized.
captions.temple-of-athena-alea-at-tegea: The ruins of the Doric temple of Athena Alea at Tegea, the chief sanctuary of Arcadian Tegea and the very monument on which Epochus was portrayed. Pausanias (8.45.7) records that the front gable, carved under the direction of the sculptor Scopas, showed the hunting of the Calydonian boar, and that there 'on the other side of the boar is Epochus supporting Ancaeus who is now wounded and has dropped his axe.' Epochus, son of the Tegean king Lycurgus, is thus given pride of place in his own city's temple holding up his stricken brother. Though the pediment's marbles survive only in fragments, this photograph of the temple platform shows the architectural setting of the lost sculptural group that immortalised him.
captions.terracotta-figurine-of-dolon: A small terracotta from the Staatliche Antikensammlungen presents Dolon in his wolf-skin kit — the Homeric spy reduced to a handheld figure of night and disguise. Even in clay, the Doloneia's doomed scout keeps his animal camouflage. Munich.
captions.the-demeter-of-knidos: Seated marble from Knidos — the sorrowful mother of the mysteries, grief read into the grain-goddess' face.
captions.demeter-and-metanira-eleusinian-hydria: Berlin hydria of the Eleusinian mysteries: Demeter with Metanira — queen of the household Homeric Hymn names as Celeus' wife. The vase stages the palace where the disguised goddess nursed Demophon and taught the rites.
captions.f272-perithoos-and-hippodameia: Attic volute-krater — Peirithous leads Hippodameia as bride while Lapiths and Centaurs explode into the wedding fight.
captions.group-the-murder-of-aegisthus-louvre-k-3: This Campanian red-figure hydria stages the end Aegisthus earned: Orestes and Pylades cut him down as he sits on a throne that was never his. The Wind Group vase freezes the Libation Bearers' revenge — the paramour king killed where he ruled. Musée du Louvre, Paris.
captions.hades-abducting-persephone-vergina-fresc: A wall painting from the Tomb of Persephone at Vergina (Aigai) in Macedonia: Hades drives a four-horse chariot as he seizes Persephone, Demeter grieving in the background. One of the rare surviving monumental Greek depictions of the abduction, it places the underworld king at the centre of a royal Macedonian burial chamber.
captions.heracles-and-auge-bronze-mirror-case-fro: This engraved bronze mirror case from Elis, dated to the late Classical period, condenses the founding violence of Auge's story into a single image: the priestess of Athena Alea confronted by a drunken Heracles. The scene depicts the assault at Tegea that, in Apollodorus' telling (Bibliotheca 2.7.4), Heracles committed 'not knowing her to be a daughter of Aleus' — the union that would produce Telephus and set in motion Auge's exile to Mysia. Now held in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens (Room 43, formerly the Stathatos collection), it is among the earliest surviving artistic treatments of the myth.
captions.painter-abduction-of-chrysippus-darius-p: Apulian volute-krater (Berlin): Laius' abduction of Chrysippus, the beautiful son of Pelops — South Italian vase-painting of the crime that precedes Thebes' curse. Not the Stoic philosopher of Soli.
captions.painter-abduction-of-chrysippus-detail: Detail of the Berlin krater: Chrysippus seized — the Pelopid youth Hyginus says Laius carried from the Nemean games.
captions.painter-apulian-volute-krater-preparatio: A monumental Apulian red-figure volute krater attributed to the Darius Painter, now in the Antikensammlung, Berlin (inv. 1984.41). The vase shows the preparation for the sacrifice of Phrixus and Helle by their father Athamas — the crisis from which the golden-fleeced ram swoops in to rescue the children, carrying Helle to her death over the sea. As one of the grandest South Italian vases of the later fourth century BC, it documents how the theatrical, suffering-laden version of the Helle and Phrixus story circulated in Greek vase painting well before its Roman afterlife.
captions.painter-jason-bringing-pelias-the-golden: Apulian red-figure calyx krater in the Louvre (K 127): Jason presents the Golden Fleece to Pelias while a winged Nike moves to crown the hero. South Italian vase painting stages the Iolcan king's impossible errand fulfilled — the prize Pelias thought would kill his nephew returned to his court.
captions.painter-pasiphae-and-the-minotaur: On the tondo of an Attic red-figure kylix from Vulci, Pasiphaë faces the child she bore — the Minotaur already horned beside his mother. Bibliothèque nationale de France, Cabinet des Médailles (De Ridder 1066).
captions.paros-bust-of-meleager-roman-copy-after-: This marble bust preserves the head of one of antiquity's most admired statue types: the Meleager attributed to the great fourth-century sculptor Skopas of Paros. The Aetolian hero is shown as an idealized youthful hunter, his tousled hair and slightly turned, deep-set gaze radiating the pathos for which Skopas was famous. Numerous Roman copies survive of the full figure — a nude Meleager resting after the Calydonian boar hunt, the boar's head and his hunting dog beside him — testifying to the type's enduring popularity. This example is in the British Museum (GR 1906.1-17.1) and stands as the canonical image of Meleager in classical art.
captions.praxiteles-hermes-and-the-infant-dionysu: A marble statue attributed to Praxiteles, discovered in 1877 in the ruins of the Temple of Hera at Olympia and now in the Archaeological Museum of Olympia. It shows Hermes pausing on his journey to deliver the infant Dionysus to the nymphs who would raise him, the god's missing right arm once dangling an object before the reaching child. The soft modelling and relaxed contrapposto have made it one of the most admired works of fourth-century BC Greek sculpture.
captions.silver-stater-of-taras-warrior-and-dolph: British Museum stater: cavalry reverse with Taras still astride his dolphin — the hero-founder keeping pace with the city's horsemen.
captions.the-argonauts-among-the-bebryces-drawing: This nineteenth-century line drawing reproduces the engraved frieze that wraps the body of the Ficoroni Cista, a celebrated Etruscan bronze toiletry casket of about 340–330 BC, signed by Novios Plautios at Rome. The continuous scene depicts the Argonauts after landing in the country of the Bebryces, where Pollux bound and boxed their king Amycus — here Pollux is shown training at a punching bag at the centre while his shipmates rest and tend the Argo. As a member of the Argo's crew listed in the catalogues of Apollonius and Hyginus, the Arcadian Argonaut Amphidamas is among the heroes who make up this landing party. The drawing, published in the Swedish encyclopedia Nordisk familjebok, preserves the legible flow of the engraving, which is one of the finest surviving examples of Italic figural metalwork.
captions.the-killing-of-atreus: An Apulian red-figure vase stages the death of Atreus — the Mycenaean king cut down in the feud his own feast had poisoned. The scene closes the circle the banquet opened: the architect of the Thyestean revenge becomes its next corpse. South Italian pottery.
captions.gold-stater-of-taras-infant-taras-and-po: British Museum gold: infant Taras with Poseidon — the founder's childhood under the sea-god who will send the saving dolphin.
captions.orestes-at-delphi-paestan-red-figure-bel: This South Italian (Paestan) red-figure bell-krater, now in the British Museum, preserves one of the canonical ancient depictions of the Erinyes in the Orestes legend. The fugitive Orestes has taken refuge at the sacred omphalos of Delphi, flanked by Apollo, Athena, and his companion Pylades; around the scene sleep and stir the Erinyes — the avenging spirits roused by the blood of his slain mother Clytemnestra — alongside priestesses of the oracle. The vase shows how the Greeks visualized the Furies as winged female pursuers of the matricide, the same chthonic powers that Aeschylus dramatized on the Athenian stage and that would ultimately be transformed into the benevolent Eumenides ('Kindly Ones').
captions.painter-abduction-of-chrysippus-baltimor: Apulian vase (Fiesole): another abduction of Chrysippus — the same Pelopid rape that vase-painters paired with underworld and bridal scenes.
Second view of the Fiesole Chrysippus abduction — Pelops' son as South Italian narrative pottery, centuries before Stoic Chrysippus of Soli borrowed the name.
captions.painter-odysseus-and-the-shade-of-tiresi: Odyssey Book 11 on a South Italian vase — the pit of blood, the seer who alone kept understanding among the dead, and the prophecy of Poseidon's wrath and the cattle of the Sun.
captions.painter-slaughter-of-the-suitors-mnester: The Ixion Painter's Campanian Mnesterophonia — Odysseus stringing the bow and cutting down the suitors in the hall.
captions.winged-thanatos-column-drum-from-ephesus: Sculpted marble column drum from the fourth-century BC Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, now in the British Museum, London. Among its relief figures stands a winged youth with a sword, commonly identified as Thanatos, beside Hermes and a veiled woman in a scene usually read as a soul's passage to the underworld.
captions.gold-stater-of-taras-taras-and-poseidon: Berlin gold stater: Taras before his father Poseidon — the dolphin-youth's genealogy struck in precious metal.
captions.painter-apulian-volute-krater-megara-and: An Apulian red-figure volute krater by the White Sakkos Painter in the Antikensammlung Kiel (B 585) stages an underworld tableau: Hades and Persephone sit in their palace while, outside to the left, Megara stands with her two sons among Hecate, the Danaids, Hermes and Orpheus. The vase keeps Heracles' Theban wife present even after death — the mother of the murdered children as a shade in the South Italian vision of the afterlife.
captions.amykos-and-pollux-praenestine-mirror: Praeneste bronze mirror: Amykos boxed by Pollux under the moon-goddess Losna — the Bebrycian duel as Etruscan luxury art.
captions.protesilaos-advancing-from-a-ship-s-prow: Thessalian drachm — Protesilaos advancing from a ship's prow, the first ashore who would be first to die.
captions.bellerophon-killing-the-chimera-hellenis: Rhodes pebble mosaic: the hero soars on Pegasus and spears the lion-goat-serpent below — Apollodorus' airborne assault in black and white stone.
captions.chairestratos-themis-of-rhamnous: Marble cult statue of Themis sculpted by Chairestratos, discovered in the goddess's small temple at Rhamnous in Attica and now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens. The goddess of divine law and right order stands draped in chiton and himation, her base preserving the sculptor's signature.
captions.judgment-tomb-rhadamanthys-lefkadia: In the Judgment Tomb at Lefkadia (ancient Mieza), painted Rhadamanthys stands among the underworld judges — Aeacus, Minos, and the Cretan son of Zeus who rules the Elysian plain in Homer and Plato. Macedonian funerary art makes the righteous judge a door-guardian of the afterlife.
captions.opheltes-small-bronze: A small bronze from the Archaeological Museum of Nemea identified with the hero Opheltes — the infant whose heroon and games made Nemea a Panhellenic sanctuary. Cult objects keep Archemorus present where the Seven paused on the road to Thebes.
captions.silver-didrachm-stater-of-the-aetolian-l: This Hellenistic silver didrachm struck by the Aetolian League depicts the federation's mythical eponym, Aetolus, the son of Endymion who fled the Peloponnese after a fatal chariot mishap and gave his name to the land of Aetolia. The hero is shown as a youthful warrior at rest, seated against a rock with his lance and sword, a heroic hunter type that the Aetolian confederacy adopted as its civic emblem. The choice of Aetolus on state coinage was a deliberate genealogical claim: by minting their founder onto their money, the Aetolians declared their region's identity to be rooted in his myth. Numismatic Museum of Athens.
captions.menelaus-bearing-the-body-of-patroclus-t: The Pasquino Group — Menelaus (or Ajax) bearing Patroclus' corpse, Hellenistic pathos that made the body's recovery a sculptural type.
captions.mosaic-of-a-cetus-sea-serpent-from-kaulo: Excavated at the ancient Greek colony of Kaulon (Kaulonia) in Calabria and now in the National Archaeological Museum of Reggio Calabria, this pebble-and-tessera mosaic renders the ketos in its canonical hybrid form: a coiling, dragon-headed sea-serpent with a finned, scaly body. It captures the imagined anatomy of the monster of myth — the devouring beast of the sea that Greek storytellers set against Andromeda — divorced from any single narrative scene and presented as a pure emblem of the deep.
captions.recognition-of-paris-attacked-by-deiphob: Etruscan alabaster funerary urn in the Museo archeologico nazionale di Chiusi. The relief shows Paris under attack by Deiphobus at the moment of recognition — the same fraternal assault the Volterra workshops carved for tombs across Etruria.
captions.silver-drachm-of-the-aetolian-league-art: On the reverse of this silver drachm of the Aetolian League, the eponymous hero Aetolus (Aitolos) is enthroned upon a heaped pile of captured Macedonian and Gallic shields, holding a spear, beside the league legend ΑΙΤΩΛΩΝ; the obverse bears the laureate head of Artemis with bow and quiver. The image fuses myth and politics: Aetolus, ancestral founder of the Aetolian people, presides in triumph over the arms of the Gauls defeated when they were repulsed from Delphi in 279 BC, the victory that made the league a great power. Minting their founder as a warrior atop spoils, the Aetolians turned their distant mythic eponym into a living symbol of federal strength. Staatliche Münzsammlung, Munich.
captions.capaneus-struck-by-zeus-etruscan-urn-rel: An Etruscan ash-urn relief (Würzburg) shows Capaneus blasted from the Theban wall — Zeus' bolt answering the hero who said even the gods could not stop him.
captions.head-of-helios-archaeological-museum-of-: This radiate Helios head from Rhodes names the island's sun-god consort — the husband Pindar gives to the nymph Rhodos when the new island rises from the sea. Cult sculpture of Helios is the visible half of the pair after whom Rhodes is named.
captions.menelaus-holding-the-body-of-patroclus: This view of the Pasquino Group type shows a helmeted warrior supporting a naked dead companion — long identified as Menelaus retrieving Patroclus' corpse from Iliad 17. Whether read as Menelaus–Patroclus or Ajax–Achilles, the group entered Menelaus' visual afterlife as the Spartan king's aristeia over his fallen comrade. Marble group type (Loggia dei Lanzi and related copies).
captions.the-winged-victory-of-samothrace-nike-of: Carved from Parian marble around 200–190 BC, this monumental statue shows Nike, goddess of victory, alighting on the prow of a warship, her great wings still spread and her wind-whipped chiton plastered against her surging body — the very image of triumph descending. Discovered in 1863 in the Sanctuary of the Great Gods on the Aegean island of Samothrace, it was likely a thank-offering for a naval victory. The dramatic forward lean, the spiraling drapery and the sense of rushing air make it the supreme surviving embodiment of Nike as the divine personification of victory, the swift winged daughter of the Titan Pallas and the Oceanid Styx who, in Hesiod's Theogony, stood beside Zeus in his war against the Titans. It is now one of the most celebrated treasures of the Musée du Louvre, Paris (Ma 2369).
captions.tomb-of-the-judgement-rhadamanthys: A closer view of the Lefkadia Judgment Tomb figure identified as Rhadamanthys — the Cretan lawgiver turned judge of the dead. The painted panel is among the clearest ancient portraits of the triad that weighs souls.
captions.urn-with-the-killing-of-myrtilus: This urnetta from the Hypogeum of the Volumnii (Perugia) again freezes Myrtilus' death: Pelops' betrayal of the charioteer who had helped him win. Etruscan funerary art repeats the scene as an emblem of broken faith — Hermes' son as the murdered helper whose last words damn a dynasty.
captions.messene-head-of-demeter-from-the-lycosou: The colossal marble head of Demeter from the cult group Damophon carved for the Temple of Despoina at Lycosoura in Arcadia, now in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens (inv. 1734). Alongside Despoina, Artemis and the Titan Anytus, the goddess sat as mother of the mysteries in one of the great Peloponnesian sanctuaries; the surviving head — veiled, grave, and monumental — is among the finest Hellenistic images of Demeter as a mystery cult divinity rather than a harvest allegory alone.
captions.aether-against-the-giants-pergamon-altar: Another angle on the same south-frieze combat in Berlin: Aether's body twists above the fallen Giant as the marble still carries the drama of Hellenistic baroque. For a figure rarely given a cult image of his own, the Pergamon frieze remains the canonical ancient portrait of the upper air at war.
captions.aether-battling-a-lion-headed-giant-perg: On the south frieze of the Great Altar of Pergamon, now in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin, the primordial god of the bright upper air strides into the Gigantomachy against a lion-headed Giant. The Hellenistic workshop gives Aether a winged, sky-borne energy — the luminous aithēr itself turned warrior — in one of the few monumental images that isolate him from the broader cosmogony.
captions.aether-in-the-gigantomachy-pergamon-alta: A closer view of the Aether group on the Pergamon Altar's Gigantomachy frieze: the deity of the clear sky grapples amid the swirling combat of gods and Giants. The relief is among the principal ancient monuments to name Aether as a fighting presence rather than a mere cosmogonic abstraction.
captions.asteria-fighting-giants-pergamon-altar: On the Great Altar of Pergamon in Berlin, the Titaness Asteria appears among the gods of the Gigantomachy frieze, locked in combat with Giants. The Hellenistic relief gives Coeus and Phoebe's daughter a martial identity beside her better-known sister Leto — an ancient image of Asteria as celestial power, not only as the future island of Delos.
captions.asteria-in-the-gigantomachy-pergamon-alt: A second view of the Asteria group on the Pergamon Altar: drapery and limbs surge with the altar's signature baroque motion as the Titaness presses the fight. For a figure whose later fame rests on Delos and Hecate, these Berlin slabs are the principal monumental witness to her place in the cosmic war.
captions.athena-against-alcyoneus-pergamon-altar: East frieze of the Great Altar of Pergamon: Athena and Nike overwhelm Alcyoneus as Ge rises from the earth — the Giant whose mother-earth bond the goddess must break.
captions.leon-and-aether-or-astraeus-on-the-perga: A widely published photograph of the south frieze pairing: the lion-headed Giant Leon locked with the sky-god usually identified as Aether (some scholars prefer Astraeus). The ambiguity itself is part of the reception — a luminous celestial fighter on the most ambitious Gigantomachy that survives.
captions.nereus-doris-and-oceanus-on-the-pergamon: West frieze of the Great Altar of Pergamon (Pergamonmuseum, Berlin): Doris fights beside her husband Nereus and her father Oceanus against the Giants in the Gigantomachy. The Oceanid who mothers the Nereids appears here as a warrior consort — one of the few monumental ancient portraits that name her in the cosmomachy rather than only in a genealogical list.
captions.pergamon-the-gigantomachy-frieze-of-the-: Berlin's Pergamonmuseum frieze: Olympians storm the serpent-legged Gigantes with boulders and torches — the most ambitious surviving ancient Gigantomachy, the Attalids' allegory of cosmic and barbarian defeat.
captions.pergamon-zeus-gigantomachy-detail: Detail of Zeus in the Gigantomachy frieze — the god who, with Heracles' aid, ends Porphyrion's assault. The Pergamon Altar remains the defining public image of the Giant who challenged Olympus.
captions.phoebe-in-the-gigantomachy-pergamon-alta: On the south frieze of the Great Altar of Pergamon in Berlin, the Titaness Phoebe — labeled Phoibe in the museum — lunges through swirling drapery with a torch, fighting beside her daughter Asteria in the Gigantomachy. For a figure who otherwise has almost no ancient iconography, this Hellenistic relief is the principal monumental witness to Phoebe as a martial power of the Titan generation, grandmother of Apollo and Artemis, rather than as a later lunar namesake.
captions.theia-on-the-pergamon-altar: A second view of Theia's combat group on the same frieze — drapery and stride identifying the mother of Helios, Selene and Eos among the Titan allies.
captions.theia-pergamon-altar-south-frieze: Theia on the Gigantomachy frieze of the Pergamon Altar — the Titaness of shining light fighting among the gods in Hellenistic high relief. Pergamonmuseum, Berlin.
captions.zeus-against-porphyrion-pergamon-altar: A closer photograph titles the duel: Zeus contra Porphyrion on the Great Altar now in Berlin. Apollodorus makes this Giant lust for Hera until Zeus blasts him; the frieze turns that lore into stone combat.
captions.zeus-and-porphyrion-pergamon-altar-east-: On the east frieze of the Great Altar of Pergamon, Zeus storms against the Giant identified as Porphyrion — the greatest of the earthborn beside Alcyoneus. Hellenistic marble makes the king of the Giants the thunderer's chief antagonist in the Gigantomachy.
captions.zeus-group-pergamon-altar: Another view of the Zeus combat on the Pergamon frieze: eagle, thunderbolt, and falling Giants — the sculptural stage on which Porphyrion's assault on Hera and Zeus was carved for the Attalid capital.
captions.keto-battling-the-giants-gigantomachy-fr: On the great Gigantomachy frieze of the Pergamon Altar, the sea-goddess Keto (Ceto) joins the cosmic battle against the Giants, fighting beside her father Pontus among the assembled marine deities of the south frieze. Carved in deep high relief, she is rendered not as a monster but as a stately, beautiful woman with finely modelled features and an ornate coiffure — a reminder that this 'mother of monsters' was herself named 'fair-cheeked' by Hesiod. This is the only securely identified depiction of Ceto surviving from antiquity, her name preserved by the inscribed labels that ran beneath the frieze. The marble panels, today reassembled in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin, rank among the supreme achievements of Hellenistic relief sculpture.
captions.telephus-frieze-carpenters-building-the-: Part of the great Telephus frieze of the Pergamon Altar, this Hellenistic marble relief shows carpenters constructing the boat (or chest) in which Auge is to be cast out upon the sea. The scene follows the Hecataeus variant preserved by Pausanias (8.4.9), in which Aleus, on discovering his daughter's child, set Auge adrift to drift to Teuthras' kingdom on the Caicus. As the dynastic myth of the Pergamene kings — who claimed descent from Telephus — the frieze gives Auge a prominent place in the city's foundation narrative. Now in the Pergamonmuseum, Berlin.
captions.telephus-frieze-king-teuthras-finds-auge: Panel 10 of the Pergamon Altar's Telephus frieze: King Teuthras discovers Auge stranded on the Mysian shore — the reception that plants Arcadian Auge at his Caicus court and sets the Pergamene dynastic myth in motion. Now in the Pergamonmuseum, Berlin.
captions.telephus-frieze-panels-2-3-the-court-of-: These two adjoining marble panels from the inner Telephus frieze of the Great Altar of Pergamon stage the household of Aleus, king of Tegea. Panel 2 sets the scene at the royal court of Aleos, while panel 3 shows Heracles catching sight of the king's daughter Auge in the precinct of Athena. The frieze, carved in low relief along the colonnaded inner courtyard, traces the saga of Telephus, the child Auge bore to Heracles and the legendary founder of Pergamon; the Attalid dynasty commissioned it to root its own lineage in the heroic house of Aleus. Now in the Pergamonmuseum, Berlin, it is the principal ancient image to place Aleus's court at the head of a continuous mythological narrative.
captions.telephus-frieze-telephus-receives-weapon: Telephus receives weapons from Auge on the Pergamon frieze — the Mysian hero armed before the Achaean clash.
captions.antioch-venus-de-milo: A Hellenistic marble statue generally identified as Aphrodite, discovered on the island of Melos in 1820. Renowned for its serene beauty and famously missing arms, it has become one of the defining images of the goddess and of classical sculpture itself. It is displayed at the Louvre, Paris.
captions.death-of-myrtilus-etruscan-cinerary-urn: An Etruscan cinerary urn stages Pelops casting Myrtilus from the chariot — the murder that turns the helpful (or treacherous) driver into a dying curse. Carved in the second century BC for a Volterran tomb, the relief shows how central the charioteer's fall was to Italic reception of the Olympian foundation myth.
captions.diomedes-roman-copy-after-kresilas: Louvre Ma 890: the athletic Argive type — taut, alert, the warrior of the great day when Athena made him match even the gods in battle.
captions.doris-in-the-sea-thiasos-altar-of-domiti: Relief detail from the so-called Altar of Domitius Ahenobarbus (Glyptothek Munich, inv. 239): Doris, mother of the bride Amphitrite, carries two torches to light the marine wedding procession of Poseidon and Amphitrite. The Roman-era sea thiasos makes the Oceanid visible as matron of the Nereid line — torch-bearer for her daughter's marriage to the sea-king.
captions.duel-of-eteocles-and-polynices-etruscan-: An Etruscan cinerary urn freezes the brothers' duel — the Seven's climax carried into Italic funerary art.
captions.marble-tondo-with-heracles-and-auge: A circular marble relief (tondo) showing Heracles seizing Auge, recovered from the villa of Herodes Atticus in Arcadia — the very region of Auge's home city of Tegea, where she served as priestess of Athena Alea. Pausanias (8.47.4) located the encounter at a Tegean fountain. The Hellenistic composition treats the moment of the assault that begets Telephus, framing the local Arcadian heroine within the visual language of mythological relief sculpture. The tondo survives in the collections documenting the Herodes Atticus villa finds.
captions.megarian-bowl-with-idomeneus-fragmentary: A fragmentary Megarian relief bowl in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (1980.11.2a–c) names the Cretan king in clay: from left to right, inscribed Idomeneus attacks Phaistos as he steps into his chariot, while Athena and Ares watch Homeric duels from the banks of the Skamandros. The bowl closely follows Iliad 5 — one of the rare ancient vessels to label Idomeneus by name.
captions.nereus-battling-the-giants-gigantomachy-: In the great marble Gigantomachy frieze of the Pergamon Altar, now reconstructed in Berlin, the sea-god Nereus appears among the marine deities who join the Olympian gods in the war against the Giants. Carved in the dramatic high relief of the Hellenistic Pergamene school, with its deep undercutting, straining muscles and swirling drapery, the Old Man of the Sea is shown amid the writhing tangle of bodies that wraps the altar's monumental base — a rare large-scale ancient depiction of a figure who otherwise survives mainly on vase-painting.
captions.original-sleeping-hermaphroditus-palazzo: The Palazzo Massimo sleeper — another Roman cast of the Hellenistic type that made Salmacis' myth marble.
captions.paris-attacked-by-deiphobus: Etruscan alabaster cinerary urn in the Museo Guarnacci, Volterra. Deiphobus assaults Paris while Aphrodite, Hector, Hecuba and Priam look on — the recognition scene in which the herdsman-prince is attacked by his own brother before the house of Troy claims him.
captions.telephus-threatening-the-infant-orestes-: The Pergamon Telephus frieze: Telephus threatens infant Orestes — the hostage bargain that forces Achilles to heal the wound he made.
captions.tralles-farnese-bull: The colossal marble group in Naples — Amphion and Zethus binding Dirce to the bull that will drag her to death — is antiquity's most famous image of the Theban queen's punishment. Found in the Baths of Caracalla and restored in the Renaissance, it made Dirce's cruelty and doom a landmark of Roman sculpture.
captions.tralles-the-farnese-bull: The colossal Naples group shows Amphion and Zethus binding Dirce to the bull — the twin sons of Zeus and Antiope avenging their mother, Amphion the lyre-builder of Thebes cast as a marble giant.
captions.warriors-lifting-the-body-of-patroclus-e: Etruscan relief of warriors lifting Patroclus — Italic reception of the Iliad's most mourned corpse.
captions.poseidon-of-melos: Hellenistic marble statue of Poseidon found on the island of Melos, now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens. The sea god stands in a commanding pose, his raised right hand once gripping a trident, with a dolphin at his feet supporting the figure.
captions.pan-teaching-daphnis-to-play-the-pipes: This Roman marble group, copied from a Hellenistic Greek original, shows the goat-horned Pan leaning close to instruct the young herdsman Daphnis in the art of the syrinx. The sculpture embodies Pan's role as the divine source of pastoral music: it was Pan, the Arcadians said, who first discovered the music of the pipes at Melpeia on the Nomian Mountains, and the reed flute he invented passed from the god to mortal shepherds. The intimate, tender grouping reflects the bucolic charm prized in Hellenistic art.
captions.phaedra-with-an-attendant-pompeii-fresco: This small Pompeian fresco (21.5 × 28.5 cm) in the British Museum (1856,0625.5) shows Phaedra seated in distress beside a standing attendant, almost certainly her nurse — the go-between of Euripides' tragedy. Recovered from Pompeii and later in the Fejérváry and Bööcke collections, the panel proves how early Roman domestic art already treated the lovesick queen as a recognizable mythic type.
captions.achilles-healing-telephus-with-the-rust-: Achilles heals Telephus with spear-rust — the oracle that only the wounder can cure, unlocking the fleet's road to Troy.
captions.cephisodotus-eirene-with-the-infant-plou: This life-size marble is the best-preserved Roman copy of the celebrated bronze group by Cephisodotus the Elder that stood in the Athenian Agora, the canonical 'Cephisodotus type' of Eirene (Εἰρήνη), the goddess of Peace. Heavily draped in a peplos and himation, the matronly goddess stands with maternal calm and cradles the naked infant Ploutos (Wealth) on her left arm, while her lost right hand once held a scepter; the child reaches up toward her, his presence proclaiming the truth that only in peacetime can prosperity be born and nursed. Erected after the Common Peace of 375/4 BC, the original embodied Athens' new state cult of Eirene. Now in the Glyptothek, Munich (inv. 219).
captions.eurus-tower-of-the-winds-athens: Southeast face of the Horologion of Andronikos in the Roman Agora: the relief of Eurus (Euros), the east-southeast wind, cloaked and bringing rain. The eight Anemoi of the Tower of the Winds remain the east wind's most famous ancient image in stone.
captions.fresco-of-vesta-hestia-from-a-pompeian-l: A lararium fresco from Pompeii (VII 12 11) depicting Vesta — the Roman form of Hestia — as the goddess of the domestic hearth, the quiet centre of household cult. Painted for a private shrine rather than a public temple, it shows how the Greek goddess of the sacred fire lived on in Roman domestic religion: the same veiled, matronly presence who received the first and last offerings of every sacrifice, here keeping watch over a Campanian house.
captions.hercules-and-iolaus-fountain-mosaic-from: This Roman wall mosaic, recovered in 1930–31 from the villa Sarsina Aldobrandini at Anzio (ancient Antium) and now in the Museo Nazionale Romano (Palazzo Massimo alle Terme, Rome), pairs Heracles with his nephew and faithful companion Iolaus. The two blond, nude heroes are set side by side in the polychrome glass-tessera style favoured for nymphaeum fountain decoration, an image of the inseparable bond between the hero and the charioteer who drove him to Lerna and seared the Hydra's severed necks. The mosaic is a rare monumental depiction in which Iolaus stands as Heracles' equal rather than a background attendant.
captions.mint-comet-caesar-roman-denarius: Roman denarius reverse with Caesar's comet — the daylight omen Augustan propaganda and Ovid's Metamorphoses XV made proof of apotheosis.
captions.notos-south-wind-tower-of-the-winds: On the octagonal Horologion of Andronikos Kyrrhestes in the Roman Agora of Athens, the relief of Notos faces due south: a winged youth emptying a water jar, the classical image of the warm, rain-bearing south wind that Hesiod and later poets paired with Boreas, Zephyrus, and Eurus. The Tower of the Winds remains the most famous architectural personification of the Anemoi, and this face is the canonical ancient portrait of Notus as storm-bringer.
captions.painter-the-laestrygonians-hurl-rocks-at: From the oldest surviving painted cycle of the Odyssey, dug from a house on the Esquiline: the giants tear boulders from the cliffs while the ships below are speared like fish.
captions.paris-and-oenone-house-of-the-labyrinth-: Fresco remains from Pompeii's House of the Labyrinth preserve Paris with Oenone in a Roman domestic cycle — the Idaean couple painted for a Campanian villa long before Helen's name eclipsed hers.
captions.the-three-graces-from-pompeii-roman-wall: Detached from a Pompeian wall in Regio VI, Insula Occidentalis, this Roman fresco shows the three Charites in their canonical embrace — nude, intertwined, the two outer sisters facing the viewer while the central figure turns away, hands resting on her companions' shoulders. The composition descends from a lost Hellenistic group and fixes the iconography of the Graces for all later art. Among the sisters stands Aglaïa (Ἀγλαΐα), 'Splendour' or 'Radiance', the eldest and brightest of the trio whom Hesiod names as the youngest daughter of Zeus and Eurynome and the bride of Hephaestus. Now in the Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Naples (inv. 9231).
captions.type-the-hera-farnese: A Roman Imperial marble statue of Hera from the Farnese Collection, now in the Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli (inv. 6027). Of the Ephesus-Vienna type after a Greek Classical original of the fourth century BC, the goddess stands veiled and diademed in the severe matronly pose that became the canonical image of Olympian queenship. Once displayed among the Farnese antiquities in Rome, it remains one of the most widely reproduced sculptural portraits of Hera in the Western tradition.
captions.agesander-laocoon-and-his-sons: The Vatican Laocoön — snakes crushing the priest who warned against the horse, Virgil's omen of Troy's last night made marble.
captions.mint-augustus-denarius-with-sidus-iulium: Silver denarius: Augustus' coinage of the Julian star — the sidus Iulium that Romans read as Caesar's soul ascending.
captions.relief-of-pax-tellus-east-frieze-of-the-: This allegorical panel from the east front of the Altar of Peace in Rome shows a serene enthroned goddess amid a flowering landscape, twin infants at her lap and the fruits of the earth in her embrace, flanked by personifications of the breezes of land and sea. Commissioned by the Senate to consecrate the Pax Augusta, the relief gives Roman form to the same idea the Greeks crowned in Eirene: Peace as the source of fertility and plenty. The monument frames its goddess within the luxuriant acanthus scrollwork of its lower walls, and the figure has been read as Pax — the Latin counterpart of Eirene — her olive-wreath aspect and burgeoning abundance translating the Cephisodotus image of Peace-nursing-Wealth into the visual language of Augustan Rome. Ara Pacis Museum, Rome.
captions.polyphemus-and-galatea-boscotrecase: Third-Style fresco from Boscotrecase: Polyphemus among his flock as Galatea rides a dolphin — the Sicilian romance before Ovid.
captions.phrixus-and-helle-fresco-from-the-masser: A Fourth-Style Pompeian fresco from the Masseria di Cuomo (Insula Occidentalis VI, 17), now in the Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli (inv. 8889). It depicts Helle and her brother Phrixus aboard the flying golden ram as they flee their murderous stepmother Ino. The composition isolates the fatal instant of the flight across the sea, the episode in which Helle loses her grip and plunges into the water, giving her name to the Hellespont (the Dardanelles). The painting is among the best-preserved Roman renderings of the myth and a key witness to its diffusion in Roman household art.
captions.achilles-and-briseis: Pompeian wall painting: Briseis is led away from Achilles' tent while the hero turns aside — the Iliad's quarrel frozen in Roman domestic space.
captions.actaeon-torn-by-dogs-terracotta-lamp: Roman lamp of Actaeon's death — Autonoe's son destroyed by his own hounds, the Cadmean mother's grief cast in clay for everyday light.
captions.athens-knucklebone-players-giocatrici-di: This painted marble pinax from Herculaneum, signed by Alexander of Athens and now in the National Archaeological Museum of Naples (inv. 9562), names its figures in Greek. Phoebe stands among Leto and Niobe while two Niobids play knucklebones below — a rare inscribed ancient image of the Titaness in a domestic mythic gathering, far from moon allegory, and one of the few classical works to label Phoebe herself.
captions.bc-hermes-ludovisi: A Roman marble of Hermes Logios — the orator Hermes — in the Palazzo Altemps, Rome. The god stands with one arm raised as if mid-address, the caduceus once completing the gesture; the type descends from a Classical Greek original and became a Renaissance favourite for the messenger as eloquent guide of souls and speech.
captions.building-the-argo: British Museum terracotta — Athena oversees the Argo's yard, the vessel the flower of Greece will take to Colchis.
captions.daedalus-presenting-the-wooden-cow-to-pa: From the House of the Vettii at Pompeii, the fresco shows Daedalus unveiling the wooden cow to Queen Pasiphaë — the craft that lets her mate with the bull and stain Minos' house. Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli (inv. 8979).
captions.dionysos-and-ikarios-farnese-relief: Farnese relief — the god visiting Icarius with the vine, the hospitality myth before the shepherds' murder.
captions.drunken-hercules-and-queen-omphale-pompe: Pompeian fresco — drunken Hercules and Omphale, Roman domestic myth of the hero unarmed.
captions.fresco-depicting-calliope-the-muse-of-ep: This Roman wall-painting from Pompeii, buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79, identifies Calliope by the attributes of epic verse: a scroll or writing tablet held by the standing Muse. Such Muse cycles adorned the dining rooms and gardens of Campanian houses, where Calliope — eldest of the nine daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne and patroness of heroic poetry — presided over the literary culture the Romans inherited from Greece. The fresco attests how deeply the imagery of the Muses, and of Calliope as their chief, was woven into everyday domestic decoration in antiquity.
captions.gaia-entrusts-erichthonius-to-athena: A Roman marble relief in the Louvre (Ma 579) staging the Attic foundation myth: Gaia rises from the ground to hand the infant Erichthonius to Athena, with Hephaestus looking on. The earth mother becomes the midwife of Athens — the primordial goddess folded into the city's own origin story.
captions.hecate-gilt-bronze-statuette-in-triple-f: A small gilt-bronze statuette in the Capitoline Museums in Rome (inv. S 2173) showing Hecate in her three-bodied aspect, three figures joined around a column with their attributes raised. Such portable hekataia condense the goddess's iconography — the twin torches she carries to light the way through night and the underworld, and the keys that open the gates between worlds — into a votive object for household and crossroad worship. As the goddess Hesiod's Theogony singles out for honor across earth, sea and sky, and the deity who alone aided Demeter in the search for Persephone by torchlight, Hecate was invoked at thresholds, and triple bronzes like this carried her protection into the home.
captions.hemera-day-from-the-sebasteion-at-aphrod: A relief from the Sebasteion at Aphrodisias, now in the Aphrodisias Museum, personifies Day as Hemera among the imperial mythological programme of the Julio-Claudian complex. The goddess of daylight stands as a classical allegory of the bright half of the cosmic cycle — Hesiod's daughter of Night translated into Roman civic marble.
captions.heracles-and-the-hind-roman-bronze-statu: This Roman-era bronze, held in the Staatliche Antikensammlungen in Munich (SL54), depicts Heracles overpowering the Ceryneian Hind, likely derived from a lost Greek prototype of the type associated with Lysippus. The hero presses down upon the deer, whose folded legs and arched neck convey the exhaustion of the year-long chase ended at the river Ladon. As a freestanding sculpture in the round, it translates the third Labour from the flat narrative of vase-painting into a fully modelled group, emphasising the physical mastery by which Heracles took the sacred animal alive.
captions.heracles-deianira-and-the-centaur-nessus: This Roman wall painting from the House of the Centaur at Pompeii (152 x 124 cm, now in the Naples National Archaeological Museum, inv. 9001) captures the prelude to Heracles' doom and gathers his whole family into a single frame. Heracles strides forward carrying his small son Hyllus in his arms, while Deianira lingers beside the river and the centaur Nessus, who has offered to ferry her across, looks back toward them. Within the myth this is the fateful moment before Nessus attempts to violate Deianira and Heracles shoots him with a poisoned arrow, leaving the dying centaur's blood that will one day kill the hero. Hyllus appears here not as the grown leader of the Heraclid Return but as the infant heir cradled by his father, anchoring the future avenger at the very origin of his family's tragedy.
captions.heracles-finding-the-infant-telephus-suc: This Roman fresco from Herculaneum, now in the National Archaeological Museum of Naples, renders the foundational image of the Telephus legend: the hero Heracles discovering the son he fathered on the Tegean priestess Auge. Exposed as an infant on Mount Parthenius, the babe was suckled by a doe that had just cast its fawn — the marvel that, by Apollodorus' etymology, gave the child his name (Bibliotheca 2.7.4). The painting personifies the Mysian landscape as a seated woman of Arcadia, with the eagle of Heracles, a lion, and the nursing deer gathered around the muscular figure of the hero, who gazes at the child he does not yet know.
captions.heracles-saving-hesione: This Pompeian wall painting (Naples MAN inv. 9445) shows Heracles rescuing Hesione from the sea-monster sent against Troy when Laomedon cheated Apollo and Poseidon. The Trojan princess — later the prize of Telamon and mother of Teucer — is the chained figure at the coast, the visual hinge between Heracles' eastern labours and the house of Priam. It remains the principal ancient image of her deliverance.
captions.hercules-and-deianira-pompeian-fresco: Pompeian wall painting of the conjugal pair whose story Achelous recounts at his harvest feast — the serene face of the wife who will send the fatal tunic.
captions.hermaphroditus-and-salmacis: Louvre relief from the Albani collection: Salmacis coils around Hermaphroditus at the fountain — Ovid's Carian nymph frozen in marble embrace.
captions.hippolytus-phaedra-and-the-nurse: Herculaneum fresco: lovesick Phaedra and her nurse opposite the chaste Hippolytus — Euripides' confession scene on a Campanian wall.
captions.io-watched-by-argus-pompeii-fresco: Pompeian fresco — Io as white heifer under Argus' gaze, the wander still ahead across continents to Egypt.
captions.leochares-diana-of-versailles: A marble statue of the huntress goddess striding beside a small deer, reaching over her shoulder toward her quiver — a Roman copy associated with a Greek original attributed to Leochares. Long a fixture of the French royal collections, it is displayed at the Louvre, Paris.
captions.marforio-oceanus: Colossal Roman river-god statue long identified as Oceanus, now the fountain figure in the courtyard of the Palazzo Nuovo at the Capitoline Museums. One of Rome's talking statues, Marforio keeps the world-encircling Titan as a public face of the city.
captions.meleager-and-atalanta-wall-painting-from: Pompeian fresco: Meleager and Atalanta in the quiet after the hunt — the charged regard that Ovid makes the seed of Calydon's family quarrel.
captions.melpomene-muse-of-tragedy: A colossal Roman statue of the first century AD, said to come from the Theatre of Pompey in Rome and now in the Louvre, monumentalizes Melpomene as the presiding genius of the tragic theatre. She stands draped in a heavy himation, crowned with vine leaves, and grasps an oversized tragic mask, while the cothurni lift her among the actors she patronizes. The grand scale, fitting for a building dedicated to dramatic performance, makes explicit the link between the Muse and the physical stage on which tragedy was enacted.
captions.metamorphosis-of-cyparissus-house-of-the: Pompeian fresco: Cyparissus beside the stag whose death will turn him into the funeral evergreen.
captions.nemesis-rhamnous-type: Miniaturised Roman replica of the Rhamnous cult image — Nemesis reduced to a handheld scale of justice. National Gallery Prague, Kinský Palace.
captions.orestes-and-electra-palazzo-altemps: The marble group in Rome's Palazzo Altemps pairs Orestes with Electra in a quiet standing embrace — the siblings of the Libation Bearers just before or after the recognition that leads to Clytemnestra's death. A Roman copy of a Hellenistic type, it fixes Orestes as the returned avenger beside the sister who kept the vow alive. Museo Nazionale Romano, Palazzo Altemps.
captions.orestes-and-pylades-before-thoas-and-iph: Pompeii fresco (VI.15.1): King Thoas presides as Orestes and Pylades stand before Iphigenia the priestess — Euripides' Taurian court in Roman domestic paint.
captions.orestes-and-pylades-in-tauris-roman-fres: A Roman fresco keeps the pair before the Taurian altar — Pylades still at Orestes' shoulder as Iphigenia's recognition approaches. Ancient wall-painting of the friendship that opera later made famous.
captions.orestes-and-pylades-san-ildefonso-group-: The Prado's San Ildefonso Group — long read as Orestes and Pylades — shows two youths in sacrificial quiet, one resting an arm on the other's shoulder. Whether cast as the Dioscuri or the Oresteia's inseparable pair, the sculpture has entered Orestes' afterlife as the image of the friend who shares exile, Tauris, and the blood-debt. Museo del Prado, Madrid.
