captions.original-bronze-head-of-hypnos: A bronze head of Hypnos with a wing springing from his temple, the god's distinguishing attribute, his downcast features evoking the gentle onset of sleep. It is a Roman copy after a lost Hellenistic original; the celebrated bronze it reproduces is held in the British Museum, and the photograph shows a cast moulded from that head.
captions.pelias-recognizes-jason-fresco-mann-inv-: Pompeian fresco from the House of Jason (IX.5.18), now MANN inv. 111436: King Pelias halts on a temple stair as he sees the one-sandaled youth — the omen that the man who will take his throne has arrived. The usurper of Iolcus is caught at the instant the Argo's voyage is born.
captions.perseus-and-andromeda-casa-di-sappho-fre: A Roman wall painting from the Casa di Sappho at Pompeii in which Perseus, having freed Andromeda, holds up the severed head of Medusa so that she may safely view its reflection in a pool of water. The tender, intimate treatment captures the couple at the threshold of the marriage from which Gorgophone — daughter of Perseus and Andromeda — would be born. It is preserved in the Naples National Archaeological Museum (Inv. 8995).
captions.phrixus-and-helle-crossing-the-dardanell: Roman mosaic from the Villa of San Marco at Stabiae: Phrixus and Helle ride the golden ram across the strait that will take her name. Floor decoration turns the boy's escape into domestic spectacle — the same voyage that ends with Phrixus' welcome in Colchis and the fleece hung in Ares' grove.
captions.phrixus-and-helle-fleeing-on-the-golden-: A Roman wall painting from Pompeii showing the siblings Phrixus and Helle carried over the sea by the winged, golden-fleeced ram Chrysomallus. Helle is shown slipping toward the waves as her brother clings to the animal — the moment just before she falls and drowns in the strait that would bear her name, the Hellespont. The fresco is now in the Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli (inv. 9478). It is one of the canonical ancient images of the escape that opens the saga of the Golden Fleece, evidence of how popular the story of the two refugee children was in Campanian domestic decoration.
captions.poseidon-and-amphitrite-pompeii-mosaic: Roman floor mosaic from Pompeii's House of the Grand Duke of Tuscany: Poseidon and Amphitrite ride a sea-chariot drawn by hippocamps, a domestic image of the divine couple who rule the deep. Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Naples.
captions.roman-statue-of-aesculapius: A Roman marble Aesculapius in the Walters Art Museum, Baltimore — the healing god as a standing philosopher-physician, staff coiled with a snake.
captions.sculptors-head-of-odysseus-sperlonga-gro: The pilos-capped hero from the colossal marble groups of the Sperlonga grotto — brow knotted, mouth parted, the face of endurance itself, found smashed in Tiberius' dining cave in 1957.
captions.selene-and-endymion-wall-painting-from-p: Recovered from a house in Pompeii (insula VI 9, 6–7) and now in the National Archaeological Museum of Naples, this Roman fresco depicts the moon goddess Selene approaching the slumbering Endymion. The shepherd reclines in the relaxed pose that became the canonical formula for the myth across antiquity, while the goddess descends from above to gaze upon him. The painting attests to the popularity of the Endymion theme in domestic Roman decoration, where the image of beauty preserved in eternal sleep—forever visited by divine love—carried funerary as well as amorous resonance.
captions.the-death-of-neoptolemus-at-delphi-pompe: Pompeian fresco — Neoptolemus slain at Delphi, the Return's end after the Molossian kingdom.
captions.the-education-of-achilles-chiron-teachin: This Roman wall painting, recovered from the Basilica of Herculaneum and now in the Naples National Archaeological Museum, shows the wise centaur Chiron guiding the young Achilles' hand across the strings of a lyre. The image distills Chiron's central role in myth as the great tutor of heroes, who fostered Achilles on Mount Pelion and schooled him not only in hunting and medicine but in music and the civilizing arts. The composition became one of antiquity's most copied images of the master-and-pupil pair.
captions.the-florentine-niobids: The Florentine Niobids — Roman marble group that taught Europe the myth as sculpture: children dying, mother already turning to stone.
captions.the-lady-of-ephesus: A marble cult statue of Artemis in her distinctive Ephesian form, the torso covered with rows of oval protuberances and the tight skirt paneled with rows of animals. The image embodies the Anatolian mother-goddess aspect of Artemis worshipped at her great temple in Ephesus. It is preserved in the Ephesus Archaeological Museum.
captions.the-marriage-of-telamon-and-hesione-troj: This fresco survives on the wall of the triclinium in the House of Octavius Quartio at Pompeii, part of a continuous painted frieze that narrates the legend of Troy. The scene shows Telamon, the Salaminian companion of Heracles who was first through the walls in the first sack of the city, together with Hesione, the Trojan princess he won as his prize of war and by whom he fathered Teucer. The episode is read as the marriage of Telamon and Hesione, or as Hesione's farewell to her brother Priam, with Heracles and Telamon standing in attendance at the right. Buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79, the painting is a rare surviving ancient depiction of Telamon by name, fixing him within the Trojan cycle that his sons Ajax and Teucer would carry into Homer's war.
captions.the-three-graces-wall-painting-from-pomp: A Roman fresco recovered from a house at Pompeii (Regio IX, Insula 2, no. 16) and now in the Naples National Archaeological Museum (inv. 9236). It shows the three Charites — Aglaea (Splendor), Euphrosyne (Mirth), and Thalia (Good Cheer), daughters of Zeus by the Oceanid Eurynome — interlocked nude in the canonical embrace, two facing the viewer with the central figure turned away, arms looped over one another's shoulders. Euphrosyne, whose name means "good cheer" or "merriment," stands among her sisters as the embodiment of the laughter and joy the Graces brought to feasts, dances, and the company of the gods. The composition fixed by this ancient type would be revived again and again from the Renaissance onward.
captions.the-torment-of-pentheus-house-of-the-vet: A Pompeian fresco restages the sparagmos: Pentheus torn by bacchants — the scene whose climax, in the Bacchae, is Agave waking to her son's head in her hands.
captions.theseus-victorious-over-the-minotaur: Pompeian fresco: Theseus stands over the crumpled bull-man as the freed Athenian youths crowd forward — the labyrinth's end painted for a Campanian house.
captions.workshop-alcmaeon-killing-his-mother-eri: Pompeian fresco (Naples MANN): Alcmaeon strikes down Eriphyle — the matricide for Harmonia's necklace that opens his Erinyes-driven wanderings.
captions.workshop-danae-arriving-at-seriphos-with: Roman fresco: Danaë cradles baby Perseus as their drifting chest reaches Seriphos — the ancient landfall that begins the island childhood.
captions.terracotta-plaque-with-king-oinomaos-and: Roman plaque of King Oenomaus and his charioteer — the Pisa tyrant whose races killed suitors until Pelops came.
captions.terracotta-plaque-with-pelops-and-hippod: This Augustan or Julio-Claudian Campana plaque in the Metropolitan Museum of Art shows Hippodamia beside Pelops in the chariot — the couple whose race against Oenomaus became Olympia's founding legend. About 38 cm high, the Roman domestic relief carries Pisa's bridal prize into villa decoration, Hippodamia as the living stake of the contest.
captions.admetus-and-alcestis-receiving-the-oracl: A Roman wall painting from Herculaneum, buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD, showing King Admetus of Pherae seated beside his wife Alcestis as they receive the fateful oracle that he may escape death only if another agrees to die in his place. The seated couple's troubled gazes capture the dread that sets the tragedy in motion. It is held in the National Archaeological Museum of Naples (MAN inv. 9026) and is one of the earliest surviving images of the pair.
captions.alcestis-and-admetus-receiving-the-oracl: An ancient Roman wall painting from the Vesuvian cities (Herculaneum/Pompeii), now in the National Archaeological Museum of Naples (inv. 9027), showing Admetus and Alcestis as they receive the fatal oracle. Admetus, son of Pheres and heir to the throne of Pherae, learns that he must find someone willing to die in his place — the decree that drives the whole Alcestis story. The fresco fixes the moment from which Pheres' own role flows: in Euripides' play the aged Pheres, despite his years, refuses to surrender his life for his son, so it is Alcestis who steps forward. The painting is a key witness to how the saga of Pheres' house was kept alive in Roman domestic art.
captions.lycurgus-and-ambrosia-mosaic-from-hercul: Herculaneum mosaic — Lycurgus raising his axe against Ambrosia as she becomes the vine that will bind him.
captions.menelaus-captures-helen-pompeii-fresco: A fresco from the Casa dell'Efebo at Pompeii shows Menelaus seizing Helen amid the fall of Troy — the Spartan king at the moment wrath becomes recovery. The wall-painting preserves the same night the vase-painters loved: Helen's beauty disarming the husband who came to kill her. Pompeii.
captions.omphale-and-hercules-fresco-tondo: Fresco tondo of Omphale and Hercules — the Lydian queen still holding the hero who sacked Laomedon's Troy.
captions.penelope-recognizing-the-returned-odysse: Pompeian fresco — Penelope recognizing the returned Odysseus, the test of the immovable bed made domestic myth.
captions.pentheus-torn-by-maenads-house-of-the-ve: Pompeii's House of the Vettii — Pentheus torn by maenads on the wall, Euripides' Bacchae in Roman domestic myth.
captions.the-encounter-of-jason-and-pelias-house-: A Roman fresco on the east wall of exedra g in the House of the Golden Cupids (regio VI.16.7) at Pompeii, sealed by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79. It depicts the fateful meeting at Iolcus between the usurping king Pelias and the young Jason, who arrives wearing a single sandal — the omen Pelias had been warned of. This is the episode in which Amythaon plays his one recorded narrative role: in the tradition he travels to Iolcus to back his nephew Jason's claim and his petition before Pelias, standing as one of the Aeolid kinsmen of Iolcus (brother of Jason's father Aeson). The painting is among the best-preserved Pompeian treatments of the Argonautic prelude and shows how the dynastic conflict of Tyro's descendants, Amythaon's family, was still being staged on Roman house walls centuries later.
captions.the-sacrifice-of-iphigenia-pompeii-fresc: Pompeian fresco of the Aulis sacrifice — the Cypria episode that buys the winds so the fleet can sail for Troy.
captions.eurus-virginia-museum-of-fine-arts: Relief image of Eurus in the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts (Richmond 51.13): the east wind as a winged or cloaked Anemos, one of the four cardinal winds who also stand for the seasons in later allegory.
captions.frieze-showing-the-hunt-for-the-calydoni: A Roman carved frieze in the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford, depicts the assembled hunters and the boar in the chase at Calydon. As a relief of the full hunting party, it stands for the gathering in which Plexippus, a son of Thestius and brother of Althaea, joined his kin and the visiting heroes. The fatal quarrel over the boar's hide that immediately followed the kill — recorded by Ovid (Metamorphoses 8.440–444) and Hyginus (Fabulae 174, 244) — is the moment in which Meleager struck down Plexippus together with a second uncle.
captions.hephaestus-and-the-cyclopes-forging-the-: A marble bas-relief in the Capitoline Museums (Palazzo dei Conservatori, Rome) showing Hephaestus and his Cyclopes hammering at the anvil, with Athena watching at left and a goddess (Thetis or Hera) at right. The Cyclopes are the divine smith Hephaestus' assistants at the forge — the same brawny one-eyed craftsmen Hesiod names Brontes, Steropes, and Arges. Steropes embodies the forge-Cyclops as a metalworking power, and reliefs of the workshop of Hephaestus/Vulcan are the principal surviving way the three smiths, him among them, were pictured.
captions.heracles-and-ladon-guardian-of-the-golde: A Roman relief plate (the decorated disc of a terracotta oil lamp) of the late imperial period, showing Heracles and the serpent Ladon coiled about the tree of the golden apples of the Hesperides. The dragon's sinuous body winds up the trunk, embodying the watchful guardian whom the hero must overcome in his eleventh labour. From the Loeb Collection, the piece is held in the Staatliche Antikensammlungen (State Collection of Antiquities) in Munich, catalogued as SL 89. It is a characteristic example of the mass-produced figural lamps through which mythological imagery, including the labours of Heracles, circulated widely across the Roman world.
captions.orpheus-taming-wild-animals: Roman mosaic — Orpheus taming wild animals, the songs episode fixed in stone for a villa floor.
captions.sarcophagus-of-orestes: This Roman marble sarcophagus compresses the Oresteia into a continuous frieze: the murder of Aegisthus and Clytemnestra, the pursuit by the Furies, and the refuge at Delphi. Orestes appears as the cycle's central actor — killer, hunted, and suppliant. Cleveland Museum of Art.
captions.teucer-with-seated-heracles-amethyst-int: A Roman intaglio of Teucer with seated Heracles — the hero whose Cypriot foundation keeps Telamon's line alive overseas.
captions.melpomene-muse-of-tragedy-b73cf1: This over-life-size Roman marble of the Hadrianic period, unearthed at the Villa of Cassius near Tivoli and now in the Vatican Museums, presents Melpomene with her canonical attributes as the Muse of tragedy. She wears a long chiton and the cothurnus, the high tragic boot, and once held a tragic mask, the emblem by which she was distinguished from her eight sisters. Her grave, statuesque bearing embodies the elevated suffering of the tragic stage, fixing in stone the iconography that ancient and later artists alike would reuse for the patroness of tragedy.
captions.statue-of-thalia-muse-of-comedy-from-the: This Roman marble of the Hadrianic period, unearthed at the Villa of Cassius near Tivoli and now in the Vatican Museums, depicts Thalia as the Muse of comedy. She is identified by the comic mask she carries and by the pastoral shepherd's crook associated with her patronage of idyllic and bucolic poetry. The figure once belonged to a sculptural ensemble of the nine Muses, a favourite theme for adorning aristocratic Roman villas.
captions.marine-cortege-from-acholla-bardo-nation: Another view of the Acholla marine cortège in the Bardo: the same Trajanic bath pavement that groups Pontus's children as a swimming thiasos. Within that procession the Phorcys–Ceto–Thaumas triad is the rare ancient image of Thaumas, father of Iris and the Harpies — wonder made flesh among the older sea-gods.
captions.phorcys-ceto-and-triton-mosaic-from-the-: This late Roman floor mosaic from the Trajan Baths at Acholla (in modern Tunisia) presents three deities of the deep: at the right is Ceto, beside her brother-husband Phorcys at the centre, with Triton — or, by another reading, her brother Thaumas — at the left. The sea-gods are pictured in their fearsome marine aspect, with fish-tails, spiky crustacean skin and crab-claw forelegs, fitting for the divine couple who in Hesiod's Theogony begot the Gorgons, the grey Graeae and the apple-guarding serpent Ladon. The mosaic, now in the Bardo National Museum in Tunis, is among the very few ancient images to name and pair Ceto with Phorcys, illustrating the watery genealogy of monsters that runs through Greek myth.
captions.achilles-strikes-thersites-roman-sarcoph: Detail of a sarcophagus in the Antalya Museum: Achilles kills Thersites for mocking his grief over Penthesilea — the Cyclic sequel to the Iliad, carved in marble for a Roman tomb.
captions.birth-of-athena-puteal-relief: Madrid puteal (cast in Pushkin): the birth in continuous relief — Zeus seated, Athena emerging, Eileithyia assisting the cry of war.
captions.helle-on-a-ram: This Metropolitan Museum relief isolates Helle on the golden ram — Nephele's daughter mid-passage, the cloud-mother's gift made visible as a single rider. The Fleece story begins with Nephele's rescue long before Jason sails.
captions.mosaic-of-poseidon-and-the-giant-polybot: A mosaic in the Palace of the Grand Master, Rhodes, restages Poseidon against Polybotes — the Giant chased through the sea and buried under the broken island. Floor art keeps the Cos–Nisyros etiology vivid in the Dodecanese.
captions.oenomaus-and-myrtilus: Relief of Oenomaus and Myrtilus — the charioteer whose treachery and curse seed the Atreid doom.
captions.personification-of-the-river-eurotas-sal: Floor mosaic from the Roman baths at Salamis on Cyprus: the river-god Eurotas reclines beside the wings of a swan in the southern sudatorium. The swan links the personification to Leda's myth on the Spartan stream, while the bath context treats Eurotas as a cooling water-power — the same Laconian river that Late Antique floors elsewhere name beside Sparta herself.
captions.relief-of-maia-and-mercury: A Gallo-Roman relief in the Musée gallo-romain of Lyon shows Maia with Mercury, mother and messenger side by side in provincial stone. The pairing carries the Cyllenian birth into the cult landscape of Roman Gaul — Maia as both Pleiad and local goddess of increase.
captions.sarcophagus-of-pelops-and-hippodamia: This Roman sarcophagus in the Tipaza Archaeological Museum retells the chariot race for Hippodamia in continuous relief — horses, drivers, and the bridal prize carved for a North African tomb. Imperial workshops favoured the story as victorious love and dynastic founding; the Tipaza chest shows how far Oenomaus' daughter travelled as an emblem of the won bride.
captions.the-augean-stables-villa-chiragan-relief: Marble relief from the Villa Chiragan (Martres-Tolosane), now in the Musée Saint-Raymond, Toulouse: Heracles at the Augean stables, the Labour that made King Augeas of Elis proverbial. Provincial Roman sculpture repeats the Olympia theme far from the Alpheus — dung, rivers, and a bad employer.
captions.leochares-apollo-belvedere: A marble statue of Apollo shown just after loosing an arrow, traditionally considered a Roman copy after a Greek bronze attributed to Leochares. For centuries it was hailed as the supreme ideal of classical male beauty. It stands in the Vatican Museums, Rome.
captions.medea-sarcophagus-berlin: Roman sarcophagus: the children carry poisoned wedding gifts to Creusa — Corinth's crimes carved beside the infanticide.
captions.achilles-and-troilus: Roman marble group in the Naples National Archaeological Museum (inv. 5999), often read as Achilles seizing the boy Troilus. The warrior lifts the struggling youth — the ambush at the fountain that vase-painters made Troilus' defining death, here carved as a single fatal grasp.
captions.andromeda-mosaic-zeugma: A floor mosaic from Zeugma (Gaziantep Museum) returns to the Ethiopian royal myth Cepheus rules: Andromeda's ordeal as provincial Roman floor spectacle — the king's household story carried east along the Euphrates.
captions.base-with-reliefs-of-the-birth-of-zeus: Marble statue base in the Capitoline Museums: on one face Rhea gives Cronus the swaddled stone; on another the Curetes clash shields while Amalthea nurses the infant Zeus. Rome's sculptural summary of the mother who outwitted Time.
captions.bc-hermes-belvedere: A monumental marble Hermes in the Museo Pio-Clementino of the Vatican Museums, long admired beside the Apollo Belvedere. The god stands in quiet contrapposto, cloak falling from one shoulder — an Imperial Roman copy of a late Classical Greek type that fixed Hermes as the graceful, almost contemplative courier of Olympus.
captions.bellerophon-and-pegasus-fighting-the-chi: Discovered in 1950 on the boulevard Gambetta in Nîmes and now held at the Musée de la Romanité, this Gallo-Roman floor mosaic forms one panel of a larger Bellerophon cycle. It shows the hero astride Pegasus as the pair confront the fire-breathing Chimera, the winged horse and rider above, the hybrid beast lunging below. The subject was a favorite of Roman provincial patrons, who saw in Bellerophon's victory over the monster an emblem of order triumphing over chaos — a theme repeated across the empire from Roman Britain to North Africa during the second and third centuries AD.
captions.bellerophon-and-stheneboea-antioch-mosai: Antioch Four Seasons mosaic: Stheneboea (Anteia) with Bellerophon — the queen whose false accusation sends the hero to Lycia, preserved in Roman pavement at Antakya.
captions.bellerophon-and-stheneboea-mosaic-detail: A closer view of the same Antioch panel — Stheneboea and the hero who rejected her, the Proetid court intrigue as late-antique floor myth.
captions.bellerophon-riding-pegasus-and-killing-t: Autun floor mosaic: Bellerophon on Pegasus plunges his lance into the Chimera — the Greek kill as Roman provincial emblem of order over chaos.

This Roman floor mosaic, now in the Musée Rolin in Autun, France, depicts the favourite Greco-Roman pairing of Pegasus and his rider in the act of slaying the Chimera. The winged horse strides forward in profile, his single great wing rising behind the spear-wielding Bellerophon, while the composite lion-goat-serpent monster recoils beneath. Worked in coloured tesserae, the panel shows how the myth of Pegasus, born from Medusa and tamed with Athena's bridle, remained a popular decorative subject across the Roman world, prized as an emblem of victory over chaos and monstrous evil.
captions.boy-heracles-strangling-a-snake: Capitoline marble: the chubby child grips a writhing serpent — the cradle miracle sculpted as innate heroic strength.
captions.copy-the-ludovisi-ares: A Roman marble statue of Ares seated at rest, his weapons set aside and a small Eros playing at his feet — the god of war momentarily disarmed by love. Restored by Gian Lorenzo Bernini in 1622, it is displayed in the Palazzo Altemps, Rome.
captions.death-of-penthesilea-amazonomachy-sarcop: Detail from a Roman marble Amazonomachy sarcophagus in the Louvre (Ma 2119): Achilles cradles the mortally wounded Amazon queen amid the crush of Greeks and Amazons. The relief carries into imperial funerary art the same hinge as the epic cycle — Penthesilea dying in the arms of the hero who killed her, love arriving a breath too late.
captions.fragment-of-a-sarcophagus-with-odysseus-: A Roman marble sarcophagus fragment in the Museo Barracco, Rome, shows Odysseus reunited with his aged father Laertes. The orchard recognition of Odyssey XXIV — scar, trees, and tears — becomes funerary relief, the nostos carved as a son's return to an old man among his vines.
captions.hecate-chiaramonti-triple-bodied-marble-: This Roman marble in the Vatican's Museo Chiaramonti (inv. 1922) gives the canonical triple form of Hecate: three identical women set back-to-back around a central pillar, each facing a different direction so the goddess watches every road at once. The arrangement embodies her cult title Trioditis or Trivia, 'she of the three ways' — the deity of crossroads honored at the junctions where her shrines and offerings stood. The sculptural type, known as the hekataion, was set up at gates and triple roads to ward off harm by night, and this triple-bodied image is the most widely reproduced ancient representation of the torch-bearing goddess of the crossroads.
captions.heracles-abducting-iole: This Roman marble relief in the Archaeological Museum of Piraeus shows Heracles carrying off Iole after the sack of Oechalia. Identifiable by his club and lion-skin, the hero seizes the daughter of Eurytus as his captive, the spoils of the war he waged to punish the king who had cheated him of his archery prize. The relief crystallizes the abduction that, through Deianira's fear of a rival, would lead to the poisoned robe of Nessus and the hero's death on Mount Oeta.
captions.king-lycurgus-of-thrace-relief-from-the-: Philippi theatre relief — the Edonian king in the scaenae frons of a city under Dionysus' patronage.
captions.medea-and-absyrtus-four-seasons-mosaic-a: Antioch mosaic panel (Antakya Museum): Medea and Absyrtus named in tesserae — the Colchian siblings fixed in a Roman floor narrative of the Argonaut saga.
captions.medea-sarcophagus-terme: Another Roman Medea sarcophagus (Museo Nazionale Romano): the Corinthian catastrophe in marble — wedding gifts, fire, and the royal household Creon cannot save.
captions.mosaic-of-oceanos-and-tethys: Another Zeugma Museum view of the Oceanos and Tethys floor: the Titan couple framed by fish and dragon-like ketos — nourishing waters laid in stone for a Euphrates villa.
captions.mosaic-of-the-nymph-cyrene: A North African floor mosaic from Lambaesis names Cyrene as a nymph — a provincial image of the Libyan figure Apollo set among the western nymphs, the same country that received her after the abduction from Haemonia.
captions.nemesis-of-rhamnous-type-farnese: Roman marble copy of the cult statue Agorakritos carved for Nemesis' sanctuary at Rhamnous in Attica. The goddess stands draped and measured — retribution as classical calm. Farnese Collection, Naples.
captions.oceanus-and-tethys-zeugma-detail: A closer view of the Zeugma Oceanus–Tethys pavement in Gaziantep: the sea-mother's face and watery crown amid the tesserae of the world-river.
captions.oceanus-and-tethys-zeugma-mosaic: Roman floor mosaic from the ancient city of Zeugma on the Euphrates, now in the Zeugma Mosaic Museum in Gaziantep, Turkey. It portrays Oceanus beside his consort Tethys amid fish and sea creatures, an image of the world-encircling river the Greeks imagined girdling the earth.
captions.original-the-campana-hera: A monumental marble statue of Hera, a Roman copy of the second century AD after a Greek original. The goddess stands veiled and crowned with a diadem, an image of regal, matronly dignity befitting the queen of Olympus. Named after the Campana collection from which it was acquired, the statue is now in the Louvre, Paris.
captions.original-the-farnese-atlas: A Roman marble statue of the Titan kneeling under the weight of the heavens, copied from a Hellenistic original. The globe on his shoulders is carved with figures of the classical constellations, making it the oldest surviving representation of the ancient celestial sphere. It is held in the National Archaeological Museum, Naples.
captions.original-the-farnese-eros: A Roman marble copy of the second century AD after a lost Greek original of the fourth century BC attributed to Praxiteles. It presents the love god not as a mischievous child but as a graceful, contemplative youth. Part of the Farnese collection, it is now in the National Archaeological Museum, Naples.
captions.pontus-from-the-oceanus-mosaic-of-acholl: A detail from a polychrome Roman floor mosaic excavated at Acholla in present-day Tunisia, now in the Bardo National Museum, in which the primordial sea-god Pontus is rendered as a bearded marine head rising from the deep, his hair and beard tangled with seaweed and crowned with crustacean claws in the manner the Romans used for Oceanus and the personified Sea. The mosaic belongs to a wider ocean program of marine deities and sea creatures; Pontus, the 'fruitless deep' born of Gaia alone in Hesiod's Theogony, is here named and visualized as the living face of the sea itself.
captions.roman-asclepius: A Roman marble of the god of medicine in the Galleria Borghese, Rome — draped, calm, and carrying the serpent-staff that later became medicine's emblem.
captions.sarcophagus-with-the-myth-of-orestes: A Roman marble sarcophagus compresses the Oresteia into a continuous frieze — including the killing of Aegisthus beside Clytemnestra as the cycle of blood closes on the usurper. Aegisthus appears as the palace lover whose death is the first payment Orestes exacts. Marble relief.
captions.sleeping-ariadne: The Vatican's reclining marble freezes the abandoned princess asleep on Naxos — antiquity's most famous image of the island vigil before Bacchus arrives.
captions.sleeping-hermaphroditus: The Borghese Hermaphrodite — the Carian fountain's afterlife in marble, languid until the other side reveals the biform body.
captions.statue-of-fortuna-and-pontus-patron-deit: This Roman-era marble group, now in the National History and Archaeology Museum of Constanța, Romania, shows the city-goddess Fortuna of ancient Tomis enthroned with a cornucopia, while the primordial sea-god Pontus stands much smaller at her feet. As the personification of the Black Sea on whose shore the Greek colony of Tomis was founded, Pontus appears here as the city's maritime patron paired with Fortuna's civic protection — a rare instance of the ancient Sea, child of Gaia and father of Nereus, Phorcys and Ceto, given his own sculpted form. It is the single image of Pontus carried on his Wikipedia article.
captions.statue-of-podalirius: A standing statue identified as Podalirius — the Asclepiad physician of the Trojan War, brother of Machaon. Roman sculpture keeps the healer-prince visible where vase-painters rarely named him alone.
captions.thalia-on-the-muses-sarcophagus-louvre-m: A relief detail from a Roman sarcophagus carved with the nine Muses, now in the Musée du Louvre (Ma 475), showing Thalia among her sisters. As Muse of comedy she holds the comic theatrical mask, her standard attribute, alongside the shepherd's staff that marks her dominion over pastoral poetry. Such Muse sarcophagi expressed the deceased's claim to learning and culture, ranging the whole sisterhood of the arts across the casket's front.
captions.thisbe-and-pyramus-house-of-dionysos-mos: Floor mosaic from the House of Dionysos: Thisbe and Pyramus with the lion and mulberry already in the scene — Ovid's lovers as Roman domestic pavement myth.
captions.ulysses-and-the-sirens-bardo-mosaic: A Roman floor mosaic from Dougga (ancient Thugga, in present-day Tunisia), now in the Bardo National Museum in Tunis. It depicts Odysseus' ship gliding past the Sirens' rocky island: the hero is bound to the mast, gesturing toward the singers, while his crew bend to the oars. The three Sirens are shown as bird-women perched on their crags, faithful to the classical form attested by Pausanias (9.34.3) and Hyginus rather than the later fish-tailed mermaid. The scene shows how enduringly the Homeric episode lived on in domestic Roman decoration across the Mediterranean.
captions.wall-mosaic-of-mnemosyne: A Roman wall mosaic of the mid–late second century AD naming Mnemosyne, Memory personified among the powers that govern recollection. Tesserae rather than canvas: the Titaness as a cult and decorative presence in the Imperial house, the goddess whose name still anchors every mnemonic.
captions.original-statue-of-asclepius-from-epidau: A monumental marble Asclepius from his sanctuary at Epidaurus, now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens — the bearded healer with staff and serpent, copied from a Classical Greek type.
captions.sarcophagus-relief-castor-and-pollux-sei: On this carved marble Roman sarcophagus of about 160 CE, the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, are shown carrying off the daughters of King Leucippus, Hilaeira and Phoebe, the legendary brides whose seizure binds the house of Leucippus to the twin gods. The dense, high-relief composition, with its tangle of horses and grasping figures, shows how popular the abduction story was in Roman funerary art, where scenes of carrying-off symbolized the soul's passage. The piece is preserved in the Walters Art Museum, Baltimore.
captions.bronze-medallion-of-heracles-and-iolaus-: A bronze medallion issued by the city of Ephesos under Antoninus Pius, now in the Cabinet des Médailles, Paris, pairs Heracles and Iolaus on the reverse. The civic coinage keeps the nephew-charioteer in the public face of Heraclean cult — proof that Iolaus travelled with his uncle not only through myth but through the mints of Asia Minor.
captions.althaea-kills-meleager-side-relief-of-a-: Carved in white marble around AD 170–180, this side relief of an urban Roman sarcophagus stages the climactic act of Althaea, queen of Calydon: the destruction of her own son Meleager. The Fates had foretold at Meleager's birth that he would live only as long as a brand then burning on the hearth; Althaea snatched it from the flames and hid it for years. When Meleager killed her brothers in the bitter quarrel that followed the Calydonian Boar Hunt, the grieving mother retrieved the log and cast it back into the fire, consuming her son's life with it. The sarcophagus, now in the Florence Archaeological Museum, treats this myth of doomed kinship as a meditation on death fit for a tomb.
captions.sarcophagus-with-scenes-from-the-myth-of: A Roman marble sarcophagus carved in high relief with a continuous frieze of the Admetus and Alcestis legend—from the couple consulting the oracle and Alcestis's deathbed sacrifice to Heracles leading her back from the dead to a grieving Admetus. Made for the freedman C. Junius Euhodus and his wife Metilia Acte, it used the myth of conjugal devotion and death conquered as a funerary parallel. It is preserved in the Vatican's Chiaramonti collection (inv. 1195).
captions.maia-and-mercury-silver-cup-from-the-ber: A repoussé silver cup, dedicated to Mercury by the freedman Publius Aelius Eutychus at the end of the 2nd century AD and recovered as part of the Berthouville Treasure (found in Normandy in 1830), depicts Maia together with Mercury, the Roman counterpart of Hermes. The pairing reflects the enduring identification of Maia as the mother of the messenger god, a tradition in which the Greek Pleiad was also syncretized with a Roman goddess of growth who gave her name to the month of May. The cup is preserved in the Cabinet des médailles of the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris.
captions.marine-cortege-of-acholla-phorcys-torch-: A museum photograph of the Acholla marine cortège sets Phorcys's torch-and-basket group inside its lotus-and-palmette border, clarifying the scale of the Trajan Baths procession in which the rarely carved sea-god appears. The bordered view complements the closer Tunis plate of the same panel and the separate three-deity mosaic from the complex, keeping Phorcys's scarce ancient imagery tied to one Tunisian find.
captions.phorcys-with-torch-and-basket-marine-pro: A second Acholla panel in the Bardo National Museum shows Phorcys in his characteristic late-Roman guise: red-skinned merman with lobster horns and clawed forelimbs, raising a flaming torch and a shallow basket while a sea-goddess rides the coiling cetus beside him. Distinct from the three-deity group on the same bath floor, this torch-bearing composition is the iconographic type handbooks cite for Phorcys as lord of hidden sea dangers — father, with Ceto, of the Gorgons and Graeae.
captions.sarcophagus-of-the-rape-of-the-daughters: This long Roman sarcophagus front in the Vatican Museums (Galleria dei Candelabri, inv. 2796) spreads the abduction of Leucippus's daughters across a continuous frieze of horses, Dioscuri, and struggling brides. Distinct from the Walters example, it shows how Roman workshops repeated the Leucippides myth as a funerary allegory of sudden removal and changed fate. Though King Leucippus himself is not carved among the actors, the relief is one of the principal ancient monuments of the story that made his house famous.
captions.the-calydonian-boar-hunt-meleager-sarcop: Capitoline sarcophagus: the boar Artemis sent against Calydon rears amid the heroes, Meleager poised for the killing thrust — the hunt as Roman funerary courage.
captions.hercules-and-the-stymphalian-birds-detai: This panel comes from a large Roman floor mosaic of the Twelve Labours of Hercules, executed in fine opus tessellatum and excavated at Llíria in the province of Valencia, Spain. In the scene devoted to the sixth Labour, Hercules drives off and shoots the birds that infested the marsh of Stymphalus. Dated to the first half of the third century AD, the mosaic survives in the Museo Arqueológico Nacional de España (M.A.N.) in Madrid and shows how the Greek myth was decorating elite domestic interiors across the Roman West.
captions.lysippos-farnese-hercules: The exhausted strongman after the labours — the end-state of the child who strangled serpents and was banished into Eurystheus' service.
captions.hercules-slaying-the-nemean-lion-detail-: A panel from a Roman floor mosaic of the Twelve Labours, executed in opus tessellatum with limestone tesserae and recovered from a villa at Llíria (ancient Edeta) near Valencia. The detail isolates the first labour: Hercules, nude and muscular, grapples the Nemean Lion at close quarters, the medium's bold tessellated outlines giving the struggle a vivid, almost heraldic clarity. The mosaic attests how thoroughly the labour cycle had become a standard decorative repertoire across the Roman West. Museo Arqueológico Nacional, Madrid (Room 22, inv. 38315 BIS).
captions.aion-uranus-in-the-zodiac-wheel-mosaic: Roman floor mosaic from Sentinum in Italy, now in the Glyptothek in Munich. The youthful god of eternal time, Aion — here identified with Uranus as lord of the heavens — stands inside the wheel of the zodiac, while the earth goddess reclines below with her children, the seasons.
captions.canace-roman-wall-painting-from-tor-mara: This fresco, from a villa at Tor Marancia near Rome and now in the Vatican Library's Sala delle Nozze Aldobrandine, belongs to a series of full-length heroines each labelled by inscription, all of them women undone by illicit passion. Canace stands holding the sword that names her fate, a quiet emblem of the suicide her father forced upon her after her affair with her brother Macareus. The painting's restrained, almost portrait-like dignity lets the lone blade carry the whole weight of the story.
captions.dionysus-acme-and-icarius-house-of-diony: Paphos mosaic — Dionysus bringing the first wine to Icarius, the Attic gift that will cost the host his life.
captions.fresco-of-scylla-from-a-villa-at-tor-mar: A Roman wall painting from a 3rd-century CE villa excavated at Tor Marancia, just south of Rome, part of a cycle portraying the tragic heroines of Greek drama. Here the figure identified as Scylla, daughter of Nisus, stands among these doomed protagonists — the Megarian princess whose love for Minos led her to pluck the purple lock from her sleeping father's head, dooming both her city and herself. The fresco preserves a rare ancient image of a figure who, despite her vivid literary afterlife in Ovid and Hyginus, was seldom represented in the visual arts.
captions.heracles-and-the-cretan-bull-detail-of-t: A panel from the Roman Labours pavement found at Llíria (Edeta) and now in the Museo Arqueológico Nacional, Madrid: Heracles captures the Cretan Bull, the living prize of the seventh Labour before the beast's later mythic career in Crete.
captions.heracles-cleansing-the-augean-stables-de: A panel from a Roman opus tessellatum pavement depicting the Twelve Labours of Hercules, this scene captures the fifth Labour set on the hero by Eurystheus: cleansing the dung-choked cattle-stables of Augeas, king of Elis, in a single day. Rather than shovelling, Heracles diverts the rivers Alpheus and Peneus through the yard, and the mosaic shows the hero turning the waters to flush the stalls clean. Found at Llíria (ancient Edeta) in Valencia, Spain, the mosaic is now held in the Museo Arqueológico Nacional in Madrid (inv. 38315 BIS). It illustrates the deed that won Augeas' grudging promise of a tenth of his herds — a reward the king afterward refused, setting Heracles' later war on Elis in motion.
captions.hercules-and-the-mares-of-diomedes-detai: A Roman floor mosaic panel in opus tessellatum, part of a Twelve Labours cycle now in the Museo Arqueológico Nacional, Madrid (3rd century CE). This compartment depicts the eighth labour, Heracles' confrontation with the man-eating mares of Diomedes of Thrace. Rendered in the spare, emblematic style of provincial Roman floor decoration, the scene compresses the whole episode into a single recognisable vignette of the hero and the deadly horses, one panel within the standard canonical sequence of Heracles' deeds.
captions.mosaic-of-the-three-horae-dike-eunomia-a: A floor mosaic from the West Wing of the House of Theseus at Nea Paphos, Cyprus, showing the three Horae as Hesiod named them: Dike (Justice), Eunomia (Good Order), and Eirene (Peace), the daughters of Zeus and Themis who keep the seasons and watch over the just city. Here Eunomia appears as one of a serene trio of robed maidens, the personification of lawful civic order set beside her sisters of justice and peace. The mosaic is preserved in situ at the Paphos Archaeological Park.
captions.mosaic-panel-depicting-the-madness-of-he: A Roman floor mosaic from the Villa of Torre de Palma near Monforte in Lusitania, illustrating the tragic episode in which Heracles, struck with Hera-sent madness, turns his violence upon his own household. The composition belongs to the Hercules Furens tradition that follows Megara's story to its darkest variant, in which the hero slays both the children he had by her and Megara herself before regaining his senses and seeking purification through his labours. The panel, dated to the 3rd–4th century CE, is preserved in the National Archaeology Museum of Lisbon, Portugal.
captions.poseidon-and-amymone-paphos-mosaic: House of Dionysus, Paphos: Poseidon and Amymone in tesserae — the Cypriot floor that fixed the Danaid's sea-god rescue for late antiquity.
captions.proserpina-sarcophagus: A Roman marble sarcophagus in the Aachen Cathedral Treasury whose front relief stages the Rape of Proserpina: Pluto seizes the goddess as her companions recoil. Reused for Carolingian and later burials, the chest carried Hades' myth into the heart of medieval imperial ceremony — antique underworld iconography recycled as Christian tomb.
captions.statues-of-castor-and-pollux: This pair of Roman marble statues presents the Dioscuri as standing nude youths, each accompanied by his horse and wearing the distinctive pilos, the egg-shaped cap recalling the eggshell from which the twins were said to have hatched. Castor and Pollux were widely venerated as protectors — of sailors, horsemen, and guests — and were honored across the Roman world with paired cult images such as these. The matched, mirrored poses emphasize the inseparable bond of the twins, the central theme of their myth.
captions.the-labours-of-hercules-slaying-the-lern: A panel from a Roman floor mosaic depicting the Twelve Labours of Hercules, this section shows the hero combating the Lernaean Hydra, the water-serpent rendered with multiple coiling heads emerging from the Lernaean swamp. Such labour cycles were a popular decorative program in Roman villas, presenting Hercules as a model of virtue triumphing over chaos. The mosaic, from Roman Hispania (Liria, Valencia), is preserved in the Museo Arqueológico Nacional in Madrid.
captions.sarcophagus-of-phaedra-and-hippolytus: The front of this marble sarcophagus in the Louvre (Ma 2294), found in 1853 on the Chiarone in Tuscany and once in the Campana Collection, narrates the Phaedra cycle in high relief: the queen's passion, the huntress-youth Hippolytus, and the disaster that follows Theseus' curse. Carved about AD 290 at roughly 1.1 × 2.2 m, it shows how late Roman funerary art kept the Euripidean story as a moral and mythic frieze.
captions.atropos-house-of-theseus-mosaic-paphos: Detail from the Achilles mosaic in the House of Theseus at Paphos: Atropos appears among the Fates attending the hero's infancy, the sister whose shears will one day cut even Achilles' glorious thread. A rare ancient floor image that isolates the cutter by name.
captions.eurotas-and-lacedaemon-mosaic: Late Antique mosaic in the Hatay Archaeology Museum, Antakya (inv. 826): facing personifications labelled as Eurotas and Lacedaemon (Lakedaimonia), the river-king and the land named for his line. Even far from Laconia, the pair travels as an emblem of Sparta's mythic geography — Eurotas as river and ancestor beside the personified Spartan plain.
captions.eurotas-and-lakedaimonia-mosaic-alternat: An earlier photograph of the same Antiochene pavement (Hatay Archaeology Museum, inv. 826), taken when the tesserae still sat in a different gallery light. The paired river-god and Lakedaimonia remain the clearest Late Antique image of Sparte's land-personification outside Cyprus — Eurotas and the city named for his daughter held in one emblematic couple.
captions.leda-and-the-swan-detail-the-personifica: In this richly coloured floor mosaic from the House of Aion at Nea Paphos in Cyprus, the Spartan river Eurotas appears not as a mere landscape but in fully human form. The panel stages the myth of Leda, queen of Sparta, who is about to bathe in the Eurotas when Zeus, transformed into a swan, approaches her; flanking the scene stand the personifications of the river-god Eurotas himself and of Lakedaimonia (Sparta), the land and city named for his daughter. The detail shown here isolates Eurotas beside his offspring Sparta, a Late Antique pagan composition (c. 350 AD) that gives the eponymous founder of Laconia a rare individual likeness.
captions.oceanus-and-tethys-antakya-mosaic: Late Roman mosaic in the Hatay Archaeology Museum, Antakya: Oceanus and Tethys face one another among marine creatures — the Titan sea-parents as Antiochene floor luxury.
captions.peleus-and-clotho-house-of-theseus-mosai: Detail from the Achilles bath mosaic in the House of Theseus at Paphos Archaeological Park: King Peleus stands beside Clotho (Klotho) as the spinner of fate attends the infant hero's destiny. One of the clearest ancient labels of Clotho by name in surviving floor art.
captions.pelops-mosaic-noheda: Noheda mosaic — late Roman Pelops still racing across a villa floor, the Olympia myth in tesserae.
captions.the-lycurgus-cup: British Museum dichroic cage cup — Lycurgus trapped in Ambrosia's vine as Dionysus' revenge closes, ruby by transmission, green by reflection.
captions.illuminator-cyclops-laboring-at-the-forg: A detail from the Vatican Vergil (Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Vat. Lat. 3225), one of the oldest surviving illustrated manuscripts of classical literature, made around 400 CE. The folio illuminates Virgil's Georgics, showing a one-eyed Cyclops bent over the forge with hammer in hand. In Hesiod's Theogony, Steropes ("Lightning-maker") is one of the three smith-Cyclopes — alongside Brontes and Arges — who hammered out the thunderbolt for Zeus in the fiery workshop; ancient art rarely names them individually, so a laboring forge-Cyclops such as this stands for the type to which Steropes belongs.
captions.battle-of-the-ships-ambrosian-iliad: Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana Cod. F. 205 Inf.: late antique miniature of the fight at the hulls — Hector's push to the Achaean ships as Homer's crisis of Books XIII–XVI.
captions.hunting-amazons-roman-mosaic-with-hippol: A late-antique Roman floor mosaic depicting four named Amazons at the hunt — Melanippe and Penthesileia mounted on horseback while Hippolyte and Thermodosa pursue game on foot — set amid wild animals and Eros figures in the border. The labelled figure of Hippolyte preserves the ancient image of the belt-bearing queen of the Amazons in the medium of monumental decoration, showing how her legend persisted in domestic art centuries after the classical vase tradition.
captions.the-capture-of-dolon-ambrosian-iliad: A miniature from the Ambrosian Iliad shows Odysseus and Diomedes taking Dolon at night — late antique book art preserving the Homeric ambush in gold and pigment. The spy's wolf-skin mission becomes a page of illuminated disaster. Biblioteca Ambrosiana, Milan.
captions.the-siege-of-the-greek-camp-ambrosian-il: Ambrosian Iliad: Trojans pressing the Greek camp and ships — the wall broken, the fleet at stake before Patroclus enters the fight.
captions.the-hestia-tapestry: A wool tapestry woven in Byzantine Egypt in the sixth century AD, now in the Dumbarton Oaks collection in Washington, DC. It shows the goddess enthroned as Hestia Polyolbos, 'Hestia rich in blessings', flanked by attendants bearing medallions inscribed with the gifts she bestows. It is a rare survival of the pagan goddess's imagery from a Christianizing age.
captions.silver-plate-with-ino-melicertes-and-an-: A late-antique partially gilded silver plate from Egypt, decorated in low relief and now in the Benaki Museum, Athens. It shows Ino with the child Melicertes riding upon the back of a marine ichthyocentaur (fish-tailed centaur), a maritime image that evokes the pair's rescue and transformation into sea-gods. The dish is rare material evidence that the myth of Melicertes-Palaemon remained a living subject for luxury silverware in the Eastern Mediterranean centuries after antiquity's classical heyday.
captions.notos-god-of-the-south-wind-byzantine: A Byzantine relief of Notos preserved in the Royal Ontario Museum continues the classical south-wind type into Christian-era decorative sculpture — a winged figure still named for the ancient Anemos. The piece shows how the Greek wind gods survived as directional emblems long after their cults had faded, keeping Notus recognizable as the wet southern breath of the Mediterranean year.
captions.tomb-of-antenor-padua: Padua's Tomba di Antenore — the shrine that claims the Trojan counselor as the city's founder. Homeric prudence becomes Italian foundation myth: Antenor who urged Helen's return sails on as Padua's first father.
captions.tomba-di-antenore: Another view of the Antenor tomb in Padua: stone and legend binding the Iliad's peace-speaker to the Veneto — not the Athenian sculptor Antenor of the Kore, but Priam's elder.
captions.menelaus-and-companions-battling-proteus: MET ivory game piece — Menelaus and his men holding Proteus through his changes, the Pharos ordeal carved for a medieval board.
captions.the-childhood-of-oedipus-laius-and-jocas: In Dijon Ms 562 (L'Histoire ancienne jusqu'à César), the upper register shows Laius and Jocasta with the infant who will destroy them — the exposure that tries to outrun Delphi. The medieval miniature keeps Laius present as the father who orders the child cast out, the first link in the recognition Sophocles later stages.
captions.giotto-envy-invidia: In the Arena Chapel at Padua, Giotto's vice cycle gives Envy a clenched, fire-eating female figure — the Latin Invidia that Hyginus's Preface equates with Greek Zelos (Zelus), the daimon of rivalry and jealous emulation who stands with Nike, Kratos and Bia at Zeus's throne. Fresco, Cappella degli Scrovegni: the medieval image through which Zelus's force of envious striving entered the Western gallery of the vices.
captions.prowess-of-deiphobus: Miniature from the Histoire ancienne jusqu'à César (British Library, Royal MS 20 D I, f. 126r). Deiphobus rides in armed prowess among the Trojan knights — Priam's son as a medieval chivalric hero before the sack that, in Virgil, leaves him mutilated in the underworld.
captions.pisano-phoroneus-or-legislation: Hexagonal marble relief from the south face of Giotto's Campanile in Florence: Phoroneus personifies Legislation among the liberal arts and human inventions. Medieval Florence casts the Argive first-man — son of Inachus, teacher of fire and law in Pausanias — as the inventor who brings statute to humankind.
captions.napoletano-dante-and-virgil-observing-ep: A fourteenth-century Neapolitan manuscript illumination to Dante's Inferno, Canto XXXI, in which the giants of myth are chained around the central pit of Hell. Dante and Virgil look on Ephialtes and Briareo (Briareus) before Antaeus lowers them toward the frozen lake of Cocytus. Medieval and Renaissance readers inherited Briareus from the classical poets as the archetypal hundred-armed giant of cosmic rebellion, and Dante places him among the impious Titans and Giants punished for their assault on heaven.
captions.manta-adelasia-of-montferrat-as-sinope-c: Baronial-hall fresco at Manta Castle: a medieval lady stands in for Sinope among the female Worthies — the Asopid nymph who tricked Zeus into granting her perpetual virginity, remembered as a Black Sea eponym and a model of shrewd chastity.
captions.creusa-receiving-the-burning-jewelry-fro: Medieval illumination of Glauce/Creusa as Medea's jewels catch fire — the Corinthian bride's death staged for a manuscript audience. The Latin name Creusa stands for Creon's daughter whom Euripides called Glauce.
captions.manta-deipyle-one-of-the-nine-worthy-wom: A detail from the celebrated Late Gothic fresco cycle in the Baronial Hall (Sala Baronale) of the Castello della Manta in Piedmont, painted soon after 1420 by the anonymous Master of Castello della Manta. The hall arrays the Nine Worthies opposite their female counterparts, the Nine Worthy Women, drawn from the chivalric poem 'Le Chevalier Errant' by Marquess Thomas III of Saluzzo. Among them stands Deipyle (rendered 'Deiphille'), the Argive princess and mother of the hero Diomedes, shown as an elegant courtly lady beneath an inscribed scroll and a heraldic shield (argent a griffin vert). The same figure was later identified with Eleonora of Arborea, but in the fresco she represents the mythological Deipyle herself, a rare instance of the otherwise barely depicted heroine being singled out by name.
captions.manta-the-nine-worthies-and-worthy-women: A further view of the fresco cycle in the Baronial Hall of the Castello della Manta, showing the long procession of the Nine Worthies and their female counterparts that runs around the room. Executed soon after 1420 by the anonymous Master of Castello della Manta, the program pairs legendary male champions (Godfrey of Bouillon, Charlemagne, King Arthur, Judas Maccabeus and others) with the Nine Worthy Women of myth and antiquity. Deipyle, mother of Diomedes, is numbered among these heroines, each standing in elaborate early-fifteenth-century dress with a scroll naming her, a vivid testimony to how Greek-myth figures were absorbed into medieval ideals of chivalric virtue.
captions.manta-the-nine-worthy-women-baronial-hal: A wide view of the frescoed wall of the Sala Baronale at the Castello della Manta, where the Nine Worthy Women (Neuf Preuses) process in courtly costume beneath painted trees and identifying scrolls. Painted around 1420 by the anonymous Master of Castello della Manta and inspired by Thomas III of Saluzzo's 'Le Chevalier Errant', the cycle is one of the finest surviving secular fresco ensembles of northern Italian Late Gothic art. Deipyle appears within this gallery of heroines, set among figures such as Sinope, Hippolyta, Menalippe, Semiramis, Lampedo, Tomyris, Teuta and Penthesilea, each presented as a model of female worth.
captions.ceyx-taking-leave-of-alcyone-ceyx-prenan: This fifteenth-century French manuscript illumination, from a copy of Christine de Pizan's Epître d'Othéa (Lille, Bibliothèque municipale, ms. 0391, fol. 78), depicts the parting that opens the tragedy of Alcyone, daughter of Aeolus. Her husband Ceyx leaves to consult an oracle by sea against her pleading; he will drown in the storm to come. The painter renders the leave-taking in the courtly idiom of late-medieval France, transmitting the Ovidian myth to a new audience through the moralizing frame of Christine's text. It is held by the Bibliothèque municipale de Lille.
captions.escape-of-jason-with-medea-and-the-death: Early woodcut of the Argonaut escape: Absyrtus dies as Medea flees with Jason — the brother whose murder stains the fleece's afterstory.
captions.hypsipyle-sparing-her-father-thoas: Woodcut: Hypsipyle saves Thoas while Opheltes dies in the background — the Lemnian king as father spared and later myth's crossroads.
captions.iphicles-saved-from-a-serpent-by-his-bro: This mid-fifteenth-century terracotta relief from Padua, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (2006.453), turns the infant snake episode into a Renaissance rescue drama named for Iphicles himself. The mortal twin is the figure being saved as his half-brother Hercules grapples with the serpent — a humanistic reading of the myth that makes Iphicles the title subject rather than a frightened bystander. About 51 cm wide, the relief shows how Quattrocento sculptors kept the Amphitryonid twins alive in Italian domestic and collector culture long after the Louvre stamnos had been buried.
captions.jason-received-by-king-oetes: Illuminated manuscript illustration (British Library) for Raoul Lefèvre's Histoire de Jason: Jason before King Oetes (Aeëtes) at the Colchian court. Medieval romance reception keeps the eastern king as the host who greets the Argonauts — and sets the price for the Golden Fleece.
captions.penelope-laertes-and-telemachus-bnf-fran: A fifteenth-century French miniature in the Bibliothèque nationale de France gathers Penelope, aged Laertes and young Telemachus — the Ithacan household waiting while Odysseus wanders. Laertes appears as the retired king, grief and orchard still ahead of him in the Odyssey's last books.

Another leaf from the same BnF manuscript returns to Laertes with Penelope and Telemachus, the court of Ithaca imaged as a late-medieval family group. The illuminator keeps the father of Odysseus inside the homecoming story long before the orchard recognition.
captions.testard-hypermnestra-writing: Hypermnestra writing — the one bride who spares Lynceus, breaking the sisters' bloody pact.
captions.testard-the-danaides-killing-their-husba: The Danaids killing their husbands — the wedding-night slaughter that earns the jars of Tartarus.
captions.testard-the-danaids-killing-their-husban: This BnF miniature (Français 874) stages the wedding-night massacre Hypermnestra alone refused: Danaus' daughters slay the sons of Aegyptus in their beds. The image is the visual foil to her mercy — the crime that defines the Danaids' underworld punishment and makes her the single exception named by Ovid and Apollodorus.
captions.tura-the-muse-terpsichore: This Ferrarese panel, attributed to Cosme Tura and the workshop of Angelo Maccagnino and now in the Museo Poldi Pezzoli in Milan, comes from the celebrated studiolo of Belfiore, a cycle devoted to the nine Muses commissioned by the Este court. Terpsichore is enthroned in jewel-like Renaissance splendour as the patroness of dance and the dramatic chorus, attended by small putti who echo the festive, music-and-movement world she rules. The panel reflects the humanist revival of the Muses as embodiments of the liberal arts and inspired performance.
captions.pollaiuolo-apollo-and-daphne: National Gallery, London: Apollo pursues as laurel already sprouts from Daphne's raised hands — an early Renaissance courtly chase that crowns the nymph as the poet's tree.
captions.anonymous-jocasta-and-oedipus: Hand-colored German woodcut from Steinhöwel's Boccaccio: Jocasta and her son Oedipus as a famous woman of antiquity. Early print culture already fixed the Theban queen beside the son who was also her husband.
captions.perseus-promises-polydectes-to-kill-medu: The promise that starts the quest — Perseus before Polydectes, the boast that sends him after Medusa and brings him home a founder.
captions.pollaiuolo-hercules-and-antaeus: This small but ferocious panel by the Florentine Antonio del Pollaiuolo, part of a series on the labours and deeds of Hercules, captures the decisive instant of the myth: Hercules has hoisted the giant Antaeus clear of the earth, severing him from the source of his strength — his mother Gaia, who renewed his power at every contact with the ground. Antaeus arches backward in agony, arms flung wide, as the hero crushes the life from him in a violent embrace. Pollaiuolo's obsessive study of the male body in extreme exertion makes the picture a Renaissance manifesto on movement and anatomy. Now in the Galleria degli Uffizi, Florence.
captions.pollaiuolo-hercules-and-the-hydra: This small but intensely energetic Florentine panel by Antonio del Pollaiuolo shows a nude, muscular Hercules swinging his club against the Lernaean Hydra, whose multiple snake-necks rear up and lunge at him from the marshy ground. Painted for the Medici around 1475, the work is celebrated for its anatomical dynamism and its rendering of violent motion, a hallmark of Pollaiuolo's fascination with the body in action. It hangs in the Uffizi Gallery, Florence, and is paired in conception with his companion image of Hercules and Antaeus.
captions.banquet-of-thyestes: Boccaccio's De casibus illumination (BL Royal 14 E V): the Thyestean banquet where Atreus serves Thyestes his own children — the infant Tantalus among the sons murdered for the plate that made the house of Pelops proverbial.
captions.botticelli-primavera: In Botticelli's allegory of spring in the Uffizi, Flora stands at the right in a flower-strewn gown, scattering blossoms as Zephyrus seizes Chloris behind her — Ovid's Fasti transformed into a Florentine garden of eternal May. The Roman flower-goddess becomes the painting's most recognizable figure of seasonal return.
captions.botticelli-the-birth-of-venus: Botticelli's Uffizi tempera: foam-born Venus arrives on a scallop shell, Zephyrs blowing her shoreward while a Hora waits with a flowered cloak — Hesiod's birth as the Renaissance's most famous image.
captions.costa-the-argonauts: Costa's Ferrarese crew aboard — the mustered heroes packed into the ship that leaves Iolcus for the fleece.
captions.botticelli-venus-and-mars: A Renaissance panel painting showing Mars sunk in deep sleep while a watchful Venus reclines opposite and infant satyrs make sport with his lance and armor. An allegory of love disarming war, it hangs in the National Gallery, London.
captions.cosimo-the-death-of-procris: Piero's National Gallery panel: Procris lies by the shore, slain by the unerring javelin she gave Cephalus — love undone by suspicion.
captions.giovanni-king-aeetes: Quattrocento panel figure from the Argonauts-in-Colchis cycle: Aeëtes as crowned Colchian king, son of Helios and keeper of Phrixus' fleece. Florentine narrative painting gives the eastern monarch a face — the father whose daughter Medea will betray him for Jason.
captions.giovanni-the-myth-of-io: Cassone panel cycling Io's story — transformation, Argus, and the long road that ends beside the Nile.
captions.perugino-apollo-and-marsyas: Perugino's Louvre panel — lyre against pipes in Umbrian calm, the deadly rivalry still a quiet pastoral exchange.
captions.bartolome-chaos: A panel from the Ciudad Rodrigo altarpiece imagines the primordial void before creation — Chaos as swirling disorder from which the ordered world will emerge, now in the University of Arizona Museum of Art.
captions.durer-the-death-of-orpheus: Dürer's Hamburg drawing — Thracian women killing the bard who refused their love after Eurydice, Northern Renaissance violence for Apollodorus' and Ovid's Maenad murder.
captions.carpaccio-the-embassy-of-hippolyta-to-th: Carpaccio's Venetian pageant: Hippolyta's embassy to King Theseus — the Amazon queen and the Athenian hero before war or marriage.
captions.michelangelo-bacchus: Bargello marble: a swaying, drunken Bacchus raising his cup while a satyr nibbles grapes behind him — intoxication carved in stone by the young Michelangelo.
captions.testard-hypsipyle-saves-thoas: BnF illumination (Français 599): Hypsipyle smuggles her father Thoas from the Lemnian massacre — medieval Boccaccio reception of the Argonaut island's spared king.
captions.testard-laodamia-writing-from-ovid-s-her: Testard's Heroides — Laodamia writing to the husband who leapt first from the black ships.
captions.boltraffio-narcissus: This Milanese Renaissance panel presents Narcissus as a half-length youth leaning over a stone basin, his face mirrored in the water — the myth reduced to its essential trap of sight and self. Long associated with Leonardo's circle through Boltraffio, the painting holds the National Gallery, London.
captions.bosch-table-of-the-mortal-sins-detail-in: Bosch's tabletop allegory of the Seven Deadly Sins isolates Invidia as a domestic scene of corrosive jealousy — the Latin personification Hyginus names as the counterpart of Zelus. Detail from the panel in the Museo del Prado, Madrid: envy as a lived social poison, the mortal afterlife of the winged emulous spirit who attends Zeus.
captions.durer-hercules-killing-the-stymphalian-b: Dürer restages the sixth Labour for Northern Renaissance eyes — Hercules loosing arrows at the man-eating birds of the Stymphalian marsh.
captions.mocetto-amymone: Mocetto's engraving isolates Amymone — the Danaid of the Poseidon encounter, Venetian print culture's face for the Lernaean bride.
captions.cronus-castrating-uranus: A French Renaissance miniature of the Theogony's founding crime: Cronus raises the sickle against Uranus — Heaven cut from Earth at the dawn of the Titans.
captions.durer-nemesis-the-great-fortune: A copperplate engraving by Albrecht Duerer, among the most celebrated prints of the Northern Renaissance. The winged goddess balances on a sphere high above an Alpine valley, holding a goblet and a bridle, emblems of the reward and the restraint she dispenses. Duerer fused Nemesis with the figure of Fortune, drawing on the humanist Poliziano's Latin poem 'Manto'; this impression is in the National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC.
captions.raphael-the-three-graces: A small panel by Raphael (1483–1520), now in the Musée Condé at Chantilly, painted at the very start of his career and possibly conceived as a companion to his "Vision of a Knight." It renders the three Charites — Aglaea, Euphrosyne, and Thalia — as three nude young women, each holding a golden sphere (often read as the apples of the Hesperides), arranged in the ancient embrace with the central Grace seen from behind. As the daughters of Zeus who personify charm, beauty, and joyful good cheer, the trio became a favored Renaissance emblem of grace and harmonious love; Euphrosyne, the spirit of mirth, takes her gentle place between her sisters in Raphael's serene early classicism.
captions.conegliano-theseus-killing-the-minotaur: In a small oil on panel, Cima stages the labyrinth's climax: Theseus drives his blade into the Minotaur's body while the bull-man's hybrid form collapses. Now in the Museo Poldi Pezzoli, Milan (on deposit from the Pinacoteca di Brera), the intimate scene distills the Cretan combat into a Renaissance cabinet piece.
captions.titian-the-legend-of-polydorus: Titian's Padua fresco cycle turns on Polydorus — Priam's youngest, murdered for Trojan gold by Polymestor in Thrace. Early Titian makes the boy's fate a civic moral for Padua: hospitality betrayed, a prince's corpse the spark of Hecuba's revenge.
captions.buonarroti-the-fall-of-the-giants-sistin: On the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel, Michelangelo stages the Gigantomachy as naked colossi hurled from heaven by the wrath of Olympian gods — the visual tradition Apollodorus compresses into named duels at Phlegra, where Heracles the mortal ally was required before any Giant could fall.
captions.michelangelo-the-cumaean-sibyl-sistine-c: Michelangelo's monumental prophetess on the Sistine vault — massive limbs and an open book, the Cumaean Sibyl as Renaissance theology's pagan witness to the Word.
captions.pinturicchio-the-return-of-odysseus: A Sienese chamber fresco turned gallery panel: suitors crowd the loom with gifts and music while, through the window, the ship is already in the harbour.
captions.titian-orpheus-and-eurydice: An early Titian (or Titianesque Venetian) treatment of the lovers in a darkening landscape, now associated with the Accademia Carrara. Eurydice's pale form already belongs more to death than to daylight — the myth told as Venetian colour and shadow rather than as underworld spectacle.
captions.cosimo-perseus-freeing-andromeda: Piero di Cosimo's Florentine panel crowds the shore with spectators as Perseus, winged and armored, strikes the fantastical sea-dragon before the bound Andromeda. The rescue that makes the Gorgon-slayer a husband unfolds as a busy Renaissance pageant. Oil on panel, Uffizi Gallery, Florence.
captions.pichore-the-suicide-of-canace-miniature-: An illumination by the Parisian master Jean Pichore for a French manuscript of Ovid's Heroides, translated by Octovien de Saint-Gelais (Bibliothèque nationale de France, MS Français 874, fol. 47v). Illustrating Heroides 11 — Canace's letter to her brother and lover Macareus — the miniature stages the grim conclusion of her story: having borne a child in secret, Canace receives the sword her father Aeolus sends, and the composition draws together discovery, the sword, and her impending death. The richly coloured Renaissance setting transposes the ancient Aeolid tragedy into a French courtly idiom.
captions.the-three-fates-flemish-tapestry: A Flemish tapestry of the early sixteenth century, now in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London. It shows the three Fates, Clotho, Lachesis and Atropos, standing in triumph over the prostrate figure of Chastity, an allegory of the Triumph of Death drawn from Petrarch's poem 'The Triumphs'. Lachesis, the apportioner who measures the thread of each life, stands among her sisters at the centre of the scene.
captions.piombo-death-of-adonis: An early High Renaissance lament in the Uffizi: Venus and her companions gather around Adonis's corpse as the landscape opens behind them — the dying beloved as Venetian tragedy.
captions.raphael-the-triumph-of-galatea: Raphael's fresco in the Villa Farnesina, Rome, shows the Nereid Galatea riding a shell chariot drawn by dolphins amid a swirl of tritons and cupids. Painted for Agostino Chigi, it is the High Renaissance's most famous image of the sea-nymph — beauty in motion, independent of Polyphemus' jealous gaze.
captions.montagna-birth-of-adonis: Montagna's engraving in the National Gallery of Art shows the infant Adonis delivered from Myrrha's transformed trunk. Early Renaissance printmaking fixes the Cypriot princess as the tree that both punishes and preserves her — bark as womb.
captions.sesto-leda-and-the-swan-after-leonardo-d: Leonardo da Vinci's lost composition of Leda and the Swan, known today through faithful copies such as this one by his Milanese follower Cesare da Sesto, established one of the Renaissance's most influential treatments of the myth. Leda, the Aetolian princess and wife of the Spartan king Tyndareus, stands nude and demure, one arm curving around the neck of the swan into which Zeus has transformed himself to seduce her. At her feet, broken eggshells release the four children born of the union and of that same night with her husband: Helen and Clytemnestra, Castor and Pollux. Leonardo fuses the human figure with the lush fertility of the surrounding landscape, casting the episode less as abduction than as a serene allegory of generation and the cycle of life.
captions.gossaert-neptune-and-amphitrite: Gossaert's Gemäldegalerie panel crowns Poseidon and Amphitrite as a Renaissance sea-couple — shell, trident, and nude majesty standing for the ocean's royal household.
captions.titian-flora: Titian's half-length goddess in the Uffizi holds roses and jasmine against loose white linen — Flora as Venetian beauty rather than calendar rite. The soft light and open bodice made this one of the Renaissance's most copied images of the flower goddess.
captions.melzi-vertumnus-and-pomona: Melzi's Leonardesque orchard — Vertumnus in disguise wooing Pomona, Ovid's Latin courtship as High Renaissance hush.
captions.the-calydonian-boar-woodcut-for-ovid-s-m: This woodcut illustrates Book VIII of Ovid's Metamorphoses in Raphael Regius's Venetian edition (c. 1518), the very passage that gives the fullest account of Ancaeus. Ovid names the double-axe-bearing Arcadian who scorns Atalanta and is then gored in the groin by the boar's twin tusks (‘concidit Ancaeus’). The print renders the hunt as a crowded melee of heroes and hounds around the rampaging boar, visualizing the literary scene in which Ancaeus meets his death—the wounds the dying Meleager would later call ‘happy.’
captions.pontormo-vertumnus-and-pomona: Pontormo's villa fresco of the orchard goddess and the shape-shifting year-god — Ovid's Latin courtship in Medici green.
captions.cranach-pyramus-and-thisbe: Cranach's German Renaissance take — the lion, the bloody veil, and the double suicide that dyes the mulberry.
captions.dossi-harpy: Dosso Dossi's oil in the Museo del Prado (58.4 × 167.8 cm) presents a lone Harpy in a horizontal landscape — the Ferrarese painter's eerie take on the classical bird-woman. Without naming Ocypete, Aello, or Celaeno, the canvas belongs to the same iconographic family as the Argonautic sisters: divine punishment delivered on the wing. It is one of the finest High-Renaissance paintings of the type.
captions.titian-bacchus-and-ariadne: On Naxos Ariadne turns as Bacchus leaps from his cheetah chariot — Theseus' sail already pale on the horizon, the crown of stars foreshadowed above her head.
captions.dossi-circe-and-her-lovers-in-a-landscap: In this Ferrarese Renaissance allegory, Circe sits in a wooded clearing with tablet and wand while men already half-changed into beasts gather around her — the Odyssey's Aeaean transformation staged as a pastoral court of desire and ruin. Dosso's soft light and dense foliage make the island feel both Eden and trap. Oil on canvas, National Gallery of Art, Washington (Samuel H. Kress Collection).
captions.sodoma-the-three-fates: A High Renaissance image of the Moirai attributed to Il Sodoma: three women with distaff, measure and shears. Lachesis stands in the middle office of fate — neither spinning the first thread nor cutting the last, but allotting how long each life may run.
captions.urbino-bowl-with-the-portrait-of-deidami: This Italian Renaissance maiolica bowl, painted in the workshop tradition of Nicolò da Urbino around 1525, names its subject outright: Deidamia, daughter of King Lycomedes of Scyros and, in this caption's reckoning, the bride of Achilles. Such inscribed istoriato dishes turned the heroines of antiquity into prized tableware for humanist patrons, here giving rare honor to a figure usually glimpsed only at the edge of Achilles' story. The piece is held in the Kunstgewerbemuseum, Berlin (inv. 17,39), and remains one of the very few works to depict Deidamia alone and identified by name rather than as one anonymous maiden among many.
captions.michelangelo-night: Michelangelo's marble Night reclines on the tomb of Giuliano de' Medici in Florence's New Sacristy — owl, mask, and poppies at her side. Renaissance allegory of Night that later ages read through the face of Nyx herself.
captions.cranach-the-judgement-of-paris-23b5df: An earlier Cranach reading of the same choice — Paris in armour, the goddesses unveiled, Mercury's apple still unawarded.
captions.aeneid-aeneas-and-helenus-sacrificing: Another Limoges enamel from the same Aeneid cycle, now in the Louvre (OA 7557), shows Aeneas and Helenus at sacrifice. The plaque keeps Helenus in his Virgilian role as priest-king of the rebuilt Troy at Buthrotum — the prophet who reads the gods for the exile who will found Rome.
captions.aeneid-helenus-and-andromache-give-prese: A Limoges painted enamel plaque by the Master of the Aeneid, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (25.40.1), stages Virgil's Buthrotum episode: the prophetic Trojan prince Helenus and his wife Andromache present gifts to Aeneas. Helenus appears here as the surviving twin of Cassandra — foresight that lived to counsel the Trojan remnant on their Italian voyage.
captions.aeneid-trojans-land-near-mount-etna-bene: Limoges enamel plaque (Metropolitan Museum): the Trojans beach under Etna while the Giant Enceladus lies crushed beneath the mountain — Virgil's etiology of Sicilian fire cast in Renaissance enamel.
captions.avelli-plate-with-hypermnestra-watching-: Hypermnestra watches Lynceus escape — the solitary mercy among Danaus' fifty daughters.
captions.baldung-pyramus-and-thisbe: Baldung's 1530 pair — Pyramus fallen on his sword, Thisbe discovering him, the wall's crack already behind them.
captions.buonarroti-leda-and-the-swan-after-miche: This panel in the National Gallery, London, preserves the composition of Michelangelo's celebrated but now-lost tempera Leda and the Swan, painted around 1530 for Alfonso d'Este, Duke of Ferrara. Michelangelo recast Leda in the powerful, muscular form of his sculpted Night from the Medici tombs, reclining as the swan-Zeus presses against her in an unmistakably charged embrace. The sculptural monumentality of the body, the coiled tension of the pose, and the daring eroticism made the image notorious; the original is said to have been destroyed for its indecency, leaving copies like this one to transmit one of the boldest Renaissance visions of the Spartan queen's mythical union.
captions.correggio-danae: Correggio's Borghese Danaë reclines as Eros and putti manage the golden shower — soft High Renaissance flesh for the impregnation that will father Perseus. Oil on canvas, Galleria Borghese, Rome.
captions.correggio-jupiter-and-io: Correggio's Vienna canvas — Zeus as a dark cloud embracing Io, the passion that begins her gadfly wander.
captions.correggio-leda-and-the-swan: Now in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin, Correggio's canvas was painted as one of a series of mythological 'Loves of Jupiter' and stages the encounter as a tender, luminous idyll set in a wooded riverbank. The picture unfolds the episode across time: at the center Leda sits among her companions as the swan nestles into her lap, while at the sides the bird is shown arriving and then departing. Correggio's soft sfumato, warm flesh tones, and gentle eroticism transform the seduction of the future mother of Helen of Troy into a vision of grace. The painting's later history was turbulent: an owner repeatedly mutilated Leda's head in moral outrage, and it was carefully restored, a testament to the enduring power of the subject.
captions.correggio-the-abduction-of-ganymede: Vienna companion to Jupiter and Io: the eagle lifts Ganymede from a wooded hillside as the boy turns toward the viewer, his dog barking from the ground below.
captions.cranach-the-close-of-the-silver-age: National Gallery, London: Cranach's quarreling nude race — the Silver Age tipping from soft living into the violence that ends the second race.
captions.cranach-the-golden-age: Oslo Nasjonalmuseet: Cranach's enclosed paradise of ease and play — Hesiod's first race remembered as a garden before silver and iron.
captions.die-daphne-embracing-her-father-the-rive: Another plate from the same Met series shows Daphne clinging to Peneus as nymphs bring jars — Ovid's moment when the daughter begs her river-father to change her form before Apollo arrives. The Thessalian Potamos is named and staged as the parental power behind the laurel.
captions.die-river-gods-consoling-peneus-for-the-: This Metropolitan Museum engraving (inv. 49.97.326) makes Peneus the mourner at the centre: fellow river-gods gather to console the Thessalian father after Daphne becomes the laurel. Designed after Peruzzi and cut by the Master of the Die, the print is among the clearest Renaissance images of the river-god himself, not only of Apollo's chase.
