captions.fiorentino-the-revenge-of-nauplius-vende: A fresco panel in the Studiolo of Francesco I de' Medici (Palazzo Vecchio, Florence) stages Nauplius the Wrecker: after the Greeks stone his son Palamedes at Troy, the aged Argive lights false beacon fires on the Capherian rocks of Euboea, luring the returning fleet onto the reefs. Renaissance Florence keeps the nostoi revenge as a moral allegory of cunning turned lethal — Poseidon's son by Amymone as the father who answers injustice with shipwreck.
captions.romano-the-fall-of-the-giants-sala-dei-g: Mantua's Palazzo Te: Zeus hurls thunderbolts while Giants are crushed beneath collapsing mountains — Mannerist illusion that makes the whole room cave in on the viewer.
captions.alciato-proteus-emblematum-liber: Andrea Alciato's Emblematum Liber (1531) made Proteus an emblem of mutable nature — the god who assumes many forms rather than reveal his counsel freely. The woodcut became one of the most influential Renaissance images of the name, from which the English adjective "protean" ultimately derives, and it circulated independently of Homer's Egyptian episode while reinforcing the myth's core idea of elusive transformation.
captions.avelli-cup-with-eurydice-aristaeus-and-o: Urbino maiolica: Aristaeus pursues Eurydice while Orpheus looks on — the chase that kills the nymph and dooms Aristaeus' bees.
captions.bronzino-the-flaying-of-marsyas: Bronzino's Hermitage panel stages the musical contest itself — Florentine Mannerism before the flaying.
captions.avelli-dish-with-hermaphroditus-and-the-: Xanto's maiolica dish: Salmacis and Hermaphroditus as table spectacle — Renaissance Urbino ceramics keeping the fountain myth in bright glaze.
captions.romano-victory-janus-chronos-and-gaea: A Mannerist allegory by Giulio Romano in which Gaea reclines among personifications of victory, beginnings, and time. The primordial earth is no longer a Hesiodic genealogy figure alone but a Renaissance emblem of the world's body, painted for the Mantuan court that made Romano Raphael's heir in mythological invention.
captions.avelli-amphiaraus-betrayed-by-his-wife-m: Urbino istoriato maiolica by Francesco Xanto Avelli: Amphiaraus betrayed by Eriphyle, the wife who sold him into the Theban war for a necklace. The bowl turns the Argive household drama into colorful Renaissance narrative ware — the seer's forced departure painted for the table.
captions.parmigianino-saturn-and-philyra: Parmigianino's drawing (Royal Collection) isolates the nymph with the horse-formed Titan — Mannerist line for the myth that makes Philyra mother of Chiron on Mount Pelion.
captions.titian-venus-of-urbino: An oil painting of Venus reclining nude on a couch in a Venetian palace interior, her gaze meeting the viewer's with calm directness. Titian brings the goddess of love out of myth and into an intimate domestic setting, in an image that shaped centuries of reclining nudes. It hangs in the Uffizi Gallery, Florence.
captions.penni-the-treacherous-sinon-brought-into: Mignon's etching after Luca Penni shows shepherds leading the bound Greek into the Trojan camp — the first act of Virgil's trap, before Sinon speaks. The horse waits; the city still believes it chooses its own doom. Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
captions.michelangelo-minos-detail-from-the-last-: Detail from Michelangelo's Last Judgment on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel: Minos, judge of the underworld, stands among the damned with ass's ears and a serpent coiled about his body. The Cretan king of myth becomes Dante's infernal magistrate — the face Renaissance Rome gave to eternal judgment.
captions.bos-jupiter-and-alcmene: An engraving from the Renaissance series of the Loves of Jupiter, designed by the Flemish painter Michiel Coxie and cut by the Southern Netherlandish engraver Cornelis Bos. It depicts the central deception of Alcmene's myth: Zeus (Jupiter), having taken the likeness of her absent husband Amphitryon, comes to Alcmene by night — the union that, in the night prolonged threefold, conceives Heracles. The sheet survives in the Rijksmuseum print collection in Amsterdam.
captions.cranach-hercules-and-omphale: Cranach's exchange of genders — Heracles at Omphale's spindle, the Lydian year of soft bondage between Troy and the later labours.
captions.cranach-the-judgement-of-paris: Cranach's German Renaissance Ida: armoured Paris between the three goddesses and the apple of Eris — the contest restaged as courtly spectacle before the war.
captions.atreus-and-thyestes-urbino-maiolica: Urbino istoriato ware paints the brothers of Mycenae facing each other across the curse — Atreus and Thyestes locked in the rivalry that will end at a table of forbidden flesh. Renaissance maiolica turns Seneca's horror into a bright ceramic narrative. Tin-glazed earthenware.
captions.barbiere-amphiaraus: Fontainebleau-school engraving by Domenico del Barbiere in the Metropolitan Museum of Art: the Argive seer Amphiaraus, who foresaw his death in the war of the Seven against Thebes yet marched when Eriphyle, bribed with Harmonia's necklace, forced his hand. Renaissance print culture made the reluctant prophet a type of doomed foresight.
captions.primaticcio-odysseus-fighting-the-beggar: Primaticcio's Odysseus fighting Irus — the beggar bout that precedes the slaughter in Odyssey 18–22.
captions.tintoretto-deucalion-and-pyrrha-praying-: Tintoretto's flood survivors kneel before the cult image of Themis — the goddess of right counsel who tells them to cast their mother's bones (the stones of Earth) behind them and remake humankind.
captions.ghisi-danae-and-the-infant-perseus-cast-: Ghisi's engraving (Metropolitan Museum of Art) stages the exile: Acrisius sets his daughter and grandson into the vessel that will float to Seriphos — the grandfather's fear made into a Mannerist print.
captions.moro-danae-and-perseus-set-in-a-boat: A Rijksmuseum etching after Ghisi's design repeats the same Argive sentence: Acrisius consigns Danaë and Perseus to the water, hoping to outrun the discus that will still find him at Larissa.
captions.beham-hercules-abducting-iole-from-the-l: A miniature engraving by the German 'Little Master' Hans Sebald Beham, part of his celebrated series on the labours and deeds of Hercules. It depicts the violent climax of the Eurytus story: Hercules, avenging the insult of King Eurytus of Oechalia, has slain the king and his sons and now carries off the king's daughter Iole as his prize. Years earlier Eurytus had offered Iole to whoever could outshoot him and his sons, only to renege when Hercules won the contest — and here the hero takes by force what was denied him. The print is held in the Cleveland Museum of Art.
captions.bronzino-andrea-doria-as-neptune: Bronzino casts the Genoese admiral Andrea Doria as the classical sea god — nude, trident in hand, a living allegory of maritime power. The Mannerist portrait fuses Renaissance statecraft with Poseidon's iconography; Pinacoteca di Brera, Milan.
captions.bronzino-venus-cupid-folly-and-time-dece: A Mannerist allegorical oil painting in which Venus and Cupid embrace amid personifications of Folly and Time. Behind the pleasures lurks a girl usually identified as Deceit, offering a honeycomb while concealing a serpent's body and sting — an emblem of love's hidden falsehoods. The painting hangs in the National Gallery, London.
captions.cellini-perseus-with-the-head-of-medusa: Cellini's Loggia bronze — Perseus astride Medusa's body with the severed head aloft, the cycle's Gorgon climax cast for Cosimo's Florence.
captions.scultori-sinon-deceiving-the-trojans: Ghisi's engraving after Scultori stages Aeneid Book II: Sinon stands among the Trojans and the looming horse, spinning the lie that Minerva demands the offering. Renaissance print culture made him the face of polished betrayal. National Gallery of Art, Washington.
captions.tintoretto-jupiter-and-semele: Tintoretto's Jupiter and Semele — Venetian drama of the visitation that seals Thebes' wine-god lineage.
captions.davent-callisto-and-arcas-raised-to-the-: Fontainebleau-school etching in the Rijksmuseum (RP-P-2010-94), attributed to Léon Davent after Léonard Thiry: Jupiter snatches Callisto from Arcas's arrow and sets mother and son among the stars. Arcas's destiny as the Bear-warden (Boötes) is the celestial sequel to the hunt that nearly made him a matricide.
captions.titian-sisyphus: Titian's Sisyphus — the boulder forever rolling, Tartarus' emblem of futile labour.
captions.titian-tityus: Titian's Tityus — the giant's liver forever eaten in Tartarus for assaulting Leto.
captions.henri-ii-as-tiphys: French royal-entry allegory: Henri II cast as Tiphys at the helm — the Argonaut steersman as Renaissance emblem of the king who guides the ship of state.
captions.ajax-and-odysseus-contest-the-arms-of-ac: Rijksmuseum print: Ajax and Odysseus quarrel over the armor — the Little Iliad's judgment that drives Sophocles' madness.
captions.amphion-building-the-walls-of-thebes: A Rijksmuseum allegory titles the miracle: Amphion's lyre draws the stones into Thebes' walls — 'suaviter et fortiter,' soft music as civic force.
captions.armorial-dish-the-story-of-king-anius: Metropolitan Museum istoriato dish titled for King Anius — the Delian host whose wine, wheat and oil daughters feed the Trojan fleet.
captions.armorial-dish-the-story-of-king-anius-al: Second photograph of the Anius maiolica — Renaissance tableware that made the Delian king a dining-room myth.
captions.borcht-jason-and-medea-beside-talos: Van der Borcht's engraving stages the Argonauts before the bronze giant — Renaissance print culture keeping Talos' ankle-pin death in circulation.
captions.bos-jupiter-and-aegina-from-jupiter-s-lo: A Renaissance engraving by the Netherlandish printmaker Cornelis Bos, part of a series illustrating the amorous adventures of Jupiter. The print stages the god's seduction of the nymph Aegina within an ornate Mannerist composition, translating Ovidian and Apollodoran myth into the sophisticated print culture of sixteenth-century Northern Europe. Such series circulated the loves of Jupiter as a learned and decorative theme; this sheet is preserved in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (RP-P-BI-2783).
captions.calamelli-cadmus-and-harmonia-transforme: Maiolica dish — the Theban founders' serpent end for a Renaissance table, Ovid glazed in colour.
captions.caravaggio-castration-of-uranus: A drawing after Polidoro's Roman façade invention, later touched by Rubens: Saturn's assault on the sky-god — the succession myth circulating as a collector's sheet.
captions.carracci-king-latinus-predicts-aeneas-ar: A Carracci-school scene of Latinus as prophetic host — the king who reads the omen of the foreign son-in-law. Italian disegno keeps him the Latian ruler of the Aeneid’s second half, not Hesiod’s Circean Latinus.
captions.cousin-cassandra-preventing-deiphobus-fr: Drawing by Jean Cousin in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Cassandra restrains Deiphobus as he raises a weapon against Paris — the brother who later inherits Helen after Paris' death, here still the rival who would have ended the war by ending the abductor.
captions.cousin-eva-prima-pandora: Cousin's Louvre masterpiece fuses Eve and Pandora on one reclining nude — the first woman as both biblical fall and Hesiodic jar. Renaissance France's great allegory of curiosity and ruin.
captions.daughters-of-anius-changed-into-doves: Rijksmuseum print: Anius' daughters transformed into doves — Ovid's sequel when Agamemnon's Greeks try to seize the girls who feed armies.
captions.die-daphne-consulting-her-father: Daphne kneels before the enthroned river-god — Peneus as the father who yields her wish for perpetual virginity before the pursuit begins. Early-modern print culture made this consultation a fixed beat of the Apollo and Daphne cycle.
captions.die-the-wedding-of-jason-and-creusa: A Metropolitan Museum print stages the Corinthian wedding Creon arranged for Jason and his daughter Creusa/Glauce — while Medea leads the children away at left. The king of Corinth is the host whose match will burn his house.
captions.farinati-pandora-offers-the-jar-to-epime: Veronese-school drawing in which Pandora presents the fatal jar to Epimetheus, the brother who accepted Zeus's gift against Prometheus' warning. Farinati freezes the moment before the lid lifts — afterthought already too late.
captions.gassel-pyramus-and-thisbe: Gassel's panoramic landscape nests the mulberry rendezvous in a Flemish world-view — tiny lovers, vast hills, and the lion that started the misunderstanding. Ovid's wall-split romance as world landscape.
captions.gheeraerts-the-labours-of-hercules-alcme: A narrative engraving from the Flemish-English artist Marcus Gheeraerts the Elder's series on the Labours of Hercules. Within a single sheet it combines the grown hero battling centaurs with the famous childhood prodigy: Alcmene and her husband Amphitryon look on as the infant Hercules throttles the two snakes Hera dispatched against him. Amphitryon is explicitly named as one of the witnessing parents in the print's own inscription, making this one of the clearer narrative images to place him by name within the Heracles birth-and-infancy cycle.
captions.heemskerck-the-colossus-of-rhodes: Heemskerck's wonder engraving imagines Helios as harbour giant on Rhodos' island — the sun god's bronze standing where the nymph personifies the land. Reception of Rhodes as Helios' bride keeps her name in every retelling of the Colossus.
captions.heracles-and-laomedon: A Valle Sabbia museum panel stages Heracles confronting Troy’s king — the sequel to the unpaid walls and the Hesione bargain. Laomedon appears as the mortal who cheats gods and heroes alike until the city falls the first time.
captions.hercules-and-iole-woodcut: A Renaissance book woodcut, preserved through the Penn Provenance Project, illustrating Hercules and Iole. Drawing on the late tradition that paired her with Omphale's emasculating power over the hero, the print shows Hercules clothed at once as man and as woman beside Iole, a moralizing emblem of love's power to unman even the strongest of heroes. It exemplifies how the figure of Iole survived into early printed mythography as a cautionary image.
captions.hercules-slays-geryon-and-his-hound: A Dutch engraving from a Works of Hercules series (Rijksmuseum, RP-P-1944-1074) shows Hercules in the tenth labour cutting down the three-bodied Geryon while the two-headed hound — Orthrus — falls at their feet. The print keeps the Hesiodic pairing of master and watchdog intact for early-modern viewers: the cattle of Erytheia cannot be driven until both the giant and his dog are slain. It is a clear Northern-Renaissance sequel to the archaic vase tradition of Orthrus.
captions.illustrator-hypermnestra-lynceus-and-the: Early printed woodcut of the Danaid crisis names Lynceus beside Hypermnestra — the bridegroom who lived when forty-nine brothers died. Book illustration kept the Argive pair legible for readers of Ovid’s Heroides.
captions.ixion-embracing-a-cloud: MET engraving: Ixion clasps the cloud — the generative scene from which Centaurus, and then the centaurs, descend in mythographic tradition.
captions.jupiter-and-aegina: Another impression of the Jupiter–Aegina pursuit: Asopus' daughter as the prize — the river-father's loss that founds the Aeacid island line.
captions.mignon-the-transformation-of-actaeon: Fontainebleau etching of Ovid's hinge: Diana sprinkles the hunter as antlers rise from his brow — the transformation that spreads the myth through print.
captions.murder-and-deification-of-julius-caesar: Rijksmuseum print: the Ides murder paired with Caesar's deification — reception's hinge between Curia steel and celestial ascent.
captions.neptune-and-amymone: Metropolitan Museum print of Neptune/Poseidon with Amymone — the Danaid he rescues from a satyr and rewards with the Lernaean spring, mother of Nauplius.
captions.nosadella-thyestes-and-aerope: Nosadella paints Aerope with Thyestes — Atreus' Cretan wife whose adultery and the stolen golden lamb token open the Mycenaean feud. She is the queen whose betrayal precedes the feast that made the house proverbial.
captions.pape-plaque-with-medea-s-murder-of-absyr: Limoges plaque — Medea's murder of Apsyrtus that delays Aeetes and opens the Argo's return.
captions.piombo-procne-tereus-and-philomela: This Renaissance fresco by Sebastiano del Piombo, painted for the Villa Farnesina in Rome, brings together the three principals of the tragedy: Procne, her husband Tereus, and her sister Philomela. Rendered with the monumental grace of the High Renaissance, the figures embody the doomed family bond that the myth tears apart, leading from Tereus's betrayal to Procne's infanticidal revenge and the final transformation of all three into birds. The fresco remains in situ at the Villa Farnesina.
captions.proserpina-and-ascalaphus-as-an-owl: Rijksmuseum print: the Queen of Erebus and the owl that was Ascalaphus — the pomegranate witness under his Latin name.
captions.romano-latona-giving-birth-to-apollo-and: NGA engraving after Giulio Romano: Leto in labour on Delos as the twin archers arrive — the Homeric Hymn's birth fixed in print.
captions.romano-meleager-and-atalanta-the-calydon: Composed after a design by the Renaissance master Giulio Romano, pupil of Raphael, this scene revives the hunt that made the city of Calydon famous. Set in the wooded country around Calydon, it shows the hero Meleager and the swift huntress Atalanta amid the press of spearmen and dogs as the great boar is brought down. The episode, drawn ultimately from Ovid's Metamorphoses, gave Renaissance and Baroque artists a vehicle for muscular figures in violent motion and for the celebrated love of Meleager and Atalanta. By Giulio Romano's day the eponymous Calydon survived only as the name of a legendary place, but the hunt that bore its name remained one of the most reproduced of all classical myths.
captions.rossi-hercules-and-diomedes: A marble statue group from Vincenzo de' Rossi's cycle of the Labours of Hercules in the Salone dei Cinquecento of the Palazzo Vecchio, Florence. It seizes the climactic moment of Heracles' eighth labour: the hero hoists the Thracian king Diomedes overhead before casting him to his own man-eating mares. The Mannerist torsion of the two intertwined nude bodies and the king's flailing, upended pose dramatise the reversal by which the tyrant who fed strangers to his horses becomes their final meal.
captions.sambin-jupiter-and-lycaon: A French Renaissance relief by Hugues Sambin stages Zeus's wrath against Lycaon, son of Pelasgus of Arcadia: the impious king who served human flesh is caught at the moment of divine judgment that will turn him into a wolf. As with the Cossiers canvas and Goltzius plate, the scene visualizes the cursed heir of Arcadia's first king — Pelasgus himself remaining almost without freestanding portraiture, his house remembered through Lycaon's metamorphosis.
captions.saturn-and-the-nymph-philyra: Dutch print culture restages Saturnus with Philyra — the Oceanid whose shame at bearing a half-horse child (in some tellings) drives her to become a linden tree, while Chiron remains the immortal tutor of heroes.
captions.saturn-in-the-guise-of-a-horse-being-suc: A Metropolitan Museum engraving titles the scene outright: Saturn as a horse nursed or attended by Philyra. The Oceanid of Pelion is fixed as the nymph of Cronus' equine metamorphosis and Chiron's conception.
captions.solis-byblis-loves-her-brother: Solis' Metamorphoses woodcut: Byblis writing or pursuing Caunus — the Renaissance plate that fixed her letter and chase.
captions.solis-ceyx-in-the-tempest-illustration-t: A sixteenth-century engraving by the Nuremberg printmaker Virgil Solis (1514–1562), made for an illustrated edition of Ovid's Metamorphoses. The plate shows Ceyx, king of Trachis, aboard his ship as a violent storm overwhelms the vessel, the moment of the king's death at sea that sets in motion the lovers' grief and ultimate metamorphosis. Solis's densely worked composition exemplifies the way Renaissance book illustration popularized the classical myths for a broad European readership.
captions.solis-lycaon: Woodcut/engraving by the Nuremberg printmaker Virgil Solis (1514–1562) from his widely copied illustrated edition of Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book I, lines 209–243). The compact image captures the metamorphosis of the Arcadian king Lycaon into a wolf as punishment for his cannibal feast: Jupiter presides while Lycaon, half-man and half-beast, flees the scene. Solis's broadly disseminated Ovid plates served as a visual model for later painters and engravers across Europe, making this one of the most influential early depictions of the Lycaon legend.
captions.solis-morpheus-appears-to-alcyone-illust: In this engraving by Virgil Solis (1514–1562) for Ovid's Metamorphoses, the dream-god Morpheus, having taken on the form of the drowned Ceyx, appears at Alcyone's bedside to reveal her husband's death. The somber visitation is the narrative hinge of the myth: it is Alcyone's grief at this apparition, and her subsequent discovery of Ceyx's body on the shore, that moves the gods to transform the faithful couple into halcyon birds. The plate belongs to one of the most influential Renaissance picture-cycles of the Ovidian fables.
captions.solis-myrrha-and-cinyras: Solis' Metamorphoses woodcut reduces the Cypriot scandal to a print: Cinyras and Myrrha as a standard Ovid plate — the father whose unknowing crime seeds Adonis' birth.
captions.stradanus-saturn-and-philyra: Cronus (Saturn), transformed into a stallion to hide from Rhea, couples with the Oceanid Philyra — the union that will bear the centaur Chiron. Renaissance mythography loved this equine disguise; the print keeps Philyra as mother of the wisest of the Centaurs.
captions.zethus-and-amphion-binding-dirce: Rijksmuseum engraving of the Farnese subject: Zethus named in the title as he and Amphion lash Dirce to the horns — print culture spreading the bull revenge.
captions.titian-jupiter-and-antiope-the-pardo-ven: Titian's great Louvre canvas (also called the Pardo Venus) stages Zeus as a satyr unveiling the sleeping Theban Antiope — the encounter that begets Amphion and Zethus. It is the Renaissance's most famous image of this Antiope, not the Amazon queen.
captions.phoenix-son-of-agenor: Print titled Phoenix Agenor filius — Agenor's son as the eponym of Phoenicia, proof of the Tyrian house the father ruled.
captions.rouille-minos: Woodcut portrait of King Minos from Guillaume Rouillé's Promptuarii Iconum Insigniorum (Lyon, 1553). The Renaissance emblem book freezes the Cretan lawgiver and labyrinth-lord as a classical ruler in profile — Minos as one of the emblematic kings of antiquity.
captions.rouille-palamedes-promptuarii-iconum-ins: Rouillé's Promptuarii woodcut — Renaissance emblem of Palamedes, the wise Achaean undone by envy.
captions.titian-venus-and-adonis: Titian's warning and farewell — Venus clinging to the youth who will not heed the boar, the anemone still to rise from his blood in Ovid's telling.
captions.titian-perseus-and-andromeda: Titian's poesie: Andromeda chained to the rock as Perseus dives sword-first at the sea-monster — the Ethiopian rescue as Venetian storm of flesh and foam.
captions.bordone-athena-scorning-the-advances-of-: This Venetian canvas depicts the prelude to Erichthonius' birth: the smith-god Hephaestus reaches for the virgin Athena, who turns away and rebuffs him. According to the myth, his frustrated desire spills upon the goddess and is wiped to the earth, and from that contact with Gaia the autochthonous child Erichthonius is conceived. Bordone, a follower of Titian, treats the encounter with cool mythological eroticism and rich coloring. The painting situates Erichthonius' origin in the awkward, half-divine union that the Athenians wove into their claim of descent from the soil itself.
captions.ligorio-echidna-sacro-bosco-parco-dei-mo: Carved from the living volcanic peperino rock of the Sacro Bosco (Sacred Wood) of Bomarzo in Lazio, this Mannerist sculpture realizes Hesiod's 'mother of monsters' exactly as the Theogony describes her: half a fair-cheeked maiden, half a vast speckled serpent. The figure rises from a coiling double tail flanked by lions, fusing the beautiful upper body of a nymph with the awful chthonic snake that, in myth, dwells in a hollow cave beneath the secret parts of the earth. Commissioned by Pier Francesco Orsini and attributed to the architect-antiquarian Pirro Ligorio, the colossal figure is part of the deliberately strange, emblematic garden begun around 1555 — one of the few monumental Renaissance treatments of a goddess who, despite her central place in Greek genealogy as the consort of Typhon and dam of Cerberus, the Hydra, the Chimera and Orthrus, has almost no surviving ancient image of her own.
captions.titian-diana-and-actaeon: Titian's poesie for Philip II: Actaeon parts the curtain on Diana's bath at Gargaphie — the fatal glance that will turn the hunter into a stag.
captions.titian-diana-and-callisto: Titian's poesie: Diana points in judgement as Callisto's companions strip her garment — the pregnancy that betrays the vow and starts the road to the bears.
captions.titian-the-death-of-actaeon: The grim sequel: Actaeon already sprouting antlers collapses under his own hounds while Diana strides in with drawn bow — metamorphosis as late Titian storm.
captions.bruegel-landscape-with-the-fall-of-icaru: A ploughman keeps his furrow and a galleon sails on while two white legs vanish into the green sea — the fall reduced to a splash nobody notices. Long attributed to Bruegel and now generally thought an early copy of his lost original, the painting in Brussels inspired Auden's Musée des Beaux Arts.
captions.cort-atreus-farnese-speculum-romanae-mag: Cort's engraving for Lafreri's Speculum records the so-called Farnese Atreus — a colossal antique statue Renaissance Rome read as the Mycenaean king. The print freezes Atreus as a standing tyrant of marble before the feast that would make his name proverbial. Engraving, Metropolitan Museum of Art.
captions.gherardi-the-mutilation-of-uranus-by-sat: Ceiling painting from the Sala degli Elementi of the Palazzo Vecchio in Florence, rendering Hesiod's pivotal cosmogonic act: Cronus unmans his father Uranus with the adamantine sickle Gaia forged, and from the blood and foam the Erinyes, Giants and Aphrodite will spring. The image anchors the succession myth that opens the Theogony and the whole cosmic cycle shelf.
captions.schiavone-the-childhood-of-jupiter: Schiavone’s Venetian canvas of infant Zeus among Cretan nurses and Curetes — the Dictaean cave milieu where Apollodorus places Ida and Adrasteia. Mannerist colour keeps the mountain-nymph’s world even when the title names the child, not the nurse.
captions.titian-danae: Titian's Prado Danaë receives Zeus as a rain of gold while a maid gathers coins — the impregnation that fathers Perseus before Acrisius' chest and the Seriphos landfall.
captions.titian-the-rape-of-europa: Titian's late poesie sends Europa over the waves on Zeus' bull, her companions stranded on the shore — the Phoenician princess's abduction as Venetian colour and terror. Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, Boston.
captions.heemskerck-momus-criticizes-the-gods-cre: A painting by the Dutch Mannerist Maerten van Heemskerck illustrating the classical fable in which Momus, the personification of fault-finding, is asked to judge the creations of the gods and mocks them all in turn, a man, a bull and a house among them. The episode, known from Aesop and retold by Lucian, made Momus the patron figure of carping critics, and for his unrelenting censure he was cast out of Olympus.
captions.solis-deucalion-and-pyrrha: Solis's Metamorphoses woodcut freezes the oracle's command: husband and wife hurl stones over their shoulders while new bodies form — the print that carried Greece's Noah story through Renaissance editions.
captions.solis-the-rape-of-philomela-by-tereus: The rape of Philomela — Tereus' crime that starts the Thracian house's metamorphosis into nightingale, swallow, and hoopoe.
captions.boyvin-aeetes-accepts-the-dismembered-co: Mannerist engraving from The History of Jason and the Conquest of the Golden Fleece (Yale University Art Gallery): Aeëtes receives the scattered remains of his son Absyrtus, slain so Jason and Medea can escape Colchis. The Colchian king is shown not as fleece-keeper alone but as the father whose household Medea destroys.
captions.boyvin-medea-cooking-magical-herbs-for-a: Mannerist engraving from the Histoire de Jason: Medea tends the cauldron that will renew Aeson — the print series that taught Europe Jason's father as the first beneficiary of Colchian arts.
captions.solis-cadmus-and-the-spartoi: Woodcut for Ovid's Metamorphoses: Cadmus sows the dragon's teeth and the armed Spartoi rise to slaughter one another. Echion is among the five survivors who become Thebes' founding nobles — and, by Agave, father of Pentheus.
captions.solis-iphis-and-anaxarete: Solis' Metamorphoses woodcut: Anaxarete at the window of scorn — the Salaminian maiden as Renaissance emblem of hardness of heart.
captions.vasari-vulcan-s-forge-la-fucina-di-vulca: Giorgio Vasari's oil-on-copper Vulcan's Forge (c. 1564), now in the Uffizi in Florence, sets the smith-god Vulcan and his Cyclops assistants at the anvil while Minerva looks on. From the third-century BC poet Callimachus onward, the Hesiodic Cyclopes — Brontes, Steropes, and Arges — were imagined as the smiths who served at the divine forge, hammering the thunderbolts of Zeus and the weapons of the gods. Vasari's muscular forge-workers carry forward this tradition, and Arges, "the Bright," stands among the brotherhood of single-eyed craftsmen the painting depicts.
captions.macchietti-allegory-of-prudence: Macchietti’s Florentine allegory personifies Prudence — the Latin afterlife of Greek mētis, counsel and cunning. Catalogued with the Oceanid Metis on Commons, the panel stands in for a figure almost never painted in her own right: Zeus’s first wife survives in art chiefly as the virtue that bears her name.
captions.momper-landscape-with-the-fall-of-icarus: Stockholm Nationalmuseum's Flemish panorama nearly loses the boy in the vista — travellers and peaks keep moving while one winged figure falls, the Bruegel lesson restaged as mountain theatre.
captions.cort-tityus-punished-in-hell: An engraving by the Netherlandish printmaker Cornelis Cort reproducing Titian's painting of the tormented giant, now in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. The print disseminated Titian's image of Tityos across Renaissance Europe, showing the earth-giant pinned in Tartarus while a bird of prey gnaws at his immortal liver. Engravings such as this carried the cautionary myth — of the brute who violated Leto and suffered an everlasting penalty at the hands of Apollo and Artemis — to a wide audience beyond those who could see the original canvas.
captions.solis-cadmus-and-harmonia-cadmus-cum-uxo: Solis' Metamorphoses woodcut — the prayer answered as husband and wife take serpent form together.
captions.backer-invidia: From de Backer's Seven Deadly Sins cycle in the Museo di Capodimonte, Naples: Invidia sits as a bare, snake-haunted allegory of envy, the Latin mask of the Greek Zelus whom Hyginus places among the children of Styx and Pallas. A Mannerist emblem of the competitive jealousy that classical genealogies seat forever at Zeus's side.
captions.titian-the-flaying-of-marsyas: Titian's Kroměříž masterpiece — Apollo's assistants flay the defeated satyr hung upside down, pain and music dissolving in late paint.
captions.tito-hercules-and-iole: Painted for the Studiolo of Francesco I de' Medici in the Palazzo Vecchio, Florence, this Mannerist panel by Santi di Tito depicts the captive Iole brought before Heracles. Set within the prince's celebrated cabinet of curiosities, the work renders the heroine of Oechalia in the elegant, elongated grace typical of late Florentine Mannerism, treating her as the fatal prize whose presence in Heracles' household would provoke Deianira's jealousy and the hero's ruin.
captions.tito-the-sisters-of-phaethon: Santi di Tito’s Mannerist scene stages the Heliades’ transformation on the Eridanus bank — sisters turning to trees while the river and mourning gods close the myth of Phaethon’s fall. Florentine disegno keeps the Oceanid daughters visible as a chorus of grief before the bark seals them.
captions.cort-the-forge-of-the-cyclopes: This engraving by Cornelis Cort, made in Rome in 1572 after a ceiling painting by Titian, shows the one-eyed Cyclopes laboring in their underground smithy: several hammer a glowing mass on the anvil while another draws iron from the fire, a lion watching at the side. The subject is the very trio Hesiod names in the Theogony — Brontes, Steropes, and Arges ("Bright") — the divine smiths who forged the thunderbolt of Zeus, here imagined as Vulcan's forge-hands. As one of these labeled thunderbolt-makers, Arges belongs to the company of single-eyed craftsmen the print celebrates. Now in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (M.88.91.96).
captions.bonasone-menelaus-wrestling-proteus: Bonasone's emblem — Menelaus grappling the Old Man of the Sea on Pharos until every shape yields the truth of the returns.
captions.spranger-vulcan-and-maia: Spranger's Mannerist canvas in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna, pairs Maia with Vulcan — the Roman forge-god beside the mother of Mercury. The painting folds the Greek Pleiad into Imperial allegory: Maia as growth and May, still recognisable as Hermes' mountain mother.
captions.tintoretto-the-origin-of-the-milky-way: An oil painting by the Venetian master Tintoretto, now in the National Gallery, London. It depicts the myth in which Jupiter holds the infant Heracles to the breast of the sleeping Juno (Hera) so that the child may gain immortality; the milk that sprays upward from the startled goddess forms the Milky Way. The composition's swirling diagonals and tumbling putti are characteristic of Tintoretto's late dynamic style.
captions.tintoretto-bacchus-venus-and-ariadne: Tintoretto's Doge's Palace canvas: Bacchus rises from the sea with a ring while Venus crowns Ariadne — Naxos as apotheosis, not only abandonment.
captions.allori-odysseus-and-ino: Allori paints the Odyssey's sea rescue: Ino-Leucothea offers Odysseus her immortal veil as he struggles in the waves after leaving Calypso. The Theban queen-turned-goddess becomes the hand that saves the nostos.
captions.allori-the-blinding-of-polyphemus: Allori's Mannerist stake — Odysseus and his men drive the heated timber into the sleeping Cyclops' eye.
captions.carracci-the-sacrifice-of-king-pelias: Carracci's drawing for the Jason cycle stages Pelias at the sacrificial altar — the king whose death at his daughters' hands closes the Iolcan half of the Argonaut saga. Preparatory work linked to the Palazzo Fava frescoes in Bologna.
captions.carracci-the-sacrifice-of-pelias: Agostino Carracci's print of Pelias' sacrificial death — the same Medea-engineered murder that empties the throne of Iolcus. Bolognese reception keeps the usurper's end beside Jason's fleece as the moral hinge of the saga.
captions.giambologna-flying-mercury: A bronze statue by the Mannerist sculptor Giambologna, now in the Museo Nazionale del Bargello, Florence. The messenger god is caught in full flight, balanced on one foot upon a breath of air issuing from the mouth of a wind god, caduceus in hand and winged sandals barely touching the earth. Its weightless poise made it one of the most influential and widely reproduced sculptures of the late Renaissance.
captions.ii-the-iron-age-aetas-ferrea: Engraved Iron Age: toil, war, and broken faith — the last race Hesiod says Zeus will destroy when even the newborn are grey.
captions.spranger-glaucus-and-scylla: Vienna Mannerist panel: Spranger gives Glaucus a muscular sea-god's body as he reaches for fleeing Scylla — the Ovidian pursuit Circe will answer with poison.
captions.spranger-hermaphroditus-and-the-nymph-sa: Spranger's Mannerist embrace — Salmacis clinging in the pool as Ovid's prayer fuses two bodies into one.
captions.the-prophecy-of-calchas-from-the-story-o: A silk-and-gilt tapestry from a Macao-woven Troy cycle (Metropolitan Museum of Art, 50.97.2): Calchas reads the omens that bind the Achaean war — the seer of Aulis and the Iliad rendered for a Renaissance collector's wall.
captions.veronese-cephalus-and-procris: Veronese's Strasbourg canvas: the hunter cradles dying Procris among dogs and foliage — the fatal throw of the never-missing spear.
captions.veronese-the-death-of-procris: Oil on canvas by the Venetian master Paolo Veronese, in the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, Boston (P17w32.7). The wide horizontal format shows the fatal hunting accident at the heart of the legend of Cephalus, son of Deion: mistaking the rustle of his hidden wife for game, Cephalus has struck Procris with the unerring javelin, and she collapses among the trees as he rushes to her. Veronese's shimmering palette turns the catastrophe of Deion's descendants into a luminous pastoral, witnessing how the house of the Aeolid king lived on chiefly through this much-painted myth.
captions.veronese-venus-and-adonis: Veronese's Venetian idyll — Venus watching over the sleeping hunter before the hunt that ends the lineage of Myrrha.
captions.vicentino-venus-supervises-the-work-of-t: This canvas by the Venetian painter Andrea Vicentino, set into the ceiling of the Sala del Senato in the Doge's Palace, shows the goddess Venus presiding over the labour of the Cyclopes as they work in Vulcan's forge. The hulking smiths — Brontes and his brothers in the Hesiodic naming — hammer at the anvil and tend the fire while the goddess looks on, an allegory of arms forged under the gaze of love. Vicentino renders the forge-Cyclopes as the brawny, half-divine craftsmen of myth, the same beings whose names mean Thunder, Lightning and Brightness and who hammered Zeus's bolts into shape.
captions.solis-apollo-killing-python-illustration: An engraving by the Nuremberg printmaker Virgil Solis made to illustrate Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book I, lines 434–451), the passage in which Earth, fertilized by the sun after the great flood, brings forth the enormous serpent Python that terrorizes the new race of men. The print shows Apollo drawing his bow against the immense coiling dragon, the deed that, in Ovid, leads the god to institute the Pythian Games in commemoration. As a widely circulated book illustration it helped fix the iconography of the Apollo-and-Python episode for early-modern European readers.
captions.solis-the-birth-of-the-myrmidons-ortus-m: A woodcut engraving by the Nuremberg printmaker Virgil Solis (1514–1562), produced for an illustrated edition of Ovid's Metamorphoses (Frankfurt) and keyed to Book VII, lines 622–642. It depicts the legend by which Aeacus repopulated plague-stricken Aegina: praying to his father Zeus beside a sacred oak, the king watched a column of ants on its trunk transform into a race of men, the Myrmidons ("ant-people"), who would later march to Troy under Achilles. The print captures the moment of miraculous metamorphosis, with the new-made warriors emerging at the foot of the oak before the kneeling king.
captions.lorck-a-harpy: Melchior Lorck's 1582 woodcut isolates the Harpy as a Renaissance monster study: a woman's torso fused to a raptor's body and claws. The print belongs to the early-modern bestiary tradition that kept Ocypete's kind — the bird-maidens of the Phineus episode — alive as emblems of snatching hunger and storm, independent of any single sister's name.
captions.carracci-medea-kills-her-brother-absyrtu: Carracci's Palazzo Fava frieze freezes the murder: Medea turns on Absyrtus — Aeëtes' son cut down so the Argo can outrun Colchian pursuit.
captions.carracci-meeting-of-jason-and-king-aeete: Study for Carracci's Palazzo Fava Argonaut frieze: Jason before Aeëtes, the Colchian king who will price the Golden Fleece in fire-breathing bulls.
captions.momper-shipwreck-of-the-greek-fleet-on-t: Nationalmuseum Stockholm: returning hulls smashed on a storm coast — the Caphareus disaster tradition in which Nauplius' false beacons wreck the victors for Palamedes.
captions.galle-proteus-from-the-series-of-sea-and: A plate from Galle's Semideorum Marinorum amnicorumque sigillariae imagines, preserved in the Rijksmuseum print collection, presents Proteus as a standing sea-god identified by inscription. Such printed pantheons kept Homer’s shape-shifting Old Man of the Sea current in Netherlandish emblem-books and decorator’s handbooks long after antiquity, separate from the narrative of Menelaus but part of the same visual vocabulary of marine prophecy.
captions.galle-the-sea-god-nereus-seated-on-a-she: This engraving by the Haarlem printmaker Philips Galle, the third plate in his numbered series of river- and sea-gods, shows Nereus enthroned upon a great shell with his many daughters, the Nereids, gathered behind him. The Renaissance image gives visual form to Hesiod's catalogue of the fifty sea-nymphs born to Nereus and the Oceanid Doris, presenting the benevolent Old Man of the Sea as a patriarch of the waters surrounded by his marine progeny, complete with the antiquarian attributes — shell, beard and watery setting — that humanist artists drew from ancient sources.
captions.galle-the-sea-god-proteus-leaning-on-a-w: In Philips Galle's engraving from the series of river- and sea-gods — here in the collection of the North Holland Archives — Proteus (spelled Protheus in the Dutch inscription) leans on an amphora from which fish pour, with a harbour city behind him. The image belongs to the same marine pantheon Galle circulated alongside Nereus and other Old Men of the Sea, fixing Proteus as a bearded prophetic divinity of Egypt's coast and the changing depths.
captions.aachen-the-rape-of-proserpina: An oil by the Prague court painter Hans von Aachen showing Pluto — Hades in Roman dress — carrying Proserpina skyward as attendants scatter below. The Mannerist swirl of limbs and drapery turns the underworld king's abduction into a compact allegory of irresistible force, long circulating among Imperial Habsburg collections.
captions.galle-the-river-nymph-styx-nymphae-stygi: A rare direct portrait of Styx herself rather than her waters. This 1587 engraving by the Antwerp printmaker Philips Galle, made after his own design, is the seventeenth and final plate in his numbered series of river and water nymphs and goddesses (New Hollstein, Galle 447). The eldest Oceanid sits on a block of stone in the foreground while the flames of the underworld flicker behind her, marking her as the personified river of the dead by whose name even the Olympian gods swore their most binding oath. The print survives in the Voorhelm Schneevoogt collection of the Noord-Hollands Archief, Haarlem.
captions.goltzius-ixion-from-the-four-disgracers: Goltzius engraves Cornelis' foreshortened fall: Ixion plummets through air toward the wheel below — one of the Four Disgracers who insulted the gods and learned the measure of Tartarus.
captions.goltzius-tantalus: From The Four Disgracers: Goltzius engraves Tantalus hurtling through empty air — the king who served his son to the gods, falling toward the hunger and thirst that await him below.
captions.haarlem-the-fall-of-the-titans-the-titan: Cornelis van Haarlem's Fall of the Titans — the elder gods cast into Tartarus when Zeus' order wins.
captions.haarlem-two-followers-of-cadmus-devoured: Haarlem Mannerist canvas: the Ismenian dragon tears Cadmus' companions while the founder fights on — the price paid before the teeth are sown.
captions.goltzius-lycaon-lycaon-transformed-into-: This finely worked engraving by the Dutch master Hendrik Goltzius, part of his celebrated 1589 series illustrating Ovid's Metamorphoses, shows the punishment of Lycaon. Jupiter is seated at the king's table, his eagle at his feet and the cannibal dish before him, while amid burning buildings Lycaon flees with his head already changing into that of a wolf. The scene is the prelude to Nyctimus's reign: in the Arcadian tradition recorded by Apollodorus and Pausanias, the outrage of Lycaon's line brings down Zeus's wrath and the Deucalionic flood, and it is in the aftermath that Nyctimus — eldest son of Lycaon, who 'possessed all the power' — holds the throne before his nephew Arcas succeeds him. Goltzius's burin renders the moral horror of the moment with cool, virtuosic precision.
captions.goltzius-lycaon-transformed-into-a-wolf: Engraving from Goltzius's series illustrating Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book I, plate 9), now in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. The plate compresses the whole myth into one charged moment: Jupiter, his eagle at his feet and the cannibal dish before him, has risen from Lycaon's table as the impious Arcadian king flees through his burning palace, his head already lengthening into a wolf's snout. One of the few complete printed cycles of the Metamorphoses, Goltzius's Mannerist line renders the metamorphosis with anatomical precision, turning Ovid's tale of guest-violation and divine vengeance into a study of the human body caught mid-transformation into a beast.
captions.carracci-latona-and-the-lycian-peasants: An oil by Annibale Carracci in the Archbishop's Palace at Kroměříž. Latona — Leto — cradles the infant twins as Lycian peasants muddy the spring she asked to drink from; frogs already gather at the water's edge. Ovid's episode of maternal wrath painted with Bolognese clarity, the Titaness as both suppliant and avenger.
captions.carracci-venus-adonis-and-cupid: Carracci's Prado painting freezes a quieter moment: Venus and Adonis at rest with Cupid nearby, before the hunt. Classical bodies and cool light make the coming death feel almost inevitable.
captions.goltzius-apollo-and-coronis-ovid-s-metam: An engraving from a celebrated series illustrating Ovid's Metamorphoses, designed after Hendrik Goltzius. It depicts the encounter of Apollo and Coronis, the episode that frames the doom of Ischys: Coronis, pregnant by Apollo, takes Ischys as her lover, and the affair, betrayed by Apollo's white raven, ends in her death and in Ischys' destruction (by Apollo's arrows in one tradition, by Zeus' thunderbolt in another). The print is held at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.
captions.goltzius-apollo-kills-coronis-apollo-doo: This engraving from the Goltzius Metamorphoses series stages the violent climax that Ischys' affair sets in motion. Apollo draws his bow on the pregnant Coronis while the raven that exposed her infidelity with Ischys flies overhead; in the background the god extracts the unborn Asclepius from her body, and at the left her funeral pyre burns. Though Ischys himself is not figured here, the print renders the consequences of his fatal liaison with Coronis. It is held at the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (RP-P-1882-A-6376).
captions.goltzius-arcas-aims-his-arrow-at-callist: Haarlem workshop engraving after Goltzius (Rijksmuseum RP-P-1882-A-6371): Arcas, son of Jupiter and Callisto, levels his bow at a bear, unaware she is his mother transformed fifteen years before. At right, Jupiter places both among the constellations before the arrow can fly — Arcas as Boötes, Callisto as the Great Bear.
captions.haarlem-hercules-and-achelous: Dutch Mannerist oil: muscular Heracles locks with bull-horned Achelous — the Calydonian wrestling for Deianira as late-sixteenth-century figure painting.
captions.matham-the-three-fates: A circular engraving attributed to Jacob Matham, now in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art: the Moirai share one medallion of distaff, measure and shears. Atropos, the inexorable cutter, completes the triad that Northern print culture spread across early modern Europe.
captions.neoptolemus-and-astyanax: Neoptolemus and Astyanax — the sack's most infamous child-killing, Hector's son torn from the walls.
captions.arcimboldo-rudolf-ii-as-vertumnus: Arcimboldo's Skokloster masterpiece: Emperor Rudolf II as a composite of fruit and vegetables — Vertumnus as the season-god emperor, the most famous face the Roman orchard god ever wore.
captions.borcht-erysichthon-tormented-by-hunger-e: An etching by the Flemish artist Pieter van der Borcht the Elder, made in 1591 for an illustrated edition of Ovid's Metamorphoses (page 215) and inscribed 'ERISICHTHON FAME TORQVETVR' (Erysichthon is tormented by Famine). The scene shows the consequence of Limos's curse: the impious Thessalian Erysichthon, having earned the wrath of Demeter, is consumed by the unappeasable hunger that the famine-spirit Fames (the Roman Limos) breathed into him, devouring everything he owns until he turns at last upon his own flesh. Held in the print collection of the Museum Plantin-Moretus, Antwerp (inv. PK.OPB.0003.107), it is a key early-modern witness to the myth that gives Limos her most famous role in literature.
captions.francavilla-apollo-victorious-over-the-p: A marble statue by the Flemish-born Mannerist sculptor Pietro Francavilla, a pupil of Giambologna, now in the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore. It commemorates Apollo's first triumph: having slain the great serpent Python with his bow and arrows, the youthful god stands in graceful contrapposto with the dead monster coiled lifeless at his feet. The work celebrates the slaying at Delphi from which Apollo took the name Pythian and the oracle as his own, rendered with the elongated elegance and spiralling poise characteristic of late-sixteenth-century Florentine sculpture.
captions.wtewael-cephalus-and-procris-the-death-o: Wtewael's Mannerist collapse: Procris dies in Cephalus' arms in the forest — mistrust ending in irreversible loss.
captions.caravaggio-bacchus: Uffizi oil: the youthful wine god reclining with a shallow glass, crowned with vine leaves beside overripe fruit — Caravaggio's fleshy, faintly drowsy Bacchus as sensuality edged with decay.
captions.carracci-the-choice-of-hercules: Carracci's young hero at the crossroads of Virtue and Pleasure — the arduous path that follows the cradle and precedes Eurystheus' labours.
captions.caravaggio-medusa: Caravaggio's shield Medusa — the severed head frozen mid-scream, Perseus' trophy as a tournament-piece of terror.
captions.caravaggio-narcissus: Caravaggio isolates Ovid's hunter at the pool: a single figure bent over his own reflection, knee and sleeve catching the only light in an otherwise black void. Desire and doom collapse into one circular composition — the youth already trapped by the image that will waste him into a flower. Oil on canvas, Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Antica (Palazzo Barberini), Rome.
captions.carracci-aurora-and-cephalus: Carracci's Farnese Gallery fresco shows Aurora carrying the sleeping hunter Cephalus skyward — the dawn goddess who steals mortal beauty for her chariot. Painted for the Carracci cycle in the Palazzo Farnese, it fixes Eos as abductor and lover in one airborne embrace. Fresco, Farnese Gallery, Rome.
captions.carracci-the-cyclops-polyphemus: In the Farnese Gallery fresco cycle Carracci paints Polyphemus as the jealous giant of the Acis and Galatea legend: the one-eyed shepherd, pipe discarded, heaves a boulder toward the fleeing lovers. The Bolognese master gives the Odyssey's cannibal a second afterlife as Ovid's thwarted suitor — still Poseidon's son, still a force of rock and rage.
captions.matham-perseus-and-andromeda: Matham's engraving after Goltzius returns to the crisis Cassiopeia caused: Andromeda chained for the sea-monster while the royal parents' boast still hangs over the shore — the queen's vanity as the hinge of the Ethiopian rescue.
captions.barocci-aeneas-flight-from-troy: Barocci's Borghese canvas: Aeneas bears Anchises through the sack, Ascanius beside him, Creusa behind — Virgil's departure from the flames.
captions.giambologna-hercules-beating-nessus-herc: This towering marble by the Flemish-born Mannerist Giambologna captures the moment of reckoning at the river Evenus: Heracles, planted with brute force, grips the rearing centaur Nessus and beats him down for his attempt on Deianira. The composition coils the human victor and the half-equine abductor into a single knot of strained muscle and torsion, exploiting the dramatic figura serpentinata that made Giambologna famous and inviting the viewer to circle the group. Carved in 1599, the sculpture stands in the Loggia dei Lanzi in the Piazza della Signoria, Florence, among the city's open-air gallery of heroic statuary.
captions.anaxarete-and-iphis: Rijksmuseum Ovid print: the funeral procession that petrifies Anaxarete — Vertumnus' warning tale to Pomona restaged for Dutch readers.
captions.brueghel-latona-and-the-lycian-peasants: A cabinet landscape in the Brueghel manner: Latona with Apollo and Diana at a woodland spring while the Lycian peasants who denied her water begin their metamorphosis into frogs. Tiny myth inside a dense Flemish forest — Leto's insult and revenge folded into the pleasure of looking at leaves and water.
captions.circe-changes-picus-into-a-woodpecker: Dutch Ovid illustration — Picus as woodpecker, Canens' grief implied in the Circean revenge.
captions.cobaert-liriope-and-narcissus: Cobaert’s relief pair binds mother and son in one sculptural breath — Liriope as the naiad who bore Narcissus to Cephissus. The work belongs to the Ovidian decorative tradition that kept the nymph’s name alive beside the boy at the pool.
captions.elsheimer-aeneas-rescuing-anchises-from-: Elsheimer's night fire: Aeneas carries Anchises out of Troy's blaze — the sack reduced to a small copper of flame and piety.
captions.elsheimer-mercury-and-battus: Elsheimer's small panel of the Homeric Hymn / Ovid episode: Mercury confronts the Pierian witness of the stolen herd — Battus as the garrulous stone-to-be.
captions.fiasella-the-death-of-meleager-morte-di-: A Baroque canvas by the Genoese painter Domenico Fiasella (1589-1669), now in the Accademia Ligustica di Belle Arti in Genoa. Fiasella renders the dramatic dying of Meleager, undone as the fatal log consumes itself in the hearth, with the lamenting figures of his household pressing close in chiaroscuro shadow. These mourning women are the sisters of Meleager — the daughters of Oeneus and Althaea, the Meleagrids whose unending grief is the engine of the episode's final act. Gorge, sister of Meleager and Deianira, belongs to this circle of mourners; in Ovid's telling she and Deianira alone escaped being changed into birds by their sorrow.
captions.sweelinck-odysseus-and-teiresias: Sweelinck's Dutch underworld — the living hero and the blind seer over the blood-offering of Odyssey Book 11.
captions.wtewael-the-battle-between-the-gods-and-: Wtewael's jewel-like chaos: Olympians and Titans locked in the theogonic war Hesiod fixed as the cosmos' founding battle.
captions.caravaggio-amor-vincit-omnia: An oil painting of a grinning adolescent Cupid trampling the emblems of music, science, warfare and statecraft, illustrating Virgil's line 'love conquers all.' Caravaggio's provocative realism made the picture famous in his own lifetime. It hangs in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin.
captions.passe-althaea-killing-meleager-from-the-: This early seventeenth-century engraving by the Dutch printmaker Crispijn van de Passe the Elder, made for a series illustrating Ovid's Metamorphoses, shows Althaea throwing the fateful brand into the fire and so killing her son Meleager. The composition follows Ovid closely: in the background Meleager's grieving sisters lament his death, the mourners whom the goddess Diana would transform into guinea-hens. Now held in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, the print belongs to the great age of Netherlandish reproductive engraving that carried the visual repertoire of classical myth across early modern Europe.
captions.passe-arcas-shoots-at-callisto: From van de Passe's Ovid Metamorphoses series in the Rijksmuseum (RP-P-OB-15.903): Arcas draws on the bear that is his mother Callisto, while in the background Jupiter already lifts mother and son toward the stars. The engraving compresses Ovid's near-matricide and catasterism into a single Northern-Renaissance plate.
captions.passe-cadmus-and-harmonia-transformed-in: De Passe's engraving — Cadmus and Harmonia becoming crested snakes after Thebes' disasters gather.
captions.domenichino-apollo-and-hyacinth-fresco-p: Domenichino's Farnese fresco — the god bending over the fallen prince, athletic play reversed into mourning in Ovid's Book X.
captions.rubens-the-fall-of-phaeton: Rubens' tumbling chariot — Phaethon struck from the sky while the horses bolt and the world burns beneath Ovid's most catastrophic hubris.
captions.greco-epimetheus-and-pandora: Paired wooden sculptures by El Greco of Epimetheus and Pandora as Adam-and-Eve analogues — the afterthought brother and the gifted bride set face to face. The Toledo pair makes Hesiod's marriage visible as a Renaissance meditation on the first human mistake.
captions.tempesta-anaxarete-seeing-the-dead-iphis: MET Metamorphoses plate: Anaxarete looks on Iphis' corpse and stiffens into stone — Venus' revenge as print culture. Metropolitan Museum of Art.
captions.tempesta-ceres-giving-her-chariot-to-tri: Tempesta's Ovidian etching (LACMA): Ceres entrusts her dragon-chariot to Triptolemus so he may sow grain among the nations — the Renaissance restaging of the Eleusinian mission from Metamorphoses Book V.
captions.tempesta-ceres-nymph-telling-famine-to-s: Tempesta Metamorphoses plate (MET): Ceres' nymph carries the order that Famine enter Erysichthon's vitals — the divine machinery that turns the felled oak into endless appetite.
captions.tempesta-circe-changing-picus-into-a-bir: Tempesta after Ovid — Circe changing Picus into a bird among the Italian woods of Metamorphoses Book 14.
captions.tempesta-diana-killing-chione: Tempesta's Metamorphoses plate: Diana's arrow strikes Chione while Autolycus and Philammon look on — the twin sons Apollo and Hermes fathered the same night.
captions.tempesta-erysichthon-selling-his-daughte: Plate 81 of the same cycle: Mestra sold again and again in shifting guise while her father eats through every ransom — appetite that consumes the household.
captions.tempesta-hippolytus-saved-from-death-vir: Tempesta's Metamorphoses plate — Aesculapius restoring Hippolytus at Diana's bidding, the youth renamed Virbius as Ovid's Book XV inset ends.
captions.tempesta-lyncus-turned-into-a-lynx-while: Tempesta's companion plate (LACMA): King Lyncus tries to murder the sleeping Triptolemus and steal Demeter's gift; Ceres transforms the assassin into a lynx — Ovid's cautionary sequel to the chariot of grain.
captions.tempesta-phineus-attacking-perseus-at-th: Antique-derived attack — Phineus storming the bridal feast, the brawl Ovid inserts after Andromeda's rescue.
captions.tempesta-proserpina-turning-ascalaphus-i: Tempesta's Ovid cycle (LACMA): Proserpina sprinkles the Phlegethon on the tale-bearer, and Ascalaphus rises as owl — the Metamorphoses episode that fixed his afterlife in print.
captions.tempesta-scylla-rejected-by-minos-after-: Scylla rejected by Minos after destroying her city — the betrayal rewarded with exile and metamorphosis.
captions.tempesta-scylla-watching-minos-from-the-: Scylla watching Minos from the walls — Ovid's princess in love with the besieging king of Crete.
captions.tempesta-the-creation-of-the-world-orbis: Tempesta's Metamorphoses plate opens with earth, sea and sky parting from formless Chaos — Ovid's cosmogony as the first metamorphosis of all.
captions.tempesta-the-fury-tisiphone-at-the-palac: The companion plate opens the same Ovidian sequence: Tisiphone enters Athamas' house with snakes and torch, sowing the madness that will turn the king against his own children.
captions.tempesta-the-insane-athamas-killing-lear: Tempesta's engraving (published by Wilhelm Janson) freezes the double climax of the myth: Athamas murdering Learchus indoors as Ino and Melicertes leap toward the sea that will remake them as marine gods.
captions.konig-apollo-and-coronis: This small oil-on-copper cabinet picture, attributed to Johann König after a lost composition by Adam Elsheimer, shows Apollo with his mortal lover Coronis in a darkening landscape. It illustrates the tragic love at the heart of Ischys' story: while Coronis carries Apollo's child (the future Asclepius), her affair with Ischys, son of Elatus, will provoke the god's lethal vengeance. The intimate, twilight mood of this Northern European Renaissance work foreshadows the catastrophe to come. The painting is held at the Agnes Etherington Art Centre, Kingston, Ontario.
captions.cantagallina-idmon-and-mopsus-guided-by-: Met plate from the Medici Argonaut pageant: Apollo steers a ship carrying Idmon and the Argonaut seer Mopsus (Ampycus’ son — not the Colophonian). Festival print keeps Idmon named among the knowing prophets of the Argo.
captions.ship-of-periclymenus: A Cooper Hewitt print from the 1608 Medici wedding naval pageant: the allegorical Ship of Periclymenus sails among mythic vessels staged for Cosimo II. Florentine festival culture gives the shape-shifting Argonaut a floating emblem beside the Argo's other names.
captions.bernini-the-goat-amalthea-with-the-infan: Bernini's early Borghese marble presents Amalthea as the goat herself: the infant Jupiter and a faun drink at her udder — the Cretan nurse of Zeus carved before the sculptor's fame.
captions.elsheimer-jupiter-and-mercury-in-the-hou: Elsheimer's candlelit hut: Zeus and Hermes inside the thatched home — kindness painted as intimate German Baroque drama.
captions.domenichino-cumaean-sibyl: Domenichino's Capitoline canvas: the Sibyl as a young woman with scroll and laurel — Bolognese clarity for Virgil's guide through the underworld.
captions.greco-laocoon: El Greco transplants the priest's death to a storm-lit Toledo: the wooden horse and a spectral city watch as Troy's omen becomes apocalypse.
captions.lastman-paris-and-oenone: Lastman's pastoral stages the Idaean shepherd Paris with the nymph Oenone — the first love he abandons for Helen, whose later refusal to heal his wound seals Troy's fall. Rembrandt's teacher makes the Cebrenid nymph the quiet counterpoint to the Judgment of Paris.
captions.rubens-juno-and-argus: Rubens's Wallraf–Richartz canvas shows Juno claiming the eyes of the slain hundred-eyed watchman — Argus's gaze transferred to the peacock's tail.
captions.rubens-pan-reclining: Rubens depicts Pan in a moment of languid repose, the muscular, horned god of the wild stretched out amid the foliage of his woodland realm. The Flemish master renders the god's hybrid nature with characteristic vitality — the powerful human torso giving way to the rough goat-limbs below — capturing the sensual, earthy spirit of the Arcadian deity of fields, groves and untamed places. The work survives in the collection of the National Gallery of Art, Washington.
captions.soutman-laocoon-and-his-sons-bitten-by-s: Soutman's print after the ancient group spreads the priest's death across Europe as reproducible agony — coils, muscle, and open mouths in ink. The warner of Troy becomes a Baroque lesson in pathos for every print collector who owned a Laocoön.
captions.rubens-prometheus-bound: Rubens' Philadelphia Bound — eagle and chains after the theft, Snyders' bird tearing the liver Hesiod and Aeschylus fixed as the price of fire.
captions.rubens-the-calydonian-boar-hunt: In this oil-on-panel by the Flemish master Peter Paul Rubens (J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles), the heroes of the Calydonian hunt close in on the monstrous boar sent by Artemis. Amid the swirling, diagonal violence of dogs, spears and straining bodies, the Arcadian hero Ancaeus lies stricken on the ground at the centre of the composition—the casualty whom the boar gored after he boasted that a man's weapon would outdo a woman's. The painting distills the moment of the hunt at its most chaotic, with Ancaeus's fallen form serving as the price of his fatal pride.
captions.gentileschi-danae: Artemisia paints Danaë and a servant under the golden rain — Zeus' visit as charged exchange before the infant and the sea-chest.
captions.chryses-begs-agamemnon-for-his-daughter: Rijksmuseum engraving from the Speculum Heroicum: Chryses' supplication as a stock Homeric emblem — the priest who starts the wrath.
captions.passe-diomedes-slays-rhesus: Van de Passe's engraving — Diomedes slaying the Thracian king before Troy's walls.
captions.lastman-orestes-and-pylades-disputing-th: Lastman paints the Taurian dilemma: which friend will die for the other. Pylades offers himself so Orestes may live — Dutch history painting as a study in classical loyalty.
captions.rubens-the-death-of-adonis: Rubens' Israel Museum canvas — the boar's wound and Venus' grief, the end of Myrrha's son who would not stay.
captions.brueghel-the-banquet-of-achelous: Metropolitan Museum collaboration: Achelous hosts Theseus at a grotto feast and recounts the wrestling for Deianira — Ovid's Metamorphoses banquet where the broken horn spills as cornucopia and the Nessus tragedy waits in the telling.
captions.dyck-daedalus-and-icarus: Van Dyck shows the father fastening wax and feathers — the warning spoken before the boy climbed too close to the sun.
captions.francken-eteocles-and-polynices: Francken's fratricide: Eteocles and Polynices locked at the seventh gate — Aeschylus' and Statius' civil war in paint.
captions.giovane-dike-goddess-of-justice: A late-Renaissance Venetian allegory (Nationalmuseum, Stockholm, NMH 1486-1863) in which Palma il Giovane personifies Dike as the goddess of justice, bearing the sword and balance with which she weighs and avenges mortal deeds. The painting translates the Greek personification of righteous order into the post-classical Justitia type, preserving Dike's role as the maiden who upholds straight judgement against the crooked dealings of men.
captions.goltzius-cadmus-sows-the-dragon-s-teeth-: In this Dutch Mannerist engraving (now in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art), Hendrik Goltzius illustrates the climactic moment from the Theban foundation myth as told by Apollodorus and Ovid: Cadmus, having slain the dragon of Ares, scatters its teeth across the freshly ploughed soil, from which fully armed warriors — the Spartoi, or 'Sown Men' — rise up out of the earth. Chthonius is one of the five who survive the brothers' mutual slaughter to become an ancestor of the Theban nobility, and the print captures the very instant of the earth-born host springing to life. The composition belongs to a celebrated cycle of Goltzius's mythological prints that disseminated Ovid's Metamorphoses across early-modern Europe.
captions.janssens-the-goddess-ceres-and-the-symbo: The Flemish Baroque painter Abraham Janssens presents Ceres — the Roman Demeter — as a full-bodied allegory of agricultural abundance, crowned with grain and surrounded by the fruits, sheaves and implements of the harvest. Painted in Antwerp in the early seventeenth century, the canvas belongs to the northern tradition that translated the Greek grain-goddess into a sumptuous emblem of fertility for private collectors, keeping Demeter's domain vivid under her Latin name.
captions.rubens-bacchanalia: Rubens fills the Pushkin canvas with Silenus at the center of the revel — heavy, crowned, and half-asleep amid nymphs and goats.
captions.rubens-boreas-abducting-orithyia: Produced in the workshop of Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640), this oil panel gives the abduction of Orithyia its fullest Flemish-Baroque vigor: the powerful, dark-winged Boreas hoists the Athenian princess skyward in a swirl of muscular bodies, fluttering cherubs, and wind-blown drapery. The North Wind's seizure of Erechtheus's daughter and her flight to Thrace was a favored mythological theme, and the Rubensian treatment emphasizes the storm-god's elemental force. The painting hangs in the Neues Palais in the park of Sanssouci, Potsdam, under the Prussian Palaces and Gardens Foundation.
captions.rubens-daughters-of-cecrops-discovering-: Rubens' Courtauld oil sketch returns to the same Athenian crisis: the Cecropids uncover Erichthonius — Aglauros' curiosity as the prelude to envy, Mercury, and the stone that Ovid makes of her.
captions.rubens-hercules-and-the-nemean-lion: Rubens translates the ancient labour into full Baroque drama: a powerfully built Hercules, anatomy strained and torsion theatrical, throttles the snarling lion in a swirl of muscle and shadow. The Flemish master, steeped in classical sculpture, returns the hand-to-hand combat tradition to monumental painting, charging it with the dynamic diagonals and raw physical struggle that define his heroic mythologies. National Museum of Art of Romania, Bucharest, formerly in the collection of King Carol I.
captions.rubens-ixion-king-of-the-lapiths-deceive: Rubens stages the crime before the wheel: Ixion embraces the cloud-form of Juno while Zeus looks on — desire for the queen of heaven that will birth the Centaurs and earn the spinning punishment.
captions.rubens-the-discovery-of-the-child-ericht: Rubens stages the forbidden moment when the daughters of King Cecrops — Aglaurus, Herse and Pandrosus — open the basket Athena had entrusted to them, against her command. Inside lies the infant Erichthonius, his legs entwined with or replaced by the coils of a serpent, a sign of his earth-born nature. The sisters recoil and marvel in a sweep of luminous Baroque flesh and drapery, their curiosity about to bring on the madness and ruin the goddess decreed as punishment. The composition, now in the Liechtenstein Princely Collections in Vienna, is one of the most celebrated Flemish treatments of the myth and a study in the dangerous limits of human inquisitiveness.
captions.jordaens-the-finding-of-the-infant-erich: Jordaens, working in Rubens' Antwerp circle, gives the same episode a darker, more crowded intimacy. By torch- and candlelight the daughters of Cecrops cluster around the opened wicker chest to reveal the serpent-legged child Erichthonius, future king of Athens, whom Athena had hidden and forbidden them to look upon. The painter heightens the drama of transgression: the warm flesh of the women, the gleam of the basket and the writhing snake pull the eye into the prohibited box. Held in the Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp, the canvas exemplifies the Flemish Baroque fascination with this cautionary tale of curiosity overcoming a divine injunction.
captions.reni-hercules-and-achelous: Louvre INV 536 from Reni's Mantuan Hercules cycle: the hero wrestles the river-god for Deianira — bull-form Achelous staged as monumental Baroque combat before the horn becomes cornucopia.
captions.reni-hercules-on-the-pyre: Louvre INV 538: Reni's Mantuan cycle ends with Heracles on the funeral pile — the poisoned shirt's agony staged as monumental nude stoicism before the flames that will make him a god.
captions.rubens-the-rape-of-the-daughters-of-leuc: Rubens's celebrated Baroque canvas depicts the moment that defined Leucippus in art: the abduction of his daughters, the Leucippides Phoebe and Hilaeira, by the divine twins Castor and Pollux (the Dioscuri). Though Leucippus himself, the Messenian king, is absent from the frame, the painting turns his family's catastrophe into a swirling diagonal of straining horses, rearing riders, and the luminous flesh of the two abducted brides. Painted in Antwerp around 1617–1618 (with the landscape attributed to Jan Wildens), it hangs today in the Alte Pinakothek, Munich, and remains the single most famous visual rendering of the Leucippus myth.
captions.bernini-aeneas-anchises-and-ascanius: Bernini's Borghese marble: Aeneas carries Anchises from burning Troy while Ascanius follows — three generations in one spiral of flight.
captions.reni-hippomenes-and-atalanta: Reni's Prado canvas freezes the race's hinge: Atalanta stoops for a golden apple while Hippomenes surges ahead — Aphrodite's gift buying victory.
captions.lastman-odysseus-and-nausicaa: Lastman's Munich canvas: shipwrecked Odysseus kneels before Nausicaa while her handmaids scatter — Scheria's civilised welcome.
captions.baglione-clio-muse-of-history: The Roman painter Giovanni Baglione, a contemporary and rival of Caravaggio, depicts Kleio as a half-length figure absorbed in the act of writing, an open book and the rolled papyri of her capsa close at hand. Bathed in the dramatic chiaroscuro of early Seicento Rome, the Muse leans into her task with quiet intensity, her attributes — the scroll and the volume of records — marking her as the daughter of Memory who safeguards the chronicle of mortal and divine deeds for future ages.
captions.baglione-erato-muse-of-lyrics: The Roman Baroque painter Giovanni Baglione depicted Erato around 1620 as a richly draped young woman absorbed in music, holding her instrument as the muse of lyric song. Baglione, a rival and biographer of Caravaggio, renders the figure with dramatic chiaroscuro and a sumptuous palette typical of early Seicento Rome. By naming her Erato among the nine Muses, the work draws on the post-classical iconographic tradition in which she presides over the lyre and the poetry of love, one luminous member of the Heliconian chorus that inspires mortal singers.
captions.baglione-urania-muse-of-astronomy: The Roman Baroque painter Giovanni Baglione depicts Urania, the celestial Muse, seated with a great star-strewn globe of the heavens at her side, the constellations charted across its sphere. As one of the nine Muses born to Zeus and the memory-goddess Mnemosyne, Urania alone governed astronomy, and ancient authors made her the Muse who taught mortals to read the courses of the stars. Baglione gives her the contemplative gravity of a heavenly philosopher, her gaze turned upward toward the sky whose motions she interprets — the lone star among her sister Muses who answers to the cosmos itself.
captions.bloemaert-landscape-with-vertumnus-and-p: Bloemaert's landscape — Vertumnus and Pomona small in a Dutch orchard world, Metamorphoses Book 14 as pastoral.
captions.cadmus-and-the-spartoi-wallenstein-palac: Prague's Wallenstein mythological corridor stages Cadmus with the Spartoi — the sown warriors among whom Udaeus stands as ancestor of the Theban line of Tiresias.
captions.dubreuil-diane-entre-deux-geants-diana-b: Chambord tapestry: Artemis flanked by Otus and Ephialtes — the Naxos trap where the goddess as a stag makes the brothers spear each other.
captions.dyck-drunken-silenus: Van Dyck's Pushkin painting: Silenus supported by satyrs in a swirl of wine-skin and flesh — the tutor of Bacchus too drunk to stand alone.
captions.gentileschi-medea: Gentileschi's Baroque Medea is a solitary half-length of the Colchian witch at work — focused, armed with her craft, already past pity. One of the rare early modern images to give Medea the same fierce agency Artemisia gave Judith, it anchors the figure in the painter's gallery of wronged women who act.
captions.giambologna-hercules-and-the-dragon-lado: A bronze statuette from the workshop of the Flemish-Italian Mannerist sculptor Giambologna (1529–1608), cast in the early 17th century after a design of around 1580 for the Medici court. It captures the climax of Heracles' eleventh labour: rather than the theft of the golden apples, the artist stages the hero's violent confrontation with Ladon, the immortal serpent who guarded the tree of the Hesperides. The hero strides forward in one of the torsioned, spiralling poses characteristic of Giambologna, while the dragon writhes beneath him; the smooth, highly finished bronze surface accentuates the play of muscle and movement. Walters Art Museum, Baltimore (accession 54.695); height 41.8 cm.
captions.jordaens-meleager-and-atalanta: Jordaens stages the aftermath: Meleager awards the hide to Atalanta — the gesture of love that enrages his uncles and burns the brand of his fate.
captions.odysseus-feigns-madness: Odysseus feigning madness — the draft-dodge Palamedes exposed, the insult that seeds the forged letter and the grave.
captions.poelenburgh-apollo-and-the-cattle-of-adm: A small Dutch cabinet painting depicting the god Apollo, condemned by Zeus to serve a mortal for a year, tending the herds of King Admetus in a luminous Italianate landscape. The myth of Admetus's kindness to his divine herdsman—repaid when Apollo later won him the gift of escaping death—is rendered in Poelenburgh's polished, classicising manner. The panel illustrates the episode that bound Admetus's fortunes to Apollo's favour.
captions.reni-abduction-of-deianira: Guido Reni's Baroque masterpiece seizes the violent climax of the myth: the centaur Nessus gallops away through the surf bearing the struggling Deianira aloft, her body twisting in alarm and her drapery streaming like a banner against a stormy sky. Having been entrusted to carry her across the swollen river Evenus for hire, Nessus has instead seized the bride of Heracles and bolts for the far shore — the assault that will draw a hydra-poisoned arrow and seal both their fates. Reni dramatizes the upward spiral of bodies, the abductor's animal power set against the heroine's helpless contortion. Oil on canvas, 262 × 192 cm, now in the Louvre, Paris (INV 537).
captions.reni-atalanta-and-hippomenes: In this Baroque masterpiece, oil on canvas now in the Museo di Capodimonte in Naples, Guido Reni freezes the decisive instant of Ovid's foot-race (Metamorphoses 10.560–707). Atalanta stoops mid-stride to snatch one of Aphrodite's golden apples while Hippomenes presses ahead toward the finish, his body twisting away from her. The two nudes form a sweeping diagonal of opposed motion against a darkened sky, their fluttering drapery and outstretched limbs balanced in an almost choreographic counterpoint that became one of the most celebrated images of the myth. A second autograph version hangs in the Museo del Prado, Madrid.
captions.rubens-boreas-abducting-oreithyia: In this Baroque oil on panel (146 by 140 cm, Academy of Fine Arts Vienna), Rubens seizes the most violent instant of the myth: Boreas, the dark-winged god of the North Wind, sweeps the Athenian princess Oreithyia bodily into the air. The composition spirals upward in a tumult of straining muscle and billowing drapery, the wind-god's powerful frame and beating wings answered by the helpless, twisting body of his bride as she is carried off from the banks of the Ilissus toward wintry Thrace. Rubens transforms Ovid's account of the spurned wooer who 'fell back on his own nature' into a whirlwind of flesh and storm.
captions.tiarini-achilles-and-the-daughters-of-ly: Tiarini’s Bolognese canvas stages the same Skyrian recognition under Lycomedes’ roof — Italian Baroque light on the court that hid Achilles until the arms called him out.
captions.tournier-king-midas: Tournier's half-length Midas wears the ass's ears as royal attribute — the king who judged the music contest wrong, fixed in Caravaggesque light. Punishment become portrait.
captions.vignali-cyparissus: Vignali's Strasbourg canvas: the youth mourns the tame stag he has slain — grief Apollo will root as the cypress.
captions.bernini-the-rape-of-proserpina: Bernini's Borghese marble — Pluto seizing Proserpina for the underworld, the Hymn's abduction carved into yielding flesh.
captions.rubens-perseus-freeing-andromeda: Rubens shows the chains giving way: Andromeda steps into Perseus' arms while putti and the slain monster fill the shore.
