captions.bernini-apollo-and-daphne: The Baroque marble that fixed Ovid's chase in stone — Daphne's toes rooting, Apollo's fingers on bark that was still flesh a heartbeat before.
captions.bernini-neptune-and-triton: Early marble group by Gian Lorenzo Bernini, carved to crown a garden fountain in Rome and now in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Neptune thrusts his trident downward to command the waters while the young Triton crouches between his legs, blowing a conch shell.
captions.caullery-the-colossus-of-rhodes: Caullery imagines the lost bronze wonder: Helios as harbour giant bestriding Rhodes, ships passing at his feet — the sun god made the measure of ancient scale. Louvre, Paris (MNR 727).
captions.poussin-the-death-of-chione: Poussin stages Artemis' arrow through Chione's tongue — Daedalion's daughter punished for ranking her beauty above the goddess. Not Chione daughter of Boreas.
captions.rubens-perseus-and-andromeda: Rubens shows the aftermath of the rescue: Perseus, still helmed and winged, receives Andromeda's gratitude while putti and Pegasus fill the sky. The Hermitage canvas celebrates the hero not at the kill but at the marriage that seals his Argive destiny. Oil on canvas, State Hermitage Museum, Saint Petersburg.
captions.rubens-the-fates-spinning-marie-s-destin: The opening canvas of Rubens' Marie de' Medici cycle in the Louvre: Clotho, Lachesis and Atropos spin the queen's thread beneath Jupiter and Juno. Lachesis, the Measurer, works the allotted length — fate as court allegory, the Moirai blessing a mortal reign.
captions.guercino-semiramis-receiving-word-of-the: Guercino's canvas: the queen interrupted at her toilet by news of revolt — Baroque theatre for the ruler who would not delay justice for vanity.
captions.poussin-mercury-herse-and-aglauros: Poussin's ENSBA drawing compresses Metamorphoses II into a doorway drama — Mercury, Herse, and the sister who bars the god.
captions.poussin-midas-and-bacchus: Midas before Bacchus begging release from the gift that starves him — the golden touch as a theological bargain, not a fairy-tale joke.
captions.tiphys-batavus-frontispiece: Frontispiece to Snellius' Tiphys Batavus — the Argonaut helmsman's name borrowed for a Dutch treatise on navigation, Tiphys as early-modern science's steersman.
captions.reni-ninus-handing-the-crown-to-semirami: Reni's transfer of the crown: Ninus yields power to Semiramis — Bolognese elegance for the legendary succession that made her queen of Assyria.
captions.riminaldi-daedalus-and-icarus: Caravaggesque oil by Orazio Riminaldi showing Daedalus fastening the wings to a youthful Icarus. Strong chiaroscuro isolates the craftsman's tools and touch — the inventor of the labyrinth rendered as an intimate scene of instruction before the fatal flight.
captions.rubens-coastal-landscape-with-ulysses-an: Rubens sets the meeting on a windy Phaeacian shore — Odysseus emerging from the brush, Nausicaa and her train with the laundry carts Homer names. The Palazzo Pitti panel turns hospitality into a Baroque coastal drama.
captions.rubens-thetis-dipping-the-infant-achille: Painted around 1625 as part of Rubens's series of designs for a tapestry cycle on the life of Achilles, this dynamic oil sketch shows the sea-goddess Thetis gripping her newborn son by the heel and plunging him into the dark waters of the Styx to render him invulnerable. The three-headed hound Cerberus and the ferryman Charon's bark anchor the scene in the underworld, while the swirling Baroque composition foreshadows the hero's single mortal weakness — the heel by which his mother held him.
captions.vouet-polyhymnia-muse-of-eloquence: By the French Baroque painter Simon Vouet, leader of the Parisian school after his return from Rome, this work portrays Polyhymnia, the Muse of sacred song and eloquence. Veiled and pensive, she is rendered with the gravity and downcast absorption that ancient and Renaissance tradition assigned to her, the most solemn of the nine Muses. As the patroness of hymns addressed to gods and heroes and of the persuasive, measured word, Polyhymnia stands apart from the music and dance of her sisters; Vouet's contemplative figure captures the inwardness of a Muse associated with silence, devotion, and the dignity of speech.
captions.ribera-drunken-silenus: Ribera's Capodimonte canvas: the aged companion of Dionysus sprawls naked and laughing while satyrs crown him with vine — Silenus as flesh, wine, and prophecy.
captions.poussin-midas-washing-at-the-source-of-t: Poussin's Metropolitan canvas — the Phrygian king scrubbing the golden curse from his hands in the Pactolus, Ovid's remedy made landscape.
captions.poussin-the-triumph-of-flora: Poussin's Louvre triumph stages Flora in a chariot amid putti and blooming nymphs — a classical procession of spring drawn from Ovid and Roman festival memory. Order, dance, and flowers fuse the goddess with the season she governs.
captions.rubens-the-rape-of-europa: Rubens copies and recharges Titian's invention for the Spanish court: Europa's white flesh against the dark bull, putti and sea spray framing the ride that founds Crete. Museo del Prado.
captions.poussin-echo-and-narcissus: Poussin's classical pastoral shows Narcissus already fading by the water while Echo collapses in grief and a putto mourns nearby — Ovid's metamorphosis rendered as ordered landscape tragedy. The youth who loved only himself becomes part of the still pool that destroyed him. Oil on canvas, Musée du Louvre, Paris.
captions.poussin-helios-and-phaeton-with-saturn-a: Poussin stages the petition before the fall: Phaethon before Helios amid Saturn and the Seasons — the fatal request that will burn the world. Oil on canvas, Gemäldegalerie, Berlin.
captions.boeckhorst-apollo-and-diana-kill-the-chi: Boeckhorst's Baroque massacre — the twins' wrath among the Niobids, maternal boast answered in blood.
captions.brueghel-aeneas-and-the-sibyl-in-the-und: Brueghel's Met panel crowds Aeneas and the Cumaean Sibyl through a hellscape of monsters and fire — Aeneid VI as Flemish cabinet drama.
captions.dyck-thetis-receiving-the-weapons-of-ach: An oil on canvas showing the sea nymph Thetis receiving from Hephaestus the divine armor forged for her son Achilles, the episode recounted in Book 18 of the Iliad. Van Dyck stages the exchange amid attendant figures and putti at the god's forge. The painting is in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna.
captions.ii-the-persecution-of-the-harpies: Quellinus' Baroque canvas drives the Boreads through the air after the Harpies — Calais in the winged pursuit that defines his brief heroic career among the Argonauts.
captions.jordaens-the-battle-of-the-lapiths-and-c: Jordaens' Baroque tumult — Centaurs seize brides, Lapiths strike back, Hippodameia's feast wrecked at the centre.
captions.jordaens-the-childhood-of-zeus: Jordaens' Louvre canvas: the infant Jupiter among Corybantes and the goat Amalthea — Cretan nurture after Rhea's deceit.
captions.jordaens-the-infant-jupiter-suckled-by-t: Jordaens' Flemish pastoral fills the Cretan cave with satyrs and the nursing goat — Amalthea as the living source of the hidden god's strength.
captions.poelenburgh-the-goddess-calypso-rescues-: Italianate landscape by Cornelis van Poelenburgh in which Calypso draws the shipwrecked Odysseus from the sea onto Ogygia. Before the long detention and Hermes' summons, the nymph appears as rescuer — the Homeric welcome that will become a seven-year captivity.
captions.poussin-selene-and-endymion: Poussin's Detroit canvas: the moon goddess descends in her chariot toward the sleeping shepherd — Selene's nightly love staged as cool classical theatre.
captions.poussin-the-infant-jupiter-nurtured-by-t: Poussin's classical landscape seats nymphs and the goat around the infant Jupiter — Amalthea's milk as the quiet opening of Olympian power.
captions.rembrandt-andromeda-chained-to-the-rocks: Rembrandt isolates the princess alone on the rock — no Perseus yet, only the chain that waits for the monster Cassiopeia's boast has summoned.
captions.romanelli-the-sacrifice-of-polyxena: Romanelli's Met canvas: the Trojan princess is led to Achilles' tomb while the Greeks demand her blood — Polyxena's last dignity painted as a baroque altar-piece.
captions.rubens-achilles-vanquishes-hector: Rubens' Achilles tapestry design: the duel outside Troy's walls — Hector falls, Achilles' spear the hinge of Iliad 22.
captions.rubens-briseis-given-back-to-achilles: Rubens' Detroit oil sketch: Briseis returns to Achilles after Patroclus' death — the prize restored too late, flesh and drapery in baroque rush.
captions.rubens-the-fall-of-the-titans: Rubens' workshop Fall of the Titans — Baroque bodies tumbling as the ten-year war ends in the abyss.
captions.rubens-the-three-graces: Rubens's late masterpiece renders the Charites as three full-bodied women linked by a garland in a lush garden, a cornucopia of blossoms above and Hephaestus's fountain spilling water at their feet. Painted for the artist's own collection and now in the Museo del Prado, Madrid, it celebrates the goddesses of grace, beauty and gladness as the embodiment of generous giving. The radiant figure at the center carries the role of Aglaïa, 'Splendour', the brightest Grace and consort of the smith-god — her luminous flesh the painterly equivalent of the dazzling brilliance her Greek name proclaims.
captions.rubens-the-wrath-of-achilles: Rubens' Iliad storm: Achilles' wrath erupting when Agamemnon seizes Briseis — the quarrel that keeps the Achaeans dying at Troy.
captions.velazquez-apollo-in-the-forge-of-vulcan: An oil painting of the moment Apollo, crowned with laurel, arrives at the forge to tell Vulcan that his wife Venus is betraying him with Mars. Velazquez renders the smith god and his stunned assistants with striking naturalism, pausing mid-labor over the glowing metal. Painted during the artist's first Italian journey, it hangs in the Museo del Prado, Madrid.
captions.reni-the-abduction-of-helen: Reni's Louvre canvas freezes the departure from Sparta: Helen, half-reluctant, is led toward Paris's waiting ship as attendants and putti swirl around the pair. The Bolognese baroque turns the abduction into a luminous pageant — the moment Menelaus's marriage becomes Troy's casus belli. Oil on canvas, Musée du Louvre, Paris.
captions.gentileschi-clio: Painted in 1632 for a patron connected to the Capponi family, Artemisia Gentileschi's Baroque allegory casts the Muse of history as a commanding figure who holds the trumpet of fame in one hand and an open book in the other, a laurel wreath crowning her head. The trumpet proclaims renown across the ages while the book preserves it, embodying Clio's role as the Muse whose office is to make great deeds outlast death. Gentileschi signed and dated the work prominently, turning the personification of recorded glory into a vehicle for her own claim on artistic posterity.
captions.rembrandt-the-abduction-of-europa: Rembrandt's rare mythological oak panel stages Ovid's bull-ride with a Dutch landscape behind it: Europa mounted, attendants crying out as Zeus carries her toward Crete. J. Paul Getty Museum.
captions.ribera-ixion: Ribera's Ixion — bound to the flaming wheel for his crime against Hera.
captions.ribera-tityus: Jusepe de Ribera's harrowing treatment of the punished giant, of which this version belongs to the Museo del Prado in Madrid. With the unflinching tenebrist naturalism for which the Spanish-Neapolitan master is famed, Ribera shows Tityos chained on the floor of Hades as a great bird sinks its talons and beak into his side to devour his ever-renewing liver. The painting was conceived as a pendant to Ribera's 'Ixion', both illustrating the legendary sinners whose insolence toward the Olympians earned them perpetual torture in the underworld described by Homer and Apollodorus.
captions.rubens-the-judgement-of-paris: Rubens' National Gallery Judgment: Paris awards the apple on Ida — the Cypria's spark that wins Helen and dooms Troy.
captions.capitelli-the-death-of-meleager: An elongated horizontal etching of about 1633 by the Sienese printmaker Bernardino Capitelli (1589-1639), held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. The friezelike composition unfolds the climax of the Calydonian saga: the dying Meleager collapses while his mother Althaea destroys the brand on which his fate depends, and the women of the family lament around him. The mourning sisters gathered at the hero's side are the Meleagrids, the daughters of Oeneus and Althaea — Gorge among them, named by Ovid as one of the two siblings (with Deianira) who kept their human form when the others became birds. The print embodies the very grief that defines Gorge's place in the myth.
captions.jordaens-the-golden-apple-of-discord: A Baroque oil painting of the wedding feast of Peleus and Thetis, the banquet of the gods into which the uninvited Eris hurls the golden apple inscribed 'to the fairest.' Her act ignites the rivalry among Hera, Athena and Aphrodite that leads to the Judgment of Paris and, ultimately, the Trojan War. The painting is in the Museo del Prado, Madrid.
captions.thulden-odysseus-recognized-by-his-dog-a: From the print series The Works of Odysseus: the beggar bends to the old hound on the dung-heap — the one recognition on Ithaca that needs no scar and no test.
captions.rembrandt-flora: Rembrandt paints his bride Saskia as Flora: staff, flowers, and a soft Amsterdam light that turns the Roman goddess into a private wedding allegory. The Hermitage canvas remains one of the most intimate modern faces given to the Sabine flower deity.
captions.zurbaran-hercules-and-the-erymanthian-bo: One of the ten canvases Francisco de Zurbarán painted in 1634 for the Hall of Realms of the Buen Retiro palace in Madrid, now in the Museo del Prado. Set against a darkened, tenebrist background, a muscular Heracles bends forward to seize the snarling boar by its haunches, pinning the struggling animal as he drives it through the deep snow into which, according to Apollodorus, the exhausted beast had been chased. Zurbarán reduces the myth to a single charged act of brute physical effort, his stark chiaroscuro and earthy palette transforming the ancient Labour into a Baroque meditation on heroic strength.
captions.zurbaran-hercules-fighting-with-antaeus: Painted by Francisco de Zurbarán for the Hall of Realms in Philip IV's Buen Retiro palace, this canvas belongs to a cycle of ten Labours of Hercules conceived as a mythic genealogy for the Spanish monarchy. Against a dark, smoky ground Hercules grapples the giant Antaeus from behind, lifting him from the earth to deny him the regenerating touch of his mother Gaia. Zurbarán renders the two muscular bodies with tenebrist drama, the hero's resolve set against the giant's failing struggle. Now in the Museo Nacional del Prado, Madrid.
captions.jordaens-mercury-and-battus: Jordaens' Boijmans canvas: Hermes tests the old herdsman who saw him drive Apollo's cattle — Battus bribed to silence, then turned to stone for speaking. Not Battus of Cyrene.
captions.lemaire-daedalus-and-pasiphae: Lemaire stages the carpenter's gift: Daedalus presents the hollow wooden cow to the Cretan queen whose desire for Poseidon's bull will beget the Minotaur. Oil on canvas, Musée des Beaux-Arts d'Agen (Louvre deposit).
captions.rembrandt-the-abduction-of-ganymede: Dresden's Rembrandt subverts the beautiful-youth tradition: a terrified, bawling infant snatched in the eagle's grip, urinating in fright — the cupbearer's rape made earthbound and unheroic.
captions.rubens-bellerophon-pegasus-and-the-chime: In this dynamic Baroque oil sketch, Rubens captures the climactic moment of the Chimera's defeat: the hero Bellerophon, mounted on the winged horse Pegasus, drives his spear down into the fire-breathing monster. Pegasus is the muscular pivot of the composition, wings outspread and forelegs lashing as he rears above the writhing beast, the immortal steed sprung from Medusa whose flight makes the aerial assault possible. The swirling diagonals, taut musculature, and turbulent energy are hallmarks of Rubens, who treats the ancient myth as a study in heroic motion. The work is held in the Musée Bonnat-Helleu in Bayonne.
captions.rubens-diana-and-callisto: Rubens' Prado wood: bathing nymphs turn on the disgraced Callisto — Ovid's exposure scene before Hera's wrath and the twin constellations.
captions.rubens-neptune-calming-the-tempest-quos-: Rubens stages Virgil's Quos ego: Neptune rises from the surge to still the storm, his trident the axis of command while winds and sea-horses scatter. Painted for Antwerp's festive entry of the Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand and now in the Harvard Art Museums (Fogg), it remains the Baroque image of the sea god as weather itself.
captions.cossiers-jupiter-and-lycaon-jupiter-y-li: Oil on canvas (120 × 115 cm) by the Antwerp painter Jan Cossiers, made after a design by Peter Paul Rubens for the Spanish court and today in the Museo del Prado, Madrid. The Baroque composition stages the climax of Ovid's first metamorphosis: Jupiter, attended by his eagle and hurling lightning, blasts the palace of King Lycaon, who had tested the god's divinity by serving him human flesh. Lycaon recoils as his form begins to twist toward the wolf's, the swirling drapery and storm-lit sky giving Flemish drama to the punishment that, in Ovid, prompts the great flood of Deucalion.
captions.gowy-the-fall-of-icarus: Prado oil after Rubens for the Torre de la Parada: Daedalus still climbs while Icarus plunges headlong, wax and feathers scattering — the Baroque fall as pure kinetic catastrophe.
captions.rembrandt-danae: Rembrandt's Hermitage Danaë waits in shadowed light as Zeus' golden visitation arrives — the bronze-tower conception that opens the Seriphos birth saga.
captions.rubens-cadmus-sowing-the-dragon-s-teeth: Rijksmuseum panel: Cadmus, guided by Minerva, watches the Spartoi rise from the furrows and turn on one another — the prodigy that seeds Thebes.
captions.rubens-deucalion-and-pyrrha: Rubens' Prado sketch for the Torre de la Parada: the flood survivors cast stones that become a new human race — Ovid's Greek deluge as Baroque energy after the waters fall.
captions.rubens-hercules-and-cerberus: Rubens' Baroque oil-sketch translates the ancient labour into churning, muscular drama: a powerfully built Hercules drags the three-headed dog of Hades from the mouth of the underworld while the heads snarl and twist away from the unfamiliar light — exactly the detail Ovid notes, the beast turning its eyes aslant and shaking the air with triple howls. Painted for the decorations of the Torre de la Parada hunting lodge near Madrid, it now hangs in the Museo del Prado. The work shows how the chthonic guardian of Greek myth was reimagined as a trophy of heroic force in early-modern European painting.
captions.rubens-jupiter-and-semele: A Torre de la Parada oil sketch by Rubens for Philip IV: Jupiter arrives in splendour before the Theban princess — the same myth Moreau would later jewel into Symbolist ecstasy.
captions.rubens-mercury-and-argus: Rubens' Prado scene — Hermes lulling hundred-eyed Argus so Io the heifer may escape Hera's watch.
captions.rubens-orpheus-and-eurydice: Painted for Philip IV's Torre de la Parada and now in the Museo del Prado, Rubens stages the underworld bargain: Orpheus leads Eurydice past Hades and Persephone as the fatal glance still hangs unmade. Eurydice is the luminous prize of the ascent — the bride the lyre almost brings home.
captions.rubens-pallas-and-arachne: Rubens paints Athena's fury as Arachne's loom is struck — the mortal weaver's victory met by the goddess who will turn her into a spider.
captions.rubens-saturn-devouring-his-son: Commissioned for the Torre de la Parada, Rubens depicts Cronus tearing into an infant son beneath his scythe — the devouring that Hesiod places between the castration of Uranus and the birth of Zeus. The painting visualizes the second age of the cosmos, when Rhea would save the youngest child with a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes.
captions.rubens-tereus-confronted-with-the-head-o: Tereus confronted with Itys' head — the recognition that turns the Thracian king into the pursuing hoopoe.
captions.rubens-the-birth-of-the-milky-way: Painted for the Torre de la Parada hunting lodge of Philip IV of Spain and now in the Museo del Prado, Rubens's Baroque treatment of the same myth Tintoretto had staged: Jupiter presses the infant Heracles to the breast of the sleeping Juno, and the spray of divine milk that starts up becomes the Milky Way. Hera is the startled axis of the composition — queen, stepmother, and cosmic fountain — rendered with the fleshy energy and swirling putti of Rubens's late mythological cycle.
captions.rubens-the-rape-of-ganymede: Prado canvas for Philip IV's Torre de la Parada: Jupiter's eagle sweeps the Trojan youth into the heavens where he will serve as cupbearer of the gods — Ovid's Metamorphoses in Baroque flight.
captions.rubens-the-wedding-of-peleus-and-thetis: Rubens's luminous oil sketch on panel stages the celebrated wedding feast of the mortal Peleus and the goddess Thetis, attended by the assembled Olympian gods. It is at this banquet that the slighted goddess Eris hurls the golden Apple of Discord 'to the fairest,' setting in motion the Judgment of Paris and ultimately the Trojan War. Peleus, the only mortal granted a divine bride, presides over a union whose celebration sows the seeds of catastrophe. The panel is in the Art Institute of Chicago (1947.108).
captions.rubens-vertumnus-and-pomona: Rubens' Torre de la Parada Pomona — the shape-shifting year-god and the fruit goddess in Baroque abundance.
captions.jordaens-apollo-as-victor-over-pan: Jordaens' Prado contest paints Midas among the judges who prefer Pan's pipes to Apollo's lyre — and earn the donkey ears. The Phrygian king as bad critic: taste punished in fur and long ears.
captions.reni-the-rape-of-europa: Reni's cool Bolognese classicism sets Europa on the bull against a clear sky — the abduction as poised, almost serene motion. National Gallery, London.
captions.ribera-apollo-flaying-marsyas: Ribera's Brussels canvas — luminous Apollo peels the skin from Marsyas in a shaft of light, the contest's aftermath as Spanish tenebrism.
captions.rubens-the-consequences-of-war: A Baroque oil painting in which Mars is dragged toward destruction by the Fury Alecto while Venus vainly tries to hold him back. Painted during the Thirty Years' War as an allegory of a Europe ravaged by conflict, it is held in the Palazzo Pitti, Florence.
captions.lemaire-theseus-finding-his-father-s-swo: Poussin and Lemaire — Theseus recovering his father's arms under the rock, then turning toward Athens on foot.
captions.baur-erysichthon-and-mestra: Baur's Metamorphoses etching: Erysichthon bargains over Mestra while Ceres' hunger still claws at him — seventeenth-century print culture's stock image of the Thessalian curse.
captions.baur-isis-and-iphis: Baur's Ovid plate — Isis granting the transformation that lets the Cretan wedding proceed.
captions.assereto-tantalus: Assereto's Tantalus — fruit and water forever out of reach, the feast denied.
captions.fabritius-hera-hiding-during-the-battle-: A rare mythological canvas by Carel Fabritius, Rembrandt's gifted pupil, now in the Pushkin Museum, Moscow. While the Gigantomachy rages, Hera draws her mantle close and turns aside — the queen of the gods caught not in triumph but in wary withdrawal. The quiet, half-shadowed figure stands apart from the usual Baroque storm of Olympian combat, an intimate psychological reading of the goddess who so often directs myth from the edge of the fray.
captions.hyre-glaucus-and-scylla: Getty canvas: La Hyre stages Glaucus' plea with cool French clarity — blue sea-flesh and the nymph's recoil before Circe ruins the strait.
captions.knupfer-hercules-obtaining-the-girdle-of: This small oil panel by the German-born Dutch painter Nikolaus Knüpfer stages the climax of Heracles' ninth labour: the hero confronting Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons, to win the war-belt of Ares she wore in token of her supremacy. Knüpfer renders the encounter as a turbulent baroque drama of armed warriors and rearing horses, evoking the moment Apollodorus describes when Hera, disguised as an Amazon, spread the rumor that the strangers were abducting the queen, turning a promised peaceful handover into bloodshed. The painting is held in the Hermitage Museum, Saint Petersburg.
captions.rubens-the-death-of-semele: Rubens' Death of Semele — Hera's jealous counsel fulfilled as the thunderbolt that births Bacchus kills his mother.
captions.vouet-helen-offering-menelaus-the-potion: Vouet's Egyptian gift — Helen pours Polydamna's nepenthe for Menelaus, Odyssey IV's drug of forgetfulness from the Nile court.
captions.baur-morpheus-in-the-house-of-ceyx-befor: Baur's Ovid etching: Morpheus wears the drowned king's face to Alcyone's sleep — the dream that reveals the wreck.
captions.atalanta-and-hippomenes-from-game-of-myt: MET engraving from the Jeu de la Mythologie: the race reduced to a playing-card emblem — golden apples and the suitor who will not be outrun.
captions.lorrain-odysseus-returns-chryseis-to-her: Claude stages the Iliad's first reconciliation as a luminous seaport: Odysseus escorts Chryseis back to Chryses amid classical quays and morning light. The priest's daughter whose ransom opened Book I becomes a quiet figure in a vast harbour world. Oil on canvas, Musée du Louvre, Paris.
captions.brun-daedalus-and-icarus: Attributed to Charles Le Brun: Daedalus binds the wings to Icarus against a luminous sky, the moment before their leap from Crete. French classicism turns the craftsman's caution into a moral tableau — skill and hubris paired in a single embrace.
captions.jordaens-jupiter-and-mercury-in-the-hous: Jordaens fills the cottage with Flemish abundance as the disguised gods accept the meal — Ovid's hospitality as festive welcome.
captions.lorrain-landscape-with-cephalus-and-proc: Claude's National Gallery light: Diana reconciles the couple and bestows the hound and javelin that will later doom them.
captions.perrier-acis-and-galatea: Perrier's French Classical painting pairs the shepherd Acis with Galatea against a coastal setting, freezing the idyll before Polyphemus' jealous violence. The canvas is in the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Carcassonne.
captions.perrier-acis-galatea-and-polyphemus: Perrier's Louvre canvas: Galatea and Acis slip away while Polyphemus watches from the rocks — the boulder already waiting.
captions.sacchi-daedalus-and-icarus: Baroque canvas by Andrea Sacchi in which Daedalus adjusts the wax-and-feather wings while Icarus looks skyward. Sacchi stages the Athenian inventor as both tender father and master artificer — the mind that built the labyrinth now building an escape from it.
captions.guercino-atlas-holding-up-the-celestial-: Guercino's Baroque Atlas strains beneath a starry globe — the Titan's eternal punishment painted as heroic musculature and night sky.
captions.brun-the-sacrifice-of-polyxena: Le Brun stages the knife above the tomb: Polyxena as the war's final price, Hecuba's daughter offered so the winds will let the fleet sail home.
captions.rembrandt-medea-or-the-marriage-of-jason: Rembrandt's etching for Jan Six's Medea — Jason and Creusa at the altar while the Colchian's tragedy gathers offstage.
captions.thijs-atalanta-and-meleager-hunt-the-cal: Flemish Baroque hunt: Atalanta among the heroes as the bristling boar and straining hounds fill the canvas — first blood and the prize that will ruin a house.
captions.poussin-landscape-with-polyphemus: Poussin's Hermitage landscape — the Cyclops tiny on the mountain above Arcadian calm, Odyssey IX's giant as a speck of threat.
captions.achilles-fighting-scamander-and-simois: Rijksmuseum print: Achilles locked with both river-gods — Simois as Scamander's partner in the flood that almost drowns the hero.
captions.achilles-fighting-the-river-god-scamande: Rijksmuseum print from an Achilles life series: the hero locked with Scamander — the river of Troy personified as opponent.
captions.achilles-in-combat-with-scamander-and-si: Another Rijksmuseum plate of the double river battle — Simois named in the title as Troy's second watery foe.
captions.aeneas-on-delos: Drawing of Aeneas' stop at Delos — Anius' island sanctuary where the Trojan remnant hears Apollo's oracle of Italy.
captions.alecto-rousing-latinus-against-aeneas: LACMA print of Alecto poisoning Latinus’ house against the Trojans — Virgil’s Fury at work on the Latin king. The image names Latinus as the mortal whose court becomes the fuse of the Italian war.
captions.alpheus-and-arethusa: A Metropolitan Museum print from the Metamorphoses cycle shows Alpheus closing on Arethusa — the river that Ovid says mingles with her Sicilian waters.
captions.anius-and-aeneas: Print of Anius receiving Aeneas on Delos — Apollo's son and priest-king hosting the Trojan exile as Virgil tells in Aeneid 3.
captions.apollo-and-cyparissus: Dutch Ovid engraving: Apollo with Cyparissus and the doomed stag — pastoral friendship before the accidental shot.
captions.apollo-and-mercury-visit-chione: Print of the double visitation: Apollo and Hermes both claim Chione in one night — Philammon and Autolycus as her twin divine gifts before Diana's arrow.
captions.bol-aegina-waiting-for-the-arrival-of-ze: A Dutch Golden Age painting by Ferdinand Bol (1616–1680), a pupil of Rembrandt whose influence shows in the rich chiaroscuro and golden light enveloping the figure. The nymph Aegina is shown in a moment of anticipation, awaiting the god Zeus, who in this telling approaches her in the guise of an eagle. The warm, theatrical lighting isolates her against a dark ground, lending the mythological encounter an air of intimate suspense before the abduction that will carry her from her father Asopus to the island later named for her. Oil on canvas, Meininger Museen, Meiningen.
captions.boullogne-la-naissance-de-minerve: Boullogne's French academic birth: Minerva rises armed from Jupiter's brow — the Renaissance–Baroque restaging of the Hesiodic axe-blow.
captions.briot-heracles-kills-periclymenus-in-the: Isaac Briot's engraving for an Ovidian Metamorphoses cycle shows Heracles striking down Periclymenus as the Neleid shape-shifter takes eagle form at the sack of Pylos. Poseidon's gift of metamorphosis cannot save Neleus' son when Heracles hunts the Pylian house.
captions.calais-and-zetes-led-by-boreas-and-oreit: This Metropolitan Museum print presents the winged twins with their parents Boreas and Orithyia — Calais as wind-born Argonaut before the Harpy chase, already marked by the gift of flight.
captions.carpioni-iris-as-messenger-in-the-realm-: This Baroque canvas by the Venetian painter Giulio Carpioni, now in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna (GG 1608), illustrates the episode from Ovid's Metamorphoses in which Juno dispatches Iris to the shadowy cave of Hypnos, god of Sleep. Iris glides in upon her luminous rainbow, her wings and bright drapery cutting through the dim, dream-haunted realm to deliver the goddess's command. The painting captures Iris in her defining function as the gods' winged messenger, the radiant courier who descends on a bridge of coloured light to carry Olympus's will into the farthest corners of the cosmos.
captions.cinyras-tries-to-kill-his-daughter-myrrh: A Rijksmuseum theatrical print shows Cinyras turning on Myrrha once he knows — the Cypriot king between Aphrodite's cult, incestuous darkness, and the chase that ends in her arboreal metamorphosis.
captions.cortona-the-oath-of-semiramis: Cortona's Ashmolean composition: Semiramis and the oath that seals her rule — High Baroque rhetoric for the Babylonian queen of Greek legend.
captions.cuyp-orpheus-charming-the-animals: Cuyp's Orpheus among the beasts — the grove songs after Eurydice, trees and animals gathered to the lyre.
captions.cyparissus-changed-into-a-cypress: Rijksmuseum climax: the boy becomes the cypress — endless mourning made evergreen.
captions.dorigny-pan-and-syrinx: Dorigny's Baroque pursuit: goat-legged Pan and fleeing Syrinx — the moment before metamorphosis, painted as French classical chase.
captions.erigone-with-grapes-after-guido-reni: Metropolitan Museum print after Reni: Erigone leans over a platter of grapes — the Attic heroine reduced to Bacchic beauty, still named for Icarius' daughter whose dog Maera found the unburied body.
captions.flemal-l-enfance-d-hercule-the-infancy-o: An oil painting (65 × 88 cm, Musée départemental Georges de La Tour, Vic-sur-Seille) by the Liégeois Baroque master Bertholet Flémal showing the infant Heracles strangling the two serpents Hera sent to kill him in his cradle. The scene is set in the Theban household of Amphitryon, the mortal foster-father who reared the child after his exile from Tiryns; the alarmed adult onlookers belong to that household drama, with Amphitryon's distinction from the divinely sired twin (his own son Iphicles cowers while Heracles triumphs) at the heart of the moment depicted.
captions.gelton-paris-and-helen-surprised-by-mene: Gelton stages the casus belli as a bedroom shock: Menelaus bursts in on Paris and Helen, the wronged husband interrupting the elopement that will launch a thousand ships. The Danish canvas keeps Menelaus as the war's personal spark — Sparta's king before the walls of Troy. Oil on canvas, Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen.
captions.giovanni-aurora-and-tithonus: Giovanni da San Giovanni's Aurora and Tithonus — the immortal lover dwindling while Dawn rises forever young.
captions.hollar-typhon-from-a-series-of-the-greek: Hollar's Typhon — the snake-legged storm-giant of the last theogonic war, etched for a series of the Greek gods.
captions.ii-achilles-among-the-daughters-of-lycom: Quellinus packs Lycomedes’ household into Flemish Baroque theatre — the Skyrian king’s daughters and the youth who will leave them for Troy. The title keeps Lycomedes the frame even when Achilles steals the eye.
captions.isis-changes-iphis-into-a-man: Theatrical Ovid print of the transformation Telethusa prayed for — Isis' answer the morning Iphis was to marry Ianthe.
captions.jordaens-momos: In this Flemish Baroque canvas by Jacob Jordaens, now in Malmö Konstmuseum, Momus appears as a half-length figure of ridicule — the winged fault-finder of Greek myth who carped at the gods until Olympus cast him out. Jordaens gives the daimon a blunt, satirical presence rather than a crowded Lucianic contest of creations, concentrating the whole character of mockery into a single gaze and gesture. The painting stands among the rare post-antique portraits that treat Momus himself as the subject, not merely an allegory tucked into a larger pantheon scene.
captions.jordaens-telemachus-leading-theoclymenus: Jordaens' Nationalmuseum drawing: Telemachus presents the fugitive seer Theoclymenus to Penelope — Odyssey XV–XVII as Flemish baroque narrative.
captions.jupiter-transforms-king-lycaon-into-a-wo: A Dutch Metamorphoses print in the Rijksmuseum (RP-P-2014-67-13, New Hollstein Dutch 540) returns to Ovid's banquet of Lycaon: Jupiter's judgment and the king's wolf-metamorphosis, the catastrophe after which Nyctimus inherits Arcadia. Together with Cossiers and Goltzius, the plate completes a three-work reception of the Lycaon crime that frames Nyctimus's brief kingship and the flood that ends it.
captions.langetti-tantalus: A Venetian tenebrist treatment of the standing sinner: Tantalus half-submerged, straining toward what he cannot grasp — the classic Tartarean punishment of the feast denied.
captions.langetti-the-torture-of-ixion: Langetti's Venetian tenebrism locks the king to the fiery wheel — muscle and flame in the dark, the Lapith's eternal spin rendered as raw underworld theatre.
captions.latona-with-diana-and-apollo-on-delos: Rijksmuseum print: Latona with the newborn twins on the sacred isle — Delos as the only land that would receive the birth.
captions.liberi-the-nymph-syrinx: Liberi's Venetian Syrinx alone — the Arcadian nymph before Pan's pursuit, flesh and landscape waiting for Ovid's reed transformation.
captions.lorrain-coast-scene-with-the-landing-of-: Rijksmuseum engraving after Claude: the Trojan landing that opens the Italian war books — destiny stepping onto Latin soil.
captions.lorrain-landscape-with-the-landing-of-ae: Claude's coast: Aeneas' ships touch Latium — Virgil's Italian arrival staged as golden light on the Tiber shore.
captions.medea-draining-the-blood-of-aeson: Wellcome Collection engraving of the grisly first step: Medea drains Aeson's blood to refill him with her brew — Ovid's surgery made into a print of medical wonder and mythic horror.
captions.metamorphoses-iphis-and-ianthe: Metamorphoses plate — Iphis and Ianthe at the Cretan wedding Isis will make possible.
captions.minos-and-scylla: A 17th-century etching of the Megarian tragedy: Scylla, daughter of Nisus, is drawn to the besieging Cretan king Minos — the fatal infatuation that will cost her father his purple lock and Megara its walls. Minos appears as the remote, dazzling object of a love that Ovid makes disastrous.
captions.moncornet-peleus-and-telamon-argonauts-g: Baroque etching of the Argonaut pageant: Peleus and Telamon ride the festive ship guided by Thetis — Telamon remembered as Jason's companion and father of Ajax long before the walls of Troy.
captions.odysseus-companions-open-the-bag-of-wind: The sequel plate: while Odysseus sleeps, his jealous crew unbind Aeolus' gift and the released storms drive the ships back from Ithaca's sight. The print completes the Homeric episode that made Aeolus' bag proverbial.
captions.odysseus-receives-from-aeolus-the-bag-of: Odysseus receives Aeolus' bag of contrary winds — the gift that nearly ends the voyage when the crew unties it in sight of Ithaca.
captions.phaethon-s-sisters-become-poplars-and-hi: Rijksmuseum Ovid print: beside the Heliades turning to poplars, Phaethon's friend becomes a swan — Cycnus of Liguria, Ovid's mourner who shuns the sky that killed his companion.
captions.phineus-interrupts-the-wedding-of-perseu: Dutch Ovid cycle — Phineus interrupting Perseus and Andromeda's wedding, Metamorphoses Book 5 as narrative strip.
captions.poussin-landscape-with-orpheus-and-euryd: Poussin's landscape — Eurydice's snakebite that opens the whole Orpheus saga.
captions.printmaker-death-of-iphis: Rijksmuseum RP-P-2014-34-82: Iphis hanged — the humble lover Anaxarete mocked until Aphrodite’s revenge. Northern Ovid cycles made his suicide a stock warning against hard-heartedness.
captions.printmaker-fight-between-odysseus-and-ir: Rijksmuseum RP-P-1890-A-15578: the palace fistfight that strips Irus of his place at the suitors’ door. Northern print tradition made the Ithacan beggar a stock Odyssey vignette.
captions.printmaker-iphis-transformed-into-a-youn: Dutch engraving of Ovid IX — the body remade on the eve of the rites so Iphis may marry Ianthe.
captions.printmaker-telethusa-and-iphis-pray-to-i: Mother and child before Isis — Ligdus' vow answered by the Egyptian goddess who walks Ovid's Crete.
captions.regnier-the-punishment-of-midas: Régnier shows Apollo fastening the donkey ears on Midas after the verdict for Pan. The golden-touch king here is pure hubris of judgment — ears as the visible price of preferring the wrong music.
captions.ribera-tantalus: A Prado canvas in Ribera's manner keeps the lost Furia alive: the underworld king twisted in shadow, still reaching for the water and fruit that slip away — Tantalus as Spanish Baroque torment.
captions.romanelli-boreas-abducting-oreithyia: In this Italian Baroque canvas, the Viterbo-born painter Giovanni Francesco Romanelli (1610-1662) renders the abduction of the Athenian princess Orithyia, daughter of King Erechtheus, by Boreas, the winged god of the North Wind. Spurned in his courtship, Boreas sweeps the frightened maiden aloft on a gust of swirling drapery, his dark wings beating against a turbulent sky. Romanelli's blend of dramatic movement and classicizing grace, learned in the Roman circle of Pietro da Cortona, romanticizes a violent moment from Ovid's Metamorphoses. The painting is held in the Galleria Spada, Rome.
captions.sandrart-laomedon-refusing-payment-to-po: Baroque canvas of the Trojan king stiff-necked before the gods who built his walls: Poseidon and Apollo stand unpaid while Laomedon’s court watches the perjury that will bring Heracles’ sack of Troy. The painting isolates the cheat that defines Laomedon in Apollodorus and the Iliadic backstory.
captions.school-the-sisters-of-phaethon-transform: An Ovidian plate freezes the sisters mid-change: bark climbing limbs, arms still raised in lament for Phaethon. The print tradition made the Heliades’ poplars and amber tears a standard Metamorphoses vignette for European readers who knew the sun-god’s daughters chiefly through that Latin grief.
captions.statue-of-notus-palace-of-the-four-winds: On the façade of Warsaw's Pałac Pod Czterema Wiatrami (Palace under the Four Winds) on ulica Długa, a Baroque statue personifies Notus among the four cardinal winds. The European palace tradition of the Four Winds kept the Greek Anemoi — Boreas, Zephyrus, Eurus, and Notus — as civic ornaments; this figure is the southern member of that quartet, the classical south wind translated into Central European stone.
captions.steen-erysichthon-sells-his-daughter-mes: Rijksmuseum oil: Steen stages Ovid's cruel sequel — Erysichthon, wasting under Demeter's hunger-curse, sells shape-shifting Mestra for food. Sacrilege rewritten as market-day desperation.
captions.stella-semiramis-called-to-arms: Stella's Lyon canvas: Semiramis rising from her toilet to answer the call of war — the same anecdote Guercino painted, in French classical calm.
captions.telethusa-and-iphis-pray-to-isis: Another Metamorphoses plate of the same prayer — Telethusa as the mother who dared Isis rather than expose the infant.
captions.the-death-of-king-laius: This anonymous oil in the National Galleries of Scotland (NG 1829) returns to the crossroads murder: the Theban king cut down on the road from Corinth. Without a named painter, the canvas still carries Laius as the first casualty of the Labdacid curse — the father Oedipus must discover he has already killed.
captions.the-death-of-pentheus-from-ovid-s-metamo: A Metropolitan Museum plate after Ovid titles the horror plainly: Pentheus torn by his mother and sisters — Agave's madness as a set-piece of the Metamorphoses cycle.
captions.the-harpies-driven-from-the-table-of-kin: A Metropolitan Museum print names both Boreads at Phineus' table: Calais and Zetes scatter the Harpies — the Argonautic rescue fixed as a titled engraving for collectors of the Metamorphoses cycle.
captions.the-infant-jupiter-fed-by-the-goat-amalt: Louvre nursing scene: Amalthea feeds the hidden thunderer — the Cretan childhood that will end Cronus' reign.
captions.thulden-ulysses-receiving-the-winds-in-a: A Metropolitan Museum print from the Odyssey cycle shows Hippotades Aeolus handing Odysseus the sealed bag of contrary winds — the gift that will almost bring the hero home until his crew opens it. This is the Homeric wind-keeper of the floating island, not a later Roman conflation.
captions.vazquez-the-erinyes: Vázquez paints the Furies as a Spanish Mannerist trio — Megaera with Alecto and Tisiphone as winged tormentors, the named Erinyes of the later mythographic lists.
captions.vecchia-tiresias-transformed-into-a-woma: Della Vecchia's Tiresias transformed into a woman — the snake-strike that begins the quarrel of Hera and Zeus and ends in blindness.
captions.vouet-euterpe-the-muse-of-music-and-lyri: A Baroque single-figure portrayal by Simon Vouet, court painter to Louis XIII, isolating Euterpe from her eight sisters to celebrate her alone. The Muse of music and lyric poetry is shown absorbed in playing a wind instrument, the Renaissance and Baroque heir to the double flute (aulos) that classical tradition assigned her. Vouet's warm palette and turning, sculptural pose give the abstract personification a living presence, presenting Euterpe as the divine source of melody whom poets invoked for inspiration.
captions.wijnen-medea-rejuvenating-eson: Dutch cabinet painting of Medea's laboratory: Aeson (Eson) as the patient of Colchian magic — the father for whose throne Jason sailed, restored before the Pelias daughters ask for the same rite.
captions.young-mercury-stealing-cattle-from-apoll: Rijksmuseum panel: the child Mercury leading Apollo's herd — the Hymn's dawn cattle-raid restaged as Dutch cabinet myth.
captions.poussin-stormy-landscape-with-pyramus-an: Poussin's stormy landscape — the lovers under the mulberry, Ovid's Babylonian tragedy as classical weather.
captions.dujardin-pallas-athene-visits-invidia: Oil on wood (Akademie der bildenden Künste, Vienna): Athena descends into the cave of Invidia to send envy against Aglauros, the Ovidian episode (Metamorphoses 2.760–796) that gave Latin literature its fullest portrait of the daimon Hyginus lists as Zelus. Dujardin's small cabinet picture stages that Roman Invidia as a living body of rivalry — Zelus under his Latin name.
captions.kircher-typhon-from-oedipus-aegyptiacus: Kircher's Typhon from Oedipus Aegyptiacus — early-modern scholarship's face for Hesiod's youngest challenger of Zeus.
captions.sueur-clio-euterpe-and-thalia: Painted for the cabinet de l'Amour of the Hôtel Lambert in Paris and now in the Musée du Louvre, this canvas groups three of the nine Muses in a serene woodland. At the center sits Euterpe, Muse of music and lyric song, identified by the wind instrument she holds — the reed pipe descended from the ancient aulos that is her constant attribute — flanked by Clio with her book of history and Thalia with the mask of comedy. Le Sueur's restrained classicism makes Euterpe the harmonious pivot of the trio, embodying the music that the Greeks held the Muses to inspire in poets and singers.
captions.sueur-the-muse-calliope-clio-euterpe-and: From a cycle of the Muses painted by the French Baroque master Eustache Le Sueur for the Hôtel Lambert in Paris and now in the Louvre, this panel presents Calliope amid her sisters, identified by the attributes of epic poetry. Crowned and absorbed in study, she holds the book and writing instruments that mark her as the chief of the Muses and the inspiration of Homeric song. Le Sueur's serene, classicizing composition reflects the seventeenth-century French reverence for the Muses as guardians of poetry and learning, with Calliope foremost among them as 'the eldest' invoked by Hesiod and the epic poets.
captions.sueur-the-muse-terpsichore: Painted by the French Baroque master Eustache Le Sueur and now in the Musee des Beaux-Arts in Marseille (a version of his Louvre Muses cycle), this canvas isolates Terpsichore, the Muse of dance and choral song, from the nine-Muse cluster. She is shown seated and turning gracefully as if caught mid-movement, holding her traditional attribute the lyre, the instrument whose rhythm governs the dancing chorus over which she presides. The poised, dance-ready posture embodies her name, 'she who delights in dance'.
captions.bourdon-the-sacrifice-of-iphigenia: Bourdon's Aulis canvas gathers the priestly circle around the altar where Calchas names Artemis' price — the seer whose reading turns Agamemnon's fleet into a daughter's death.
captions.desubleo-ulysses-and-nausicaa: Desubleo's Bolognese oil gathers Nausicaa and her companions around the half-naked stranger — the Homeric ball game interrupted by awe. The princess's calm gesture steadies the scene as Athena's plan unfolds.
captions.blommendael-paris-and-oenone: Blommendael's Dutch canvas returns to the lovers on Mount Ida: Paris crowned with flowers, Oenone the river-nymph who will outlive his betrayal. Baroque pastoral keeps her as the abandoned healer of the Trojan cycle.
captions.castiglione-deucalion-and-pyrrha: Castiglione's Denver canvas isolates the couple in a rocky waste as they throw their 'mother's bones' — the stones of earth that rise as men and women after Zeus' flood.
captions.diepenbeeck-amphion: From the Temple of the Muses series: Amphion with his lyre — the Theban twin whose music, Hermes-gifted, made masonry follow the tune.
captions.poussin-achilles-on-skyros: Nicolas Poussin's late Baroque canvas of 1656 stages the moment Odysseus, disguised as a merchant, exposes Achilles hidden among the daughters of Lycomedes on Scyros: as the hero seizes a sword from the peddler's wares, his disguise falls away. Deidamia, the king's daughter who has secretly borne Achilles a son, stands among the startled women, her closeness to the unmasked hero marking her apart from her sisters. Painted with Poussin's measured classical gravity, the work hangs in the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, Richmond (acc. 57.2), and renders the episode that binds Deidamia forever to the father of Neoptolemus.
captions.lorrain-acis-and-galatea: Claude's golden pastoral: the lovers at ease before the Cyclops' jealousy — Sicilian idyll as classical landscape.
captions.velazquez-las-hilanderas-the-fable-of-ar: Velázquez's Prado masterpiece folds the weaving contest into a tapestry workshop — Athena's challenge and Arachne's pride as Baroque art about art itself.
captions.poussin-blind-orion-searching-for-the-ri: Poussin's Metropolitan landscape — blind Orion carried toward the healing sunrise, the hunter's myth as cosmic weather.
captions.rembrandt-philemon-and-baucis: The moment the old couple see leaves sprouting from each other's limbs — oak and linden guarding the temple ever after.
captions.baur-althaea-casts-the-brand-of-meleager: An illustration to Ovid's Metamorphoses by the German etcher Johann Wilhelm Baur, published in 1659, capturing the irreversible instant in which Althaea hurls the hidden firebrand back into the flames. By destroying the log on which Meleager's life secretly depended, she avenges the brothers her son had slain — and at the same moment dooms herself, for in most tellings she dies of grief once the deed is done. Baur, known for his finely detailed small-scale etchings, distils the whole tragic mechanism of the myth into a single domestic hearth scene.
captions.velazquez-mercury-and-argus: Velázquez's Prado fable — Argus already asleep as Mercury reaches for the sword, Io's prison about to open.
captions.carpioni-artemis-and-chione: Carpioni's Blanton canvas pairs the huntress with her victim — Chione of Daedalion's house as Venetian Baroque myth.
captions.carpioni-liriope-bringing-narcissus-befo: A second Carpioni treatment of the same Metamorphoses III consultation: Liriope, the river-nymph mother, and the prophet who answers with a riddle. Together the canvases form the rare early-modern gallery that names Liriope rather than only her self-doomed son.

Carpioni’s Kunsthistorisches Museum canvas (GG 1646) shows the naiad Liriope presenting infant Narcissus to blind Tiresias — Ovid’s opening of the Echo myth. Venetian color keeps the mother visible as the figure who asks the fatal question: will the boy live long if he never knows himself?
captions.giordano-vulcan-s-forge-the-forge-of-vul: In this Baroque painting of about 1660 the Neapolitan master Luca Giordano shows the underground workshop of Vulcan as a scene of tremendous physical labour: the Cyclopes, the god's gigantic one-eyed assistants, swing their hammers in unison to beat out the thunderbolts of Jupiter on a glowing anvil. Hesiod's Theogony makes these forge-Cyclopes — Brontes, Steropes and Arges — the very smiths who armed the sky-god with his lightning, and Giordano captures the din of their work, the sparks and the strain of their bodies, turning the myth of Brontes and his brothers into a study of heat, muscle and elemental force.
captions.rosa-glaucus-and-scylla: Rosa's dark coastal drama: transformed Glaucus stretches toward Scylla on a rocky shore while the sea behind them promises Circe's revenge — Ovid as a storm of desire.
captions.sirani-melpomene-the-muse-of-tragedy: The Bolognese Baroque painter Elisabetta Sirani gives Melpomene an intimate, half-length treatment, distinct from the towering ancient statues. The Muse turns toward the viewer holding the tragic mask, her contemplative expression and rich drapery translating the gravity of tragedy into the warm chiaroscuro of seventeenth-century Bologna. As one of the most celebrated women artists of her age, Sirani revisits a classical personification and reclaims it through her own hand, locating Melpomene among the long line of painters who depicted the Muses to allegorize the arts.
captions.zanchi-sisyphus: The Venetian Baroque painter crowds the eternal sentence into a dark, muscular canvas: Sisyphus locked against the rock that will always roll back down. Oil on canvas in the Mauritshuis, The Hague (inv. 335) — the crafty king of Corinth reduced to raw, repeating effort.
captions.bol-aeneas-before-latinus: Bol’s Rijksmuseum canvas (SK-A-614) shows Aeneas received at Latinus’ court — embassy, gifts, and the king who must weigh an oracle against Turnus’ claim. Dutch classicism keeps Latinus the seated authority of Latium’s first contact with Troy.
captions.mitelli-sinon-as-a-captive-before-the-wa: Mitelli's engraving after the Carracci Aeneas frieze in Palazzo Fava shows Sinon bound and brought before the Trojans — the staged prisoner whose confession will persuade them to drag the horse inside. The print freezes the moment deceit puts on the mask of vulnerability.
captions.bray-the-discovery-of-achilles-among-the: Jan de Bray's oil of 1664, drawn from Ovid's Metamorphoses, captures the pivotal scene on Scyros: Odysseus and his companions watch as Achilles, raised in girlish disguise among Lycomedes' daughters, snatches up a weapon and reveals himself. The painter gathers the women in animated reaction, and within their company is Deidamia, the princess who had become the secret companion of the hidden hero and the mother of his child. Measuring 129 by 179 cm, the work is preserved in the National Museum in Warsaw (inv. M.Ob.530).
captions.maes-athamas-tearing-apart-his-children: A pen-and-wash design for Ovid's Metamorphoses: Athamas dashes Learchus against the palace while Ino flees with Melicertes and Tisiphone still haunts the stair — the Fury's visit made legible as domestic slaughter.
captions.poussin-apollo-in-love-with-daphne: Poussin's unfinished Louvre late masterpiece gathers the Ovidian episode into lucid classical landscape: Apollo pursues, Daphne flees toward her river-father, metamorphosis begins at the grove's edge.
captions.rosa-astraea-leaves-the-earth-the-depart: Salvator Rosa's canvas (Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna, GG 9823) depicts Astraea, the star-maiden aspect of Dike, abandoning a corrupt humanity at the close of the Golden Age. As mortals descend into violence and injustice she withdraws from the earth to ascend into the heavens, where, following Ovid and Aratus, she becomes the constellation Virgo. The work captures the elegiac other half of Dike's myth: the just virgin who, unable to bear the wickedness of men, departs the world for the sky.
captions.wolfgang-jove-turns-lycaon-into-a-wolf: Etching on laid paper (15 × 14.6 cm) by the German printmaker Georg Andreas Wolfgang the Elder, in the National Gallery of Art, Washington. The small plate illustrates the same episode from Ovid's Metamorphoses: enthroned Jupiter unleashes his thunderbolt over the table of the Arcadian king Lycaon, whose body contorts into lupine form as his house collapses around him. A characteristically dense seventeenth-century narrative engraving, it folds the banquet, the divine wrath, and the transformation into a single frame as part of an illustrated Ovidian series.
captions.zanchi-myrrha-and-cinyras: Zanchi's Baroque crime — the incest that begets Adonis and drives Myrrha into the myrrh-tree.
captions.marsy-the-latona-fountain-versailles: A monumental fountain in the gardens of Versailles, with sculpture by the brothers Gaspard and Balthazar Marsy. It depicts Latona, the Roman name of Leto, with her children Apollo and Diana, appealing to Jupiter as the Lycian peasants who insulted her are transformed into frogs, an episode told in Ovid's Metamorphoses. The subject is often read as a political allegory for Louis XIV, the triumph of royal order over insolence and revolt.
captions.eeckhout-vertumnus-and-pomona: Eeckhout, Rembrandt's pupil, paints Pomona half-turned toward the god's disguise — soft Dutch light on Ovid's autumn romance. Google Art Project scan of the orchard pair.
captions.giordano-picus-and-circe: Giordano's Picus and Circe — the Ausonian king before the cup that will leave Canens singing herself into air.
captions.gole-the-bronze-age-l-aage-d-airain: Rijksmuseum print from a Four Ages series: the Bronze Age as armed strife — Hesiod's ash-born warriors who destroy one another.
captions.lairesse-eteocles-and-polynices-admonish: Rijksmuseum print (CC0): Jocasta stands between her warring sons, pleading for peace before the Seven march on Thebes. The queen as mediator — the mother who cannot stop the brothers' mutual slaughter that will leave Creon the throne.
captions.lairesse-hermes-ordering-calypso-to-rele: Rijksmuseum oil: Mercury delivers Zeus' command — the order that ends seven years on Ogygia.
captions.liberi-jupiter-and-asteria: The Venetian painter Marco Liberi stages Zeus's pursuit of the Titaness Asteria, sister of Leto: the god descends upon the starry nymph who, in Apollodorus and later mythographers, fled his advances and became the floating island later called Delos. Held in the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest, the canvas is among the rare Baroque treatments that name Asteria herself rather than only her island aftermath.
captions.steen-the-sacrifice-of-iphigenia: Steen's Dutch Baroque Aulis — crowd, priest, and victim packed into the moment before Artemis' intervention.
captions.marsy-fountain-of-enceladus: Marsy's gilded-lead Giant writhes under rock in the Versailles bosquet — Enceladus buried as at Etna, water standing in for volcanic fire. Photographed by Eugène Atget for the Cleveland Museum of Art.
captions.leclerc-king-polydectes-petrified-by-the: Leclerc's engraving — King Polydectes petrified, the return that frees Danae and Dictys.
captions.bloemaert-minerva-and-cecrops: This Baroque engraving by Cornelis Bloemaert (c. 1603-1692), after a design by Pietro da Cortona, shows Minerva (the Roman Athena) appearing before Cecrops, the legendary serpent-tailed first king of Athens. It belongs to the series 'Heroicae virtutis imagines' (Images of Heroic Deeds) published by Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi, reproducing the lunette frescoes of the Sala di Venere in the Palazzo Pitti, Florence. The pairing of goddess and king evokes Cecrops' role as Athena's earthly partner: the king who judged her victory over Poseidon and established her worship in the new city of Athens. The print is held in the British Museum's Prints and Drawings collection.
captions.colombel-atalanta-and-hippomenes: Colombel's late-Baroque runners restage the footrace — the huntress who races suitors to the death, slowed by gold that will cost them both.
captions.giordano-perseus-turning-phineus-and-his: After Giordano — Perseus raising Medusa's head at the wedding, Phineus and his men freezing mid-assault.
captions.lairesse-achilles-discovered-among-the-d: Lairesse’s Mauritshuis painting freezes the trumpet-and-weapons test in Lycomedes’ hall — Achilles seizing steel while the king’s daughters scatter. Dutch classicism made Skyros’ court the European image of the concealed hero.
captions.lairesse-selene-and-endymion: Lairesse's Rijksmuseum overmantel: Cupid's torch leads Selene to Endymion while the moon breaks through cloud — lunar desire painted for a royal bedchamber.
captions.lubieniecki-circe-turning-king-picus-int: Lubieniecki — Circe turning King Picus into a woodpecker, Ovid's Latin metamorphosis of love refused.
captions.luyken-jupiter-in-the-guise-of-amphitryo: A pen-and-ink drawing by the Dutch printmaker and poet Jan Luyken (1649–1712), now in the Städel Museum, Frankfurt. It renders the same pivotal moment of Alcmene's story told by Apollodorus: Zeus assumes the exact form of her husband Amphitryon and is received by the unsuspecting Alcmene. The intimate, small-scale sheet (roughly 158 by 203 mm) treats the divine masquerade as a quiet domestic scene rather than a triumphant mythological tableau.
captions.maratta-alpheus-and-arethusa: Maratta paints the river-god in pursuit — Alpheus of Elis hunting the Naiad whose spring on Ortygia he will still seek beneath the sea.
captions.mehus-the-apple-of-discord-thrown-among-: The Flemish-Italian Baroque painter Livio Mehus stages Eris's insult as airborne drama: the golden apple flies into the assembly of the gods while Discord herself still hangs in the air. The canvas isolates the instant before Hera, Athena and Aphrodite claim the prize — strife as a projectile aimed at Olympus.
captions.wijnen-phineus-interrupting-the-wedding-: Van Wijnen's interruption — the uncle's claim on the bride answered by the Gorgon's stare.
captions.brissart-frontispiece-of-moliere-s-amphi: Engraved frontispiece for the 1682 printed edition of Molière's comedy Amphitryon, itself drawn from Plautus's comic treatment of the myth. The scene crystallizes the legend's central deception: the god Jupiter (Zeus), having taken on the exact likeness of the Theban general Amphitryon, descends from Olympus borne on an eagle, with Mercury (Hermes) beside him, to intrude upon the mortal household. Amphitryon's identity — usurped and doubled by the disguised god while Alcmene is misled — is the engine of the whole drama, making this image one of the most reproduced early-modern depictions of the Amphitryon story.
captions.lorrain-ascanius-shooting-the-stag-of-sy: Claude's late Ashmolean landscape restages Aeneid 7: Ascanius' arrow kills Silvia's stag and lights the war in Latium — the boy's hunt as the spark that turns Trojan refugees into Italian enemies.
captions.picart-the-furies-urge-althaea-to-burn-m: Etched and engraved by Bernard Picart after a design by the French court painter Charles Le Brun, this print from a Meleager series shows two vengeful deities — the Furies — pressing the anguished Althaea to throw the wooden brand into the fire. The image dramatises the moral agony at the heart of the myth: the mother torn between love for her son and grief for the brothers he has killed, goaded by the powers of vengeance to destroy her own child. Picart produced the drawings and prints while overseeing the translation of Le Brun's Meleager tapestries into engravings; this impression is in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam.
captions.giordano-acis-and-galatea: Giordano stages Ovid's Sicilian triangle at the fatal instant: Galatea with Acis while Polyphemus looms with the rock that will crush him.
captions.seiter-diana-next-to-the-corpse-of-orion: Seiter's Diana beside Orion's corpse — the goddess and the giant she loved and killed, before the stars took him up.
captions.weissenkircher-helios-on-his-chariot: Weissenkircher's Baroque detail shows Helios driving the four-horse solar team across the sky — the daily circuit of the sun god as ceiling splendour.
captions.granier-ino-and-melicertes-ino-frappee-d: A near three-metre marble group carved for Louis XIV's gardens by the sculptor Pierre Granier, standing in the demi-lune beside the Apollo Basin in the Park of Versailles. It captures the climactic instant of the myth: Ino, driven mad by Juno (Hera), plunging from the cliff into the sea clutching her infant son Melicertes. Conceived as part of the grand iconographic programme of Versailles, it is among the most monumental surviving depictions of the child whose drowning transformed him into the sea-god Palaemon, honoured ever after at the Isthmus of Corinth.
captions.rayol-ino-queen-of-thebes-leucothea: Rayol's white marble for the Bosquet des Dômes at Versailles shows Ino transformed into the sea-goddess Leucothea, receiving sailors' offerings. Cadmus' daughter who leapt with Melicertes rises here as protectress of those who sail — Theban queen remade as white goddess of the surf.
captions.giordano-aeneas-and-turnus: The final duel of Aeneid 12: Aeneas faces Turnus — the cost of founding Latium paid in the Rutulian king's blood.
captions.houasse-morpheus-awakening-as-iris-draws: Oil on canvas by Rene-Antoine Houasse, commissioned in 1688 for the Chamber of Sleep at the Grand Trianon, Palace of Versailles. The painting shows the rainbow-goddess Iris descending on a cloud to the cavern of Sleep, where she rouses Morpheus, chief of the Oneiroi, the dream-shaping sons of Somnus. The scene follows Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book XI): at Juno's bidding Iris orders Morpheus to take on the likeness of the drowned Ceyx and visit his widow Alcyone in a dream. Houasse presents the Oneiros as a winged, languid youth surrounded by sleeping putti, the classic Baroque image of a dream-god summoned to his nightly errand.
captions.granier-ino-and-melicertes: Granier's marble group for the demi-lune of Apollo's Basin at Versailles shows Ino with Melicertes at the moment of their sea-change. Mother and child become Leucothea and Palaemon — the Theban flight cast in stone for Louis XIV's gardens.
captions.kraus-ascalaphus-turned-into-an-owl: Baroque engraving for Ovid's Metamorphoses: Ascalaphus, the underworld witness of the pomegranate, becomes the screech-owl — Demeter and Persephone's punishment made visible.
captions.krauss-anaxarete-turns-to-stone-at-iphis: Krauss freezes Ovid’s climax: Anaxarete watches Iphis’ funeral pass and hardens into stone. The youth’s death is the moral engine of the Cypriot metamorphosis.
captions.laguerre-apotheosis-of-julius-caesar: Laguerre's Chatsworth ceiling: Julius Caesar lifted toward the gods — Baroque apotheosis for the dictator Ovid ends as a star.
captions.coysevox-amphitrite: Coysevox's marble Amphitrite in the Louvre rides a dolphin-borne wave — Poseidon's queen as French Baroque allegory of the sea's calm power.
captions.ricci-phineas-and-the-sons-of-boreas: Ricci's Baroque rescue — Calais and Zetes driving the Harpies from Phineus, Apollonius' episode as Venetian theatre.
captions.lepautre-aeneas-and-anchises: Marble group by Pierre Lepautre in the Musée du Louvre, Paris. Aeneas supports Anchises, who clutches the Palladium — the sacred image that will travel with them from burning Troy toward the destiny Virgil charts for Rome.
captions.altomonte-alexander-cutting-the-gordian-: Altomonte's Baroque history painting packs soldiers and priests around the chariot as Alexander raises his blade over Gordius' inextricable knot. The Phrygian king's wagon — and the prophecy tied to it — become the stage for decisive force.
captions.bertin-the-danaides-in-hell: Bertin's underworld canvas shows the Danaids at their leaking vessels — eternal labour for murdering Aegyptus' sons on their wedding night. The French baroque scene keeps Aegyptus present as the bereaved twin: his fifty heirs become the crime that fills Tartarus with water that never stays.
captions.boullogne-juno-asking-aeolus-to-release-: Boullogne's painting follows Virgil rather than Homer: Juno bribes the keeper of the winds to wreck Aeneas' fleet. Reception often merges this Aeolus with the Odyssey's Hippotades; the canvas shows how later art kept the wind-king as a single theatrical figure.
captions.coypel-the-apotheosis-of-hercules: Coypel's oil restages the cloud-borne ascent: the labourer of Trachis and Oeta lifted among the immortals — Hesiod's Hebe-wedding afterlife in French classical colour.
captions.guidobono-medea-rejuvenates-aeson: Guidobono paints Ovid's miracle: Medea restores Jason's aged father Aeson with her cauldron-brew — the Iolcan king made young again while Pelias still waits for the same gift.
captions.halbax-the-feast-of-atreus-and-thyestes: This Baroque mural at Zákupy Castle stages the Thyestean banquet: Atreus serving his brother the flesh of Thyestes' own children. The painting makes Atreus the host of horror — the king whose revenge taught Europe how far a Mycenaean feud could go. Wall painting, Zákupy Castle.
captions.hoet-pan-and-syrinx: Hoet's Google Art Project panel: Pan and the nymph among trees and water — Dutch golden-age quiet before the reeds become the syrinx.
captions.po-the-fight-between-aeneas-and-king-tur: LACMA print from the Aeneid cycle: Aeneas and Turnus locked in combat — Rome's founding war as graphic epic.
captions.baur-philomela-and-procne-showing-the-he: Engraving by Johann Wilhelm Baur from a 1703 illustrated edition of Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book VI, lines 621-647). It dramatizes the moment of revenge in which Philomela and her sister Procne reveal to the Thracian king Tereus that the banquet he has just eaten was the flesh of his own son Itys, holding up the boy's severed head. Baur's tightly packed Baroque composition condenses the table, the shocked king, and the avenging sisters into a single charged scene, just before all three are metamorphosed into birds.
captions.solimena-aurora-taking-leave-of-tithonus: Francesco Solimena's Aurora taking leave of Tithonus — the dawn goddess rising from the bed of her immortal, aging lover.
captions.houasse-minerva-and-arachne: Houasse's Versailles canvas from the Story of Minerva cycle: the goddess confronts Arachne at her loom — Ovid's contest as court allegory of skill and hubris.
captions.picart-jupiter-and-asteria-jupiter-as-ea: Picart's Paris etching-engraving, now in the Rijksmuseum (RP-P-OB-51.261), shows Jupiter in eagle form wrestling with Asteria before her metamorphosis. The print crystallizes the same flight-and-capture tradition that makes the Titaness the mythic seed of Delos — Zeus as raptor, Asteria still in human shape.
captions.ricci-selene-and-endymion: In this exuberant Venetian Rococo composition, Sebastiano Ricci paints the moon goddess Selene descending through a luminous sky in her chariot to visit the sleeping Endymion, whose eternal youth and beauty Zeus has preserved in unending sleep. Putti and billowing drapery animate the heavens while the shepherd reclines below with his flock, his crook beside him, oblivious to the divine visitation. Ricci's airy palette and dynamic diagonal of swirling clouds capture the tender, recurring nocturnal union of immortal and mortal that lies at the heart of the myth.
captions.lemoyne-the-death-of-hippolytus-la-mort-: Lemoyne's Louvre marble — Poseidon's sea-bull wrecks the chariot, the death Ovid's inset must reverse before Virbius rises.
captions.watteau-jupiter-and-antiope-nymph-and-sa: Watteau's Louvre painting returns to the same Theban myth: a satyr-like Jupiter discovers the sleeping Antiope. The soft Rococo handling keeps the subject of Zeus' love for the mother of Amphion and Zethus.
captions.panini-alexander-the-great-cutting-the-g: Panini's Walters Art Museum canvas stages Alexander before an altar of Zeus as he slices the yoke-knot on Gordius' wagon at Gordium — the oracle that whoever loosed it would rule Asia. Baroque architecture frames the Phrygian founder's riddle as a single sword-stroke.
captions.balestra-theseus-discovering-his-father-: The Venetian late-Baroque painter Antonio Balestra shows the muscular young Theseus straining to heave aside the rock that conceals his father's hidden arms, his mother Aethra at his side directing him to the treasure. The dynamic diagonal composition and warm Venetian palette dramatize the heroic effort, but it is Aethra who supplies the narrative key: only she knew where Aegeus laid the tokens, and the painting renders her as the indispensable witness to her son's first feat of strength.
captions.conca-boreas-abducting-oreithyia: The Neapolitan late-Baroque master Sebastiano Conca (1680-1764) stages the rape of Orithyia with theatrical élan: the muscular, wind-borne Boreas clasps the recoiling princess as the two are lifted into a vortex of cloud and billowing cloth. The North Wind had glimpsed Orithyia gathering flowers by the Ilissus near Athens and, finding entreaty useless, seized her by force, carrying her off to Thrace where she bore him the winged Argonauts Zetes and Calais. Conca's luminous palette and dynamic diagonals typify the decorative grandeur prized by his eighteenth-century patrons.
captions.crespi-hecuba-blinds-polymestor: Oil painting by the Bolognese painter Giuseppe Maria Crespi, in the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, Brussels. Hecuba takes her revenge on Polymestor, the Thracian king who murdered her youngest son Polydorus for his gold: with the captive Trojan women she falls upon him and blinds him, a scene told in Euripides' Hecuba and in Ovid's Metamorphoses.
captions.picart-calais-and-zetes-deliver-phineus-: French engraving — the winged sons of Boreas delivering Phineus, the chase that ends the pollution of the feast.
captions.restout-alpheus-and-arethusa: Restout's academic canvas pairs the god and the nymph at the moment of flight — Alpheus as desire that will not stop at the shoreline of Sicily.
captions.sarrabat-hercules-brings-eurystheus-the-: The French Baroque painter Daniel Sarrabat (1666–1748) reimagines a moment from the Labours in oil: Heracles presents the captured girdle of the Amazon queen Hippolyta to King Eurystheus, the prize of the ninth Labour, which Eurystheus had demanded on behalf of his daughter Admete. Where the ancient vases render Eurystheus as a quailing figure in a jar, Sarrabat stages a theatrical court scene in which the hero delivers his trophy before the enthroned, watchful king, casting Eurystheus in his role as the relentless commissioner of Heracles' tasks.
captions.trevisani-urania-muse-of-astronomy: Attributed to the late-Baroque Roman painter Francesco Trevisani, this canvas isolates Urania among the nine Muses as the patroness of the stars. She is shown with the celestial globe and pointer that ancient iconography assigned to her alone, the instruments with which she charts the firmament. Daughter of Zeus and Mnemosyne and named for the 'heavenly' realm (Ourania, 'the celestial one'), she embodies the Greek conviction that the study of the night sky was itself a form of divine inspiration, the Muse turning the order of the heavens into knowledge and song.
captions.troy-pan-and-syrinx: De Troy stages the chase at the riverbank — Syrinx already turning toward the reeds while Pan's desire closes in. French Regency myth as soft pastoral crisis.
captions.hogarth-charon-and-cerberus-the-parcae-m: Hogarth's plate for William King's Pantheon gathers the underworld court: Minos, Rhadamanthus ('Rada'), and Aeacus among Fates and Furies. Eighteenth-century English mythography keeps the Cretan judge in the standard triad of the dead.
captions.ricci-arcas-and-callisto: This shimmering late-Baroque canvas by the Venetian master Sebastiano Ricci (1659–1734) captures the climactic moment of the Arcas myth as told by Ovid (Metamorphoses 2.496–530). The young hunter Arcas, son of Zeus and Callisto, has come upon a she-bear in the Arcadian forest — in truth his own mother, transformed by Juno's jealous curse. Ricci freezes the instant of near-matricide: Arcas stands in a heroic pose with his javelin poised to strike, arrested by the beast's strangely human, pleading gaze. The bear's eyes are rendered with deliberate emphasis, the visual key that reveals an apparent hunting scene to be a tragedy of unwitting recognition. Above, Jupiter is shown intervening to avert the crime and bear both mother and son into the heavens as the constellations Ursa Major and Boötes (Arctophylax, the Bear-warden). Praised for its theatricality and luminous tonality, the work is among the rare paintings to depict Arcas himself rather than the more frequently illustrated seduction or discovery of Callisto.
captions.tiepolo-eteocles-and-polynices-detail: Detail from Tiepolo's treatment of the Theban brothers: armour, gesture, and the locked struggle that leaves both kings dead on the same field. The Venetian painter keeps the duel as a flash of Baroque motion — Eteocles still the brother who held the city, Polynices the exile who came back with the Seven.
captions.boucher-the-death-of-meleager: Painted by the young François Boucher around 1727 and now in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, this oil sketch stages the death of the Calydonian hero Meleager, who wastes away as his mother Althaea burns the fated brand that holds his life. Boucher fills the chamber with the stricken women of the house of Oeneus — the Meleagrids, the hero's grieving sisters. Among them are Gorge and Deianira, the only two daughters whom Ovid (Metamorphoses 8.542-546) says were spared transformation into birds; the rest of the sorrowing sisters were turned by Latona into guineafowl. Gorge is thus a constant, if rarely named, presence in this most painted of Calydonian scenes.
captions.boucher-the-death-of-meleager-la-mort-de: An early history painting by François Boucher, made during his years in Italy and now in the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Rennes. The young Calydonian hero Meleager collapses at the left, his strength ebbing as his mother Althaea consumes the fated brand on which his life depends; his grieving household presses around the couch. Among the women gathered at the dying hero's side is his wife Cleopatra (Alcyone), daughter of Idas and Marpessa — the wife whom Homer makes pivotal to Meleager's story and who, Apollodorus tells, hanged herself in grief after his death. Boucher renders the moment in warm, fluid Baroque drama, with anxious attendants and a dog completing the deathbed group.
captions.wit-jupiter-and-mnemosyne: An oil by Jacob de Wit in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (SK-A-3886). Jupiter, disguised as a shepherd, courts Mnemosyne in a pastoral landscape while his eagle wheels above — the nine nights that will father the Muses staged as Rococo gallantry, Memory herself the object of divine pursuit.
captions.scotin-orion-libretto-frontispiece: Engraved frontispiece for Lacoste's opera Orion: the hunter and Diana framed for the stage — the myth as Parisian libretto ornament.
captions.solimena-boreas-abducting-oreithyia: Solimena paints the North Wind carrying Oreithyia — the abduction that begets Chione, Cleopatra, Zetes and Calais. Chione is the snow-daughter of that Thracian marriage, mother of Eumolpus by Poseidon.
captions.solimena-boreas-abducting-oreithyia-vien: Kunsthistorisches Museum version of the same rape: the founding scene of Chione's Boread house.
captions.pittoni-the-sacrifice-of-polyxena-a14efe: A second Pittoni version in the Hermitage — the maiden led to the tumulus, the priest's steel, Hecuba's last child taken from her arms.
captions.solimena-the-abduction-of-orithyia: Francesco Solimena (1657-1747), the leading painter of late-Baroque Naples, depicts the episode from Ovid's Metamorphoses in which Boreas, god of the North Wind, abducts Orithyia, daughter of the Athenian king Erechtheus, from amid her attendant maidens after she has refused his suit. Fluttering cupids attend the passion-driven flight, while Solimena's signature contrasts of flickering light and shadow heighten the maiden's distress. A version after the artist's compositions of the early eighteenth century, the painting is held in the Walters Art Museum, Baltimore.
captions.lemoyne-the-apotheosis-of-hercules: Versailles Salon d'Hercule ceiling: after Oeta's pyre, Hercules is received on Olympus by Jupiter and Juno — the death that becomes godhead painted as Rococo triumph.
