captions.telemachus-and-nestor-embracing: Dutch embrace — Telemachus and Nestor, the old counsellor's welcome that Homer makes the foil to every wrecked return.
captions.picart-alcyone-and-ceyx-transformed-into: Picart's engraving of the climax: Alcyone finds Ceyx's body and both become kingfishers — the origin of the halcyon days.
captions.pittoni-the-sacrifice-of-polyxena: Pittoni's Rococo staging — Polyxena at Achilles' tomb, Neoptolemus and the grieving Trojans, the rite Ovid placed on the Thracian shore before the fleet sailed home.
captions.pittoni-polyxena-before-the-tomb-of-achi: Louvre Pittoni: Polyxena stands before Achilles' tomb as the Greeks close in — the sacrifice delayed one breath into a luminous Venetian tableau.
captions.pittoni-the-sacrifice-of-polyxena-at-the: Pittoni's Stuttgart canvas — Achilles' sepulchre in the background, the virgin's voluntary death before the son of the hero whose shade demanded her.
captions.coypel-fury-of-achilles: Coypel's fury scene from the Trojan cycle — Achilles' rage that drives him into Scamander's flood in the Iliad's river battle.
captions.nattier-thalia-muse-of-comedy: In this Rococo allegory the French court portraitist Jean-Marc Nattier presents Thalia, the Muse of comedy and pastoral poetry, as a smiling young woman crowned with an ivy wreath and holding the grinning comic mask that is her defining attribute. The mask and the lighthearted, idyllic mood announce her domain over comedy and bucolic song, distinguishing her from her tragic sister Melpomene; the picture belongs to the eighteenth-century vogue for portraying living sitters in the guise of the nine Muses.
captions.tocque-allegorical-portrait-of-urania-mu: In this elegant Rococo allegory, the French portraitist Louis Tocqué casts his sitter in the guise of Urania, the Muse who presided over astronomy and the order of the heavens. She rests one hand upon a celestial globe — her unmistakable attribute, its surface marked with the constellations — while the other holds a slender pointer for tracing the stars, the small compass-like instrument by which she measures the sky. The conceit of the 'portrait historié,' dressing a noblewoman as the heavenly Muse, flatters her learning by aligning her with the daughter of Zeus and Mnemosyne who, in Hesiod's Theogony, sings of the wheeling cosmos.
captions.zuccarelli-cadmus-killing-the-dragon: Zuccarelli's Arcadian kill: Cadmus spears Ares' serpent at the spring — Ovid's bloody prelude to the sowing that will found Thebes.
captions.troy-jason-taming-the-bulls-of-aeetes: De Troy's Jason taming Aeëtes' fire-breathing bulls — the first Colchian labour Medea's charms let him survive.
captions.widmann-latona-with-her-children-apollo-: LACMA marble group of the protective mother with the infant twins — Delos' birth translated into Enlightenment collectible form.
captions.batoni-the-infant-hercules-strangling-se: An oil painting by the leading Roman Rococo master Pompeo Batoni (1708–1787) depicting the famous proof of Heracles's divine parentage: the snakes Hera sent against Alcmene's infant twins, which the baby Heracles throttles in his cradle while his mortal brother Iphicles cries out. This episode in the household of Alcmene and Amphitryon first reveals to the family, through the seer Tiresias, that the child is the son of Zeus.
captions.tiepolo-apollo-and-daphne: Tiepolo lightens the chase into Venetian air: Apollo lunges as Daphne's fingers leaf into laurel — Ovid's panic restaged as Rococo luminous theatre.
captions.batoni-achilles-at-the-court-of-lycomede: Batoni’s Uffizi canvas fills Lycomedes’ Skyrian palace with daughters and a disguised Achilles — the king’s court as the stage where Odysseus will unmask the hero. Neoclassical polish keeps Lycomedes the named host of the most painted episode of Achilles’ youth.
captions.batoni-achilles-and-the-centaur-chiron: In this Italian Rococo painting, Pompeo Batoni depicts Chiron instructing the boy Achilles in archery, the centaur's powerful equine body coiled behind his youthful pupil as he steadies the bow. Batoni, the leading history painter of mid-18th-century Rome, treats Chiron not as a wild creature but as a noble preceptor, embodying the Enlightenment ideal of the hero shaped by a wise teacher on the slopes of Pelion.
captions.tiepolo-bellerophon-on-pegasus: Painted for the ceiling of the Palazzo Labia in Venice, Tiepolo's luminous Rococo fresco sends Pegasus soaring through an airy, light-filled sky. The winged horse, bearing the youthful Bellerophon aloft, embodies the Venetian master's love of upward-spiralling, di sotto in sù compositions in which figures seem to float free of gravity. Here Pegasus serves as an allegory of glory and fame ascending toward immortality, his beating wings and pale coat set against luminous clouds. Tiepolo transforms the mythic steed into a vision of weightless triumph characteristic of eighteenth-century ceiling decoration.
captions.doyen-the-sacrifice-of-iphigenia: Doyen's French academic staging of the Cypria/Euripidean rite — the princess on the altar so the ships may sail for Troy.
captions.aeneas-fleeing-troy-with-anchises-creusa: A Metropolitan Museum print after Aeneid 2 names Creusa among the fleeing household — wife, father, and son in the moment before she is lost.
captions.amphion-and-zethus-yusupov-palace: Decorative pair in the Yusupov Palace, Saint Petersburg: Amphion and Zethus as twin founders — Zethus the strength that raised Thebes' walls.
captions.bacchus-and-attendants-visiting-icarus: After-antique visiting scene — Bacchus at Icarius' door with the wine that Attica will learn to fear and celebrate.
captions.batoni-aeneas-fleeing-from-troy: Batoni's flight through the burning streets — the last scion of the house of Troy carrying Anchises from the city's fall.
captions.calvi-chryses-persuading-apollo-to-send-: Chryses persuading Apollo to send the plague — Iliad 1's opening wound: the priest's prayer that empties Achaean ranks.
captions.calvi-chryses-vainly-soliciting-the-retu: Calvi stages Iliad 1: the priest of Apollo Smintheus before Agamemnon's tent — wreaths, ransom, and the refusal that will empty the Achaean camp.
captions.eileithyia-assisting-at-the-birth-of-the: This engraving in the print collection of the Statens Museum for Kunst (KAS320), reproducing an antique relief composition, is titled in the museum catalogue 'Eileithyia helping at the birth of the child Dionysos, with Hermes standing at left.' The goddess of childbirth bends to the newborn god while Hermes waits to carry the infant away, an intimate threshold scene between deliverance and rescue. It shows Eileithyia in her core role beyond the Olympian births: the bringer of light who attends each delivery and hands the new life onward.
captions.erigone-ensnared-by-dionysus: Print of Erigone and the vine — the daughter of Icarius caught in Dionysus' gift that named her grief among the stars.
captions.gamelin-the-return-of-idomeneus: Jacques Gamelin's painting of the Cretan king's nostos, now in the Musée des Augustins (Palais Niel), Toulouse, stages the storm-tossed return that will force Idomeneus into his fatal vow to Neptune. The canvas belongs to the French academic tradition that treated Homeric homecomings as moral dramas of oath, sacrifice, and exile.
captions.giaquinto-medea-rejuvenating-aeson: Giaquinto's Metropolitan Museum canvas stages the Metamorphoses scene: Aeson on the couch as Medea's herbs reverse years — the rightful king of Iolcus briefly returned to youth.
captions.locrian-ajax: French academic study of Ajax Locrien — the Oilean hero whose name means Athena's violated altar.
captions.lusitano-hippolytus-saved-and-named-virb: Vieira Lusitano's Ovid scene — Diana's impulse, Aesculapius' revival, and the new name Virbius in the sacred grove.
captions.odysseus-beats-thersites-iliad-book-ii-p: Plate from an illustrated Pope Iliad: in the assembly of Book II, Odysseus strikes Thersites with Agamemnon's sceptre — the epic's rare punishment of a common soldier for mocking kings.
captions.orestes-and-pylades-before-iphigenia: Rijksmuseum plaque from an Iphigenia series: the recognition scene under Taurian law — Thoas' kingdom as the stage Euripides, Goethe and Gluck never left.
captions.ricci-aurora-and-tithonus: Aurora and Tithonus — the gift of immortality without youth, the dawn forever leaving a diminishing husband.
captions.sterope: Statens Museum for Kunst drawing titled Sterope — the Pleiad named as an individual sister among the Seven Sisters.
captions.telemachus-visits-nestor-at-pylos: Dutch engraving — Telemachus received at sandy Pylos, Odyssey Book 3's safe nostos at Nestor's table.
captions.trautmann-view-of-burning-troy: Trautmann's blazing Troy — the night Virgil names when neighbouring Ucalegon's house already burns, the Trojan counsellor who became a proverb for the neighbour whose roof is on fire.
captions.tiepolo-the-death-of-hyacinth-la-morte-d: Tiepolo's Thyssen canvas updates the fatal sport with tennis racquet and balls — Apollo's grief under a luminous Rococo sky.
captions.batoni-aeneas-fleeing-from-troy-a61b0e: Batoni's neoclassical flight: the Trojan house leaves Ilion with the Penates — exile as polished Roman destiny.
captions.giaquinto-ulysses-and-diomedes-in-the-te: Giaquinto's night raid — Odysseus and Diomedes in Rhesus' tent, Iliad X as Baroque theatre.
captions.tiepolo-latinus-offering-his-daughter-la: Tiepolo stages King Latinus as the host who yields Lavinia to the Trojan stranger — the oracle-bound father of Latium in Aeneid VII. Baroque gesture makes the Latin king the hinge between welcome and the war Alecto will kindle.
captions.lagrenee-the-abduction-of-deianeira-by-t: Exhibited at the Salon of 1755, Lagrenée's polished academic canvas stages the centaur Nessus mid-flight as he carries off Deianira, her arms flung out and her gaze turned back toward the shore in mute appeal for rescue. The French painter balances classical restraint with movement: cool flesh tones and ordered drapery temper the abduction's violence into an elegant, theatrical tableau in the manner of mid-eighteenth-century history painting. The episode is the pivot of Heracles' downfall, for Nessus's dying gift of poisoned blood will later destroy the hero. Oil on canvas, 157 × 185 cm, Musée du Louvre, Paris (INV 5552).
captions.tiepolo-eurybates-and-talthybius-lead-br: Tiepolo's Venetian draft of the seizure: heralds escort Briseis from Achilles' tent — the Iliad's insult painted as airy, cruel pageantry.
captions.tiepolo-the-sacrifice-of-iphigenia: Tiepolo's airy altar: Iphigenia as the price of the voyage — the Cypria's Aulis crisis in Venetian light.
captions.tischbein-acis-and-galatea: Tischbein's Rococo treatment of Ovid's lovers keeps Acis and Galatea in a soft pastoral embrace, the Sicilian myth translated into eighteenth-century elegance before the Cyclops' rock falls.
captions.boucher-jupiter-in-the-guise-of-diana-an: Boucher's Rococo deception: Zeus as Diana embraces Callisto — the assault that will make Arcas, then the Great and Little Bears.
captions.boucher-pan-and-syrinx: Boucher's National Gallery canvas: Pan reaches as Syrinx dissolves into reeds at the Ladon — Rococo flesh for Ovid's Arcadian escape.
captions.albacini-statue-of-isis: Albacini’s Hermitage marble continues the Greco-Roman Isis who crossed from Egypt into the Mediterranean mystery cults — the same goddess Ovid later plants in a Cretan temple to answer Telethusa and remake Iphis. Neoclassical polish keeps Isis as a classical deity of salvation, not a tourist Tutankhamun prop.
captions.lagrenee-ulysses-in-the-palace-of-alcino: Lagrenée stages Odyssey 7: the shipwrecked stranger clasps the knees of Alcinous and Arete — Nausicaa's counsel made into a palace tableau of Phaeacian hospitality.
captions.tiepolo-the-building-of-the-trojan-horse: Tiepolo's companion canvas — Epeius' horse rising on the shore, the stratagem that will empty Priam's halls.
captions.tiepolo-the-procession-of-the-trojan-hor: The end of the house that began with a cow and a Palladium — citizens haul the horse through the gate while the dynasty's last king watches the stratagem close the saga Homer sang.
captions.deshays-the-departure-of-briseis: Deshays stages Briseis leaving Achilles' camp — the captive between tents and heralds, the quarrel's human cost before David's sharper geometry.
captions.wilson-the-destruction-of-the-children-o: Woollett's celebrated engraving after Richard Wilson's 1760 landscape made Niobe a Georgian print sensation — the Theban queen's ruin set in a Claudian vista of rock and storm. British Museum, London.
captions.bracci-oceanus-of-the-trevi-fountain: Colossal marble statue of Oceanus presiding over the central niche of the Trevi Fountain in Rome, carved by Pietro Bracci to Nicola Salvi's design. The sea Titan rides a shell-shaped chariot drawn by winged sea-horses — one calm, one restive — guided by tritons, an allegory of the ocean's changing moods.
captions.tischbein-diana-and-orion: Tischbein circle — Diana and Orion as courtly myth, the hunter still alive in the goddess's company.
captions.bayeu-olympus-the-fall-of-the-giants: Bayeu's Spanish Baroque canvas: the Giants tumble from Olympus as Zeus's lightning clears the mountain — the earthborn revolt restaged for an eighteenth-century ceiling imagination.
captions.carmontelle-jean-baptiste-brizard-as-nar: This watercolour-and-crayon drawing by Louis Carrogis Carmontelle records a Comedie-Francaise performance of Voltaire's Merope, showing the actor Jean-Baptiste Brizard as Narbas in Act III. Narbas is the loyal old servant who, in Voltaire's recasting of the myth, secretly raised Merope's surviving son far from Messenia and protects the family from the usurper Polyphontes - the dramatic counterpart of the guest-friend and the grandfather Cypselus who shelter the infant Aepytus in Hyginus and Apollodorus. The drawing is a vivid eighteenth-century witness to how Merope's revenge saga was staged for the living theatre. Executed in black crayon, sanguine and watercolour; later engraved by Jean-Baptiste Delafosse. Public domain.
captions.halle-the-race-between-hippomenes-and-at: Hallé's Louvre Rococo race: Atalanta hesitates over scattered apples as Hippomenes runs on — Ovid's contest as courtly allegory of love conquering pride.
captions.mengs-helios-as-the-personification-of-m: Mengs paints Helios as Noon for Maria Luisa of Parma's boudoir cycle of the times of day — radiant crown and classical body making the Titan sun into Enlightenment allegory.
captions.west-hector-taking-leave-of-andromache-t: West's engraving freezes Iliad 6: the infant Astyanax shrinks from Hector's crested helmet as Andromache holds him — the child already named 'lord of the city' in the moment his father rides out to die.
captions.west-pylades-and-orestes-brought-as-vict: West's National Gallery canvas turns to Iphigenia in Tauris: the priestess of Artemis faces the two Greek strangers she must sacrifice, not yet knowing one is her brother Orestes. The painting freezes Euripides' recognition drama — the sister Artemis saved at Aulis, now almost the instrument of a second family blood-debt. Oil on canvas, National Gallery, London.
captions.boucher-phocus-receives-cephalus-illustr: A copperplate engraving from the lavish 1767 Paris edition of Ovid's Metamorphoses in Latin and French, illustrating the seventh book. Phocus, the young son of King Aeacus of Aegina and the Nereid Psamathe, welcomes the Athenian envoy Cephalus and the sons of Pallas at the palace. Struck by Cephalus's curious gold-tipped wooden javelin, Phocus asks about its origin, drawing from his guest the sorrowful tale of how that very weapon killed his wife Procris. Phocus is the rare named figure of the Aeacid line to appear in a narrative image at all: best remembered for his death at the hands of his envious half-brothers Peleus and Telamon, he is shown here in the gentler role of attentive host, the listener whose question frames one of the poem's most poignant stories.
captions.greuze-aegina-visited-by-jupiter: In this large Rococo-Neoclassical canvas, the French painter Jean-Baptiste Greuze (1725–1805) renders the moment the nymph Aegina, daughter of the river-god Asopus, is approached by Jupiter (Zeus), who descends to her disguised in the form of a flame or eagle. Aegina reclines in languid, luminous nudity, her body bathed in warm light against shadowed drapery, while the god manifests as a radiant celestial presence above her. The union depicted here will produce Aeacus, the future king of the island that bears her name and grandfather of Achilles. Oil on canvas, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
captions.hamilton-hebe-giving-drink-to-the-eagle-: The Scottish Neoclassical painter and antiquarian Gavin Hamilton depicts Hebe in her Olympian office as cupbearer, here serving not the assembled gods but the great eagle of her father Zeus (Jupiter). Seated amid clouds, the goddess of youth inclines toward the bird with a shallow vessel, the intimacy of the gesture underscoring her domestic place within the divine household of Zeus and Hera. Hamilton's restrained classicism and idealized form are characteristic of the eighteenth-century revival of antique subjects.
captions.lagrenee-mercury-herse-and-aglaurus: Lagrenée's Nationalmuseum canvas: Mercury at the threshold, Herse the prize, Aglauros the envious sister who will turn to stone — Ovid's Cecropid triangle.
captions.brenet-aethra-showing-her-son-theseus-th: Brenet's Troezen — Aethra shows Theseus where Aegeus hid the sword and sandals, the tokens that start the Isthmus road.
captions.kauffmann-hector-taking-leave-of-androma: Kauffmann's Sceafton parting — Hector, Andromache and Astyanax at the Scaean Gate before the champion returns to the wall.
captions.altomonte-aurora-awakening-morpheus: A ceiling or decorative oil by Bartolomeo Altomonte in which Aurora, goddess of dawn, rouses Morpheus from sleep. Light breaks over the dream-god's limbs — the daily contest between daybreak and the architect of dreams, painted for an Austrian Baroque interior.
captions.coustou-hippomenes-and-atalanta: This marble group seizes the climactic instant of the foot-race: the suitor strides forward at full sprint while Atalanta breaks stride to stoop after a golden apple rolling at her feet, her body twisting against the line of the race. The sculptor renders in stone the trick by which the hero — called Melanion in the Arcadian tradition and Hippomenes in the Boeotian — used Aphrodite's apples to overtake the unbeatable runner and claim her as his bride. The work is held in the Musée du Louvre, Paris.
captions.bause-portrait-of-christiane-henriette-k: Johann Friedrich Bause's Metropolitan Museum print shows the actress Christiane Henriette Koch costumed as Pelopia — Thyestes' daughter and mother of Aegisthus in the Atreid horror. Eighteenth-century stage culture kept the Sicyonian tragedy of the sword and the unrecognized incest alive as a role for leading ladies.
captions.fuseli-ixion-worshipping-hera-disguised-: Fuseli again: Ixion before the false Hera — the cloud that will birth Centaurus, father of the wild centaur kind (distinct from wise Chiron).
captions.gandolfi-selene-and-endymion: Bolognese Rococo: Selene leans from the night sky over the eternally sleeping youth — the moon's visit rendered as soft flesh and silver light.
captions.david-jupiter-and-antiope: David's early canvas (Musées de Sens) shows Jupiter as satyr approaching the sleeping Antiope — a Neoclassical essay on the Theban mother whose twin sons will later avenge her against Dirce.
captions.restout-morpheus-sleep: An oil by Jean-Bernard Restout in the Cleveland Museum of Art, exhibited as Morpheus or Sleep. A nude youth sinks into oblivion on dark drapery — the Oneiros who takes human form in dreams reduced to pure, academic repose, the body as the vessel of night.
captions.tischbein-epimetheus-opening-pandora-s-b: Oil by Anton Tischbein in the Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen (KMS1006): Epimetheus himself pries open Pandora's box while ills pour into the world. The canvas shifts Hesiod's agency onto the husband who looked too late.
captions.west-chryseis-returned-to-her-father: West's grand-manner canvas reunites Chryses with his daughter after Apollo's plague forced Agamemnon's hand — the priest's prayer answered, the captive restored beneath the god's statue. A companion piece in the New-York Historical Society's collection, it treats Chryseis as the moral hinge of Iliad Book I.
captions.david-apollo-and-diana-attacking-the-chi: David's Rome prize canvas — Apollo and Diana raining arrows on Niobe's children, the Metamorphoses slaughter as neoclassical terror.
captions.goya-the-rape-of-europa: Young Goya paints Europa's bull-ride with Rococo lightness — the Phoenician princess still aloft on Zeus, the myth that named a continent restaged for an eighteenth-century Spanish wall.
captions.jombert-the-children-of-niobe-killed-by-: Jombert's Prix de Rome — the Niobids falling under Apollo and Diana, Leto's insult paid in a mother's emptied arms.
captions.kauffman-penelope-awakened-by-eurycleia-: Kauffman's Eurycleia waking Penelope — the nurse's news that the beggar is the husband, recognition before the bed-test.
captions.lagrenee-landscape-with-salmacis-and-her: Lagrenée's pastoral landscape nests the fountain encounter in soft trees and water — Salmacis as Rococo desire before the waters fuse the pair.
captions.kauffmann-ariadne-abandoned-by-theseus: Kauffmann isolates the Naxos morning: Ariadne alone on the shore, the thread-giver left after the labyrinth, Catullus' abandoned heroine restaged for neoclassicism.
captions.abildgaard-the-wounded-philoctetes: Abildgaard's Copenhagen canvas — the Lemnos exile whose bow the Little Iliad must fetch before Troy can fall.
captions.antenor-prato-della-valle-padua: Statue of Antenor among Padua's Prato della Valle worthies — the Trojan hero still named as civic ancestor centuries after Homer seated him at the Scaean Gate.
captions.graff-portrait-of-sophie-friederike-seyl: The Swiss-German painter Anton Graff portrays the celebrated actress Sophie Friederike Seyler in the title role of Merope, the Messenian queen whose grief and resolve made her a favourite heroine of eighteenth-century tragedy. Graff captures the actress in costume and in character, embodying the widow of Cresphontes who hides her infant son Aepytus and waits years for revenge on the murderer Polyphontes. Painted in 1775, the portrait belongs to the era when Voltaire's and Maffei's Merope dominated the European stage, and it is one of the most direct surviving images of the figure herself. Hamburger Kunsthalle.
captions.hamilton-priam-pleading-with-achilles-fo: Hamilton's ransom — the old king pleading before the seated hero, the poem's quietest and greatest scene of pity.
captions.lagrenee-helen-recognising-telemachus-so: Lagrenée's neoclassical painting stages Odyssey 4 in Menelaus' hall at Sparta: Helen recognises the prince by his likeness to Odysseus at the feast where the host will tell how Proteus in Egypt revealed that the king of Ithaca still lives. Eidothea does not appear on canvas, but the scene is the direct fruit of her instruction — the first sure news of Odysseus that Telemachus receives on his voyage.
captions.david-the-combat-of-diomedes: Albertina drawing by the young David: Athena-fired Diomedes rampages across the Trojan plain — Iliad 5's aristeia as neoclassical frenzy, the mortal who wounds Aphrodite and Ares.
captions.west-helen-brought-to-paris: West's Helen — the prize Menelaus fought for on the plain while she watched from Troy's wall.
captions.stubbs-the-fall-of-phaeton: Stubbs, the anatomist of horses, paints Phaethon's team thrashing as the chariot breaks — the sun-ride as equine panic and mortal overreach. Oil on canvas, National Trust, Saltram House.
captions.david-the-funeral-of-patroclus: David's funeral pyre — Patroclus' body at the centre of Iliadic grief, the games and sacrifice that follow Hector's kill.
captions.abildgaard-odysseus-takes-counsel-with-t: Abildgaard's counsel at the trench — Odysseus hearing Tiresias among the dead, Nekyia's prophecy of the road home.
captions.barbier-the-birth-of-heracles: A neoclassical composition by the French painter and engraver Jean-Jacques-François Le Barbier (1738–1826) showing the labour and delivery of Heracles. Alcmene reclines as the central figure attended at the birth, with the goddess of childbirth Eileithyia (Lucina) and the cunning servant Galanthis — who, in Ovid's telling, tricks the goddess into releasing the obstructed delivery. The scene illustrates the dramatic difficulty of Heracles's birth caused by the jealous Hera.
captions.binet-cadmus-goes-in-search-of-his-siste: Ovidian print of Cadmus' quest: Agenor's command that his sons find Europa or not return — the Phoenician king's order that empties Tyre and founds Thebes.
captions.fuseli-teiresias-foretells-the-future-to: Fuseli's second Nekyia — Tiresias rising to foretell Poseidon's wrath and the cattle of the Sun.
captions.fuseli-tiresias-appears-to-ulysses-durin: Over the blood-trench the blind seer rises like smoke given shape, and the hero shrinks back sword in hand — the moment the living must ask the dead the way home.
captions.jeune-aeacus-and-telamon: An engraving by the French draughtsman and book illustrator Jean-Michel Moreau le Jeune (1741–1814) showing Aeacus, the pious king of Aegina and son of Zeus by the nymph Aegina, in the company of his son Telamon. Renowned in antiquity for his justice and reverence toward the gods, Aeacus founded a line that would produce the greatest heroes of the Trojan War — through Telamon came Ajax, and through his other son Peleus came Achilles. The composition pairs father and son in the neoclassical idiom of late-eighteenth-century French printmaking, presenting the dynasty's patriarch as the embodiment of righteous kingship.
captions.monnet-telemachus-and-mentor: Monnet's Telemachus and Mentor — Athena in disguise urging the prince against the devouring suitors.
captions.smith-mercury-inventing-the-lyre: Yale Center print: Mercury fashions the tortoise-shell lyre — the Hymn's other dawn invention, the bargain that will buy Apollo's forgiveness.
captions.downman-the-ghost-of-clytemnestra-awaken: Downman stages the sequel the murder demands: the queen's shade rouses the Erinyes against Orestes — blood calling for blood after Agamemnon's death.
captions.goddyn-the-greek-sinon-before-priam: Sinon before Priam: the captive whose false tale persuades Troy to accept the horse — the verbal half of the stratagem.
captions.kauffman-telemachus-and-the-nymphs-of-ca: In this Metropolitan Museum pendant of 1782, Kauffman stages Telemachus among Calypso's nymphs — the island episode from Fénelon's Les Aventures de Télémaque in which the son nearly forgets Ithaca. Pastoral landscape and graceful grouping translate Homeric wandering into Rococo-Neoclassical charm. Together with The Sorrow of Telemachus, the pair became a staple of Anglophone collecting and of Telemachus's afterlife beyond the Odyssey's first four books.
captions.kauffmann-calypso-abandoned-by-odysseus: Kauffmann's Ogygia shore: Calypso watches the ship leave after Hermes' release — immortality offered, home chosen.
captions.regnault-the-education-of-achilles-by-th: Painted for the French academy and now in the Louvre, Regnault's Neoclassical canvas shows the centaur Chiron training the young Achilles in the open air, the muscular tutor demonstrating the use of a weapon while his pupil watches intently. The picture, with its cool clarity and heroic nudity, presents Chiron as the model educator of antiquity, transmitting strength, virtue, and skill to the future hero of the Trojan War.
captions.tischbein-the-muse-euterpe: From Johann Heinrich Tischbein the Elder's series of the Nine Muses (1782), this Neoclassical study depicts Euterpe as Muse of music. Following the iconographic convention codified since antiquity, Tischbein equips her with a flute — the modern stand-in for the aulos, her traditional emblem — marking her out as the one star among the nine-Muse cluster who governs instrumental song. The painting reflects the eighteenth-century revival of the Muses as embodiments of the individual arts, with Euterpe presiding specifically over music and lyric melody.
captions.david-andromache-mourning-hector: David's reception piece: Andromache grieves beside Hector on his bier — the lament that answers the duel and closes the Iliad's greatest death.
captions.derby-penelope-unraveling-her-web: By a single lamp the queen picks the day's weaving apart while Telemachus sleeps and Odysseus' armour gleams in the dark — the nightly untelling that holds a kingdom in suspension.
captions.duclos-merope-act-iv-scene-2-illustratio: This copper engraving by Antoine-Jean Duclos after a design by Jean-Michel Moreau le Jeune illustrates the climactic recognition scene (Act IV, Scene 2) of Voltaire's tragedy Mérope (1743), the most celebrated dramatic retelling of the Messenian saga of Cresphontes. The Heraclid Cresphontes, who had won Messenia by his trick with the lots and made Stenyclerus his seat, is dead before the play begins, murdered with his elder sons by the usurper; his widow Merope, forced into the tyrant's house, raises a weapon over a young stranger she takes for her husband's killer, only to be stopped at the last instant by the old retainer Narbas, who reveals the youth is her own surviving son Aepytus. The image captures the suspended axe and the cry of recognition that turns the avenging blow aside and sets in motion the slaying of the usurper and the recovery of Cresphontes' kingdom.
captions.kauffman-the-sorrow-of-telemachus: Kauffman's Sorrow of Telemachus — the prince's despair under the suitors' siege of his house.
captions.david-the-oath-of-the-horatii: David's oath before battle — the spirit of the sacrificial truce Pandarus' arrow would shatter on the Trojan plain.
captions.duclos-merope-illustration-to-voltaire-s: Surviving ancient art almost never depicts the Messenian Merope, so her image lives chiefly in the great early-modern stage tradition of her story. This engraving by Antoine-Jean Duclos after a design by Jean-Michel Moreau (Moreau le Jeune) was made for the 1784 edition of Voltaire's complete works (Oeuvres complètes, Theatre, vol. III), illustrating his hugely popular tragedy Merope. The play dramatizes exactly the myth recorded by Apollodorus and Hyginus: the widowed queen, forced toward the usurper, who at the climax all but kills her own disguised son before recognizing him. The print stages this tense recognition-and-revenge moment in neoclassical theatrical dress. Held by the ETH-Bibliothek, Zurich; public domain.
captions.gagneraux-the-blind-oedipus-commending-h: Gagneraux's blind king entrusting his children to the gods — the aftermath that Colonus will turn into Athens' hidden blessing.
captions.tischbein-mourning-electra: Tischbein's grieving princess sits in dark classical dress, eyes lowered over the murdered king's memory. The German neoclassical portrait isolates Electra as the Oresteia's mourner-in-chief — the daughter who will not let Agamemnon's death grow quiet. Oil on canvas.
captions.fuseli-danae-and-perseus-on-seriphos: Fuseli's Yale canvas: the chest washes onto Seriphos — Danaë and the infant Perseus delivered from Acrisius' sea sentence to Dictys' shore.
captions.moreau-les-pelopides-voltaire: Moreau's illustration for Voltaire's Pelopid tragedy keeps Aerope's generation on the Enlightenment stage — the adulterous queen still written into the curse that runs from Tantalus to Agamemnon.
captions.peyron-alceste-mourante-the-dying-alcest: Neoclassical oil painting by Jean-François Pierre Peyron in the Musée du Louvre, Paris. Alcestis, queen of Pherae, sinks dying among her grieving family, having volunteered to surrender her own life so that her husband Admetus might be spared the death fated to him. Painted as a pendant to David's 'Death of Socrates,' it became a touchstone of late-eighteenth-century French history painting on the theme of self-sacrifice.
captions.regnault-pygmalion-praying-venus-to-anim: Regnault's Origin of Sculpture shows Pygmalion before Venus, begging life for the ivory maiden — the prayer that precedes the kiss. Painted for the French crown and still at Versailles.
captions.tilliard-hegesippus-summons-philocles-at: An etching from the 1785 Didot edition of Fénelon's Les Aventures de Télémaque shows Idomeneus seated beneath a tree reading a letter while Hegesippus stands beside him. In Fénelon's political romance the Homeric Cretan king becomes a ruler whose court Telemachus must navigate — the mythological Idomeneus translated into Enlightenment didactic fiction.
captions.fuseli-oedipus-cursing-his-son-polynices: Fuseli's storm-lit canvas shows the blind Oedipus blasting Polynices, the exile who has come to Colonus seeking a blessing for his war on Thebes. The painting freezes the curse that will send the Argive-backed brother to mutual slaughter with Eteocles.
captions.canova-psyche-revived-by-cupid-s-kiss: A Neoclassical marble group by Antonio Canova capturing the moment from Apuleius's tale when Cupid revives the lifeless Psyche with a kiss, his wings rising above their embrace. The tender interlocking of the two figures made it one of the most celebrated sculptures of its age. It is now in the Louvre in Paris.
captions.borel-thetis-immerses-her-son-achilles-i: The French painter and printmaker Antoine Borel (1743–1810) returns to the same myth in a Neoclassical key. Thetis is shown lowering the infant Achilles into the dark current of the Styx in the hope of rendering him invulnerable, the river's underworld setting evoked around her. As in every telling, the heel she clasps remains untouched by the water, so the scene quietly fixes the boundary of the Styx's power and the origin of the hero's fatal vulnerability.
captions.david-the-loves-of-paris-and-helen: David's Louvre lovers: the abduction the Judgment purchased — Helen in Paris' chamber as the Cypria's human cost.
captions.kauffmann-a-scene-from-troilus-and-cress: Engraving by Luigi Schiavonetti after Angelica Kauffmann's 1789 painting of Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida, Act V, Scene ii. Troilus watches as Cressida yields to Diomedes — the medieval romance of the Trojan prince restaged as bitter theatrical betrayal.
captions.abildgaard-ismene-and-antigone-plead-wit: SMK Copenhagen: Oedipus' daughters petition Athens' king — Theseus as public monarch of Attica, the hospitable ruler of Colonus and the Panathenaea.
captions.anonymous-creon-king-of-thebes-costume-d: BnF costume maquette labelled Creon roi de Thebes: the Theban king as a late-Ancien Régime stage figure in cloak and crown. Theatre's stock image of the uncle who holds the city after Oedipus falls.
captions.carstens-talos-argonaut-cycle: Carstens' neoclassical plate from the Argonautenzug: Talos as monumental bronze threat — late-eighteenth-century line for the guardian of Crete.
captions.flaxman-apollo-and-marpessa: This marble relief by the English neoclassical sculptor John Flaxman, held by the Royal Academy of Arts in London, renders the abduction with cool linear restraint. Apollo, the radiant god of the lyre and prophecy, strides forward attempting to carry off Marpessa, the Aetolian princess he loved. Flaxman, celebrated for the clarity of his outline drawings after Homer, translates that purity of line into low relief, reducing the violent struggle to elegant, balanced contours. The work belongs to the era's revival of Greek myth as moral and aesthetic ideal, isolating the instant of pursuit before Marpessa would reject the god in favor of the mortal Idas.
captions.flaxman-study-for-the-fury-of-athamas: Flaxman's chalk study for his marble group (Ickworth) abstracts Athamas' frenzy into a neoclassical knot of bodies — the king, the murdered child, and Ino's flight distilled for sculpture.
captions.flaxman-the-fury-of-athamas: This colossal white marble group, carved in Rome by the English Neoclassical sculptor John Flaxman for Frederick Hervey, 4th Earl of Bristol, depicts the climax of Learchus's brief and tragic life. Driven mad by the wrath of Hera, King Athamas seizes his elder son Learchus by the ankle and swings the child overhead to dash him against the rocks, while his wife Ino recoils with the infant Melicertes. The straining, helpless body of Learchus is the dramatic pivot of the composition, his outflung limbs embodying the horror of a father destroying his own son. Commissioned for Ickworth in Suffolk, where it remains in the National Trust collection, the piece took Flaxman more than three years and stands as one of the most ambitious sculptural treatments of the Athamas myth drawn from Ovid's Metamorphoses.
captions.fuseli-perseus-returning-the-eye-of-the-: A pen-and-wash drawing by the Anglo-Swiss Romantic artist Henry Fuseli depicting the close of Perseus's encounter with the Graeae. Where most images fix on the theft of the eye, Fuseli stages its return: having forced the grey sisters to reveal the road to the Gorgons, Perseus restores their single eye to the clustered, eyeless old women. Fuseli's characteristically charged, muscular figures and dramatic chiaroscuro turn the strange shared-eye motif into a moment of taut negotiation between the cunning hero and the primordial daughters of Phorcys and Ceto, sisters and watchful guardians of the Gorgons.
captions.kauffmann-the-death-of-alcestis: Oil painting by the Swiss Neoclassical artist Angelica Kauffmann depicting the deathbed of Alcestis. The scene captures the moment of her sacrificial farewell, surrounded by her mourning husband Admetus and their children, as she gives up her life to ransom his. The subject, drawn from Euripides' tragedy, allowed Kauffmann to dwell on the virtue and conjugal devotion that made Alcestis a model of the faithful wife in antiquity.
captions.kauffmann-venus-induces-helen-to-fall-in: Kauffmann paints the divine persuasion behind the abduction: Venus (Aphrodite) softens Helen toward Paris while Cupid aims his bow. The Hermitage canvas makes Helen's choice a goddess's work — desire staged as mythology rather than mere elopement. Oil on canvas, State Hermitage Museum, Saint Petersburg.
captions.landi-hebe-offering-a-cup-to-jupiter-in-: The Italian Neoclassical painter Gaspare Landi shows the youthful Hebe extending a brimming cup toward Zeus, who has assumed the shape of his sacred eagle. As daughter of Zeus and Hera and cupbearer to the Olympians — the role Homer assigns her in the Iliad, where 'the queenly Hebe poured them nectar' — she embodies eternal youth and the ritual hospitality of the gods. Landi balances tender attention with classical grace, the goddess's flowing robes and the powerful bird forming a harmonious mythological group.
captions.monsiau-the-birth-of-adonis: Monsiau's Myrrha-tree — Adonis born from the bark that hid his mother's crime, Ovid's Cypriot metamorphosis made visible.
captions.nahl-telemachus-recognizes-odysseus-in-t: Oil in the Weimar Schlossmuseum: Nahl stages the recognition of Odysseus by Telemachus inside the swineherd's house, with Eumaeus' steading as the setting Athena chooses for the plot's turning point. The painting keeps the humble hut — not the palace — as the place where the royal family first reunites.
captions.carstens-sorrowful-ajax: Carstens' Neoclassical Ajax broods after losing the armor — wounded honor before the cattle slaughter and the sword.
captions.girodet-the-sleep-of-endymion: Girodet's celebrated Neoclassical canvas, painted in Rome and exhibited at the Salon of 1793, shows the shepherd Endymion stretched out in a languid, almost weightless slumber while a beam of cool moonlight—the disembodied presence of his lover Selene—caresses his nude body. The winged figure of Zephyr parts the branches to admit the goddess's radiance, transforming the silvery light itself into the erotic protagonist. The dreamy androgyny of the sleeping youth and the diffuse luminism mark a deliberate break from David's severe classicism, making the work an early icon of pre-Romantic sensibility. It now hangs in the Louvre, Paris.
captions.meynier-hecuba-discovering-the-body-of-h: Oil painting by the French Neoclassicist Charles Meynier, painted during his Prix de Rome years in Italy and now in the Horvitz Collection. On a stormy shore after Troy's fall, Hecuba stretches toward the washed-up corpse of Polydorus while her companions restrain her — the shock that, in Euripides and Ovid, turns a captive queen toward revenge on Polymestor.
captions.bacciarelli-allegory-of-justice-themis: Bacciarelli's Warsaw allegory: Themis as Justice with scales and sword — divine order translated into the Enlightenment courtroom's emblem.
captions.flaxman-ulysses-and-his-dog: Flaxman's outline engraving for the Odyssey freezes the recognition: Argos lifts his head from the dung-heap as the disguised Odysseus passes — the twenty-year wait ended in a single glance.
captions.kauffman-orpheus-and-eurydice: Angelica Kauffman's Neoclassical canvas softens the catastrophe into tender parting: Orpheus reaches as Eurydice is drawn downward. Painted by one of the eighteenth century's most celebrated women artists, the picture makes Eurydice the emotional centre of the glance that undoes the rescue.
captions.lebrun-portrait-of-anna-pitt-as-hebe: In this mythological portrait, the celebrated French painter Élisabeth Vigée-Lebrun casts her sitter, Anna Pitt, in the guise of Hebe, goddess of youth. The young woman reclines among clouds beside Zeus's eagle, holding aloft the cup of nectar that is Hebe's emblem as cupbearer of the gods. The conceit — flattering a living beauty by likening her to the eternally youthful daughter of Zeus and Hera — was a favorite of eighteenth-century portraiture, and Vigée-Lebrun renders it with luminous color and effortless charm, the eagle's wing sheltering the radiant figure.
captions.singleton-manto-and-tiresias: Singleton's Manto and Tiresias — the blind seer led by his daughter, sight traded for prophetic knowledge.
captions.flaxman-ajax-defending-the-greek-ships-a: Flaxman's outline for Church's Story of the Iliad: Telamonian Ajax alone at the prow while Hector calls for fire — the ship-fight distilled to a single stubborn defence.
captions.flaxman-polydamas-advising-hector-to-ret: Flaxman: Polydamas urges caution at the trench before Hector presses on to the ships — the omen ignored on the road to the fleet.
captions.flaxman-sleep-and-death-conveying-the-bo: A nineteenth-century illustration of the Homeric cortege: Sleep and Death carry Sarpedon home to Lycia — the Iliad's most solemn funeral flight.
captions.flaxman-thetis-calling-briareus-to-aid-z: John Flaxman's neoclassical line engraving illustrates the episode Thetis recounts to Achilles in Iliad I.396-406: when Hera, Poseidon and Athena conspired to bind Zeus, Thetis summoned the hundred-handed giant Briareus, whom the gods call Aegaeon, to Olympus, where his sheer strength so overawed the rebels that they abandoned the plot. Briareus is shown as the towering, many-armed defender of Zeus's rule, the rare Homeric moment in which a Hecatoncheir appears as the gods' ally rather than their primordial weapon against the Titans.
captions.garnier-hippolytus-after-the-confession-: Garnier's Salon canvas — Hippolytus recoiling after Phaedra's confession, the instant that sets Theseus' curse in motion.
captions.head-iris: This study of the rainbow goddess by Guy Head, held by the National Galleries of Scotland (NG 2756), isolates Iris as a winged figure poised in motion against an open sky. Daughter of the Titan Thaumas and the Oceanid Electra, Iris personifies the rainbow itself — the shimmering arc that the ancients saw as her path between the realm of the gods and that of mortals. Head renders her with the buoyant grace of a herald caught mid-descent, the iridescent atmosphere around her standing for the prismatic colours of her sign.
captions.head-iris-carrying-the-water-of-the-rive: Painted around 1793 by the English Neoclassicist Guy Head and now in the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, this canvas shows Iris in full flight, her great wings spread and her drapery streaming as she races across a turbulent sky bearing an ewer of the sacred water of the Styx — the river by which the gods swore their unbreakable oaths. As the swift winged messenger of the Olympians, Iris is the divine courier who runs the errands of heaven; the storm-grey clouds and the goddess's headlong momentum embody her role as the speeding bridge of light between Olympus and the world below.
captions.piroli-otus-and-ephialtes-holding-mars-a: Flaxman/Piroli Iliad plate: the Aloadae bind Ares in a bronze jar for thirteen months — Homer's giant twins overpowering the war-god.
captions.fuseli-odysseus-between-scylla-and-chary: The strait as pure vertigo — the hero braced on a heaving deck between the whirlpool's mouth below and the six-fold shadow falling from above.
captions.fuseli-odysseus-in-front-of-scylla-and-c: In this dramatic oil on canvas (126 × 101 cm, Aargauer Kunsthaus, Aarau), the Swiss-British Romantic Henry Fuseli stages the most perilous moment of Odyssey 12: the passage of the narrow strait between Scylla and divine Charybdis. Odysseus, muscled and heroic, stands braced on the bow of his ship with his shield raised, while his oarsmen strain below to drive the vessel through the churning water. Charybdis is rendered not as a body but as the deadly whirlpool itself — the seething, sucking sea that Homer likens to a cauldron boiling on a great fire — embodying Circe's warning that not even Poseidon could save a man caught when she draws the black water down.
captions.jr-illustration-for-seven-chiefs-against: A preparatory drawing by John Flaxman for his Aeschylean outline series shows the Seven Chiefs Against Thebes in the spare neoclassical line that would dominate nineteenth-century Greek-tragedy illustration. Parthenopaeus belongs to that doomed company as Atalanta's son and the youngest champion; Flaxman's sheet, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, is the studio origin of the oath and march imagery later reprinted in popular editions such as Church's Stories from the Greek Tragedians.
captions.blake-hecate-or-the-night-of-enitharmon-: William Blake's color-printed drawing in the Tate (c. 1795, Butlin 316), long known as 'Hecate', shows a brooding triple figure of the goddess crouched over a book in restless spectral light, flanked by two shadowy companions who echo her into a single three-headed presence. Around her gather the creatures of her nocturnal domain — an owl, a bat, a thistle, a serpentine ass and a long-snouted beast — emblems of the night, witchcraft and the lunar underworld over which Hecate, the Greek goddess of the crossroads, magic and the dark of the moon, was thought to preside. Blake fuses the classical triple Hecate of the crossroads with his own mythic vision, making this the most celebrated post-classical image of the goddess.
captions.fagan-orestes-and-electra: Fagan pairs the siblings in a quiet clasp: Electra and the returned Orestes before the matricide that will avenge Agamemnon. The National Trust canvas gives visual form to the Libation Bearers' reunion — conspiracy and recognition held in one embrace. Oil on canvas.
captions.flaxman-bia: A single-figure study of Bia drawn from Flaxman's 1795 Prometheus Bound cycle, isolating the personification of Force from the larger binding scene. Stripped to clean Neoclassical outline, the taut, athletic female figure leans forward mid-effort, her muscular tension distilling the silent violence that Aeschylus gives to Zeus's enforcer. As the sister of Kratos, Nike and Zelus and child of Pallas and Styx, Bia is rarely portrayed alone; this isolated profile lets her stand as the pure image of compelling might rather than a bystander to Prometheus's torment.
captions.flaxman-kratos: John Flaxman's neoclassical line illustration for Aeschylus isolates Cratos himself, the divine personification of Strength who in the drama commands Hephaestus to fetter Prometheus. Stripped to pure contour in Flaxman's signature outline style, the figure is conceived as sheer enforcing power — stern, unyielding muscle in the service of Zeus — the very emblem of the daimon whom the Titan curses as the cruel hand of tyranny.
captions.flaxman-the-binding-of-prometheus-fronti: Flaxman's spare Neoclassical line engraving, made for Richard Porson's 1795 translation of Aeschylus, shows the chaining of Prometheus exactly as the tragedy's prologue describes it. The Titan is held at the centre while Hephaestus rivets him to the mountainside; flanking him are Kratos and Bia, the silent strong-arm daimones of Zeus, pinning his body so the fetters can be fixed. Bia, the wordless agent of Force in the play, leans her full weight into the captive, embodying the raw compulsion that makes the divine sentence inescapable.
captions.flaxman-to-phoebus-at-his-birth-from-aes: Flaxman's outline drawing for Aeschylus's Eumenides, now in the Yale Center for British Art, stages the Delphic succession speech of the Pythia: Phoebe, who received the oracle from Themis, presents the oracular tripod to the newborn Phoebus Apollo. The neoclassical sheet is the canonical modern image of the Titaness's one great mythic act — the birthday gift that gives Apollo his name from Phoebe.
captions.head-echo-flying-from-narcissus: The English Neoclassical painter Guy Head makes Echo the fleeing protagonist: she turns from the self-absorbed youth at the spring, her rejected love already driving her into the woods where only her voice will remain. Oil on canvas, Detroit Institute of Arts.
captions.kirk-troilus-and-cressida-act-1: Kirk's Boydell Shakespeare Gallery plate stages Act 1 of Troilus and Cressida — Pandarus as go-between for the Trojan lovers, the Homeric archer rewritten as the comic bawd of English stage tradition.
captions.meynier-the-muse-erato-writing-verses-in: This black-chalk and wash drawing by Charles Meynier, dated 1797 and held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, is a preparatory study for his series of the Muses. It shows Erato in the act that gives her her name — she who is 'lovely' or 'beloved' — setting down verses while a hovering Cupid whispers their amorous subject to her. The lyre rests within reach, and the tender exchange between Muse and winged love-god makes explicit the ancient tradition that assigned to Erato the poetry of love and eros, distinct from the epic and tragic spheres of her sisters.
captions.harriet-oedipus-at-colonus: Harriet's Colonus — the blind exile led by Antigone into Attic sacred ground, Sophocles' last Theban play as revolutionary-era pathos.
captions.lethiere-philoctetes-on-the-island-of-le: Lethière's Neoclassical Lemnos — the indispensable archer the cycle must reclaim before Paris falls to Heracles' arrows.
captions.meynier-calliope-muse-of-epic-poetry: Painted by the French Neoclassical artist Charles Meynier as part of an Apollo-and-the-Muses ensemble now in the Cleveland Museum of Art, this canvas personifies Calliope, eldest and most distinguished of the nine Muses and patroness of epic poetry. She is shown seated in classical robes holding a stylus and a writing tablet — her traditional attribute as the inspirer of heroic verse — beside a volume of epic song. As the Muse who, in Hesiod's Theogony, is 'foremost of them all' and attends upon kings, Calliope embodies the elevated, measured eloquence of the epic tradition; she is also remembered as the mother of the singer Orpheus.
captions.romney-drawing-of-the-binding-of-prometh: In this black-chalk study from his Prometheus Bound series, George Romney pins the action at the rebel Titan's feet: Cratos and Bia hold Prometheus down against the rock while Hephaestus binds his arms. The broad-shouldered Cratos is all leverage and clenched force, the muscle that makes Zeus's sentence physical — the silent, brutal counterpart to the smith's reluctance, fixing the personification of raw Strength to the act of chaining a god.
captions.gautherot-pyramus-and-thisbe: Gautherot's neoclassical canvas catches Thisbe's discovery of Pyramus — sword, blood, and the mulberry that will stain forever. Late-eighteenth-century pathos for Shakespeare's favourite Ovidian lovers.
captions.burney-the-marriage-of-telephus-and-auge: Burney's Met drawing stages the interrupted wedding at Teuthras' Mysian court — the king who would marry Auge to Telephus without knowing they are mother and son, until recognition breaks the rite.
captions.fuseli-anticlea-in-the-underworld: A nineteenth-century illustration returns to Odyssey 11: Anticleia among the shades — Odysseus' mother, dead of longing, speaking to her living son at the trench of blood.
captions.fuseli-haemon-discovering-the-body-of-an: Fuseli's gray-wash drawing (Huntington Library) freezes the Sophoclean catastrophe that defines Haemon: Creon's son finds Antigone hanged in her tomb and will turn the sword on himself. The British-Swiss Romantic stages the fiancé not as a debating prince but as a body stricken by sight — the visual counterpart to Antigone's last episode. Few images name Haemon so squarely; this one makes him the discoverer of the tragedy his father wrote.
captions.fuseli-hephaestus-bia-and-kratos-securin: Fuseli's pencil drawing stages the opening of Aeschylus's Prometheus Bound, in which Zeus dispatches his enforcers Kratos (Strength) and Bia (Force) to pinion the rebel Titan to the Caucasus. Bia is one of the two female figures pressed against Prometheus: she appears at first glance to cradle the prisoner, but in truth she steadies the stake that Hephaestus will hammer through his chest, the personification of brute violence executing the punishment her brother Kratos can only command. Now in the Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tāmaki.
captions.fuseli-king-amycus-of-the-bebryces: Fuseli's Bebrycian king — Poseidon's boxing tyrant who forces every lander into the caestus until Polydeuces kills him. Not the centaur Amycus of Ovid's Lapith war.
captions.fuseli-tekemessa-and-eurysakes: Fuseli's drawing of Tecmessa with the child Eurysaces — the son named for Ajax's broad shield. In Sophocles the doomed hero entrusts the boy and the shield before his suicide; Romantic pathos keeps mother and heir at the edge of that farewell.
captions.fuseli-the-psychostasia-of-achilles-and-: The Anglo-Swiss Romantic painter Henry Fuseli revived the ancient theme of the weighing of fates in this drawing of the psychostasia of Achilles and Memnon. Reaching back past Homer to the lost Aethiopis and the vase-painters who showed Hermes balancing the heroes' death-spirits, Fuseli stages the cosmic adjudication of doom as a sublime confrontation of mothers, gods and scales. The Keres, the personified deaths weighed in the balance, here become the engine of his characteristic drama of inexorable fate.
captions.howard-hylas-carried-off-by-nymphs: Henry Howard's British Romantic canvas stages the moment the naiads lift Hylas from the spring — limbs entangled, pitcher forgotten, the Argonaut already halfway into another world. The painting belongs to the same nineteenth-century fascination with Theocritus' Idyll XIII that later fed Waterhouse: Hylas as the beautiful youth whom water and love erase from the Argo's crew.
captions.howard-telemachus-departing-from-nestor: Howard's departure — Telemachus leaving Nestor's hospitality for Sparta, the Pylos visit closing in farewell.
captions.meynier-clio-muse-of-history: Part of Charles Meynier's Neoclassical cycle of Apollo and the Muses, now in the Cleveland Museum of Art, this canvas personifies Kleio, the Muse of history, as a serene young woman seated against a sweeping landscape. She rests an open scroll on her knee and turns toward a stone slab inscribed with names, her gaze fixed on the act of recording the past. The open roll and the chest of papyri at her side render her traditional attributes — the keeper of memory who, as Hesiod sang in the Theogony, was born to Mnemosyne and so gives deeds their immortality in the written word.
captions.meynier-erato-muse-of-lyrical-poetry: Painted in 1800 by the French Neoclassical artist Charles Meynier and now in the Cleveland Museum of Art, this canvas presents Erato as the patron of amorous song. Crowned with roses and seated in a serene pastoral setting, the Muse cradles a golden lyre — her defining attribute — while a small winged Eros at her side identifies the love poetry that is her particular gift among the nine sisters of Helicon. Meynier conceived the picture as one of a series of individual Muses, isolating Erato so that her cool, idealized grace embodies the inspiration the ancient poets invoked when they sang of desire.
captions.meynier-polyhymnia-muse-of-eloquence: Painted by the French Neoclassical artist Charles Meynier as part of an Apollo-and-the-Muses ensemble now in the Cleveland Museum of Art, this canvas personifies Polyhymnia, the Muse of sacred hymn and solemn eloquence. She is shown in the meditative pose that became her hallmark — wrapped in a plain enveloping mantle and leaning thoughtfully, lost in contemplation rather than performance. As the most grave and inward of the nine daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne, Polyhymnia presided over the hymns sung to the gods and over the silent, pondered word; Meynier's restrained, classicizing figure embodies exactly that reflective solemnity that distinguished her from her livelier sisters.
captions.meynier-telemachus-urged-by-mentor-leavi: Meynier's neoclassical canvas stages Fénelon's episode in which Mentor (Athena in disguise) pulls Telemachus away from Calypso's isle. The painting belongs to the didactic afterlife of the Odyssey's trusted friend — Mentor as the voice that turns a wandering prince toward duty.
captions.rowlandson-salmacis-and-hermaphroditus: Rowlandson's watercolour: the nymph clinging at the spring — English Regency wit applied to Ovid's most intimate metamorphosis.
captions.silvagni-eteocles-and-polynices: Neoclassical oil by Giovanni Silvagni staging the mutual slaughter of Oedipus' sons before the gates of Thebes: Eteocles and Polynices lock shields and spears in the duel that ends the Seven's war and opens Antigone's tragedy. The brothers' interlocking bodies make the fratricide a single fatal knot — the image that later painters and urn-makers return to whenever they need the Theban civil war in one frame.
captions.trioson-head-of-capaneus-the-blasphemer: Girodet's study isolates the defiant face Dante memorialized — Capaneus as the type of the blasphemer who will not bend even in Hell's burning sand.
captions.trioson-the-meeting-of-orestes-and-hermi: Girodet's Cleveland drawing isolates the Spartan princess with her cousin Orestes — the marriage Tyndareus promised and Menelaus later complicated with Neoptolemus. Neoclassical line makes Hermione a figure of contested succession: Helen's daughter as the prize that binds Atreid and Aeacid claims after Troy. The sheet is among the rare images that name her without Racine's Andromache crowding the frame.
captions.trioson-the-oath-of-the-seven-chiefs-aga: Girodet's oath of the Seven — the sealed pact that binds Adrastus' army to Polynices' claim.
captions.wicar-electra-receiving-the-ashes-of-her: Wicar stages the cruel trick of Sophocles' Electra: the urn said to hold Orestes' ashes is placed in her hands while the living brother stands unrecognized beside her. The painting turns the recognition scene into neoclassical pathos — the sister who has kept the house of Atreus awake for revenge. Oil on canvas.
captions.wilson-ceyx-and-alcyone: A classic illustration of the Trachinian couple — married love that Ovid carries past shipwreck into birds and calm seas.
captions.broc-the-death-of-hyacinthos: Broc's Neoclassical canvas — Apollo cradling the Spartan youth struck by the discus, the flower still to rise from the spilled blood.
captions.gandolfi-athamas-killing-ino-s-son: Gandolfi's oil shows the Boeotian king in the grip of Hera's madness: Athamas seizes the infant Learchus while Ino recoils with Melicertes — the Ovidian catastrophe that ends in the leap from the Molurian rock and the children's sea-change into Palaemon and Leucothea.
captions.ingres-achilles-receiving-the-ambassador: Ingres' Prix de Rome canvas: Odysseus speaks while Phoenix and Ajax attend Achilles and Patroclus — neoclassical calm for the embassy that cannot bend the hero.
captions.meynier-la-danse-terpsichore: A Neoclassical oil study by the French painter Charles Meynier, held in the Musee Magnin in Dijon, made in preparation for his larger composition of Apollo and the Muses. Terpsichore personifies the dance: rendered as a single radiant figure in the crisp linear manner of the Davidian school, she carries the lyre that marks her, the Muse who leads the choral dance under Apollo. Lifted out of the full Muse ensemble, the sketch presents her as one luminous star among the nine sisters of Helicon.
captions.migliarini-athamas-seized-by-the-furies-: A Neoclassical painting by Arcangelo Michele Migliarini, preserved at the Accademia di San Luca in Rome. It shows King Athamas in the grip of the avenging Furies, the divine madness that turns him against his own family. The infant Learchus appears among the imperilled figures of the household alongside Ino and Melicertes, the young child rendered as the vulnerable victim at the center of the unfolding violence. Produced as an academic competition piece, the work exemplifies how the Athamas-and-Learchus episode served around 1800 as a vehicle for the heightened pathos and dramatic gesture prized in late-eighteenth- and early-nineteenth-century history painting.
captions.gerard-flora-caressed-by-zephyr: Gérard's Grenoble painting: Zephyr leans from the air to kiss Flora — Neoclassical tenderness for the breeze that brings the year's first blossoms.
captions.guerin-phedre-et-hippolyte-phaedra-and-h: Bought by the French state at the Salon of 1802 and now in the Louvre (INV 5182), Guérin's Neoclassical canvas stages Racine's Act IV: Hippolytus denies before Theseus the charge that Phaedra, counselled by Oenone, has laid against him. Marble architecture and hunting dogs frame a palace confrontation in which the stepmother's false accusation seals the curse that will destroy her stepson — a cold, calculated drama that made Guérin's reputation.
captions.smirke-cave-of-trophonius: Smirke's Cave of Trophonius — the Lebadeian oracle-mouth where consultants descend in terror and return forever changed.
captions.tischbein-odysseus-and-eurycleia: Tischbein's Odysseus and Eurycleia — the nurse recognizing the scar as the beggar-king's true identity.
captions.west-arethusa: West's High Museum canvas isolates the Sicilian spring-nymph — Arethusa after Artemis opened the earth beneath her, risen on Ortygia as the fountain that still bears her name.
captions.thorvaldsen-jason-with-the-golden-fleece: Thorvaldsen's neoclassical Jason after the Colchian ordeal — fleece on his arm, spear in hand, the Argonautica frozen at the prize won.
captions.canova-palamedes: Canova's neoclassical Palamedes — the inventor-hero Odysseus framed, Trojan War's first judicial murder.
captions.pajou-oedipus-cursing-polynices: Neoclassical oil by Jacques Augustin Catherine Pajou of Oedipus laying his curse on Polynices while Antigone and the household look on. The canvas makes the Seven against Thebes begin not at the gates but in a father's mouth.
captions.turner-narcissus-and-echo: Turner's early mythological landscape dissolves Echo and Narcissus into luminous atmosphere — figures nearly lost in the golden haze of a classical Arcadia. The nymph's presence is felt as much as seen, a Romantic reading of Ovid in which voice and light outlast solid form. Oil on canvas, Tate, London.
captions.canova-theseus-defeats-the-centaur: Antonio Canova's monumental marble group captures Theseus astride a vanquished centaur, his fist raised to deliver the killing blow at the wedding battle of the Lapiths and Centaurs, where the hero fought alongside his friend Pirithous. Carved between 1805 and 1819 and standing some 340 cm high, the Neoclassical colossus was first commissioned by Napoleon for Milan before being acquired by Emperor Franz I of Austria. It now presides over the grand staircase of the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, an emblem of order triumphing over savagery.
captions.heath-nestor-appearing-in-a-dream-to-aga: Engraving by James Heath after Henry Fuseli, held in the British Museum, illustrating the opening of Homer's Iliad (Book II). Here Zeus dispatches one of the Oneiroi, the personified Dreams born of Night, to the sleeping Agamemnon. The Dream-spirit assumes the shape of the aged counsellor Nestor and leans over the Greek king's couch to whisper the deceitful message that the gods have decreed Troy's fall, urging him to arm. Fuseli renders the Oneiros as a looming, shadowy apparition hovering at the bedside, capturing the dream-gods' twin nature as both messengers and deceivers of mortal sleep.
captions.bromley-odysseus-between-scylla-and-char: Bromley's engraving after a Fuseli watercolour isolates the Odyssey's second ordeal with Charybdis: Odysseus clings to the wild fig tree above the whirlpool while the vortex yawns below and Scylla coils among the rocks at left. Made as an illustration to Pope's Odyssey, the print freezes Circe's counsel made flesh — when the ship is lost, only the fig and the sucking deep remain, and Charybdis is the sea that will either drown or spit the hero back.
captions.mongez-theseus-and-pirithous-clearing-th: Mongez's brigand-clearing — Theseus and Pirithous making the road safe, the labours that name the journey to Athens.
captions.turner-the-goddess-of-discord-choosing-t: Turner's early Tate canvas shows Eris — Discordia — as an older woman in a red skirt choosing among golden apples in the garden of the Hesperides. Before the wedding feast and the Judgment of Paris, the goddess of strife selects the fruit that will unmake Troy; the Romantic landscape makes discord a figure walking among mythic trees.
captions.canova-hebe: Carved in white marble by the great Neoclassical sculptor Antonio Canova, this version of his celebrated Hebe (1808, Sculpture Gallery, Chatsworth House) shows the goddess of youth in mid-stride, drapery streaming behind her as if caught in flight. She tilts a small jug above an upraised cup, frozen in the act of pouring the nectar that keeps the Olympians forever young — her own everlasting role as cupbearer to the gods. Canova returned to the subject repeatedly; the airy poise, gauzy clinging fabric, and the figure's serene, dewy freshness made his Hebe one of the defining images of divine youth in European sculpture.
captions.ingres-oedipus-and-the-sphinx: Ingres' Louvre masterpiece freezes the Theban roadside encounter: Oedipus stands naked before the winged Sphinx, answering the riddle of the creature that has been devouring travellers. Bones litter the rock while the hero's calm profile already carries the irony of a man who will solve every puzzle except his own birth. The canvas fixed the modern West's image of Oedipus as intellect facing monster.
captions.revett-dionysus-and-the-tyrrhenian-pirat: Stuart and Revett's engraving of the Lysicrates frieze — Dionysus and the Tyrrhenian crew mid-metamorphosis.
captions.fuseli-ixion-and-nephele: Fuseli stages Ixion embracing the cloud Nephele — the union that begets Centaurus, progenitor of the horse-men. The cloud-crime before the race of centaurs spreads.
captions.langlois-priam-at-the-feet-of-achilles: Langlois' Priam at Achilles' feet — the ransom that ends the Iliad not with Troy's fall but with shared grief.
captions.russ-hecuba-with-the-bodies-of-polyxena-: Oil painting by the Viennese Biedermeier painter Karl Russ, in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna. Hecuba kneels among the corpses of Polyxena and Polydorus at Achilles' tomb — the twin losses that close her house after Troy, the daughter sacrificed to the dead hero and the son murdered for the gold entrusted to Polymestor.
captions.flaxman-demodocus-singing-to-the-phaeaci: Flaxman's outline illustration for the Odyssey shows Demodocus with his harp among the Phaeacians as Odysseus listens — the blind minstrel whose three songs (Achilles and Odysseus, Ares and Aphrodite, the wooden horse) structure the Scherian books.
captions.guerin-andromache-and-pyrrhus: Guérin's Salon scene — Andromache before Pyrrhus in Epirus, Hector's widow as the Molossian prize of Achilles' son.
captions.guerin-aurora-and-cephalus: Guérin paints the other great episode of Cephalus's life: his abduction by Aurora (Eos, the Dawn), who fell in love with the young hunter and carried him off — the very moment that draws the Phocian prince out of the mortal catalogue and into the orbit of a goddess. The amorous Dawn, robed in pale rose, lifts the beautiful sleeping youth upon a cloud, gazing down at him with longing while a winged Eros hovers nearby. A polished Neoclassical reverie of cool flesh and soft morning light, the painting follows Ovid's Metamorphoses. Oil on canvas, Musée du Louvre, Paris.
captions.guerin-morpheus-and-iris: An oil by Pierre-Narcisse Guérin showing Iris waking or addressing Morpheus, the shaper of dreams. Neoclassical flesh and cool drapery stage Ovid's dream-messenger as a sleeping youth interrupted by the rainbow goddess — sleep personified at the threshold of waking.
captions.ingres-jupiter-and-thetis: Ingres' monumental Neoclassical canvas illustrates the opening of Homer's Iliad: the sea-nymph Thetis kneels before an enthroned, colossal Jupiter to beg that her son Achilles be honoured. The artist exaggerates the supplicating Thetis with sinuous, elongated limbs and a serpentine throat as her hand reaches up to caress the god's beard, while the impassive father of the gods looms in marmoreal majesty. The dramatic contrast of scale and the tense intimacy of her plea make this one of the most celebrated visions of Achilles' divine mother. Held in the Musée Granet, Aix-en-Provence.
captions.pujol-lycurgus: Pujol's Neoclassical Thracian king — Homer's first persecutor of Dionysus staged as a moral drama of hubris.
captions.hayez-laocoon: Hayez's Neoclassical canvas restages the Vatican group's agony in paint — the priest and his sons locked with the serpents in a study of twisted anatomy and doomed warning. Romantic Italy looks back at the sculpture that taught Europe how to suffer on marble.
captions.girodet-pygmalion-and-galatea: Girodet's Louvre canvas catches the instant marble softens into flesh: Cupid's torch lights Galatea as Pygmalion kneels in astonishment. Neoclassical polish for Ovid's sculptor who loved his own work into life.
captions.blondel-hecuba-and-polyxena: Oil painting by the French Neoclassicist Merry-Joseph Blondel, now in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. After the fall of Troy, the aged queen throws a protective arm around her daughter Polyxena, whom the Greeks claimed for sacrifice at the tomb of Achilles.
captions.canova-the-three-graces: A Neoclassical marble group by the Italian sculptor Antonio Canova (1757–1822); this version, commissioned by Empress Joséphine and completed for her son Eugène de Beauharnais, is held in the State Hermitage Museum, Saint Petersburg (a second version is shared by the V&A and the National Galleries of Scotland). Canova draws the three Charites — Aglaea, Euphrosyne, and Thalia — into a single tender knot of embracing bodies, their heads inclined together and a length of drapery binding them. The daughters of Zeus, attendants of Aphrodite who bestowed beauty, festivity, and good cheer, here become an image of intimate sisterly affection; Euphrosyne, goddess of mirth and gladness, leans into the close triadic embrace at the heart of the group.
captions.canova-the-three-graces-le-tre-grazie: Canova's Neoclassical marble distills the Charites into three nude figures clustered in a single tender knot, heads inclined together and arms entwined over a shared draped column. Carved for John Russell, 6th Duke of Bedford, the group is today shared between the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, and the National Galleries of Scotland. The sisters — named in antiquity as Aglaïa ('Splendour'), Euphrosyne ('Good Cheer') and Thalia ('Festivity') — give beauty, charm and joy to the world; Aglaïa, the eldest and most radiant, the bride of Hephaestus, takes her place at the heart of the embrace.
captions.eckersberg-ulysses-revenge-on-penelope-s: Neoclassical daylight on the poem's darkest hour: the beggar in the doorway has already become the archer, and the hall's feast turns to flight.
captions.hayez-ulysses-at-the-court-of-alcinous: Hayez's vast Capodimonte canvas shows Odysseus weeping in Alcinous' hall as Demodocus sings of Troy — the Phaeacian king as the perfect host whose court hears the hero's name before the hero will speak it.
captions.morse-the-judgment-of-jupiter: Painted by the young American artist Samuel F. B. Morse (later famous as the inventor of the telegraph) during his studies in London, this ambitious neoclassical canvas in the Yale University Art Gallery stages the decisive moment of Marpessa's myth. Zeus, enthroned, arbitrates the quarrel between Apollo and the mortal Idas, who have come to blows over the princess. Rather than ruling himself, the king of the gods commands Marpessa to choose between her two suitors. The composition, indebted to the grand-manner history painting Morse absorbed under Benjamin West, dramatizes the rare instance in Greek myth in which a mortal woman is granted authority over her own fate against a god's desire.
captions.palagi-theseus-and-pirithous-abducting-h: Palagi's neoclassical abduction: the oath to marry daughters of Zeus begins with Helen at Aphidnae — the crime that sends the pair down for Persephone.
captions.alaux-briseis-mourning-patroclus: Alaux's Salon grief: Briseis weeps over Patroclus in Achilles' tent — Homer's captive given a voice of mourning in neoclassical quiet.
captions.guerin-aeneas-tells-dido-of-the-misfortu: Oil painting by Pierre-Narcisse Guérin, now in the Musée du Louvre, Paris. In a scene from the opening books of Virgil's Aeneid, the Trojan hero recounts the fall of his city to Dido, queen of Carthage, as evening falls over her court — the telling that kindles the queen's fatal love.
captions.hayez-achilles-dragging-hector-s-body: Hayez's chariot round the wall — the outrage that would move Zeus to send Priam with ransom.
captions.quincy-the-statue-of-zeus-at-olympia-rec: Plate from Antoine-Chrysostome Quatremère de Quincy's study Le Jupiter olympien, reconstructing the lost gold-and-ivory Statue of Zeus at Olympia. Phidias's colossus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, showed the god enthroned with a figure of Nike in his right hand and a sceptre in his left.
captions.reinhart-landscape-with-hypsipyle-and-op: Johann Christian Reinhart's classical landscape at the Staatliche Kunsthalle Karlsruhe sets the Lemnian queen Hypsipyle in an Arcadian Nemean wilderness with the infant Opheltes (Archemoros). The painting freezes the quiet before the snake-strike that will found the Nemean Games — Hypsipyle as nurse and tragic witness rather than Argonaut queen.
captions.bosio-aristaeus-god-of-the-gardens: Bosio's Louvre marble: the rustic culture-god of bees, oil, and the chase — the husbandry hero whose cycle Virgil made Roman farming myth.
captions.flaxman-epimetheus-receives-pandora: Outline drawing by John Flaxman for Hesiod's Works and Days: Hermes delivers Pandora to Epimetheus despite Prometheus' warning against gifts from the gods. Neoclassical line turns the brother's acceptance into a cool, fatal handshake.
captions.flaxman-the-rising-of-the-pleiades-illus: Flaxman's outline drawing for Hesiod's Works and Days: the rising of the Pleiades marks harvest time — the star-cluster that is also the seven sisters, Taygete among them, written into the farmer's calendar and the night sky.
captions.fuger-prometheus-brings-fire-to-mankind: Füger's torchbearer — the Titan carrying stolen fire down to humankind, the gift that names the myth and costs him the rock.
captions.guerin-clytemnestra-and-agamemnon: Guérin's Louvre night-scene: the returning king asleep as Clytemnestra hesitates with the dagger and Aegisthus urges the blow — Aeschylus' homecoming murder at the hinge.
captions.david-the-farewell-of-telemachus-and-euc: David's late Neoclassical oil (J. Paul Getty Museum) shows Telemachus parting from the nymph Eucharis on Calypso's island — an episode drawn from Fénelon's Télémaque rather than Homer, yet inseparable from the modern image of Odysseus's son. Painted in Brussels in 1818, the canvas pairs the youth's averted resolve with Eucharis's clinging embrace under cool, sculptural light. It is among the most famous post-Homeric portraits of Telemachus as a sentimental hero of education and duty.
captions.remond-the-isolation-of-philoctetes-on-l: Rémond's Toulouse landscape — the abandoned archer alone with Heracles' weapons until Odysseus and Diomedes return.
captions.blondel-the-sun-or-the-fall-of-icarus: A monumental ceiling painting commissioned for the Rotunda of Apollo in the Louvre, allegorizing the sun through the myth of Icarus. Blondel renders the youth tumbling backward through a brilliant solar blaze, his wings coming apart as he is overwhelmed by the very light he sought to reach. Conceived in the grand Neoclassical decorative tradition, the work casts the fall as a meditation on hubris and the limits of mortal ambition. It remains in situ in the Musée du Louvre, Paris.
captions.couder-achilles-fighting-the-river-gods-: Couder's Louvre decoration: Achilles against Scamander (Xanthus) and Simois — Iliad XXI as neoclassical flood and fury.
captions.david-the-anger-of-achilles: David's Achilles at the moment of the false marriage — the bridegroom named in Agamemnon's lie when Iphigenia came to Aulis.
captions.goya-atropos-the-fates: One of Goya's Black Paintings, painted directly onto the walls of his house, the Quinta del Sordo, and later transferred to canvas. It shows the Fates hovering in a dark sky above a bound human figure, with Atropos bearing the shears that cut the thread of life. It now hangs in the Museo del Prado, Madrid.
captions.goya-saturn-devouring-his-son: Goya's Black Painting returns Cronus' appetite as modern nightmare — the cosmogonic devouring stripped of Olympus' polish.
captions.court-achilles-gives-nestor-the-prize-of: In this companion scene by Court, Achilles awards Nestor a prize for wisdom — a pictorial gloss on the Iliad's funeral games and on Nestor's standing as the Achaeans' remembered counsellor. The king of Pylos receives the tribute of youth before assembled heroes, his age turned into public honour rather than frailty. French academic painting here cements the epithet that English still borrows: a nestor as a wise old adviser.
captions.court-achilles-presented-to-nestor: Court's Neoclassical canvas presents the boy Achilles before Nestor — the Pylian king cast as the aged arbiter of heroic education, the same voice Homer gives him in the Iliad as the eldest counsellor at Troy. Academic clarity and theatrical gesture turn the meeting into a lesson in respect for experience. The painting belongs to the nineteenth-century French taste for Homeric pedagogy, with Nestor as the living archive of the previous generation's wars.
