captions.gros-bacchus-and-ariadne: Gros returns to the Naxos meeting in the grand manner of French Romantic history painting: Bacchus' train surges toward the seated Ariadne as the island shore becomes a theatre of divine rescue. The canvas is held by the Phoenix Art Museum.
captions.hennequin-tydeus-hippomedon-and-partheno: Tydeus among the Seven — the Calydonian champion whose rage at Thebes became proverbial.
captions.lecomte-the-sleep-of-erigone: After Girodet — Erigone asleep before she finds her father's body and the Aiora swinging rites begin.
captions.pinelli-aeneas-and-the-ghost-of-his-wife: The Virgilian farewell: Creusa's shade appears to Aeneas after the sack — not to follow him west, but to free him for Italy and Lavinia.
captions.zauner-philotes-sacrificing-on-the-altar: A Neoclassical marble by the Austrian sculptor Franz Anton von Zauner (1746-1822) personifying Philotes, the Hesiodic spirit of affection, friendship and loving union born of Night. Draped in the antique manner, the young woman lays a crown of flowers upon an altar-column on which a heart burns, performing a tender sacrifice on the 'altar of friendship' that gives the work its title (Philotes sacrifiant sur l'autel de l'amitie). Since the ancients personified Philotes almost wholly in verse and left no individuated cult image, Zauner's allegory is among the rare attempts to give this abstraction a face, translating the Greek daimon of intimacy into the cool emblematic idiom of around 1800. The statuette measures roughly 83 x 31 x 20 cm.
captions.fuseli-the-erinyes-beside-the-body-of-er: Fuseli's related Louvre treatment: the Erinyes crowd Eriphyle's corpse as Alcmaeon is claimed for exile — the necklace's second harvest made visible.
captions.fuseli-the-erinyes-drive-alcmaeon-from-t: Fuseli's Kunsthaus Zürich canvas: the Furies swarm as Alcmaeon flees Eriphyle's body — Romantic terror for the pollution that drives him through Arcadia to Achelous.
captions.rude-the-death-of-cenchirias-son-of-nept: Sophie Rude paints Peirene mourning Cenchrias — the son by Poseidon whose death (by Artemis' arrow in some tellings) drives the nymph's grief into the Corinthian spring that still bears her name. Neoclassical pathos makes the naiad mother the face of the fountain's aetiology.
captions.guerin-venus-and-anchises: Oil painting by Jean-Baptiste Paulin Guérin, Salon of 1822, Louvre collection on long-term loan to the Musée des Beaux-Arts Jules Chéret, Nice. Venus claims the Dardanian herdsman Anchises — the mortal love that begets Aeneas and, in the Homeric Hymn, nearly costs Anchises his life when he boasts of the goddess.
captions.langlois-diana-and-endymion: A pupil of Jacques-Louis David, Langlois renders the moment of the goddess's nocturnal descent with polished Neoclassical clarity. Diana—the Roman Luna, identified with Selene—leans tenderly over the sleeping Endymion, a crescent moon crowning her brow, while a winged Cupid draws back the veil of night to reveal the youth. The smooth modelling, restrained gestures, and idealized anatomy reflect the discipline of the Davidian school, and the chaste eroticism of the encounter is conveyed entirely through the goddess's lingering, downward gaze upon her perpetually dreaming beloved.
captions.moyne-the-nymph-echo: Le Moyne's marble isolates Echo alone — no Narcissus, no pool — a solitary nymph whose posture already hints at the wasting that will leave only her answering voice. Neoclassical sculpture as the myth reduced to a single figure. Musée du Louvre, Paris.
captions.tischbein-achilles-and-penthesilea: Tischbein stages the aftermath: Achilles supports the dying Amazon — recognition arriving a breath too late.
captions.turner-the-bay-of-baiae-with-apollo-and-: Turner's Tate canvas: Apollo offers the Sibyl as many years as the sand in her hand — the Bay of Baiae dissolving into light while her bargain with immortality fails.
captions.bartolini-dirce: Bartolini's Louvre marble reduces the Farnese drama to a single bound nude — Dirce alone, ropes and bull implied, Neoclassical pathos instead of Hellenistic crowd. The reduced version for the Duke of Devonshire kept the Theban torment in nineteenth-century salons.
captions.blake-capaneus-illustrations-to-dante-s-: Blake's watercolour for Inferno XIV sets Capaneus under the rain of fire — Dante's blasphemer still scorning Jove, the Theban who climbed the walls and was struck by lightning.
captions.blake-cerberus-illustration-to-dante-s-i: Among the watercolours Blake made for Dante's Divine Comedy near the end of his life, this sheet depicts Cerberus as the three-headed warden of the Third Circle of Hell, where the gluttons lie in cold rain. Blake gives the monster three fully human-eyed canine faces and a swollen, beast-like body, faithful to Dante's 'great worm' yet charged with the artist's own visionary intensity. The image carries the ancient hound of Hades into the Christian afterlife, the role Virgil and Dante had assigned it, and stands as one of the most celebrated post-classical portrayals of the creature.
captions.clarke-the-simoeis-plain: Clarke's travel view of the Simoeis plain in the Troad — the mortal landscape of the river-god who fought beside Scamander.
captions.ivanov-priam-asking-achilles-for-the-bod: Ivanov's ransom — aged Priam at Achilles' feet for the son dragged around the walls, the Iliad's last mercy.
captions.norblin-antigone-giving-burial-to-polyni: Norblin's Prix de Rome canvas shows the handful of dust: Antigone burying Polynices against Creon's ban — the act that defines the Theban sister.
captions.haydon-venus-and-anchises: Oil painting by the English history painter Benjamin Robert Haydon. Venus appears to Anchises on Mount Ida — the encounter that makes a herdsman the father of Rome's Trojan ancestor, painted with the muscular neoclassical gravity Haydon prized.
captions.mongez-the-seven-chiefs-against-thebes: Mongez's Seven Chiefs — seven Argive champions arrayed for the assault on Cadmus' gates.
captions.flaxman-antigone-forced-from-her-father: British Museum lithograph after Flaxman for Sophocles' Oedipus at Colonus: Creon seizes Antigone from the blind exile who clings to her. The Theban king as political force — reclaiming the daughters for Thebes against Athens' sanctuary.
captions.guillemot-acis-and-galatea: Guillemot's Neoclassical canvas returns to the Sicilian shore: Acis and Galatea as Ovid's doomed couple, the pastoral calm already shadowed by Polyphemus' approaching jealousy.
captions.brodowski-oedipus-and-antigone: Brodowski's father and guide — Oedipus and Antigone on the road that ends at Colonus, dependence remade as piety.
captions.turner-vision-of-medea: Turner's swirling vision places Medea amid the supernatural machinery of her revenge — spells, dragons and the haze of Corinthian catastrophe. Painted in Rome and now associated with the Tate/National Gallery circle of Turner's myth subjects, it dissolves Euripides' sorceress into light and storm rather than a single dagger-blow.
captions.lohbauer-the-court-of-the-dead-die-unter: An 1829 Stuttgart lithograph by Rudolph Lohbauer reproducing the central section of a bas-relief, "Das Totengericht" (The Court of the Dead), by the sculptor Ludwig Mack (1799–1831). It shows the three judges of the Underworld enthroned together — Minos, Aeacus (here holding a scepter), and Rhadamanthys — as they interrogate the shades of the newly dead about their lives. In the afterlife tradition descending from Plato, the just king of Aegina was appointed alongside the two Cretan brothers to weigh mortal souls; Aeacus was often said to judge the shades of Europeans and to hold the keys of Hades.
captions.navez-the-nymph-salmacis-and-hermaphrodi: Navez's Neoclassical fountain — the Carian nymph and the youth at the water that will not let them part.
captions.sabatelli-ajax-the-lesser-son-of-oileus: Sabatelli's Neoclassical Locrian — the lesser Ajax isolated as the warrior whose sacrilege outlived his courage.
captions.turner-ulysses-deriding-polyphemus: Dawn bursts over the escaping fleet while the blinded giant, half cloud and half mountain, writhes above the bay — Turner's answer to Odyssey 9, all light where the cave was all dark.
captions.calvert-cyrene-and-cattle: Calvert's pastoral panel shows Apollo's Thessalian lover at rest among her father's cattle — the hunting nymph of Peneus whom the god would carry to Libya and who bore him Aristaeus, the keeper of bees and herds in Apollonius' Argonautica.
captions.blouet-heracles-and-the-cretan-bull-engr: Blouet's 1831 engraved reconstruction of the Olympia Temple of Zeus metope, published after the early excavations — a scholarly image that fixed the Early Classical struggle with the Cretan Bull for nineteenth-century viewers.
captions.ivanov-apollo-hyacinthus-and-cyparissus-: Ivanov's idyll before the discus — Apollo at music with Hyacinthus and Cyparissus, the bloom of youth that makes the later death cut deeper.
captions.scott-the-dead-sarpedon-borne-by-sleep-a: Scott's National Galleries of Scotland canvas from the Iliad: Hypnos and Thanatos bear the fallen Lycian prince — Romantic pathos for Zeus' son whom even a father could not save.
captions.thorvaldsen-hylas-and-the-water-nymphs: Thorvaldsen's neoclassical marble relief (Thorvaldsens Museum, Copenhagen) turns the rape of Hylas into a cool frieze of grasping nymphs and a yielding youth. Where Waterhouse would later drown the scene in foliage and pond-light, the Danish sculptor keeps the myth as pure outline — the Argonaut cupbearer pulled from the shore by desire. It is the academic afterlife of Apollonius' Mysian episode, carved for a Europe that read Hylas as both beauty and loss.
captions.flandrin-theseus-recognized-by-his-fathe: Flandrin's recognition — Theseus known by Aegeus at Athens, the road's end when the sword proves the son.
captions.gibert-thesee-reconnu-par-son-pere-these: Antoine-Placide Gibert treats the same Prix de Rome subject of 1832: the recognition of Theseus by King Aegeus of Athens. At the banquet arranged by the sorceress Medea to poison the newly arrived stranger, Aegeus spies the family sword Theseus carries and dashes away the deadly cup, embracing the son he had never met. The dramatic, theatrically lit composition belongs to the museum tradition of French academic history painting and is housed in the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Bordeaux.
captions.nenci-the-banquet-in-the-house-of-alcino: Nenci's academic banquet folds Homer himself into Alcinous' feast — a nineteenth-century allegory of the Odyssey's most civilized court, where song, gift, and safe passage still define the king.
captions.schinkel-uranus-and-the-dance-of-the-sta: Schinkel's Romantic sky-father: Ouranos enthroned among circling constellations — the primordial heaven as architecture of light rather than Hesiod's wounded giant.
captions.burrow-ilissus: Burrow’s romantic view of the Athenian Ilissus — the stream Hyginus lists among Oceanus’ river-sons and beside which Boreas seized Orithyia. Landscape art keeps the river-god’s watercourse when his human face is rare.
captions.rethel-nemesis: A painting by the German artist Alfred Rethel depicting the winged goddess of retribution in pursuit of a fleeing murderer, vengeance following inescapably across an open, desolate landscape. The work casts the ancient goddess in the brooding moral key of German Romanticism.
captions.thorvaldsen-achilles-and-penthesilea: Thorvaldsen's circular plaster relief (Thorvaldsens Museum, inv. A496) reduces the myth to two interlocking figures: Achilles holding the collapsing Penthesilea. The Danish Neoclassical sculptor turns the Amazon's death into a medallion of tragic recognition — the conqueror already mourning the warrior he has struck down.
captions.delacroix-medea-about-to-kill-her-childr: Delacroix's Louvre Medea — the Colchian pressed into a cave with her children and a dagger, Euripides' Corinthian revenge at the brink of the act.
captions.skene-oracular-cavern-of-trophonius: Skene's Oracular Cavern of Trophonius — a nineteenth-century vision of the underground consultation rite.
captions.chasseriau-andromeda-chained-to-the-rock: Chassériau paints the Nereids binding Andromeda to the cliff before the rescue — the sacrifice the city demands, staged for the Louvre.
captions.payne-scylla-and-charybdis-strait-of-mes: This 1840 steel engraving by the English printmaker Albert Henry Payne presents the legendary strait identified in antiquity with the Strait of Messina, where Scylla and Charybdis menaced passing ships from opposite shores. The print gives topographic, picturesque form to the Homeric geography: the rocky narrows where, in Odyssey 12, Charybdis lay beneath the great fig tree and thrice each day sucked down and belched up the sea. Such nineteenth-century engravings popularized the myth as a real-world locale, fixing the proverbial image of being caught 'between Scylla and Charybdis' — between two equally deadly hazards.
captions.troschel-zethus-and-amphion: Troschel's Neue Pinakothek sculpture: the Theban twins as nineteenth-century marble — Zethus the strong builder beside Amphion the lyre.
captions.turner-glaucus-and-scylla: Turner's late oil dissolves Ovid's sea-chase into light and spray: the blue-green fisherman-god pursues Scylla across a boiling gulf while Circe's jealousy waits offstage.
captions.daumier-heracles-cleaning-the-stables-of: Another Daumier take on the fifth Labour: Heracles mucks out — or rather floods — the stalls of King Augeas. The print keeps the focus on the king's notorious herds and the hero's river-borne shortcut, the bargain Augeas would break.
captions.daumier-the-augean-stables-histoire-anci: Daumier's lithograph for Le Charivari's Histoire ancienne series (25 September 1842), now at LACMA: Heracles confronts the filth of Augeas' stables with satirical grit. The Elean king's impossible yard becomes nineteenth-century political comedy — the labour that still names any Augean mess.
captions.barye-theseus-slaying-the-minotaur: Barye's bronze coils the hero and the bull-headed beast in one struggle — the labyrinth fight cast as Romantic animal force.
captions.cabanel-oedipus-separating-from-jocasta: Cabanel's early academic canvas freezes the palace catastrophe: Oedipus turns from Jocasta as recognition unmakes their marriage. The queen who was mother and wife stands at the hinge of Sophocles' plot — the moment before the noose.
captions.anonymous-final-scene-of-antigone-creon-: Nineteenth-century stage print of Sophocles' catastrophe: Creon (Bocage) weeps over Haemon's body while the Theban court gathers. The king who forbade burial learns too late what his decree cost — son, bride, and queen.
captions.genelli-odysseus-and-telemachus-in-the-h: Genelli's outline composition for the Odyssey: Odysseus sits by the fire as Eumaeus discovers Telemachus at the hut's entrance — the reunion of father and son under the swineherd's roof (Book 16). Eumaeus is the hinge of the scene, the loyal host whose steading becomes the conspiracy's first safe room.
captions.diotti-antigone-condemned-to-death-by-cr: Diotti's vast Accademia Carrara canvas stages the uncle-king at full authority: Creon sentences Antigone (and Ismene) while the court looks on. Thebes' rigid law made flesh — the decree that will wall the sister alive and ruin his own house.
captions.benouville-the-wrath-of-achilles: Benouville's Wrath of Achilles — nineteenth-century restaging of the same rage that opens the poem.
captions.boulanger-ulysses-and-eurycleia: Boulanger's Ulysses and Eurycleia — the foot-washing recognition in the beggar's disguise.
captions.amalthea-nursing-the-infant-zeus: A nineteenth-century French painting returns Amalthea to nymph form: the Cretan nurse offers her breast to the hidden child — the tradition in which she is woman, not goat.
captions.barre-odysseus-and-argos: Barre's print returns to the same Homeric instant: Argos knows his master at the threshold of the palace — fidelity staged as the quietest recognition in the epic.
captions.baumeister-opheltes-ensnared-by-the-snak: A handbook reconstruction after an ancient relief shows the infant Archemorus in the serpent's coils — the visual type of Opheltes' death that modern archaeology still cites beside the Nemean shrine.
captions.becker-hypsipyle-finds-opheltes-killed-b: Karl Ludwig Friedrich Becker's mural for the Niobidensaal of Berlin's Neues Museum (destroyed) staged the instant Hypsipyle discovers the infant Opheltes slain by a serpent — the catastrophe that turns a forgotten Lemnian nurse into the aetiology of the Nemean Games. The surviving reproduction keeps the nineteenth-century museum's reading of her as a figure of horrified recognition.
captions.carpeaux-hector-holding-astyanax: Carpeaux's sculpture groups father and son: Hector cradles Astyanax — the Trojan heir as a small body against the warrior who alone, Homer says, guarded Ilios.
captions.delacroix-apollo-slaying-python-apollon-: The vast central canvas of the Galerie d'Apollon ceiling at the Louvre, executed by Delacroix in oil on mounted canvas (about 8 by 7.5 metres) to complete the seventeenth-century decorative scheme begun by Charles Le Brun. Apollo, radiant in his sun-chariot at the apex of the composition, looses an arrow into the writhing, dark-coiled Python far below, who is pierced amid storm-wracked clouds and floodwater. Delacroix orchestrates the triumph of light over darkness — blazing yellows and golds around the god set against the purples and shadow of the serpent — as a cosmic allegory of order conquering primeval chaos, the divine sun-god slaying the earth-born monster of Delphi.
captions.fuseli-night-and-her-children-aither-and: Henry Fuseli's print in the Metropolitan Museum of Art stages Hesiod's Theogony genealogy: Night with her children Aether and Hemera. The Romantic sheet gives the primordial Day her Hesiodic family — sister of bright Air, daughter of Nyx — rather than the later conflation with Eos.
captions.genelli-ajax-slain-by-poseidon: Genelli's nostos punishment — Poseidon shattering the Locrian's rock after Athena's wrath at Cassandra's rape.
captions.hephaestus-and-the-scamander: Illustration of Hephaestus' fire against Scamander's flood — the Iliad's elemental duel that saves Achilles from the river.
captions.heracles-and-the-cretan-bull-drawing-aft: A BnF drawing after a red-figure vase: Heracles subdues the Cretan Bull in the formula vase-painters used for the seventh Labour — the same bull Poseidon sent to Minos and that later sires the Minotaur's line.
captions.hiltensperger-danaus-showing-the-argives: Hiltensperger's ceiling panel for the Hermitage's Gallery of the History of Ancient Painting shows Danaus presenting painted Egyptian god-figurines to the Argives — the refugee king as culture-bearer from Egypt to Argos. The scene answers Pausanias' notice that Danaus dedicated the first wooden images at Apollo Lykeios; here the father of the Danaids appears in his own right, not only through his daughters' crime.
captions.ingres-hercule-saisissant-hippolyte-rein: In this preparatory drawing the French Neoclassical master Ingres distills the violent core of the labour into pure line: Heracles overpowering the Amazon queen Hippolyta to seize the belt of Ares. Ingres, a lifelong student of antique heroic subjects, captures the wrestling tension of the two figures with the disciplined contour for which his draftsmanship is celebrated. The sheet is preserved in the Musée Ingres Bourdelle in Montauban.
captions.ingres-the-dog-of-ulysses: Ingres isolates Argos as a study of loyalty: the hound of Ithaca, neglected yet still knowing — Odyssey 17 distilled into a single animal portrait.
captions.kaselowsky-pelops-and-hippodamia: Kaselowsky's academic race aftermath — Pelops with Hippodamia, the bride won by Myrtilus' sabotage.
captions.monsiau-scylla-and-nisus: Scylla and Nisus — the lock of purple hair cut from her father's head to open Megara's gates.
captions.pandarus-and-cressida: This Metropolitan Museum print of Troilus and Cressida Act 1 Scene 2 freezes Pandarus with Cressida — Shakespeare's middleman, far from the Iliad's Lycian archer who breaks the truce, yet still named for him.
captions.preller-chryses-on-the-seashore: Preller isolates Homer's old man walking the resounding sea after Agamemnon's threats — the quiet moment before he calls Apollo.
captions.preller-dolon: Preller's Romantic reading isolates the Trojan spy in his animal disguise — the wolf-clad scout of Book X caught between courage and folly. Nineteenth-century myth illustration keeps Dolon as the night's most expendable volunteer.
captions.schopin-achilles-pursued-by-the-xanthus: Schopin's canvas: the river-god Scamander rising in waves against Achilles — Romantic water overwhelming the hero until Hephaestus intervenes.
captions.the-centaur-eurytion-carrying-off-a-lapi: Print after the Centauromachy type: Eurytion, wine-maddened at Peirithous' wedding, seizes a Lapith bride — the outrage that opens the battle of Lapiths and Centaurs. The named Thessalian centaur becomes the emblem of the feast gone violent.
captions.theseus-and-sciron: Nineteenth-century illustration of Theseus casting Sciron from the Scironian rocks — the turtle below, the brigand mid-fall.
captions.trophonius: An early-modern portrait emblem of Trophonius — the architect-hero who became Lebadeia's chthonic voice.
captions.volanakis-the-return-of-the-argonauts: Volanakis' seascape of the Argo homeward — the return voyage as Greek marine painting.
captions.bouguereau-combat-of-the-centaurs-and-th: Bouguereau's Salon machine — bodies mid-struggle from Ovid's Metamorphoses XII, the Centauromachy as academic proof.
captions.rahl-orestes-pursued-by-the-furies: Rahl's canvas: the Erinyes close on Orestes — Tisiphone among the pursuing sisters as nineteenth-century academic terror.
captions.malmstrom-odysseus-before-alcinous-king-: Malmström's Nationalmuseum painting seats Odysseus before the Phaeacian throne — Alcinous as the island king who will hear the wanderer's tale and send him home on a self-steering ship.
captions.pollet-endymion-and-selene: Pollet's academic nocturne: Selene arrives at the sleeping shepherd — nineteenth-century polish on the oldest lunar love story.
captions.gerhard-heracles-and-athena-flanked-by-d: Eduard Gerhard's nineteenth-century line drawing reproduces a late sixth-century BCE Attic amphora, now in the British Museum (1843,1103.96), published in his Auserlesene griechische Vasenbilder (Berlin, 1858, pl. 246). Heracles stands at left beside a Doric column while Athena stands at right beside an Ionic one, a deliberate pairing that figures the ancient association between Heracles and Dorian identity. That association underpins the legend of Temenus, the eldest Heraclid who, claiming descent from Heracles through Hyllus, Cleodaeus and Aristomachus, led the Dorian Return of the Heraclidae and won Argos. The vase image thus stands as the visual ancestry of Temenus's claim: the Dorian recovery of the inheritance of their hero forefather.
captions.gerome-the-death-of-caesar: Gérôme’s Walters canvas freezes the Ides: Caesar fallen, conspirators exiting the Curia. Academic history painting is the modern image of the dictator Ovid will soon lift to a comet — murder as the hinge before apotheosis.
captions.jones-thisbe-sarjeant-gallery: Another Burne-Jones Thisbe in the Sarjeant Gallery — the same Ovidian heroine as solitary figure, cloak and wall, waiting for a voice that will not save her.
captions.tadema-the-death-of-hippolytus: Alma-Tadema's shore — the bull from the waves and the wrecked hunter, Phaedra's lie completed before Diana's rescue.
captions.corot-orpheus-leading-eurydice-from-the-: Corot's descent — the cycle's heart: Orpheus leading Eurydice from the underworld before the fatal glance.
captions.degas-semiramis-building-babylon: Degas' early history painting: Semiramis surveys the rising walls of Babylon — the legendary queen as nineteenth-century builder of empire.
captions.dore-minos-inferno-canto-v: Wood engraving from Gustave Doré's illustrated Divine Comedy: Minos sits at the gate of Hell, wrapping his tail to assign each soul its circle. Doré's Romantic reading of Dante sealed the Cretan lawgiver as the iconic judge of the damned for the modern age.
captions.dore-the-giants-inferno-canto-xxxi: Doré's Inferno giants: Ephialtes chained among the Titans who heaped Pelion on Ossa — the Aloadae's assault on heaven carried into Dante's pit.
captions.dore-the-harpies-in-the-wood-of-the-suic: Gustave Doré's engraving for his illustrated edition of Dante's Divine Comedy shows the Harpies nesting in the gnarled, blood-weeping trees of the Wood of the Suicides in the seventh circle of Hell. Dante drew the creatures directly from the classical tradition of the storm-winged snatchers who tormented Phineus, recasting them as the foul-winged tormentors who feed on the leaves of the damned. Doré's dramatic chiaroscuro fixed this haunting image of the Harpies in the popular imagination of the nineteenth century.
captions.millais-iphis-and-anaxarete: National Gallery of Victoria print of Ovid's Cypriot tale: proud Anaxarete watches Iphis hang himself — before Venus turns her to stone at the funeral.
captions.pujol-the-vengeance-of-diana-against-oen: The French Neoclassical painter Abel de Pujol dramatizes the offence that set the Calydonian disaster in motion: Oeneus, having rendered first-fruits to all the gods but neglecting Artemis (Diana), incurs the goddess's wrath. The composition turns on the king of Calydon and the divine huntress whose slighted honour will loose the monstrous boar upon his fields and people. As a museum piece it crystallizes the moral pivot of Oeneus's story, the pious king's single omission, that the ancient sources name as the cause of the hunt in which his son Meleager would win and lose his life.
captions.bouguereau-orestes-pursued-by-the-furies: Bouguereau's remorse after the matricide — Orestes recoiling as the Erinyes throng, the Oresteia's blood-guilt before Athens' court.
captions.fesquet-the-shepherd-aristaeus-mourning-: Fesquet's seated grieving Aristaeus — the same Virgilian apiary disaster, second prize in the 1862 sculpture contest.
captions.hiolle-the-shepherd-aristaeus-mourning-t: Hiolle's Prix de Rome plaster: Aristaeus sunk beside an empty hive — Georgics IV's bee-loss that drives him to Cyrene and the bugonia.
captions.cabanel-the-birth-of-venus: Cabanel's Salon sensation: Venus reclining on the wave-crest beneath putti — academic polish for the same foam-born arrival Napoleon III bought at once.
captions.moreau-oedipus-and-the-sphinx: Moreau's Symbolist confrontation turns the riddle into erotic menace: the Sphinx clings to Oedipus' breast like a living puzzle, her feline body pressing against the hero who meets her gaze without flinching. Painted for the Salon of 1864 and now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, it made Oedipus a fin-de-siècle emblem of knowledge bought at a terrible price.
captions.preller-odysseus-and-nausicaa: Preller the Elder's history painting renders the Odyssean threshold: brine-caked Odysseus supplicates the composed Phaeacian princess while her maids flee. Neoclassical balance makes Nausicaa the face of civilised welcome.
captions.fedi-the-rape-of-polyxena: Fedi's marble group in the Loggia dei Lanzi: Neoptolemus seizes Polyxena for the tomb — Trojan grief carved as a nineteenth-century public monument.
captions.moreau-diomedes-devoured-by-his-horses-d: Oil on canvas (140 x 95.5 cm), Musée des Beaux-Arts de Rouen. Moreau translates the eighth labour of Heracles into a brooding Symbolist tableau: the Thracian king Diomedes, son of Ares, sprawls on the ground as his own once man-eating mares fall upon him, while Heracles looms impassively at the right. The lurid palette and the writhing tangle of horseflesh and human limbs turn the myth's poetic justice — the cruel king fed to the beasts he kept — into a meditation on retribution and the savagery beneath royal power.
captions.moreau-jason-and-medea: Moreau's Salon canvas after the fleece is taken — Jason triumphant, Medea at his side, the voyage's eastern prize already shadowed by later betrayal.
captions.moreau-orpheus: Moreau's lyre and head — the cycle's aftermath distilled into Symbolist melancholy.
captions.poynter-eurycleia-recognizing-ulysses: A Victorian classicising canvas from the circle of Edward Poynter: Eurycleia starts back as she knows her master by the scar. The scene that Homer keeps almost secret — Odysseus silencing his nurse so the suitors will not hear — becomes a polished gallery drama of loyalty and danger.
captions.cameron-cassiopeia: Cameron's albumen print (Metropolitan Museum of Art) stages the Ethiopian queen as a Victorian allegory — Cassiopeia's boast against the Nereids distilled into a single seated figure whose vanity still names a northern constellation.
captions.moreau-diomedes-devoured-by-his-horses: A watercolour (19.1 x 17.1 cm, private collection) in which Moreau revisits the subject of his 1865 oil. The intimate sheet again shows the Thracian king Diomedes thrown down and torn by his own carnivorous mares as Heracles completes the eighth labour. The jewel-like, densely worked technique characteristic of Moreau's watercolours intensifies the nightmarish atmosphere, concentrating the myth's theme of the tyrant undone by his own cruelty into a small, glowing field of colour.
captions.sandys-medea: Sandys' Pre-Raphaelite half-length shows Medea as enchantress at her work: mixing the poison for Creusa's bridal gift, a coral necklace and magic vessels before her. The painting isolates the Colchian witch's craft rather than the slaughter — intelligence and dread in equal measure. Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery.
captions.schou-chione-killed-on-the-hunt-by-offen: Schou's Danish history-painting restages Ovid: Chione fallen under Diana's anger — the blasphemy that drives Daedalion toward the hawk.
captions.blanc-the-murder-of-laius-by-oedipus: Blanc's Prix de Rome canvas freezes the fork in the road: Oedipus strikes down the older king in the chariot while attendants fall back — the patricide Sophocles' recognition will later uncover. Painted for the École des Beaux-Arts, Paris, it made Laius the corpse at the centre of the Theban tragedy, not a name in a genealogy.
captions.blanchard-the-murder-of-laius-by-oedipus: Blanchard's rival Prix de Rome entry stages the same roadside killing: Laius toppled from the chariot as the unrecognized son strikes. Now in the Musée d'art et d'archéologie, Cluny, the canvas shows how the Academy treated Laius' death as a history-painting test — the king whose oracle and exposure set the recognition in motion.
captions.henner-byblis-turning-into-a-spring: Henner paints the metamorphosis mid-flow: Byblis' body softens into the fountain that bears her name — Carian incestuous grief made liquid.
captions.regnault-esquisse-pour-automedon-avec-le: French study for the same subject: Automédon named in the title — the Iliadic driver as a nineteenth-century academic trial before the Boston canvas.
captions.regnault-sketch-for-automedon-with-the-h: Regnault's oil sketch for the finished Automedon — the charioteer already wrestling the immortal team into a single composition.
captions.constant-antigone-at-the-bedside-of-poly: Benjamin-Constant's Antigone keeps vigil over her brother's corpse — the quiet moment before defiance becomes Sophocles' tragedy.
captions.kaulbach-the-battle-of-salamis: Kaulbach's vast history painting stages the Persian defeat at Salamis with Artemisia of Halicarnassus at center-left, loosing arrows above the Greek fleet beneath Xerxes' throne — the Carian queen Herodotus praised as the only Persian-side commander worthy of naming.
captions.regnault-automedon-with-the-horses-of-ac: Regnault's Boston masterpiece: Automedon masters Xanthus and Balius — Achilles' immortal horses — before the chariot that will carry Patroclus to death and Achilles to Hector. The charioteer Homer honoured most after Patroclus made flesh in Second Empire paint.
captions.fagnani-polyhymnia: From the cycle of the Nine Muses painted by the Italian-American artist Giuseppe Fagnani and now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, this canvas presents Polyhymnia, the Muse of sacred hymn. Fagnani follows the canonical iconography of the most solemn Muse: a pensive, veiled figure draped in a plain mantle, her thoughtful gaze turning inward as though weighing the words of a hymn. In the ancient division of the arts among the daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne, Polyhymnia governed devotional song and the grave, persuasive eloquence offered to the gods, and Fagnani's quiet, contemplative portrait honours that reflective character.
captions.jones-the-garden-of-the-hesperides: Edward Burne-Jones's gouache (1869–1873, Hamburger Kunsthalle) depicts the three Hesperides circling the sacred apple tree in a slow, ritual dance, their linked rhythm echoed by the serpent Ladon spiralling up the trunk behind them. A leading Pre-Raphaelite image of the myth, it imagines the nymphs as tending and singing about the golden apples at the world's western limit — the dwelling of the daughters of Hesperus where the tree of Hera's golden fruit grew, guarded perpetually by the sleepless dragon.
captions.lehmann-calypso: Academic oil by Henri Lehmann in the Minneapolis Institute of Art: Calypso alone, idealized as a solitary goddess of the shore. Stripped of Odysseus, the portrait still names the Ogygian nymph — the detainee-hostess of the Odyssey reduced to a single contemplative figure.
captions.leighton-electra-at-the-tomb-of-agamemno: Leighton's Electra at her father's Mycenaean tomb — the Libation Bearers' vigil before Orestes returns and the axe falls again.
captions.leighton-hercules-wrestling-with-death-f: Oil on canvas by Frederic Leighton, now in the Wadsworth Atheneum, Hartford, Connecticut. It depicts the climax of the Alcestis myth as dramatized by Euripides: Alcestis lies pale and lifeless after dying in place of her husband Admetus, while at the right Heracles grapples bodily with the winged figure of Death (Thanatos) to wrench her back from the grave. Leighton's painting inspired Robert Browning's poem 'Balaustion's Adventure,' which retells the same rescue.
captions.poynter-andromeda: Poynter's Victorian Andromeda stands chained against the rock with a blue cloth at her ankle — Ovid and Apollodorus restaged as Academic spectacle, the princess as the myth's still centre before Perseus arrives.
captions.the-heraclidae-drawing-lots-for-the-pelo: Engraving after the antique gem — the Heraclidae drawing lots for Argos, Messenia, and Sparta, the Return's partition.
captions.feuerbach-medea: Feuerbach's seated sorceress holds the fatal gifts — cool neoclassical calm before the bridal fire and the children's deaths.
captions.jones-aeneas-and-the-sibyl-in-the-underw: Burne-Jones' Fitzwilliam design: the Sibyl leads Aeneas among the shades — Pre-Raphaelite stillness for Virgil's most famous katabasis.
captions.jones-night: Burne-Jones personifies Night as a solemn, draped woman drifting through a star-pricked void — Pre-Raphaelite stillness for the goddess who mothers Sleep and Death. Watercolour and bodycolour; a Victorian heir to the ancient Nyx.
captions.jones-phyllis-and-demophoon: Burne-Jones' Birmingham canvas: Phyllis, transformed into an almond tree, clasps the returning Demophon — Theseus' son who abandoned her and found her changed. Pre-Raphaelite myth turns the Athenian prince's Thracian love into a tree-embrace of forgiveness and desire.
captions.joy-laodamia: Joy's Laodamia — the widow whose grief outlived the first Achaean dead at Troy.
captions.watts-orpheus-and-eurydice: The Victorian Symbolist George Frederic Watts isolates the moment of loss: Orpheus turns and Eurydice slips back into shadow. Where Baroque painters filled the underworld with gods, Watts reduces the myth to two bodies and a glance — Eurydice as the vanishing half of the song.
captions.allar-hecuba-discovering-the-body-of-her: Bas-relief by the French sculptor André-Joseph Allar, his first-year envoi from the Villa Medici, now represented by a galvanoplastic bronze in the Musée des Beaux-Arts, Marseille. Hecuba finds Polydorus cast up on the sand — the Ovidian recognition that opens her vengeance cycle, carved by an artist who had just lost a child of his own.
captions.rossetti-pandora: Rossetti's half-length Pandora holds the sealed box against a sulphurous glow — Jane Morris as the gift the gods sent to punish mankind. The Pre-Raphaelite jar made into a jewel of dread.
captions.toudouze-farewell-of-oedipus-to-the-corp: Toudouze's Prix de Rome painting (École des Beaux-Arts, Paris) lays Jocasta among the dead of the house of Cadmus. Blind Oedipus takes leave of the queen who hanged herself when the bed's riddle was spoken — Theban ruin staged as a funeral farewell.
captions.jones-the-feast-of-peleus: Burne-Jones's Pre-Raphaelite frieze of the wedding banquet places Eris at the far right, the uninvited guest whose golden apple is already among the gods. Where Jordaens fills the table with Baroque tumult, Burne-Jones turns the same Homeric hinge into a pale, ritual procession — Discord as the quiet edge of the feast that starts the Trojan War.
captions.jones-thisbe: Burne-Jones' Birmingham panel isolates Thisbe at the wall — part of his Pyramus and Thisbe cycle, the maiden framed as patient listener before the mulberry tragedy.
captions.lefebvre-pandora: Lefebvre's academic Pandora stands with the box still closed — beauty as bait, the gift Zeus sent through Epimetheus. Salon mythology at full polish: the woman who has not yet opened the world.
captions.cabanel-pandora: Cabanel's Walters portrait casts soprano Christine Nilsson as Pandora with the casket — high-society myth, the opener as celebrity. The jar becomes an opera singer's prop in Second Empire silk.
captions.corbould-troilus-and-cressida-in-the-gar: Oil painting by the Victorian illustrator Edward Henry Corbould. Troilus and Cressida meet in Pandarus' garden — Chaucer's and Shakespeare's lovers before the war and the betrayal unmake them, the Trojan prince cast as courtly suitor rather than Achilles' victim.
captions.poynter-mercury-stealing-the-cattle-of-t: Poynter's Walker Art Gallery canvas: Mercury as cattle-thief among the herd — Victorian Academic reading of the infant god's first crime.
captions.dantan-hercules-at-the-feet-of-omphale-h: Dantan's Salon canvas — the hero at the queen's feet, club and lion-skin surrendered for the spindle.
captions.leighton-clytemnestra-from-the-battlemen: Leighton paints the watch that opens Aeschylus' Agamemnon: Clytemnestra alone on the Argive walls, waiting for the beacons that will bring her husband home to the axe.
captions.rossetti-proserpine: Rossetti's Tate Proserpine holds the bitten pomegranate — the Hymn's binding fruit that splits the year between worlds.
captions.waterhouse-sleep-and-his-half-brother-de: An early oil painting by John William Waterhouse depicting Hypnos and his brother Thanatos, Sleep and Death, resting side by side in a dim chamber. Sleep, in the lamplight, holds poppies in his lap, while Death lies in shadow behind him; their near-identical faces draw out the ancient kinship between the two brothers.
captions.bouguereau-flora-and-zephyr: Bouguereau's Mulhouse canvas: Zephyr, winged and airborne, lifts Flora among putti and roses — academic polish on the Ovidian marriage of west wind and flowers.
captions.feuerbach-gaea: A ceiling painting by the German classicist Anselm Feuerbach at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna. It presents Gaia, the primordial mother of the earth, as a serene figure enthroned in the heavens, part of the decorative program Feuerbach created for the academy in his final years.
captions.jones-pygmalion-and-the-image-the-soul-a: The last panel of Burne-Jones' Birmingham Pygmalion series: Galatea steps living from the pedestal into the sculptor's arms. Pre-Raphaelite quiet after the prayer, the myth fulfilled in soft light.
captions.lenormant-heracles-and-iphicles-heracles: This nineteenth-century line drawing, published by the antiquarian François Lenormant, faithfully unrolls the painted frieze of the Louvre stamnos (G 192) so the whole scene can be read at once. At its centre the infant Heracles throttles the two serpents; to one side his twin Iphicles bolts away in fright toward the sheltering arms of their mother Alcmene, while Amphitryon and Athena complete the family group. As the illustration that heads Iphicles' own entry, it preserves the canonical contrast of the brave child and the fearful one—the founding test of the twins distinguished in Apollodorus' Bibliotheca.
captions.rossetti-mnemosyne-the-lamp-of-memory: An oil by Dante Gabriel Rossetti in the Delaware Art Museum, also called The Lamp of Memory. The Titaness of recollection holds a lamp and wears a dark, heavy gaze — Pre-Raphaelite Memory as longing made flesh, the mother of the Muses reimagined as a late-Victorian icon of remembrance.
captions.watts-chaos: Watts's Tate allegory of the first gap: elemental titans heave from fire and vapour — Hesiod's Chaos before Earth and sky take form.
captions.moreau-hercules-and-the-lernaean-hydra: Moreau's Symbolist Hydra — the second Labour as jewelled nightmare, the many-headed marsh beast of the Heracles cycle.
captions.belleuse-the-abduction-of-hippodamia: Bronze group — a Centaur rears with Hippodameia locked against his chest, the seizure that ignites the Lapith war.
captions.jones-perseus-and-the-graiae-southampton: The earlier bodycolour version of Burne-Jones's Graiae scene, now in Southampton City Art Gallery — a preparatory masterpiece in the Perseus series. The three grey sisters and the armoured hero are already locked in the eye-theft ritual that the 1892 Stuttgart oil would monumentalise; here the design is sharper, flatter, and closer to the artist's stained-glass and tapestry thinking.
captions.morgan-cadmus-and-harmonia: De Morgan's Pre-Raphaelite close: Cadmus and Harmonia become entwined serpents — the Theban founder ending as the dragon he once slew.
captions.bocklin-medusa: Böcklin's Medusa — Symbolist isolation of the snake-haired face that turns flesh to stone.
captions.chervet-amphitrite: A bronze Amphitrite on the Place de la Marine in Agde, France — Poseidon's queen as the Mediterranean's local sea goddess, facing the harbour.
captions.eurus: Wood engraving from August Heinrich Petiscus' Der Olymp (Leipzig, 1878): Eurus as the personified east wind of autumn — cloak, seasonal attributes, and the classical schoolbook image of the Anemos who brings changeable weather from the sunrise.
captions.hestia-goddess-of-the-hearth-and-domesti: A wood engraving of Hestia published in August Heinrich Petiscus's popular mythology handbook Der Olymp oder die Mythologie der Griechen und Römer (Leipzig, 1878). The veiled goddess stands with a torch and a bowl, the Victorian schoolroom's canonical image of the hearth deity — austere, unwed, and absent from the flashier Olympian quarrels — through which nineteenth-century readers first met the quietest of the Twelve.
captions.leighton-nausicaa: The Phaeacian princess pauses in a doorway, the ball games done — the girl on the edge of womanhood who found a salt-crusted stranger on the shore and led him to her father's hall.
captions.momus-the-greek-god-of-ridicule: This nineteenth-century woodcut engraving, published in August Heinrich Petiscus's Der Olymp oder die Mythologie der Griechen und Römer (Leipzig, 1878), freezes Momus in the popular handbook image of the god of satire and blame. Cloaked and gesturing as a personification rather than a narrative actor, he embodies the Hesiodic and later comic tradition of Momus as the spirit who finds fault with everything. The print supplied generations of schoolroom and parlor readers with their visual cue for the daimon of ridicule.
captions.moreau-phaeton: Moreau's watercolour plunges Phaethon through a jewelled abyss of horses and stars — the fatal ride as Symbolist catastrophe. Watercolour on paper; Musée Gustave Moreau, Paris.
captions.morgan-night-and-sleep: An oil painting by the English artist Evelyn De Morgan, now in the De Morgan Foundation collection. Nyx, the goddess of night, drifts across the sky drawing her mantle of darkness over the world, while her son Hypnos floats at her side scattering the poppies of sleep. The intertwined pair show De Morgan's debt to Botticelli and the Pre-Raphaelites.
captions.rhea-presenting-cronus-the-stone-wrapped: Nineteenth-century wood engraving of the birth's hinge: Rhea delivers the swaddled rock while the true child is hidden for Crete.
captions.schlosser-prometheus-and-epimetheus-befo: Academic oil from Berlin's Nationalgalerie: Prometheus and Epimetheus stand before the newly fashioned Pandora, the foresighted brother already uneasy and the afterthought brother already won. Schlösser stages the gift that will undo Epimetheus as a tableau of two temperaments.
captions.tours-the-murder-of-pelias-by-his-daught: Academic canvas of Medea's trick: Pelias' daughters, convinced they will rejuvenate their father, cut him down in the cauldron. Moreau de Tours freezes the Iolcan king's end — the revenge Jason's Colchian wife visits on the uncle who stole the throne.
captions.bouguereau-the-birth-of-venus: Bouguereau's Orsay canvas returns Venus to the shell amid a ring of nymphs and tritons — the Anadyomene birth restaged as French academic spectacle.
captions.flaxman-the-oath-of-the-seven-chiefs: A neoclassical line engraving showing the seven champions of the Argive expedition swearing their oath before marching on Thebes — among them Parthenopaeus, the Arcadian son of Atalanta, the youngest and most beautiful of the Seven. The seven warriors gather over a sacrificial victim, hands raised in solemn pledge to take the city or die at its gates, an iconic moment dramatized in Aeschylus' tragedy. The plate is drawn in the austere outline manner derived from John Flaxman's celebrated designs for the Greek tragedians and appeared in Alfred J. Church's 'Stories from the Greek Tragedians' (1879). It is the principal image illustrating Parthenopaeus' role in the saga, since the youth is rarely portrayed in isolation and is most often encountered as one of the doomed band before Thebes.
captions.leighton-psamathe: Oil on canvas, 85 × 66.5 cm, in the Lady Lever Art Gallery, Port Sunlight. Leighton's late academic-classical study presents the Nereid Psamathe alone on a sandy shore, her filmy drapery slipped from her shoulders onto the sand, arms folded about her drawn-up knees as she gazes out across a luminous Aegean. Turning the sea-nymph's back to the viewer, the painter distills her into a meditation on solitude and the tide, evoking the goddess of sandy beaches whom Aeacus once seized on this very kind of strand to father Phocus.
captions.aublet-selene: Aublet's fin-de-siècle moon goddess — Selene alone as luminous nude against the dark, crescent and night condensed into one figure.
captions.cabanel-phedre-phaedra: Shown at the Paris Salon of 1880 and given by the artist to his native Montpellier, this large oil on canvas (194 × 286 cm) is the defining modern image of Phaedra: the Cretan queen, daughter of Minos and wife of Theseus, lies wasted on her bed while two attendants watch her silent agony. Cabanel's academic, faintly Orientalist staging follows Euripides and Racine — the stepmother consumed by forbidden love for Hippolytus — and remains the centrepiece of the Musée Fabre.
captions.cezanne-leda-au-cygne-leda-and-the-swan: Held at the Barnes Foundation, Paul Cézanne's Leda au cygne reimagines the ancient myth in the language of early modernism. A reclining nude Leda extends one hand to grasp the beak of the swan, the disguised Zeus who will father Helen and the Dioscuri, while the rest of the composition dissolves into Cézanne's characteristic blocks of muted color and deliberate, constructive brushwork. Stripping away the theatrical eroticism of the Renaissance versions, Cézanne treats the figure and the bird as problems of volume, contour, and pictorial structure, turning the timeless story of the Spartan queen into a meditation on form itself.
captions.collin-biblis: Collin's reclining Byblis — Third Republic Ovidian nude of the sister exhausted by forbidden desire for Caunus.
captions.harrison-dictys-discovers-danae-and-the-: Gouache with wash and black chalk, exhibited at London's Grosvenor Gallery in 1880: Harrison names the fisherman in the title and shows Dictys finding Danaë and the baby Perseus after their chest washes onto Seriphos. Where Fuseli and the Pompeian fresco stage the landfall, this Victorian sheet makes Dictys himself the discoverer — Apollodorus' rescuer caught in the act of opening the myth.
captions.moreau-nyx-night-goddess: Moreau's Symbolist Nyx rises as a jewelled vision of primordial Night — dark wings, star-dust, and the hush before dreaming. The painting names the Hesiodic goddess directly rather than a generic allegory of evening.
captions.moreau-pasiphae: Moreau's Symbolist Pasiphaë turns the queen's unnatural passion into jewelled nightmare — Helios' daughter and the bull myth as fin-de-siècle obsession rather than classical anecdote. Musée Gustave Moreau, Paris.
captions.point-biblis-changed-into-a-spring: Point's Symbolist panel: Byblis as fountain-nymph — the rejected twin whose tears become a permanent spring in Caria.
captions.poynter-a-visit-to-aesculapius: Poynter's Tate canvas imagines Venus bringing a thorn-wounded foot to Aesculapius — the Classical healer receiving a goddess in a marble grove, snake-staff at his side.
captions.stanhope-the-waters-of-lethe-by-the-plai: A Pre-Raphaelite tempera-and-gold painting in which a procession of weary souls crosses a barren plain toward the waters of Lethe, the underworld river of forgetfulness personified in Greek myth. On the far bank, those who have drunk the water of oblivion and shed the memory of earthly life rise renewed into the bright meadows of Elysium. The work is held by Manchester Art Gallery.
captions.thumann-the-three-fates: Thumann's popular Salon image distinguishes the sisters sharply: Atropos with shears, young Clotho at the weave, and modest Lachesis measuring with sprigs in hand. The Measurer of lots becomes the calm centre of a print that circulated across nineteenth-century Europe.
captions.watts-a-study-for-hyperion: A preparatory study held at Somerville College, Oxford, for Watts' Hyperion imagery. The Titan of watchful light is reduced to a concentrated figure study — Victorian idealism reaching for the Hesiodic sun before the Olympian Helios took the chariot.
captions.yvon-penelope-drawing-after-an-antique-v: Yvon's drawing after an antique vase — Penelope as the faithful type classical archaeology handed to the nineteenth century.
captions.belle-the-hercyna-and-the-cave-of-tropho: Belle's Hercyna and the Cave of Trophonius — the Boeotian spring and chasm of the hero-oracle at Lebadeia.
captions.morgan-phosphorus-and-hesperus: De Morgan’s Pre-Raphaelite pair: Phosphorus (Eosphorus), the Morning Star, clasps Hesperus, the Evening Star — Hesiod’s dawn-bringer as a luminous youth, not the Christian Satan who later borrowed Lucifer’s Latin name.
captions.thornycroft-teucer: Thornycroft's Teucer — the Telamonian archer whose exile after Ajax's death sends him to found Salamis in Cyprus.
captions.watts-artemis-and-hyperion: Watts' Symbolist canvas pairs Artemis with Hyperion, the Titan of light whose name still means 'the High One.' The painting treats the Hesiodic father of Helios, Selene and Eos as a luminous presence rather than a mere genealogy — Hyperion as living light beside the huntress.
captions.argus-building-the-ship-argo: Victorian plate — Argus at the keel Athena planned, the muster beginning as wood becomes the speaking ship.
captions.collier-clytemnestra: Collier's queen just after the deed: bloodied axe in hand on the palace threshold — Agamemnon's murder already fact behind the curtain.
captions.jones-the-tree-of-forgiveness: A later Burne-Jones reworking of Phyllis and Demophon: the almond-tree nymph still holds the Athenian king. The painting keeps Demophon's afterlife as the lover who returned too late — and was forgiven in bark and blossom.
captions.leighton-antigone: Leighton's solitary Antigone in classical drapery — conscience without Creon or corpse, the sister who chooses the dead over the city's law.
captions.baschet-oedipus-condemns-polynices-with-: Baschet's academic canvas stages the Colonus curse: blind Oedipus turns on Polynices while Ismene and Antigone frame the scene. The quieter sister is present as witness — filial piety caught between brothers already doomed.
captions.bocklin-odysseus-and-calypso: Two figures who cannot meet: the nymph glowing against her red drapery at the cave-mouth, the hero a dark back on a dark rock, staring at the sea that is the only way home.
captions.bouguereau-la-nuit-night: An oil painting by the French academic master William-Adolphe Bouguereau personifying Night as a graceful female figure gliding through the darkened sky, her dark veil billowing about her. It belongs to a group of allegorical canvases Bouguereau devoted to the times of day, rendering the ancient goddess of night in the polished idiom of nineteenth-century academic painting.
captions.bouguereau-biblis: Bouguereau's Academic nude: Byblis collapsed beside the spring she will become — after the letter to Caunus, the pursuit, and the tears that dissolve her into water.
captions.bouguereau-day-le-jour: An academic oil painting personifying Hemera, the Greek goddess of daytime, as a female figure rising in flight against the morning sky. It belongs to Bouguereau's series of allegories of the hours, alongside Dawn, Twilight and Night, and was exhibited at the Paris Salon of 1884.
captions.bouguereau-lost-pleiad: Bouguereau’s Academic nude is the modern image of the ‘lost Pleiad’ — traditionally Merope, the sister who alone married a mortal (Sisyphus) and whose star shines dimmest. Salon pathos keeps the Atlas daughter distinct from the Messenian queen of Voltaire’s tragedy.
captions.baumeister-sthenelos-and-diomedes: Nineteenth-century Baumeister plate of Sthenelus with Diomedes — the Epigone and chariot-mate whose Iliadic vaunt answers Agamemnon with Capaneus' son's pride.
captions.collier-circe: Collier's Circe — the island hostess with cup and wand, Odyssey 10's most painted enchantress.
captions.sandys-cassandra: Sandys' head of the seer — wide-eyed prophecy at the moment Troy falls, the curse Apollo set on her voice made visible.
captions.strudwick-a-golden-thread: Strudwick's Pre-Raphaelite allegory gathers the three Fates at their eternal labour: Clotho spins, Lachesis measures, and Atropos waits with the shears that no prayer can stay. The cutting sister — 'she who cannot be turned' — dominates the moral of the golden thread.
captions.vedder-study-for-the-pleiades: Metropolitan Museum study for Vedder's Pleiades canvas: the seven star-sisters take shape in chalk and wash — among them Taygete, the Laconian Pleiad whose name clings to Mount Taygetus and the Spartan line through Lacedaemon.
captions.vedder-the-pleiades: Oil on canvas, 61.3 by 95.6 cm, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (gift of George A. Hearn, 1910; accession 10.64.13). The American Symbolist painter Elihu Vedder shows the seven daughters of the Titan Atlas and the Oceanid Pleione drifting in a luminous void, each holding a thread strung with a star. Taygete, the Laconian Pleiad who became the mountain-nymph of Mount Taygetus and bore Lacedaemon to Zeus, is one of the sisters in this celestial sorority; the cluster of stars they cradle is the constellation that bears the family's name. One star hangs dark and dimmed at the lower left, a quiet allusion to the ancient tradition of the 'lost Pleiad.'
captions.watts-the-minotaur: Watts' brooding Minotaur — the creature at the heart of the cycle, waiting in Knossos for the tribute ship.
captions.bouguereau-the-return-of-spring: Bouguereau's Joslyn Art Museum canvas surrounds a nude Flora with putti and blossoms — academic spring as the goddess's bodily return. The painting made Flora a late-Victorian emblem of seasonal rebirth for American audiences.
captions.knab-the-mausoleum-at-halicarnassus: Knab’s reconstruction paints the stepped pyramid, chariot, and colonnade Pliny described — the tomb of Mausolus as nineteenth-century imagination still saw the Wonder. The king’s afterlife is architecture: his name outlived his city as a common noun for grand burial.
captions.rodin-myrrha: Rodin's sculpture isolates Myrrha as a body caught between woman and tree — the Ovidian metamorphosis made flesh. The Cypriot princess who asked to vanish from both life and death becomes a study in shame, desire and wooden transformation.
captions.schutzenberger-ulysses-attacked-by-the-d: Illustration to Odyssey 14: the disguised Odysseus approaches the swineherd's steading and is set upon by Eumaeus' dogs before the loyal slave calls them off and offers hospitality. Schützenberger makes the hut's threshold the first true welcome home — Eumaeus' dogs almost spoil the recognition that will save Ithaca.
captions.selous-thersites-accosts-achilles: Selous' Victorian illustration for Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida: the deformed railer Thersites confronts Achilles — the Iliad's insolent voice from the ranks reinvented as the play's bitter fool.
captions.solomon-ajax-and-cassandra: Solomon's sack of Troy — the Locrian Ajax tears Cassandra from Athena's sanctuary, the sacrilege that brought the thunderbolt and the Gyraean rocks.
captions.derkinderen-the-building-of-the-ship-arg: Rijksmuseum canvas — the Argo rising on the strand while Argonauts point toward the open sea from Pagasae.
captions.leighton-captive-andromache: Leighton's captive — Andromache among the spoil, the Trojan queen whose Epirote fate this nostos seals.
captions.simonet-nessus-and-deianira: Simonet's academic canvas: the centaur seizes Deianira at the Evenus — the dying deceit that furnishes the poisoned 'love-charm' and seals Heracles' pyre years later.
captions.haerdtl-briareos-spandrel-figure-natural: A carved spandrel (Zwickelfigur) by the sculptor Hugo Haerdtl on the Bellariastrasse avant-corps of the Naturhistorisches Museum in Vienna. Within a programme of mythological figures, Briareos appears as the hundred-handed son of Uranus and Gaia, embodying the primordial, earth-born forces of nature appropriate to a museum of natural history. The figure continues the long iconographic tradition of representing the Hecatoncheir as a colossus of immense, many-limbed strength.
captions.moreau-jupiter-and-semele: Moreau's Jupiter and Semele — the mortal mother consumed by the god's true form, Dionysus still unborn in the blaze.
captions.richmond-venus-and-anchises: Oil painting by William Blake Richmond. Venus draws Anchises into an embrace amid a classical landscape — late Victorian myth-painting that keeps the Dardanian lover as Aphrodite's chosen mortal rather than only the burden on Aeneas' shoulders.
captions.gerome-pygmalion-and-galatea: Gérôme's marble maiden warming into flesh under the sculptor's kiss — Ovid's festival miracle as academic theatre.
captions.thoma-hercules-delivers-hesione: Hans Thoma's late-nineteenth-century canvas restages the rescue as a German Symbolist allegory: Hercules leads Hesione from the monster's rock. The painting belongs to the modern reception that kept Laomedon's daughter alive beside Andromeda — the Trojan princess as a second chained maiden of the Greek east.
captions.bannister-leucothea-rescuing-ulysses: Bannister's American landscape-toned myth shows Leucothea — Ino deified — coming to Odysseus in the storm. The White Goddess of sailors is painted as a presence of rescue rather than court allegory, the Theban leap fulfilled as mercy on the open sea.
captions.cros-pasiphae-adorning-the-bull-with-flo: Cros's pâte-de-verre relief freezes the queen in the act of garlanding the bull — Pasiphaë's doomed courtship cast in coloured glass for the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
captions.leighton-perseus-and-andromeda: Leighton's Victorian spectacle — Perseus airborne above Andromeda as the dragon coils, Athena's gifts implied in the flight.
captions.leighton-the-return-of-persephone: Leighton's Leeds canvas — Hermes leading Persephone up to Demeter's arms, the annual reunion that brings spring back.
captions.michelena-penthesilea: Michelena's Amazon queen armed for Troy — the sovereign warrior who will die under Achilles' spear in the lost epic after Hector.
captions.moreau-the-return-of-the-argonauts: The Argonauts' homecoming — the fleece-bearing ship after Colchis, Wandering Rocks, and Corcyra.
captions.stuck-orpheus: Stuck's Symbolist Orpheus — the singer whose Metamorphoses inset songs still name music's power over living things.
captions.waterhouse-circe-offering-the-cup-to-uly: Enthroned between drugged swine and scattered herbs, the goddess lifts cup and wand at once — and in the bronze mirror behind her, small and armed, stands the man the drug will not touch.
captions.waterhouse-ulysses-and-the-sirens: Waterhouse gives the singers their old vase-form back — great birds with women's faces settling on the rigging around the bound king, close enough to touch.
captions.jones-perseus-and-the-graiae: Oil on canvas by the English Pre-Raphaelite painter Edward Burne-Jones, part of his Perseus cycle and now in the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart. The composition shows the hero Perseus, in dark armour, slipping among the three grey sisters at the decisive instant of his quest: he has intercepted the single shared eye as the Graeae pass it from hand to hand, holding it just beyond their reach. The sisters, draped in classical robes against a flat decorative ground, grope blindly toward him, while Perseus extorts from them the way to the nymphs who keep the winged sandals, the cap of Hades, and the kibisis. Burne-Jones distils the episode of Apollodorus (Bibliotheca 2.4.2) into a frieze-like ritual of outstretched hands and averted faces.
captions.leighton-the-garden-of-the-hesperides: Frederic Leighton's tondo (c. 1892, Lady Lever Art Gallery, Port Sunlight) gives the Hesperides their most famous Victorian image. Three nymphs of the evening recline beneath the golden apple tree at the western edge of the world, lapped in drowsy harmony while the immortal serpent Ladon coils around the trunk and across their laps to guard the fruit. Leighton renders the daughters of Night not as guardians on alert but as figures of languid, eternal repose — the embodiment of the far western paradise where Gaia's wedding gift to Hera was kept, and the prize Heracles came to seize in his eleventh labor.
captions.matsch-triumphant-achilles: Matsch's Achilleion fresco: Achilles drives his chariot before Troy, dragging Hector's body in the dust as the city watches from the ramparts.
captions.schenck-reconstruction-of-the-nekyia-of-: Polygnotus Nekyia reconstruction — Palamedes among the dead, the framed inventor still present in the underworld catalogue.
captions.waterhouse-circe-invidiosa: Waterhouse's tall oil (Art Gallery of South Australia) freezes Ovid's jealousy: Circe pours emerald poison into the bay where Scylla will bathe, turning Glaucus' rejected love into the strait-monster of Messina.
captions.claudel-clotho: A plaster sculpture of Clotho, the Fate who spins the thread of life, imagined not as a maiden but as a gaunt old woman ensnared in the very threads she spins. Claudel's haunting inversion of the myth makes destiny itself appear entangled in its own web.
captions.crane-king-midas-with-his-daughter: Crane's Wonder Book plate — Hawthorne's Midas discovering that the touch that gilds a rose can also freeze a child to gold.
captions.robert-epeius-in-the-iliupersis-of-polyg: A nineteenth-century scholarly reconstruction by Carl Robert of a section of Polygnotus's lost Iliupersis (the Sack of Troy), which decorated the Lesche of the Cnidians at Delphi. Pausanias, who saw the original, records that Epeius was shown in the act of throwing down the Trojan wall, above which rose the head of the wooden horse he had built. The drawing recovers, from ancient testimony, how one of antiquity's most famous fresco cycles portrayed the architect of Troy's downfall.
captions.robert-reconstruction-of-the-iliupersis-: Carl Robert's 1893 reconstruction of Polygnotus' lost Iliupersis in the Lesche of the Knidians at Delphi follows Pausanias, who places Helenus seated in deepest dejection near Helen among the captive Trojans. The modern drawing recovers the Classical image of the prophetic prince at Troy's fall — foresight that survived the sack.
captions.flaxman-diomed-and-ulysses-returning-wit: Flaxman's outline — the Achaeans returning with Rhesus' spoils and the snow-white horses.
captions.morgan-eos: De Morgan's Eos — the dawn goddess whose gift of endless life without youth defines Tithonus' tragedy.
captions.stuck-the-kiss-of-the-sphinx: Stuck's Symbolist Sphinx pins a mortal in a lethal embrace — the Theban monster remade as femme fatale, kiss and kill in one gesture. Oil on canvas, Hungarian National Gallery, Budapest.
captions.bocklin-odysseus-and-polyphemus: Böcklin's Symbolist confrontation — the hero facing the one-eyed shepherd before the wine and the name Nobody.
captions.laurens-glauce-and-thaleia: Laurens' Salon canvas pairs two Nereids — Glauce and Thaleia — as sea-sisters in quiet companionship, not the Muse Thalia of comedy. Apollodorus and Homer keep Thalia among Nereus' fifty daughters.
captions.morgan-boreas-and-oreithyia: Painted by the Pre-Raphaelite artist Evelyn De Morgan and now held at the De Morgan Centre in London, this oil reimagines the abduction as a sweeping aerial dance. The shadowy, blue-grey figure of Boreas, the North Wind, enfolds the pale Athenian princess Oreithyia as the pair are borne aloft over a cold landscape, her draperies streaming with the gusts that carry her away. De Morgan's symbolist sensibility softens the ancient theme of seizure into an image of irresistible elemental force, the chill of the north made flesh.
captions.waterhouse-hylas-and-the-nymphs: Waterhouse's Manchester canvas is the modern image of Hylas: the Argonaut youth kneels at a dark pool while seven water-nymphs rise to draw him under. Painted in 1896 for the Pre-Raphaelite twilight of Victorian myth, it freezes Theocritus' Mysian spring — beauty as a trap, Heracles' beloved vanishing into water. The painting remains the single most familiar depiction of the abduction that left the Argo without its strongest hero.
captions.waterhouse-pandora: Waterhouse's Pre-Raphaelite Pandora kneels over the fatal casket in a wooded hollow — Hesiod's first woman as curious opener, the jar restyled as a Victorian box. The moment before the world's troubles spill.
captions.watts-the-infancy-of-zeus: Watts' Symbolist infancy: the future king of the gods as a child in the mountain cave — birth myth as Victorian allegory of power waiting.
captions.siemiradzki-christian-dirce: Siemiradzki's National Museum in Warsaw canvas restages Nero's arena as a 'Dircean' spectacle: a Christian woman tied to a bull before a glittering Roman crowd. The painting turns the mythic punishment into a modern indictment — Dirce's death as template for imperial cruelty.
captions.waterhouse-phyllis-and-demophoon: Waterhouse's Phyllis and Demophon restages the reunion at the almond tree — Demophon of Athens as Pre-Raphaelite errant lover, caught by the woman he left.
captions.castaigne-alexander-cutting-the-gordian-: Castaigne's illustration for popular Alexander biographies freezes the cut: the Macedonian king, the ox-cart of Gordius, and the knot that English still calls 'Gordian.' Late-Victorian book art carried Phrygia's founder into classroom and parlour.
captions.draper-the-lament-for-icarus: Fallen Icarus lies among mourning nymphs, his great wings still spread — Tate Britain's Victorian elegy for the boy who flew too high, the myth retold as romantic martyrdom rather than unnoticed splash.
captions.klimt-pallas-athene: An oil painting of Athena in gleaming golden armor, the gorgoneion on her breast and a small nude figure of victory in her hand, her gaze level and unyielding. Painted at the height of the Vienna Secession, it became an emblem of the movement. It is held by the Wien Museum, Vienna.
captions.morgan-cassandra: De Morgan's prophetess before the burning city — she tears at her flame-red hair as everything she foretold comes true and no one will listen.
captions.morgan-helen-of-troy: De Morgan's Helen of Troy — the prize the oath was sworn to defend when Paris carries her away.
captions.the-story-of-perseus-and-the-gorgon-s-he: An illustrated page from the Perseus retelling in Charles Kingsley's The Heroes, issued in W. T. Stead's popular 'Books for the Bairns' series and held in Maastricht University's special collections. The Perseus narrative it accompanies turns on Polydectes, the king of Seriphos whose lust for Danae and demand for a wedding-gift drives Perseus to vow the Gorgon's head and ultimately to petrify the king on his return. The image belongs to the late-Victorian wave of moralizing mythology for young readers that kept the Seriphos episode, and its villain Polydectes, in wide circulation.
captions.bunny-nymph-of-salmacis: Bunny's fin-de-siècle Salmacis alone — the Carian naiad as Symbolist water spirit, desire before the embrace.
captions.gardner-salmoneus-imitating-zeus-drawing: AJA plate after Art Institute of Chicago 1889.16: Salmoneus with sword and mock thunderbolt, chains trailing his chariot — Iris watching the king who would be Zeus.
captions.vrubel-pan: Mikhail Vrubel's symbolist masterpiece transplants the Arcadian god of the wild into a Russian twilight landscape. A grizzled, blue-eyed Pan rises from the earth like a creature of the soil itself, his curling horns and shaggy goat-flesh dissolving into the birch grove and crescent moon behind him. In his gnarled hands he cradles the syrinx, the reed pipe he is said to have invented; the painting distils Pan's essence as a primordial spirit of nature, untamed, ancient and faintly unsettling — the deity whose sudden presence in lonely places gives us the word 'panic.'
captions.herter-garden-of-the-hesperides: The American painter and muralist Albert Herter set this Garden of the Hesperides (c. 1900) at the golden tree of the western nymphs. The daughters of Evening move among the laden branches that bore Hera's golden apples, the coiled guardian Ladon never far from the fruit. Herter's decorative, mural-scaled treatment places the myth in the lineage of late-nineteenth-century Aesthetic painting, presenting the Hesperides as keepers of an earthly paradise at the sunset edge of the Greek world.
captions.redon-phaeton: Redon isolates Phaethon's fall in a dreamlike swirl of horse and youth — hubris behind the sun-wheel reduced to a single, vertiginous vision.
captions.sabatte-the-daughters-of-danaus: Sabatté's Daughters of Danaus — the fifty brides whose crime becomes Argos' founding myth and the underworld's sieve.
captions.waterhouse-nymphs-finding-the-head-of-or: Waterhouse's nymphs — the Maenad murder's aftermath, the singing head that closes the cycle.
captions.britten-oenone: Britten's plate for Tennyson's early poems illustrates the monologue 'Oenone' — the nymph alone on Ida after Paris leaves for Helen. Victorian book art made her grief the English face of the Trojan prelude.
captions.bunny-heliades: Bunny’s Symbolist canvas gathers Phaethon’s sisters in a dusk of gold and mourning — bodies already half-poplar, amber tears implied in the palette. Painted in Paris for the fin-de-siècle taste for Ovidian metamorphosis, it is among the few modern pictures that name the Heliades as the subject rather than their brother’s fall alone.
captions.phrixus-and-helle: This plate after a Pompeian fresco shows Phrixus and Helle on the golden ram — the children of Athamas and the cloud-nymph Nephele, fleeing Ino's plot. Nephele's gift of Hermes' ram is the hinge of the Golden Fleece cycle even when she herself stays off-stage.
captions.waterhouse-echo-and-narcissus: Waterhouse pairs the fading nymph with the boy at the spring — Echo's last embrace refused, Nemesis' answer still to come.
captions.waterhouse-the-danaides: Waterhouse's Danaides — the sisters forever pouring into broken jars, Tartarus' punishment for the wedding-night massacre.
captions.draper-the-golden-fleece: Draper's Jason and Medea with the fleece — the prize the return voyage must carry home to Iolcus.
captions.simonet-the-judgement-of-paris: Simonet's Málaga canvas restages the herdsman-prince among the three goddesses — the Epic Cycle opening as Academic spectacle.
captions.pyle-odysseus-advises-king-tyndareus-con: Pyle's Odysseus advising Tyndareus — the counsel that binds Helen's suitors by oath before the Spartan marriage.
captions.weguelin-the-magic-of-pan-s-flute: In this luminous late-Victorian watercolour, Weguelin imagines the spell cast by Pan's pipes. The goat-legged god sits enthroned upon a rock in a moonlit clearing, piping the syrinx, while nymphs are drawn helplessly toward him to dance in the silvery light. The scene celebrates Pan as god of shepherds, flocks and pastoral music — the inventor of the shepherd's pipe whose melody, in Arcadian belief, could be heard echoing from Mount Maenalus, the mountain held especially sacred to him.
captions.morgan-demeter-mourning-for-persephone: De Morgan's winter goddess among withered stalks — the mother's grief that barrened the earth until the Kore returned.
captions.herzog-the-banks-of-lethe: A Pictorialist photogravure evoking Lethe, the Greek personification and stream of oblivion whose waters the dead must drink to forget their former lives. Herzog stages a softly lit figure beside the still river, translating the classical daemon of forgetfulness into the dreamlike idiom of turn-of-the-century art photography. The print is in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA).
captions.klimt-danae: Klimt curls Danaë into a gold-patterned coil as Zeus arrives as a shower of coin-like rain — the bronze tower myth restaged as Symbolist erotic ornament. Oil on canvas, Leopold Museum, Vienna.
captions.niceville-daedalion-transformed-into-a-h: Early twentieth-century plate of Daedalion mid-change: Apollo's pity turns the warrior's leap from Parnassus into the hawk that still hunts other birds — Ovid's aetiology of the raptor's rage.
captions.waterhouse-jason-and-medea: Waterhouse stages the Colchian pact that makes the Argonautica possible: Medea mixes the charm while Jason waits to face Aeëtes' bulls.
captions.dechenaud-philemon-et-baucis: Déchenaud's academic canvas returns the Phrygian hosts to their table — twentieth-century reception of Ovid's rewarded piety.
captions.leslie-the-devotion-of-menoeceus-the-son: Leslie’s Edwardian sculpture stages Creon’s son offering himself to Ares so Thebes may stand against the Seven — the willing death Euripides and Statius make the city’s price. Rare modern art that names Menoeceus apart from his grandfather.
captions.parrish-cadmus-sowing-the-dragon-s-teeth: Created by the American illustrator Maxfield Parrish for an early-twentieth-century edition of Nathaniel Hawthorne's retellings of Greek myth, this luminous illustration depicts Cadmus on the Theban plain at the moment he sows the dragon's teeth and the first armed figures begin to rise from the ground. The Spartoi who emerge — the earth-born brothers from whose ranks Chthonius and four others alone survive — are shown as a crop of warriors bursting into being, dramatizing the myth's eerie equation of sowing seed with raising an army. Parrish's signature saturated palette and theatrical staging made the image one of the most widely reproduced modern visualizations of the episode.
captions.waterhouse-apollo-and-daphne: Waterhouse freezes the riverbank flight: Daphne twists as bark and foliage claim her limbs, Apollo still reaching — Victorian classicist terror becoming green armour.
captions.draper-ulysses-and-the-sirens: The Edwardian nightmare version: the singers climb over the gunwale as sea-nymphs while Ulysses strains against the mast and the rowers' sealed ears hold the ship on course.
captions.parrish-jason-and-his-teacher: This luminous illustration by the American artist Maxfield Parrish, created for Nathaniel Hawthorne's retellings of Greek myth, shows the centaur Chiron with another of his celebrated pupils, the young Jason, before he set out to win the Golden Fleece. Parrish renders Chiron against his signature saturated blue sky as a gentle, sagacious mentor, a reminder that the centaur tutored not only Achilles but a whole generation of heroes, including Jason and the healer Asclepius.
captions.waterhouse-thisbe: Waterhouse's Thisbe alone at the wall — the crack through which the fairest of Babylon whispered before the tomb.
captions.frye-the-golden-touch: Frye's illustration of the stranger's cure — plunge into the river, sprinkle the water, and wash the fatal gift away.
captions.hirschl-between-scylla-and-charybdis: The Hungarian Symbolist Adolf Hirémy-Hirschl restages the proverbial strait as a late Romantic ordeal: the ship trapped between the cliff-monster and the devouring swirl. Painted around 1910, the pastel keeps Charybdis as Homer cast her — not a figured body but the thrice-daily suck of the deep — the hazard Odysseus must skirt if he is to keep any of his crew alive.
captions.vedder-the-dance-of-the-pleiades-star-lo: Published plate from William Tyler Olcott's 'Star Lore of All Ages' (G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1911), reproducing Elihu Vedder's vision of the Pleiades as a circling band of star-maidens. The engraved illustration appears in a chapter on the mythology and folklore of the Pleiades star cluster, presenting the seven sisters — among them Taygete, eponym of the Laconian mountain range and ancestress of the Spartan kings through her son Lacedaemon — as luminous dancers whose movement traces the rising and setting of the constellation across the night sky.
captions.waterhouse-penelope-and-the-suitors: The queen bends to the loom with her back to the window full of pleading men — fidelity painted as concentration, the thread held taut.
captions.bunny-amymone-rescued-by-poseidon: Bunny's Symbolist canvas: Poseidon lifts Amymone from the satyr's pursuit — Danaus' daughter as modern mythic nude, the Argive spring-myth restaged in oil.
captions.redon-the-cyclops: Redon's Symbolist oil in the Kröller-Müller Museum turns the myth toward Polyphemus' gaze: the giant's huge head rises over a hillside while Galatea sleeps nude among flowers below. The Nereid becomes the dream the Cyclops cannot possess — Ovid rewritten as modern longing and colour.
captions.draper-halcyone: Draper's Edwardian Alcyone keeps vigil for Ceyx lost at sea — Ovid's widow before the gods turn both into halcyons.
captions.stratton-idas-and-marpessa-illustration-: Helen Stratton's Edwardian pen-and-ink plate, made for Jean Lang's A Book of Myths (1915), pictures Idas with his hard-won bride Marpessa. Stratton renders the Messenian prince in the flowing Art Nouveau line of the period's golden-age book illustration, drawing not the violence of the abduction but the tender aftermath of Marpessa's choice. The image accompanies the chapter retelling how Idas defied Apollo and dared even to draw his bow against the god before Zeus stepped in to settle the contest in the mortal's favour.
