captions.philpot-melampus-and-the-centaur: Painted in 1919 by the British artist Glyn Warren Philpot RA (1884–1937) and now in Glasgow Museums, this canvas gives the Greek seer Melampus a richly atmospheric Edwardian-classical treatment, pairing the youthful prophet with a centaur in a charged encounter of human and beast. The subject suits Melampus, who in legend understood the speech of animals — a gift won when serpents he had raised licked his ears clean — and who moved easily between the human and natural worlds as Greece's first mortal seer and healer. Philpot, celebrated for his sensuous handling of the male nude and his theatrical mythological compositions, here renders the meeting with a painterly warmth that places the ancient diviner squarely within early twentieth-century British Symbolist-classicism.
captions.regnier-birth-of-minerva: Kuhn-Régnier's Art Deco plate returns Athena to the split skull — a modern illustrator's take on wisdom springing complete.
captions.school-bellerophon-sets-out-against-the-: Printed Odyssey of Bellerophon’s Lycian labours: the hero rides out against the Chimera on the quest King Iobates assigned after reading Proetus’ sealed death-letter. Schoolbook myth keeps Iobates the off-stage sender of every Pegasus exploit that follows.
captions.stuck-sisyphus: Franz von Stuck's Sisyphus — Symbolist restaging of the endless ascent.
captions.pogany-phineus-and-the-harpies: Pogány's modern illustration — Phineus and the Harpies restaged for twentieth-century myth books.
captions.pogany-polydectes-turned-into-stone-by-p: Pogány's Seriphos climax — Perseus unveiling Medusa at Polydectes' feast, the tyrant and his friends turned to stone.
captions.sargent-orestes-pursued-by-the-furies: Created by the American painter John Singer Sargent for his mural cycle at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, this large oil shows the matricide Orestes fleeing in terror across the canvas, his nude body straining forward while a swarm of Erinyes — the Furies — bears down on him with raised arms and writhing serpents. Sargent renders the avenging goddesses as a frenzied, swirling mass of female figures, dramatizing the unrelenting torment that the spirits of blood-guilt inflict on the man who has shed his mother's blood. The painting belongs to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, and remains one of the most striking modern visualizations of the Erinyes as embodiments of pursuing remorse.
captions.sargent-atlas-and-the-hesperides: Sargent's museum mural sets Atlas under the heavens while the Hesperides rest below — the Titan's burden as a modern classical ceiling vision.
captions.styka-eumaeus-chief-swineherd: Polish history painter Jan Styka isolates Homer's swineherd as a monumental pastoral figure — staff, cloak, and the weathered face of the slave who never stopped waiting for Odysseus. The canvas treats Eumaeus not as a side character but as the Odyssey's type of loyalty below the palace.
captions.bernard-oedipus-and-jocasta: Bernard's late modernist pair keeps mother and son in the same charged space — Jocasta as consort before the recognition, the double bond made visible without the Sphinx or the noose. A twentieth-century return to the Theban queen at the heart of the tragedy.
captions.kiwitz-antigone-and-ismene: Kiwitz's 1931 print pairs the sisters as a modern woodcut dialogue — Antigone's resolve set against Ismene's caution. The image keeps Sophocles' two voices in one frame, Ismene no longer a footnote but the necessary other half of the argument.
captions.manship-prometheus: Gilded bronze sculpture by Paul Manship overlooking the sunken plaza of Rockefeller Center in New York. Prometheus glides through a ring bearing the signs of the zodiac as he carries the stolen fire down to mankind, making him one of the most recognizable public artworks in America.
captions.lawrie-atlas: An Art Deco bronze statue of Atlas straining beneath an open armillary sphere of the heavens, installed in 1937 at Rockefeller Center in New York, facing Fifth Avenue. It has become one of the most recognizable modern images of the Titan's eternal burden.
captions.benton-achelous-and-hercules: Smithsonian mural: Benton restages the river-god's bull-form wrestling with Heracles as American Regionalist energy — Deianira's suitor contest as modern mythic labour.
captions.statue-of-eurotas-leonidas-monument-at-t: Part of the modern commemorative monument to Leonidas I at Thermopylae, this sculpture personifies Eurotas, the pre-Dorian king of Laconia who, according to Pausanias, drained the marsh-water of the plain by cutting a channel to the sea and gave his name to the river that remained. Set among the heroic figures honouring Sparta, the statue casts the mythic ancestor of the Spartan land as a foundational presence behind the city that later defended the pass, linking the legendary founder of the Eurotas valley to the historical Spartans who fought there.
captions.statue-of-teucer-pontevedra: The bronze Teucer in Pontevedra's Praza da Peregrina — Galicia's legendary founder cast as Homer's archer, the half-brother of Ajax who wandered west after the fall of Troy and gave the city its mythic pedigree.
captions.ayrton-talos-sculpture-cambridge: Ayrton's bronze Talos in Cambridge — modern sculpture returning the Cretan automaton as a striding metal body in the open air.
captions.vasiliev-tydeus-fighting-the-soldiers-of: A modern book illustration depicting Tydeus' celebrated aristeia at Thebes, where, sent as Argos' envoy, he challenged and overcame the Cadmeans in feats of strength and then cut down an ambush of fifty Theban youths laid by Eteocles, sparing only Maeon at the gods' bidding (Homer, Iliad 4). Drawn by N. Vasiliev for A. Ryabinin's mythological retelling 'Riddle of the Sphinx' (Saint Petersburg, 2019), it renders the favorite of Athena as the heroic father against whom his son Diomedes would forever be measured.
captions.zinonos-pontus-contemporary-illustration: A black-and-white graphic portrait of the primordial Sea, labeled Pontus, rising bearded from stylized waves with a sailboat, dolphin and fish — a modern Commons-licensed reception that keeps Hesiod's fatherless son of Gaia visible when ancient freestanding images of the god remain scarce beyond the Tomis Fortuna group and the Acholla mosaic head.
captions.chart-genealogy-of-taygete-and-lacedaemo: A schematic Pleiad genealogy naming Taygete and her son Lacedaemon — the stem by which Sparta’s eponymous king enters the Atlas line. Classroom mythography rather than salon painting, it still marks the rare places where Lacedaemon is labelled as a person.
